docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
How to define an agent, run it, and what to expect back. Agents that launch other agents are in launching-agents.md, skills in skills.md, MCP tools in mcp.md, and jobs, resuming and result stores in jobs.md.

  • Defining an agent
  • Running an agent
  • The result
  • Failures and retries
  • Checking the output
  • Tools
  • Who is asking: the identity of a run
  • Approvals: agents propose, your code acts
  • Configuration

docs.title: Defining an agent
docs.text:
An agent is a static definition: a subclass of AgentBase, with Pydantic models for its input and output. A running agent is complete and validated before it runs, and its hash identifies it, so it is easy to read, test and version. You write the class, or you build it from data (a file, a database row) when you need it: the runner sees a class either way.

from typing import ClassVar

from featherweight import AgentBase, AgentInput, AgentOutput


class ExtractInput(AgentInput):
    text: str


class ExtractOutput(AgentOutput):
    people: list[str] = []


class PeopleExtractor(AgentBase):
    name: str = "people_extractor"
    description: str = "Finds the people named in a text"
    version: str = "0.1.0"
    prompt: str = "List every person named in the text."
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = ExtractInput
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = ExtractOutput

Pydantic does the specification work: the input is validated before the model is called, and the model's reply is validated against the output model (it is sent as the structured-output schema). Give the output's task fields defaults, so that a model that wants to ask a question is not forced to invent an answer just to pass validation.

docs.title: Fields of AgentBase
docs.text:
Field Default name, description, version, prompt required Recorded in the run log with every attempt. description is what other agents see when they may launch this one. Change version when the prompt or behaviour changes model Gemini() Which model runs the agent, and how hard it thinks: Gemini, Gemma, Claude or OpenAI, or your own class. See models.md tools none The tools the agent can call. Only these are ever bound to the model recursion_limit 25 Stops a runaway tool loop inside one run; a run that hits it fails allow_user_questions False Adds a sentence to the prompt telling the model whether it may put questions in open_questions raise_conflicts False The same, for conflicts it finds in the input subagents none Agents this agent may launch. See launching-agents.md skills none Skills this agent can read. See skills.md mcp_servers none MCP servers whose tools this agent may use. See mcp.md input_model, output_model AgentInput, AgentOutput Class attributes (ClassVar)

AgentInput forbids extra fields. AgentOutput always carries open_questions: list[str], where a model reports questions or conflicts instead of guessing. It is never a failure.

docs.title: The system prompt
docs.text:
The model's system prompt is assembled from the pieces below, in this order. Its SHA-256 is recorded on every attempt (system_prompt_hash), so two runs can be compared by prompt.

  1. prompt
  2. one sentence from allow_user_questions, and one from raise_conflicts
  3. if the agent has subagents and depth left to launch: the list of agents it may launch
  4. if the agent has skills: the list of its skills (name and description)

agent.build_system_prompt() returns it.

docs.title: Running an agent
docs.text:
from featherweight import AgentRunner, SqliteDatabase

async with SqliteDatabase("featherweight.db") as db:
    job_id = await db.create_job("demo")
    runner = AgentRunner(db)
    result = await runner.run(PeopleExtractor, ExtractInput(text="..."), job_id=job_id)
    results = await runner.run_many(
        PeopleExtractor, [ExtractInput(text="..."), ExtractInput(text="...")], job_id=job_id
    )
  • run(agent_cls, agent_input, job_id=None) runs one agent. Pass the class, not an instance.
  • run_many(agent_cls, inputs, job_id=None) runs one agent over many inputs at the same time (fan-out) and returns the results in input order. It has no limit of its own: the runner's concurrency limit bounds it.
  • Several agents of one pipeline share a job_id. Without one, the run is logged with no job. A job is for one identity (who is asking): give every run of a job_id the same one.
  • A job_id is the job that the run belongs to, not the id of the run. A job is one unit of work with a status (a pipeline you run with run_job, or one you submit to a worker): it has many runs, each with a run_id, and each attempt of a run has an attempt_id.

AgentRunner(db, ...) takes these keyword arguments:

Argument Default max_attempts 3 Attempts per run retry_delay_s 1.0 Wait between attempts, without holding a concurrency slot max_concurrent FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS, else 10 Model attempts running at once max_depth, max_launches 3, 10 See launching-agents.md

The runner has no argument for choosing the model: an agent's own model settings decide it. To run an agent on a fake in a test, give it fake model settings (testing your agents).

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
run always returns an AgentResult:

Field status SUCCESS or FAILED output The validated output model, on success error The last error, on failure attempt_id The id of the last attempt, to look it up in the run log input_tokens, output_tokens Summed over the attempt's model calls. Output includes thinking tokens, and the input includes the tool results the model read attempts, latency_ms Attempts made, and total time across them model_name The model as the API reported it, which can differ from the one requested reused True when the output came from the job this one resumes, with no model call (resuming a job)

docs.title: Failures and retries
docs.text:
• A runtime failure is a result, not an exception. The pipeline decides what it means. Wrong input types and unknown job ids are programming errors, and they do raise.
  • Retries. Every failed attempt (an API error, an invalid output, a rejected check_output) is retried, up to max_attempts. A retry resamples with the same input: the error is recorded in the log but is not sent back to the model. If a retry should know what went wrong, the pipeline does that (the example's Form Filler gets the problems and its previous attempt as input).
  • No retry for errors that cannot succeed: a model that cannot be built (no API key, an unknown model) and any 4xx response other than 408, 409 and 429. These fail at once.
  • A model that returns no structured output is a failed attempt.

docs.title: Checking the output
docs.text:
Warning

Not every output model works with every model. Claude Opus, Sonnet and Fable take no dictionaries, no recursive models and at most 24 optional fields, and an agent that has them is refused when it is built. See provider limits.

Beyond the schema, two places hold the rules the output must satisfy:

class PeopleExtractor(AgentBase):
    ...

    def check_output(self, agent_input, output):
        missing = [p for p in output.people if p not in agent_input.text]
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(f"names not in the text: {missing}")  # a failed attempt, retried
  • Validators on the output model (pydantic): rules about the output alone, such as unique ids or a value from a fixed set.
  • check_output(agent_input, output): rules between input and output, such as "everything the model returned is in the input". Raise ValueError to reject.

A Gemini caveat. A nested or nullable structured-output schema can come back silently truncated (a tree with only its root). Prefer flat lists with ids, avoid X | None on nested objects, and add a check_output that compares the output with the input. The example pipeline builds its trees from flat lists for this reason.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
tools: list[BaseTool] = [my_tool]. A function decorated with langchain's @tool works. A tool that needs the job declares runtime: ToolRuntime[RunContext]; langchain fills it in and hides it from the model, so the model never passes a job id.

Ready-made tools, in featherweight.tools:

Tool calculate(expression) Exact decimal arithmetic: + - * / // % ** and parentheses. No functions current_datetime() The current UTC date and time, ISO 8601 add_to_date(date, days, weeks, months, years) Date arithmetic days_between(start, end) Whole days between two dates

Agents that can launch agents, and agents with skills, get their extra tools from the runner; they are not in tools. The tools of MCP servers are added the same way: found with search_tools and call_tool by default, or bound directly with discover=False (see mcp.md).

docs.title: Who is asking: the identity of a run
docs.text:
A tool often has to act for someone: this teacher's mail, this tenant's files. The model must not choose who, so the application tells the run, and the tools read it. An identity is a Pydantic model you define. You declare its type once, and pass a value with identity=:

from langchain.tools import ToolRuntime, tool
from pydantic import BaseModel

from featherweight import AgentRunner, RunContext


class Teacher(BaseModel):
    user_id: str
    tenant: str


@tool
async def send_email(to: str, body: str, runtime: ToolRuntime[RunContext[Teacher]]) -> str:
    """Send an email as the signed-in teacher."""
    who = runtime.context.identity  # the model never sees this parameter, and cannot set it
    if who is None or not await may_send_email(
        who.user_id
    ):  # your check: featherweight carries the identity, you decide
        return "Not allowed."
    ...


runner = AgentRunner(db, identity_type=Teacher)
result = await runner.run(Mailer, MailerInput(...), identity=Teacher(user_id="u1", tenant="uni"))
  • A declared type makes identity= required (a TypeError when it is missing or of another type), so that one code path that forgets it cannot run a tool as nobody. identity_type=Teacher | None allows runs without one. With no type declared, passing an identity is a TypeError.
  • One agent can serve different kinds of people: identity_type=Teacher | Student accepts either, and a tool that serves both annotates RunContext[Teacher | Student] and checks isinstance before it acts. Two models in one union cannot have the same class name: the name is the identity's kind on the queue, and a rename of the class while a job is queued fails that job.
  • run, run_many, stream and run_job take identity=. A job reads it as ctx.identity, and every agent it runs with ctx.run has it.
  • A launched agent has its parent's identity, and so does an agent started in the background in the same process. The model cannot set or change it.
  • Code that cannot take runtime (a tool shared by many attempts, such as an MCP tool) reads CURRENT_IDENTITY from featherweight.context.
  • A job is for one identity. run_job and submit give a whole job one identity. If you pass a job_id to run, run_many or stream yourself, pass the same identity every time: a run for another identity (or for none, when an earlier run had one) raises ValueError before anything is written. To run for someone else, use another job: a resume is a new job, so a support person can resume a user's job under their own identity.
  • A field marked exclude=True is not sent to a worker, for a value that exists only in your process. It needs a default (jwt: str | None = Field(None, exclude=True)), because the worker rebuilds the identity without it; a model without one is refused when the runner, the worker or the client is built.
  • It is carried, not used. It is never shown to the model, never part of the agent's hash, never logged and never stored. Keep it small, keep secrets out of it, and do not change it after a run has it: a tool gets a credential from the identity with your own code. Checking what the identity may do is the tool's job.
  • A job that is submitted to a worker carries it in the queue message, and the worker rebuilds it (submitted jobs).
  • Resuming a job reuses a step only for the same identity (resuming a job): a change in who the run is for may be a change in what it may do, so the old result is not relied on. Whether a person may resume a job at all is your check.

What stays yours, on purpose:

  • Authorization. A tool that ignores the identity acts for everyone. Check what the identity may do before the tool acts, and refuse in text.
  • Staleness. The identity is a snapshot taken when the job was submitted. A queued job may run after a role changed or a user left: for a sensitive action, re-check with your application by user id.
  • Credentials. Get a token from the identity with your own code, at each call: a tool that gets a token for its identity.
  • Who may resume a job. A resume reuses only steps of the same identity, but whether someone may resume a job, or read its result, is a check you make with your own records of who started it.
  • Stdio MCP servers. If users define agents, do not let them declare one (MCP).

The identity spec has the rules, the book has a chapter on it, and the recipes show how to build on it.

docs.title: Approvals: agents propose, your code acts
docs.text:
An agent does not ask for approval and does not hold a permission. It proposes; your application shows the proposal to a person; and after the yes, plain code (an API call, a pipeline, another job) executes it. Two stages, and the model never holds the permission, so a mistake or a prompt injection can only produce a proposal.

  • Give the agent no tool that does what needs approval. Its tools hold read tools and, to propose in the middle of a conversation, a propose_* tool that only writes a proposal. A sub-agent or a background job has its own tools, never its parent's, so it reads.
  • The proposal is typed: the agent's output_model, or what the tool writes. Keep it with its hash and an expiry, and draw the screen from its fields.
  • An approval is for what was shown. The client sends the proposal's id, the choice and the hash, never the arguments. The executor checks that the proposal is pending, unchanged and not expired, that this person may approve it, and an idempotency key.
  • Only the streaming agent talks to the user. Anything else returns a result, open_questions or a proposal to its parent.
  • A job asks at a boundary: its agent ends with open_questions, the job succeeds with a typed outcome, you ask the person, and a new job with resume_from reuses the finished stage at no cost. Nothing is held while you wait.

A recipe has the whole thing, another the job that asks, and the spec says what is left out (a flag on a tool, a "needs input" status, pausing a run) and why.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Every environment variable of featherweight starts with FTW_. A few settings can also be passed in code, while you try something out: the argument wins over the variable, and the variable over the default. The rest are environment only: they tune a deployment, and nobody sets them for one worker. A value is read when the runner or the worker is built; one that is not a positive number raises ValueError that names the variable. There is no way to switch a timeout off: set a very large one.

Variable Default Argument GOOGLE_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY The key of the provider the agent's model uses. See models.md FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS 10 AgentRunner(max_concurrent=) Model attempts running at once, per runner. A queued attempt shows as INIT until it gets a slot FTW_MAX_AGENT_DEPTH 3 AgentRunner(max_depth=) Most agents in one chain of launches. 1 turns launching off FTW_MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES 10 AgentRunner(max_launches=) Most launches per attempt of one agent FTW_MAX_BACKGROUND_JOBS 3 AgentRunner(max_background_jobs=) Most children one attempt may have running in the background FTW_WORKER_CONCURRENCY 10 JobWorker(concurrency=) Jobs one worker runs at once FTW_OBSERVER_TIMEOUT 1 s How long an observer hook may take before the runner goes on FTW_WORKER_RECEIVE_TIMEOUT 1 s How long a worker waits for a message before it looks again whether it is stopping FTW_WORKER_CANCEL_POLL 1 s How often a worker asks whether a job it runs was cancelled in another process FTW_JOB_LEASE 60 s How long a worker holds a job without renewing it, before another may take it over FTW_HEARTBEAT a third of the job's lease How often a worker renews the leases of its jobs and of their messages FTW_QUEUE_LEASE 60 s How long a received message stays invisible to other receivers (SqliteQueue) FTW_QUEUE_MAX_DELIVERIES 3 How many times SqliteQueue delivers a message before it marks it dead FTW_JOBS_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT 15 s How long jobs_lookup may take FTW_SKILL_READ_TIMEOUT 15 s How long a skill's aread may take FTW_DB_PATH featherweight.db the path given to SqliteDatabase The sqlite file FTW_LOG_LEVEL INFO the level given to setup_logging() Used by setup_logging()

max_attempts and retry_delay_s are arguments of AgentRunner only. The rule, and what is not configuration, is in the configuration spec.

docs.title: What the providers accept as attachments
docs.text:
A snapshot, as of 2026-11-22. Providers change their limits often and without notice, and this page is not actively maintained. Before you build on a type, a size or a count, read the provider's page (linked in each section) and try it with your model. Where two pages of a provider disagree, this page says so.

featherweight does not check any of this: it passes attachments to the model and the provider's answer comes back as a failed run (attachments). This page is for choosing what to build on.

  • At a glance
  • Anthropic
  • Google (Gemini API)
  • OpenAI
  • Ollama
  • A file returned by a tool
  • How we read it

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
"Inline" means the bytes travel in the request, as base64. "Stored" means you upload the file to the provider first and send its ID.

Anthropic Google (Gemini API) OpenAI Ollama Images inline, URL, stored inline, URL, stored inline, URL, stored inline, vision models only PDFs inline, URL, stored inline, URL, stored inline, stored; URL on Responses only not stated Other documents text files; Office files are not accepted text, HTML, CSV, JSON and more (Office types are mentioned, unconfirmed) on Responses only: text, code, Office, spreadsheets not stated Audio not stated as accepted inline, stored input_audio on Chat Completions not stated Video not stated as accepted inline, stored not stated not stated Most in one request 100 images (600 for some models); past 20 images or documents a stricter pixel limit applies no count stated for documents; 3,600 images (unconfirmed) 1,500 images; no count stated for files not stated Size of a request 128 MB (first-party API) 100 MB inline, 50 MB for PDFs (one page says 20 MB) 512 MB for images; 50 MB for all files together not stated

docs.title: Anthropic
docs.text:
Pages: PDF support, vision, the Files API.

  • How: an image or document content block with a source: base64, a URL, or a file_id from the Files API. On Amazon Bedrock and on Google Cloud, only base64 sources are available.
  • Images: JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP (an animation uses its first frame). At most 8000 x 8000 px and 10 MB each, base64-encoded (5 MB on Bedrock).
  • PDFs: 128 MB per request on the first-party API, and 600 pages (100 when the model's context window is under 1M tokens). No passwords.
  • Count: 100 images per request for models with a 200k-token context window, 600 for the others. Above 20 images or document blocks, a stricter limit applies: each image must fit within 3,000 px, or the request must stay at 20 or fewer.
  • Other documents: text/plain in a document block. .docx and .xlsx are not accepted there: convert them first.
  • Audio and video: not described as input on the pages read.
  • The Files API: upload once, send the ID. 500 MB per file, 1 TB per organization, kept until you delete it or it expires (optionally 1 hour to 90 days). The beta header is no longer needed. Not eligible for zero data retention.

docs.title: Google (Gemini API)
docs.text:
Pages: file input methods, document understanding, image understanding, and the announcement of the new limits (2026-01-12).

  • How: inline bytes, a file uploaded through the Files API (kept 48 hours), a URL, or a Google Cloud Storage object that you register.
  • Size: 100 MB per request inline, 50 MB for PDFs (the January 2026 announcement raised it from 20 MB). The image page still says 20 MB for the whole request. Files API: 2 GB per file, 20 GB per project. A URL that Gemini fetches itself: 15 MB per file.
  • PDFs: up to 1,000 pages, as far as the context window allows.
  • Types: images (BMP, JPEG, PNG, WebP; one page also lists HEIC and HEIF), audio (WAV, MP3, AIFF, AAC, OGG, FLAC and more), video (MP4, MPEG, MOV, AVI, WebM and more), documents (PDF, text, HTML, CSS, CSV, JSON, RTF, XML). The page calls its own list "initial guidance, not comprehensive".
  • Count: no per-request count of files is stated for documents, audio or video. An unread part of the image page is reported to say 3,600 images per request. The Gemini app (not the API) limits a prompt to 10 files, which is probably where "10" comes from.
  • Note on LangChain: with langchain-google-genai, an http(s) URL that is not Google's own is downloaded by your process and sent inline, not fetched by Gemini (attachments).

docs.title: OpenAI
docs.text:
Pages: file inputs, images and vision, audio in Chat Completions.

  • Chat Completions and Responses differ.
  • Chat Completions accepts only PDFs as files, inline (file_data) or by file_id. No file_url.
  • Responses accepts more: text and code, Office documents, presentations, spreadsheets, and file_url.
  • Files: each under 50 MB, and 50 MB combined for all files of the request. No count stated. For a PDF the API reads the text and the page images; for other files, text only.
  • Images: PNG, JPEG, WebP and non-animated GIF, by URL, as a base64 data URL, or by file_id. Up to 1,500 per request and 512 MB in all. A size per image is not stated; pixel and "patch" limits apply, and an image over the limit is rejected, not resized.
  • Audio: an input_audio part with base64 data and a format, documented for Chat Completions only. Limits not stated.
  • Video: not stated.

docs.title: Ollama
docs.text:
Page: vision.

  • How: an images array on a message of POST /api/chat; the REST API expects base64 (its SDKs also take paths, URLs or bytes).
  • Models: vision models only. A model without vision refuses the field.
  • PDFs, audio, video, a count of images: not stated. The usual workaround is to turn each PDF page into an image first.
  • featherweight has no Ollama provider, and langchain-ollama was not read.

docs.title: A file returned by a tool
docs.text:
An agent or a job does not carry files (attachments): it gets a reference, and a tool fetches the file. A tool can return the text of the file, which every provider takes, or an image or a file block. Checked once on 2026-11-25 (real calls, the smallest model of each provider in featherweight's settings, one small file each: a 200 px JPEG and a one-page PDF; the model had to answer from the file):

Provider (model) Image returned by a tool PDF returned by a tool Anthropic (claude-haiku-5-5) read read Google, Gemini (gemini-3.5-flash-lite) read read OpenAI (gpt-6-luna, Responses API) read read Google, Gemma (gemma-4-26b-a4b-it) not known: it did not call the tool not known

It is a snapshot from one run each, with the same warning as the rest of this page: try your provider, your model and your type of file. OpenAI's Chat Completions API was not tried (featherweight's OpenAI settings build the Responses API). The recipe shows the tool.

docs.title: What the LangChain packages do with it
docs.text:
featherweight gives the model LangChain content blocks, and these packages turn them into the provider's request. We built the request offline for each block type (nothing was sent), with langchain-anthropic 1.7.11, langchain-google-genai 4.4.2 and langchain-openai 1.8.2. This is what they did on 2026-11-22, and it changes with their versions:

Block langchain-anthropic langchain-openai, Chat Completions langchain-openai, Responses langchain-google-genai image image block, base64 image_url data URL input_image inline data PDF document block, base64; no filename file with file_data; a placeholder name and a warning without a filename input_file inline data; no filename text file document passes through, though the API takes PDFs only input_file inline data audio raises input_audio (format wav) dropped, with no error inline data video raises raises raises inline data

"Raises" is a ValueError while the request is built. A silent drop is the worst case: the model answers from the text alone. Test the type you plan to use, with your provider and your model.

docs.title: How we read it
docs.text:
• This page was written from the providers' documentation pages, read on 2026-11-22, plus the source of langchain-core 1.8.3, langchain-anthropic 1.7.11, langchain-google-genai 4.4.2 and langchain-openai 1.8.2.
  • "Not stated" means the pages we read do not say, which is not the same as "not supported".
  • Some pages were long, and parts of them were summarised, not read in full: a number marked "unconfirmed" comes from such a part.
  • We did not call any provider to check a limit.

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text:
An agent hands work to another agent and goes on. A launched sub-agent (launching agents) blocks its parent until it returns. A background job does not: the agent starts it, gets a job id at once, and the result comes back when it is ready.

Spec: Background jobs. Example: examples/background (a session that wakes itself).

  • How it works
  • Declaring it
  • Where it runs
  • Getting the result back
  • Events
  • A chat in the browser
  • How long a child lives
  • Limits
  • What is not here

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: A background job is a job that is exposed to an agent as a tool. It has a job id, events, a result in your store, and it can be cancelled, as any job. featherweight wakes nothing: it emits events, and your application decides what to do with them. The model never polls.

docs.title: Declaring it
docs.text:
from featherweight import AgentBase


class Researcher(AgentBase):
    background_jobs = [WebSearcher, Summariser]  # agent classes, or job classes
  • An agent class in background_jobs runs as a job: it gets a job of its own, with an id, a status, events and a result. (The field was called background_agents in 0.1; the tool is still start_background.)
  • The model gets one more tool, start_background(agent_name, input_json). It returns at once with {"status": "STARTED", "agent": ..., "job_id": ...}, and, like launch_agent, it never raises into the parent's run: a wrong name, an input that does not fit or the limit gives a sentence the model can read.
  • An agent may be in subagents too. Then the model chooses, per call, between launch_agent (it waits and gets the output) and start_background (it goes on). The prompt describes each agent once, as inline, background or either.
  • A streaming agent cannot be a background job. A background job cannot start background jobs.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
The same job, in your process or on a worker, by configuration:

runner = AgentRunner(db)  # here: an asyncio task in this process (the default)
runner = AgentRunner(
    db, background=client
)  # on a worker: `client` is a JobClient, and the child is submitted to its queue

Either way the child has the same job row, events and result. On a worker, the worker must list the child's job in its jobs. The runner needs a result store to read the result from (results=, or the client's): an agent with background_jobs on a runner without one is a SetupError, before any model call.

docs.title: Getting the result back
docs.text:
The tool has already returned ("started"), and a second result for the same call would be rejected by the providers. So when the child finishes, its result arrives as new information, a user message:

<background_result job_id="…" agent="Summariser" status="SUCCESS">
{ the output, as JSON }
</background_result>

A failed child has status="FAILED" and its error_type (never its error text), and a cancelled one status="CANCELLED". There is no output.

  • While the parent runs, the message is added before the next model call, after the results of the round's tool calls, once for each child.
  • A child that finishes while the turn is still running is given to that turn, and its message is in new_messages. Before you start a turn for a finished child, wait for the running turn and look for job_id="..." in your history, so that the model is not told twice (as the example does).
  • After a chat turn has ended, it is yours: start the next turn with the history and the message. await runner.background_message(job_id) builds it from the job's status and your result store (a LangChain HumanMessage).
history = [*history, await runner.background_message(job_id)]  # then start a turn with it, as for any message

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
• On a chat stream (a streaming agent, while the stream is open), two AG-UI CUSTOM events: background_started (job_id, agent) and background_finished (job_id, agent, status, error_type). They carry metadata only, never the output.
  • The child's own job events (queued, running, succeeded, ...) are the full record. Follow them with client.events(job_id), and over SSE with sse.encode, as for any job (submitted jobs). The chat events are shortcuts for the chat connection, derived from them. After a chat stream has ended, follow the job's events yourself: the job id is in background_started.

docs.title: A chat in the browser
docs.text:
The AG-UI adapter passes the events through. The Vercel adapter sends them as transient data parts, data-background_started and data-background_finished: the useChat hook gives them to onData, and does not keep them in the messages.

const [children, setChildren] = useState<Record<string, string>>({});  // job id -> status

const { messages, sendMessage } = useChat({
  onData: (part) => {
    if (part.type === "data-background_started") setChildren((c) => ({ ...c, [part.data.job_id]: "running" }));
    if (part.type === "data-background_finished") setChildren((c) => ({ ...c, [part.data.job_id]: part.data.status }));
  },
});

Show a chip for each running child, and when one finishes, call your own endpoint: it calls runner.background_message(job_id) and starts the next turn. The type of a data part depends on the version of the SDK (check how it types onData); the shape that is sent is the one above.

docs.title: How long a child lives
docs.text:
• A chat turn does not wait. It ends when the model ends it, and its children carry on. If the user stops the response, its children are cancelled.
  • A run that is not a chat waits. When the model would end its run while a child still runs, the run waits for it, adds its result, and the model goes on (within recursion_limit). Cancelling the run cancels its children.
  • A cancelled or failed child is a result like any other: the parent is told, and the model decides.
  • featherweight keeps no pending result for a parent whose turn is over. If your process restarts, what you did not store is lost; a child on a worker carries on, and its result is in your store.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Live children: AgentRunner(max_background_jobs=3) is the most children one attempt of one agent may have running. A start over the limit is refused with a sentence.
  • A background job is a job of its own, so max_depth and max_launches count within it.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
• A session that wakes itself. It is not part of the framework: it is a small class in your application (the example has one, about 40 lines).
  • Arbitrary statuses streamed by a background job ("searching 3 of 5 sources"), a tool for the model to wait for or poll a child, a durable inbox, and background jobs that start background jobs.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Issues and pull requests are welcome.

Command make build Build the image make test Unit tests (the model is mocked, no key needed, and the keys and tokens are blanked); or uv run pytest make test-core, test-tools, test-jobs, test-chat, test-patterns One suite of the tests, e.g. make test-jobs ARGS="-k lease" make coverage All the tests with coverage: fails under 95% overall or 90% in a suite, and writes the badges and the test map (the rules) make check Lint and format check (ruff) and types (ty); make lint, make format, make typecheck run one make hooks Install the git hooks: conventional commit messages, ruff, ty, the book's navigation and the docs build. They run no tests: every pull request runs them all, with the coverage gate make docs Serve the documentation site at http://localhost:8001 (make docs DOCS_PORT=9000 for another port), in the container; make docs-build builds it (strict: a broken link fails). The commit hook and the pull request check run the build make e2e The same tests on the smallest model of Gemini, Claude and OpenAI (costs money): the rules make package-check Build the package, install it into new environments and import it make pipeline ARGS="..." Run the example pipeline make example-skills Run the skills example agent make example-launching Run the example agent that launches agents make example-mcp Run the example agent that uses an MCP server make example-resume Run the example that resumes a failed job make example-jobs Run the example that submits a job to a worker

The PostgresDatabase tests run when FTW_TEST_POSTGRES_URL is set (make test starts a Postgres with docker compose and sets it). Only make test starts it: the examples, make check and make e2e run with --no-deps.

The tests check the skill, and the commit hook and CI check the book.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Read CONTRIBUTING.md first: what a change needs, spec-first design, and the rules for changes made with AI tools. Run make hooks once. Commit messages follow Conventional Commits (feat(runner): ..., fix: ...), and make check and make test must pass. Each change updates the docs, the specs and the skill with the code. How a release is made: Releasing.

docs.title: Example pipeline: doclearn
docs.text:
examples/doclearn is a worked example of a pipeline on top of featherweight: learn the template of a document family from a few examples, then write a new document from a few facts. It is a demonstration of what the harness makes easy, not a finished product, and it is not specific to any domain. The sample documents (project proposals and incident reports) are in examples/doclearn/samples.

  • What it does
  • Running it
  • The agents
  • The learning pipeline
  • The generation pipeline
  • What it shows about the harness
  • Limits

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Learn a template from several documents of one category. Structure, standard wording and the values that change come from the whole set, not from one document.
  • Generate a new document from the learned template and the facts of a new case (a case is one new document and its facts). Standard wording is copied; only the case-specific parts are written.
  • Check both. The learned template is verified against its sources, and every generated document is checked before it is accepted.

Four rules shaped it: 1. The model does only what needs a model: reading text into structure, judging whether two names mean the same, and writing the parts that vary. Everything else is code. 2. Agents are small and know nothing about each other. The pipeline functions own the order, the hand-offs and what a failure means. 3. Every model output is checked in code before it is used. 4. Every pipeline is a job, so every agent input and output of a run is in the run log.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env     # set GOOGLE_API_KEY
make build
make pipeline ARGS="examples/doclearn/samples/project_proposals --category project_proposals"

Without Docker: uv sync, then PYTHONPATH=src:examples/doclearn uv run python -m doclearn.cli examples/doclearn/samples/project_proposals --category project_proposals.

It learns from the documents, shows what it learned (the tree, the template, the inputs, and how well each source document conforms to the tree), then fills the form: manual opens the inputs in $EDITOR, auto has an agent invent a case and a story, which you accept, edit or redo. Last it generates the document. --fill manual|auto skips the question and -v shows every log line. Everything is saved in out/<time>_<category>/ (doclearn.log, learned/, facts.json, story.txt, generated.md, summary.md) and in featherweight.db. Exit codes: 0 done, 1 failed, 2 stopped before generating.

docs.title: The agents
docs.text: Agent Model Calls Task Document Analyzer (analyzer.py) gemini-3.8-flash, low one per document, in parallel Read a document into typed blocks, mark the case-specific values as {{spans}}, record the markdown style of each element type Reconciliation Agent (reconciler.py) gemini-3.8-flash, medium one for the set Give every element type and field name one standard name, because documents name the same thing differently Semantic Alignment (alignment.py) gemini-3.8-flash, low one per section, in parallel Learn one subtree from the same section of every document: which blocks are fixed, which are slots, which are generated, which are conditional Generator (generation.py) gemini-3.8-flash, low one, with tool rounds Write the document from the compiled tree, the facts and optional guidance. Tools: calculate, the date tools, check_document Form Filler (autofill.py) gemini-3.5-flash-lite, low one, retried on problems Invent a coherent case for a learned template, for demos and tests

docs.title: The learning pipeline
docs.text:
Documents in, a learned template out. Three artifacts are saved together, tagged with the category:

  • Learned tree: the document as a tree of blocks. Each has a type, the standard text (with {{field}} placeholders), and a kind: fixed (the same in every document, copied verbatim), slot (the same sentence with placeholders) or generated (varies with the case, written each time). It can have alternatives (other wordings), conditions (the block is included only if they hold) and children.
  • Template: the element types with their markdown patterns.
  • Facts schema: the inputs a user has to give, derived in code from the tree.

The steps: the Analyzer reads each document (in parallel); the Reconciler gives names one standard form; code splits any merge that would give one field two values in a document; code matches the sections of the documents by their heading text; Semantic Alignment learns one subtree per section (in parallel); code assembles the tree, checks it and derives the facts schema; and last, each source document is parsed against the tree and must be at least 80% reproduced, or the job fails and nothing is saved.

Where the model was unreliable, there is code: - Flat output, tree in code. Nested schemas came back silently truncated, so agents return flat lists with parent ids and code builds the tree. - Contexts, not values, for the Reconciler. Shown only values, it merged a subtotal into an item that happened to have the same amount. Each name is shown with the line it is used in. - The agent decides one thing per block, whether it is generated. Code derives the rest of the kind from the text; asked for the kind directly, the model contradicted its own text. - An output check on the alignment: the subtree must have at least half the blocks of the largest input section, so a reply with only a root is rejected and retried.

What goes wrong What happens A model call fails or returns invalid output The runner retries (3 attempts); auth and config errors fail fast One document cannot be analyzed It is skipped and reported; the rest carry on. None left: the job fails One section cannot be aligned The job fails: a hole in the tree is worse than no tree Documents do not fit the tree (below 80%) The job fails and nothing is saved Any failure The job is marked FAILED with the error, and every agent output stays in the trace

docs.title: The generation pipeline
docs.text:
Code first: every given fact must be a field of the tree and every required input must have a value (or it raises before any model call), and blocks whose conditions do not hold are cut out, so the agent never sees a condition. Then the Generator copies fixed blocks (with small grammatical adaptations), fills slot blocks with the facts exactly as given, writes generated blocks in the style of the example from the facts only, and computes totals with calculate.

check_document is the only way to hand the document in. It is a tool that runs code, not a model: no {{placeholder}} is left, every fixed and slot block is present and within 85% similarity of one of its wordings, the blocks are in the tree's order, and every fact appears exactly as given. If it passes, the document is stored as accepted. If it fails, the problems go back to the agent. After the third failed check the document is accepted as it is and the remaining problems are returned in the result.

docs.title: What it shows about the harness
docs.text:
• A pipeline is an ordinary async function, learn_document_tree(runner, store, documents, category, job_id=...). It calls runner.run and runner.run_many, runs code between the calls, and runs inside a job (run_job, with a typed input and output).
  • Typed agents make hand-offs cheap: the output model of one agent is the input of a function, which builds the input model of the next.
  • Retries and check_output absorb an occasional bad reply; pipeline code decides what is fatal (one section failing) and what is not (one document failing).
  • The trace is what makes development bearable: the prompts were improved by reading the attempts rows of failed attempts, not by guessing.

To build your own: define the agents, write the pipeline as an async function of (runner, ..., job_id), run it with run_job, and test it with a mocked model. The recipes have a scripted fake chat model and a whole test file. Add a few real-model tests on small fixtures for what mocks cannot show.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
This is a prototype, and these were left out on purpose, to keep the scope small.

  • No tests and no evaluation. The example has no tests of its own, and make pipeline runs it. There is no held-out set, prompt comparison or quality metric. The conformance score is computed against the Analyzer's own reading of each source, and a generated block accepts any text of its type, so it measures self-consistency, not quality.
  • No personal-data handling. Documents go to the model as they are and are kept in plaintext in the run log. The examples are invented; do not run it on real client documents.
  • Generation is lenient. Fixed text is checked by similarity (85%), so a small but meaningful edit, such as a changed negation, can pass; rendering fixed blocks in code is what a product should do. Totals are computed by the model with calculate and are not re-checked. generated blocks are not verified, only present and in order.
  • Few, very different documents can be learned as optional slots instead of a generated block. Required inputs follow the examples. Repeated items are not modelled as lists.
  • Gemini only, one language per category, markdown in and out. Learning from a user's edits and detecting documents unlike the examples are designed but not built. A failed job can be resumed with run_job(..., resume_from=...) (resuming a job), but the example does not use it.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Install it, write an agent, run it. For a guided path that builds one small project from a first agent to workers, read the book.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install featherweight
pip install 'featherweight[anthropic]'    # or mcp, openai, postgres, otel
pip install 'featherweight[all]'          # all of them

Python 3.12 or later. Import what you use: from featherweight import AgentBase, AgentRunner. (import featherweight as ftw works too.)

docs.title: With a coding agent
docs.text:
There is a skill that teaches a coding agent to build with featherweight. In Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add aadhithya/featherweight
/plugin install featherweight@featherweight

Other tools that read Agent Skills: copy skills/featherweight into their skills folder.

docs.title: An agent
docs.text:
An agent is a class. Its input and output are Pydantic models, and check_output checks what a schema cannot.

from typing import ClassVar

from featherweight import AgentBase, AgentInput, AgentOutput


class ExtractInput(AgentInput):
    text: str


class ExtractOutput(AgentOutput):  # also carries `open_questions: list[str]`
    people: list[str] = []


class PeopleExtractor(AgentBase):
    name: str = "people_extractor"
    description: str = "Finds the people named in a text"
    version: str = "0.1.0"
    prompt: str = "List every person named in the text."
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = ExtractInput
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = ExtractOutput

    def check_output(self, agent_input, output):  # rules a schema cannot express; raise to reject and retry
        missing = [p for p in output.people if p not in agent_input.text]
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(f"Not in the text: {missing}")

A malformed agent is refused when the class is built, so it never reaches the model.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
import asyncio

from featherweight import AgentRunner, Status, SqliteDatabase


async def main():
    async with SqliteDatabase("featherweight.db") as db:
        job_id = await db.create_job("demo")
        result = await AgentRunner(db).run(
            PeopleExtractor, ExtractInput(text="Anna Berger met Tom Okafor on Monday."), job_id=job_id
        )
        if result.status == Status.SUCCESS:
            print(result.output.people)
        else:
            print(result.error)  # a failed run is a value, not an exception


asyncio.run(main())

Set GOOGLE_API_KEY first. The default model is Gemini, and the other providers take their own key. runner.run_many(Agent, inputs, job_id=...) runs one agent over many inputs at once.

The run log is a sqlite file here. For a deployment, PostgresDatabase ships in the package (pip install 'featherweight[postgres]'), and switching is one line: see persistence.

The job_id is the job the run belongs to; each run has a run_id and each of its attempts an attempt_id (agents).

  • Launching agents, MCP tools, skills, models.
  • Streaming agents for chat, and submitted jobs for work that runs in the background.

docs.text:
cp .env.example .env          # set GOOGLE_API_KEY (the other keys only for Claude or OpenAI agents)

Each example has a README that says what to look at; they are listed in examples/.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
A job is a pipeline with a name, an id, a status and events. How to declare one, run it in your process, follow it, and resume it after a failure. To run a job on a worker from a queue, see submitted jobs; what the run log keeps, and where results are stored, is in persistence; an agent that starts a job and goes on is in background jobs; traces are in observability. Agents are in agents.md.

  • Declaring a job
  • Running a job
  • Following a job: events and SSE
  • Resuming a job

docs.title: Declaring a job
docs.text:
A job is a declared class, like an agent (@job, below, builds one from a function):

class Shout(Job):
    name = "shout"
    version = "1"
    input_model = ShoutInput  # Pydantic
    output_model = ShoutOutput

    async def run(self, ctx: JobContext, input: ShoutInput) -> ShoutOutput:
        result = await ctx.run(Shouter, ShouterInput(text=input.text))  # an agent, run in this job
        ...

The name, the version and both models are checked when the class is defined, and Shout.job_hash() changes when any of them (or either schema) does. ctx.run and ctx.run_many run agents in the job, so they share its trace and its resume. A plain agent can be a job too (as_job(Shouter): its name, its models, and its agent_hash); a streaming agent cannot.

For a job that is just a function, @job builds the class from it, reading the models from the annotations:

@job  # or @job(name="shout", version="2", timeout=120)
async def shout(ctx: JobContext, input: ShoutInput) -> ShoutOutput: ...

The name is the function's, the version "1" (the version of the job is the version of the pipeline: change it when its behaviour changes), the timeout 600 seconds (a job that runs longer fails with JobTimeout; timeout=None for no limit), and the result is a Job class, usable wherever one is (the function is shout.function).

docs.title: Running a job
docs.text:
A job is a pipeline declared as a class with typed input and output, like an agent. It runs in your process with run_job, or on a worker (submitted jobs), and it is the same job either way. run_job creates it, marks it RUNNING, runs it and marks it SUCCESS, or FAILED with the error. A job that raises comes back as a failed JobOutcome, not an exception.

from featherweight import AgentRunner, JobContext, job, run_job


@job
async def my_pipeline(ctx: JobContext, input: PipelineInput) -> PipelineOutput:
    return PipelineOutput(...)  # plain async Python: ctx.run and ctx.run_many run agents in this job


outcome = await run_job(AgentRunner(db), my_pipeline, PipelineInput(...))
# outcome.status, outcome.result (the output model, on success), outcome.error ("ExceptionType: message", on failure)

The output is also written to the runner's result store if it has one (results=None keeps nothing; you still get it back). To run in the background and hand the caller the id first, create the job with db.create_job and use asyncio.create_task(run_job(runner, my_pipeline, input, job_id=job_id)). For a quick try, SqliteDatabase(":memory:") keeps everything in memory: no file, no service.

docs.title: Following a job: events and SSE
docs.text:
Every change of a job's status is an event (queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled, cancel_requested, and lost: the job's worker was lost and the job went back to the queue to be taken over), and the database writes it in the same transaction as the change, whoever makes it (run_job, a client, a worker). An event is metadata only (seq, job_id, type, status, the error's type and hash, at). job_events(db, job_id, after=0) streams them: the stored ones first, then each as it happens, ending after a final one. A stream that starts late replays what it missed, and one that reconnects passes the seq of the last event it had.

async for event in job_events(db, job_id):
    print(event.type)  # queued, running, succeeded
row = await wait_for_job(
    db, job_id, timeout=60
)  # the same stream, until the job is final (a convenience for scripts and tests)

In the process that wrote an event, the listener hears it at commit, with no polling. From another process, the table is read by one reader task per Database object, with a short, growing delay, for every open stream together: a hundred open streams cost one query, not a hundred. Polling is in that one place.

SSE is the one way events are streamed to a client. sse.encode turns the stream into server-sent events (id is the seq, so Last-Event-ID resumes; a comment goes out every 15 seconds to keep the connection open) and sse.HEADERS has the headers. featherweight runs no server: your API sends the response.

@app.get("/jobs/{job_id}/events")
async def events(job_id: str, request: Request):
    after = int(request.headers.get("last-event-id", 0))
    return StreamingResponse(sse.encode(job_events(db, job_id, after)), headers=sse.HEADERS)

docs.title: Resuming a job
docs.text:
A pipeline fails at step 2. Run it again with resume_from, and step 1 is not paid for twice. The first job has to opt in before it runs, because featherweight keeps no outputs unless you ask:

first = await run_job(runner, my_pipeline, PipelineInput(...), resumable=True)  # fails at step 2
outcome = await run_job(runner, my_pipeline, PipelineInput(...), resume_from=first.job_id)
  • resumable=True keeps the output of each step of the job, in a result store. Without it nothing is kept, and resume_from that job raises ValueError ("it did not keep its results"), before any model call. To run everything again, run the pipeline without resume_from.
  • The result store is where the outputs are kept: AgentRunner(db, results=...). The default is a SqliteResultStore, a table in the run log's sqlite file, which is for local development. results=None keeps nothing, and then resuming a job is a SetupError. To keep outputs somewhere else (a database per tenant, a bucket), write a ResultStore.
  • Resuming is up to you. Nothing retries a failed job by itself. The attempts of one run are retried automatically (max_attempts), but a failed job is resumed by the person or the code that decides to, for example a retry button that calls run_job(..., resume_from=...).

This creates a new job that records resumed_from, and is resumable itself, so that a third attempt is possible. Your pipeline runs again from the top, with its own loops and decisions. Only the runs are answered from kept results. It is replay, not pausing: featherweight is not a workflow engine. To create the job first, use db.create_job(name, resume_from=old_job_id) and pass its id with job_id (run_job refuses job_id together with resume_from or resumable). examples/resume runs a pipeline that crashes halfway and resumes, with the default result store and Claude Haiku (make example-resume).

For each run that your pipeline starts in the new job, the runner looks in the old job for a row that

  • has status SUCCESS,
  • has the same agent_hash (the same agent: prompt, version, model settings, tools and so on),
  • has the same input (input_hash),
  • has the same identity (identity_hash, made from the kind of the identity, the name of its class, and its fields: who the run is for; a run with none matches only a run with none), and
  • is a top-level run (depth 1).

A job is for one identity, and a resume is a new job: to resume a user's job as someone else (a support person), give the new job their identity, and every step reruns.

If there is one, the runner gets its output from the result store, and checks that it still validates against the output model and passes check_output. If so, it does not call the model and takes no concurrency slot. It writes a SUCCESS row of its own in the new job, with zero tokens, the kept output and reused_from_attempt_id, copies the result to the new job (so deleting the old job never affects it), and returns an AgentResult with reused=True and zero tokens. The log says run_reused .... If the output no longer validates, the log says run_reuse_rejected reason=... and the agent runs as usual. If the store has no result for a step that the log says succeeded (it was never kept, or was lost), the log says result_missing and the agent runs. A store that fails to keep a result never fails the run: that step just cannot be reused later. With several matches (the same input twice in one run_many), any one answers. run_many resumes per input: one failed section of ten reruns only that section.

Changing the prompt, bumping version or changing a model setting changes agent_hash, so that step runs again, and so does any step whose input depends on its output.

What to know:

  • The code between agents must be deterministic: no clock, no random, no unordered iteration. It is your code, so it is your responsibility, and featherweight does not check it. If it takes another path, the agents get other inputs, nothing matches, and they run again.
  • State outside the result store is not kept. Outputs come from the result store. A reused step does not run, so anything it kept in memory (a counter, a dict) is not rebuilt. Do not rely on it for anything a resume needs.
  • Side effects are not undone or repeated. A tool that sent an email in the failed job is not rerun when its agent's result is reused. An agent that failed halfway runs whole again.
  • Rows from before agent_hash existed are never reused, and neither are FAILED, INIT and RUNNING rows.
  • Depth 1 only. A run launched by a model (a sub-agent) is never looked up. A parent that succeeded is reused whole, and its children never launch. A parent that failed runs again, and so do its children. Reusing children is not included.
  • A crash inside your pipeline code runs that code again, and its agent calls are answered from the log.

docs.title: Agents that launch agents
docs.text:
An agent can hand part of its work to another agent: it launches it, waits, and reads the result. This page says how that is declared, what the model sees, what is limited, and how it is traced. Defining agents is in agents.md.

  • Declaring it
  • What the model sees
  • Behaviour
  • Limits
  • Concurrency
  • Tracing
  • What is not supported

To see it run: examples/launching is an Editor that may launch a summariser and a translator (make example-launching). It prints the runs of each request as a tree.

docs.title: Declaring it
docs.text:
class Researcher(AgentBase):
    name: str = "researcher"
    description: str = "Finds facts about a topic"  # this is what the parent's model reads
    ...


class Planner(AgentBase):
    ...
    subagents: list[type] = [Researcher, Writer]  # the only agents Planner can launch

subagents holds agent classes. It is the allow-list: an agent can launch exactly those, and nothing else. There is no global registry, so there is nothing to register and a rename is a normal refactor.

Checked when the agent is built (a programming error that raises, not a failed run): - every entry is an AgentBase subclass; - an agent cannot list its own class; - the names of its sub-agents are distinct.

Agent A listing B while B lists A is allowed; the depth limit stops it.

docs.title: What the model sees
docs.text:
An agent with sub-agents, and depth left to launch, gets two additions.

In the system prompt: the agents it may launch, by name and description, and how to use them. Not their schemas.

You can launch other agents to do part of the work. You may launch only these agents:
- researcher: Finds facts about a topic
- writer: Writes a short text from facts
Before you launch an agent, call `get_agent_schema` ...

Two tools, built by the runner for each attempt:

Tool get_agent_schema(agent_name) The agent's name, description, input_schema and output_schema (JSON schemas), as JSON. The model asks for this when it needs an agent's input, so the prompt stays small launch_agent(agent_name, input_json) Validates input_json (the input as a JSON string) against the agent's input model, runs the agent to the end and returns the result

The input is a string, not an object, because Gemini function declarations can reject an object parameter that has no declared properties. It was checked with the real model.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
launch_agent always returns text, so the model can read what happened and carry on. It never raises into the parent's run.

A launched agent runs with the identity of its parent (who is asking); the model cannot change it.

Case What comes back The child succeeds {"status": "SUCCESS", "agent": "...", "output": {...}}, the child's output as JSON The child fails (after its own retries) {"status": "FAILED", "agent": "...", "error": "..."} A name that is not on the allow-list 'x' is not an agent you can launch. You can launch: ... The input does not fit the child's input model The input for 'x' is not valid: <the validation errors>. Check get_agent_schema and try again. The depth or the launch limit is reached A sentence saying which limit
  • The child is an ordinary run. It has its own retries, its own tools, its own rows in the log, and its own skills and subagents.
  • The child shares the job, so its runs are in the same job's log, and a resume looks at them with the parent's.
  • The result is the child's output only. The parent reads it as a tool result, so it counts in the parent's input tokens on its next model call. The child's own tokens are in its own rows.
  • A model may launch several agents in one turn. They run at the same time.
  • A retried parent attempt launches its children again. The earlier children stay in the log, under the failed attempt that launched them.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Limit Default Set with Depth 3 FTW_MAX_AGENT_DEPTH, or AgentRunner(max_depth=...) The most agents in one chain, the first one included. 3 means A launches B launches C, and C cannot launch Breadth 10 FTW_MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES, or AgentRunner(max_launches=...) The most launches one attempt of one agent may make
  • A depth of 1 turns launching off.
  • At the depth limit an agent is given no launch tools and no mention of them in its prompt. The tool also refuses a call made anyway.
  • Invalid launches do not count against the breadth limit; only launches that ran do.
  • The breadth limit is per attempt of one agent, not per job, so a tree is bounded but can be wide: with the defaults, up to 1 + 10 + 100 = 111 agents in one tree, before retries. Lower FTW_MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES or FTW_MAX_AGENT_DEPTH if that is too many for your budget.
  • These are different from recursion_limit on an agent, which only bounds the steps of one run's own tool loop.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: Every attempt holds one concurrency slot while it runs (FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS). A parent waiting for its child would hold a slot the child needs, and with enough waiting parents nothing could finish. So a parent gives up its slot while its launches run, and takes one again when the last of them is done, also when it launched several at once. The limit on model calls at one time still holds, because a waiting parent is not calling the model.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
Children are in the same job. Each row in attempts records:

  • parent_attempt_id: the attempt that launched it (empty for a top-level run);
  • depth: 1 for a top-level run, 2 for the agent it launched, and so on.

The whole tree of a job is one query:

sqlite3 featherweight.db "select depth, agent_name, attempt, status, parent_attempt_id from attempts where job_id = '<job id>' order by seq"

The log has one line per launch: agent_launch parent_attempt_id=... child=... depth=2 launch=1/10.

The attempt_started log line lists the tools an agent had, launch_agent and get_agent_schema among them (tools=...). The run log keeps only tools_hash, which changes when they do: a tool's name can be client-specific, so names are not stored.

docs.title: What is not supported
docs.text:
• Finding agents. An agent knows only its own allow-list. There is no tool to search for agents.
  • Launching in the background. launch_agent waits for the child. An agent that goes on is a background job.
  • Reusing a launch when a job is resumed. A parent that succeeded is reused whole; one that failed runs again with its children (resuming a job).
  • A limit on the number of launches per job, or on cost. Depth and breadth are the only limits.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text:
An agent can use the tools of MCP servers. The agent declares the servers; the runner connects to them and gives the agent their tools next to its own. Defining agents is in agents.md. The design and what was checked is in specs/mcp-tools.md.

  • Declaring a server
  • Running an agent that uses MCP
  • What the model gets
  • Finding tools by search
  • Failures
  • Connections
  • Logging
  • Caveats
  • What is not supported

docs.title: Declaring a server
docs.text:
from featherweight import HttpMCPServer, StdioMCPServer


class Triager(AgentBase):
    ...
    mcp_servers: list[StdioMCPServer | HttpMCPServer] = [
        StdioMCPServer(
            name="github",
            command="npx",
            args=("-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"),
            env_from=("GITHUB_TOKEN",),  # names of environment variables, never values
            tools=("search_issues", "get_issue"),  # only these; leave it out for all of them
        ),
        HttpMCPServer(name="docs", url="https://example.com/mcp", bearer_from="DOCS_TOKEN"),
    ]

Both are frozen Pydantic models, checked when they are built. Install the extra: pip install 'featherweight[mcp]'. The models import without it; it is needed when a server is connected.

Field Default name required Lowercase letters and digits joined by single underscores, up to 20 characters. It is the prefix of the tool names: the tool get_issue of github is github_get_issue. Unique within the agent tools all The server's own tool names that the agent may use. A name the server does not have fails the attempt, because it is usually a typo timeout_s 60 For one call, and for starting the server max_result_chars 20,000 The cap on the text of one result (see below) discover True True: the server's tools are found with search_tools and run with call_tool, and none is bound to the model. False: they are bound directly. See below description empty What the server is for. With discover, the model reads it to know what to search for command, args, env_from, cwd A stdio server: the process to start, and the names of the environment variables to pass it url, bearer_from, headers_from A streamable HTTP server. bearer_from is the name of the environment variable that holds a token, sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>. headers_from maps other header names to the name of the variable that holds the value

Secrets are names. The definition holds the name of the variable. The value is read when the server is started, and it is in no log line, run row, error or prompt hash. A variable that is not set (or is empty) fails the attempt and names the variable.

A server that stdio starts gets a default environment (PATH, HOME and the like) plus the variables in env_from.

A stdio server runs a command on your server. If your users define agents (from a form or a file), do not let them declare one: allow HttpMCPServer, or servers from a list you control (agents built from JSON). A server that acts for a user needs a token issued for that server, not the one your own API was given; per-user connections are not built in yet.

docs.title: Running an agent that uses MCP
docs.text:
Nothing special: run it like any agent.

result = await AgentRunner(db).run(Triager, TriageInput(...), job_id=job_id)

A server is started when a run needs it and stopped when the last run using it ends, so nothing is left running. Starting costs time (npx can take seconds), so when you run agents with the same servers more than once, keep them up with async with:

async with AgentRunner(db) as runner:  # the servers stay up between runs, and stop when the block ends
    await runner.run(Triager, ...)
    await runner.run(Triager, ...)

await runner.aclose() does the same as leaving the block. The block is optional and changes only how long servers live.

docs.title: What the model gets
docs.text:
The tools of a server with discover=False are bound to the model like the agent's own, with their schemas. (The default is to find them by search instead, and this section is about what a tool returns either way.) An agent's own tools, MCP tools and the tools the runner adds (launching, skills) are checked together before the model sees any: two tools with one name fail the attempt, and so does a name Gemini would refuse. The attempt_started log line lists them all (tools=...); the run log keeps tools_hash.

The tool returns The model gets Text The text An image, or a file that is part of the result It, as the model's own image or file input A link to a file A line of text: Resource link: <uri> (<type>). The link is not fetched Structured data and no text The data as JSON text Audio, or anything the adapter cannot convert A line of text saying so

The text is capped at the server's max_result_chars, over all the text blocks of one result. Longer text is cut and ends with [truncated: 48,213 characters, showing the first 20,000]. A result counts in the next model call's input tokens, and an oversized one can exceed the context limit and fail the attempt. Images and files are not capped.

docs.title: Finding tools by search
docs.text:
By default an MCP server's tools are not bound to the model. A server can offer dozens, and binding all of them puts every schema in every model call. The model gets two tools instead, and the prompt names the servers it can search:

You can find more tools by searching. These servers have tools you can search for:
- github: Issues, pull requests and code search
Tool search_tools(keywords) The best 5 matching tools, each with its name, description and input schema. Matched by BM25 over the tool's name, description and argument names call_tool(name, args_json) Runs a tool. args_json is a JSON string. It is checked against the tool's real schema first, and a call that does not fit returns the errors and the schema, so the model can fix it without searching again
  • Search only when the tool is not in an earlier result. Results stay in the conversation, and the prompt says so.
  • call_tool needs no earlier search. The agent's tools filter is the boundary. A name that is not a tool of the agent gets a message to search for it.
  • A discovered tool has the same timeout, size cap and failures-as-text as a bound one.
  • Opt out with discover=False for a small server, where one native call beats a search and a call. One agent can bind one server and search another. The agent's own tools are always bound.
  • The tools= of the attempt_started log line shows search_tools and call_tool, not the tools behind them. Each search logs tool_search ... keywords=... hits=... and each call tool_call_via_search ... status=ok|invalid.

specs/tool-discovery.md has the design.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
Nothing an MCP server does raises into the agent's run.

Case What happens The tool returns an error The model gets the error text and carries on A call exceeds timeout_s The model gets The call to 'x' timed out after 60s The server dies, or the connection drops, during a call The model gets MCP server 'x' is unavailable: .... The next attempt or run opens a new connection Bad arguments The server validates them, and its error text goes to the model A missing variable, a command that does not exist, an HTTP server that answers 4xx (such as a wrong token: 401), an unknown tool in tools, two tools with one name The attempt fails at once, without retries, and the message names the server or tool The server fails to start for another reason, or does not start in time An ordinary failed attempt, which is retried

docs.title: Connections
docs.text:
Two parts, with different jobs:

Is shared? Does Connections (featherweight/mcp_connections.py) Yes: one per runner, across agents, runs and retries Starts, shares and stops servers. Hands out a server's own tool list and its session. Knows nothing about an agent's names, filters, timeouts or caps The agent's tools (featherweight/mcp_tools.py, added to the attempt's registry) No: one per attempt of one agent Applies the agent's declaration to the server's tools: the tools filter, the <server>_ prefix, the timeout and cap, and turning failures into text

What can differ between two agents that share a server is on the agent's side. What cannot is on the connection's side.

  • Nothing connects when the runner is created. A server starts when a run first needs it, before its attempt takes a concurrency slot, so a slow start (npx downloading) holds none.
  • A run holds a lease on its servers, from its first attempt to its last, so a retry does not start a server again. A server stops when its last lease is released, or, inside async with, when the block ends.
  • One connection per distinct server. Agents whose servers have equal connection settings (the command, args, cwd and variable names, or the URL and header names) share one process, also while they run at the same time.
  • Each connection has an owner task that opens and closes it, because the MCP library requires one task to do both.
  • A launched agent uses the servers it declares itself, through the same runner, and holds its own lease.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Each call logs mcp_call attempt_id=... server=... tool=... status=ok|error|timeout|unavailable ms=..., and starting and stopping a server logs mcp_open server=... transport=... and mcp_close server=.... Arguments and results are not logged. No new table or column: the tools of an attempt are in the attempt_started line, and tools_hash is in the run log.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text: Gemini's conversion of tool schemas is lenient and lossy. It does not raise, but nested optional fields can come out as required, a oneOf collapses to its first type, a dictionary with typed values becomes a bare object, and format, minimum and maximum are dropped. The server still validates a call, and its error text reaches the model. If a tool behaves oddly, look at the schema the model was given. This is the same kind of limit as the structured-output caveat in agents.md.

docs.title: What is not supported
docs.text:
• Finding tools of the agent's own tools, skills or agents. Only MCP tools are found by search.
  • SSE and websocket transports, OAuth for HTTP servers, and MCP resources, prompts and sampling.
  • A refresh of a server's tool list while it runs. It is read when the connection is opened.
  • Using a tool's annotations (destructiveHint and so on) as policy.

docs.title: Migrating from 0.1
docs.text:
Everything that breaks between 0.1 and the next release, what to search for in your project, what to write instead, and how to check. It is for people, and for the coding agents that work on projects that use featherweight: the last section is written for them, and the skill carries the same page.

The rename of the units is specified, and a test checks the names of its tables against the code (the Python, SQL, settings, spans and logs, and the steps for coding agents).

  • What breaks, in the order you are likely to meet it
  • The run store is gone
  • background_agents is background_jobs
  • Runs, attempts and executions
  • A Database you wrote
  • A queue you wrote
  • Stricter checks: identity, job names and skills
  • Attachments in a chat
  • Typed output: what is now refused
  • Settings, logs and spans
  • Your database upgrades by itself
  • What is new, and does not need a change
  • For coding agents

docs.title: What breaks
docs.text:
# Change You are affected if you... 1 The run store is gone use RunStore, AgentRunner(store=), RunContext.store or the tools store_get and store_set 2 background_agents is background_jobs give an agent background_agents 3 agent_run_id is attempt_id, and the other words read result.agent_run_id, use the run log's methods, rows or table, or implement observers 4 A Database you wrote implemented Database yourself 5 A queue you wrote implemented JobQueue yourself 6 Stricter checks: identity, job names and skills pass one job_id to runs for several identities, declare an identity model with an exclude=True field and no default, name jobs freely, or write a skill's aread 7 Attachments in a chat serve a chat at all (files are now accepted by default), use the Vercel adapter with a client that can send files, send an empty attachment, match the text of an error, or catch ValueError around runner.stream() 8 Settings, logs and spans set MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENT_RUNS, MAX_AGENT_DEPTH or MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES, pass a timing or lease argument to a runner, worker or queue, import a runner constant, read the logs, or have dashboards or alerts on the spans 9 Typed output: what is now refused use Claude for an agent with typed output: a dict, a recursive model or many optional fields on Opus, Sonnet or Fable, or tools on Haiku (the default Claude model)

If you use none of these, upgrade and run your tests.

docs.title: The run store is gone
docs.text:
Agents do not share state: information moves through outputs and return values. The in-memory store (one per runner and process) could not be shared by workers anyway.

Gone Instead RunStore, from featherweight import RunStore Keep state in your own store, or in a dict keyed by the job id when it lives in one process AgentRunner(db, store=...) Drop the argument RunContext.store Drop the use the tools store_get and store_set Drop them from tools, and from prompts that name them the fakeredis dependency Nothing to do

Search: RunStore, store_get, store_set, store=, .store. Check: your tests pass, and git grep -n "store_get\|store_set\|RunStore" is empty.

docs.title: background_agents is background_jobs
docs.text:
The field of an agent takes agent classes and Job classes, and an agent class in it runs as a job of its own, so the name says what it holds.

# before
class Researcher(AgentBase):
    background_agents = [WebSearcher, Summariser]


# after
class Researcher(AgentBase):
    background_jobs = [WebSearcher, Summariser]

There is no alias for the old name, and it is not ignored: a class that still declares a field background_agents is refused when it is declared (TypeError, which names background_jobs).

There is no alias. The tool start_background and the events background_started and background_finished keep their names. The agent's hash does not change, so a resume of a job made before the upgrade still reuses its steps. Search: background_agents. Check: git grep -n background_agents is empty.

docs.title: Runs, attempts and executions
docs.text:
Each word now names one unit (the spec): a run is one call of an agent, with its retries; an attempt is one try within a run; an execution is one start of a job by a worker; a job is a declared pipeline. "Invocation" is retired, and the id that was called agent_run_id was an attempt's, so it is attempt_id. The table:

Python

Before After result.agent_run_id result.attempt_id (and result.run_id is new: the id of the run) runtime.context.agent_run_id (in a tool) runtime.context.attempt_id (and run_id) CURRENT_AGENT_RUN_ID CURRENT_ATTEMPT_ID db.list_runs(job_id=..., invocation_id=...) db.list_attempts(job_id=..., run_id=...) db.get_run, create_run, mark_run_running, finish_run db.get_attempt, create_attempt, start_attempt, finish_attempt db.find_reusable_run(job_id, agent_hash, input_hash, identity_hash) db.find_reusable_attempt(...) AgentRunRow AttemptRow RunStart, RunEnd (in featherweight.db, and exported from featherweight) AttemptRecord, AttemptFinish row.agent_run_id, row.parent_agent_run_id, row.reused_from_agent_run_id, row.invocation_id row.attempt_id, row.parent_attempt_id, row.reused_from_attempt_id, row.run_id job_row.parent_agent_run_id job_row.parent_attempt_id the same fields of the observers' records attempt_id, run_id, parent_attempt_id, reused_from_attempt_id AgentRunFailed RunFailed RunStatus Status (same members: INIT, RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED, CANCELLED) ReusedRun (observer record) RunReused AgentRunner(max_background=...) AgentRunner(max_background_jobs=...)

A streamed run (runner.stream): run.run_id is the id of the run, the one that its events carry and that runner.cancel takes, and the row of the run log has its own id, run.attempt_id. It used to be one id. So await db.get_attempt(run.run_id) (the old db.get_run(run.run_id)) now returns None, with no error: look the row up with get_attempt(run.attempt_id), or with list_attempts(run_id=run.run_id) (its run_id column is the run's).
