SQL, if you query the run log yourself: the table agent_runs is attempts; the columns agent_run_id, invocation_id, parent_agent_run_id (also in jobs) and reused_from_agent_run_id are attempt_id, run_id, parent_attempt_id and reused_from_attempt_id. The database is migrated for you: see below.

Check: the old names are gone from your code (git grep -n "agent_run_id\|invocation_id\|list_runs\|AgentRunRow" is empty), and your tests pass.

docs.title: A Database you wrote
docs.text:
• Your methods are renamed as in the table above (create_attempt, start_attempt, finish_attempt, get_attempt, list_attempts, find_reusable_attempt), and the records and rows too.
  • find_reusable_attempt takes identity_hash (who is asking): a step is reused only when the old attempt's identity_hash equals the new one, and None matches only None. The attempt record has an identity_hash field.
  • Your schema has the table attempts with the renamed columns and a nullable identity_hash column.
  • It has a new abstract method, job_has_other_identity(job_id, identity_hash): whether the job has an attempt whose identity is not the one given (a job is for one identity). A Database that lacks it cannot be built.
  • Run testing.check_database against it, which checks all of this.

docs.title: A queue you wrote
docs.text: A message has two new fields, identity (a JSON mapping or None) and identity_kind (the name of the identity's class, or None): carry them unchanged. Your queue stores them with the other fields, and returns them. testing.check_queue checks that it does, and a queue that drops either fails. SqliteQueue(db) takes no lease or max_deliveries any more (they are FTW_QUEUE_LEASE and FTW_QUEUE_MAX_DELIVERIES); testing.MemoryQueue(lease=) keeps its argument.

docs.title: Stricter checks: identity, job names and skills
docs.text:
These were accepted before, or failed late. Now they are refused where they are made. Each is a change of code or of a data model, not a rename.

What Now You are affected if you... Do A job is for one identity A run that names a job_id raises ValueError ("a job is for one identity") when the job already has runs for another identity (or for none, and the reverse) pass one job_id to runs for several users Use one job id for each identity identity_hash covers the class name of the identity Hashes recorded before differ, so a resume of a job that was resumable and in flight reruns its steps once resume jobs across the upgrade Nothing: the steps run again, once An identity model with a field marked exclude=True and no default TypeError when the runner, the worker or the client is built (a worker rebuilds the identity without that field) have such a field, for a token that stays in the process Give the field a default (None) A union of identity models with two classes of one name Refused when built (the class name travels in the queue) name two identity classes alike Rename one JobWorker(identity_type=...) TypeError when built if its runner does not accept that type give a worker and its runner different identity types Use one type run_many([]) Checks the identity, as a call with inputs does (TypeError if it is missing or of the wrong type) call it with an empty list and no identity Pass the identity A job name Must match ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*$ in full: a name with a newline at the end is refused (TypeError for a class). A message whose name does not match fails with UnknownJob, and jobs_lookup is not asked build job names from user input Choose the names yourself jobs_lookup Cancelled after FTW_JOBS_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT (15 s); the job fails with JobLookupError have a lookup that can take longer Make it quicker, or set the variable get_skill with a resource path Refused when it has .., starts with /, has a backslash or a control character, or is over 256 characters; ./ and // are tidied. Skill.read and aread never see a refused path have a skill that is read with such a path Use plain relative paths Skill.aread Must return text: None or bytes is a failed read. Cancelled after FTW_SKILL_READ_TIMEOUT (15 s) wrote an aread Return str; keep it quick

Check: your tests pass, and a worker starts (it builds its checks when it starts).

docs.title: Attachments in a chat
docs.text:
Warning

A chat now accepts files, and sends them to the model's provider, without any change of yours. 0.1 took text only. Every streaming agent now takes up to 10 attachments and 15 MiB of decoded data in a conversation. Files cost tokens, and their contents leave your application for the provider. No error tells you.

What arrives In 0.1 Now A file part of a user message, through the Vercel adapter, with a data: URL Ignored: the model got the text An attachment: the file goes to the model The same with another URL, such as https: Ignored The whole request is refused (BadRequest) Content that is not text in an AG-UI request or a ChatInput, such as an inline image Refused Accepted when the data is inline (a URL is still refused)

Files in the Vercel messages of the assistant are still ignored.

Decide whether your application takes files. If it does: check who may send what, and set max_attachments and max_bytes on the agent (attachments). If it does not:

class Support(StreamingAgent):
    max_attachments = 0  # no files: a conversation that has one is refused

This refuses, it does not ignore: runner.stream() raises AttachmentLimitError (answer it with a 413), also when the file is in an earlier message, so a chat whose history holds one fails on every turn.

To go on ignoring files, as the Vercel adapter did, take them out of the request before you parse it. This also takes out the links that would be refused. A message that had only files is left empty, so decide what your application answers to one:

import json


def without_files(body: bytes) -> dict:
    """The request of `useChat` with no file parts. Then: `vercel.parse_request(without_files(body))`."""
    request = json.loads(body)
    for message in request["messages"]:
        message["parts"] = [part for part in message["parts"] if part.get("type") != "file"]
    return request

The other changes:

What Now You are affected if you... Do An empty attachment (no bytes) Refused when a ChatInput is built (ValueError, a BadRequest through an adapter). It used to fail at the provider, in the run send one, or have a stored conversation that has one Drop the part before you build the ChatInput The error for data that is not base64 Names the likely cause: a data: URL, line breaks or spaces, the URL-safe alphabet, missing padding. The form that is taken is stated: what base64.b64encode and btoa give. Nothing that was taken is refused now, except the empty one match the text of the error Match the type (ValueError), not the text The limit error AttachmentLimitError, a subclass of BadRequest (so still a ValueError), from runner.stream(). A handler for BadRequest now answers it too (a 422); a handler for the subclass can answer 413 catch ValueError around runner.stream(), or let it reach your framework (a 500 before) Add a handler for AttachmentLimitError that answers 413, before the one for BadRequest BadRequest Defined in featherweight.errors. featherweight.BadRequest, featherweight.adapters.BadRequest and featherweight.adapters.errors.BadRequest are one class import it from the old module Nothing The messages of an adapter's BadRequest Both adapters word a refusal alike: messages[0].content[0] is image content ..., and a missing mime type reads messages[0].content[0].source.mimeType: Field required; the AG-UI adapter no longer says "Value error," or "body:" match the text Match the type

A file is not carried from one agent to another, or through a queue, on purpose: pass a reference. The limits (max_attachments 10, max_bytes 15 MiB) have not changed.

docs.title: Typed output: what is now refused
docs.text:
Warning

An agent that used to work may now raise, and a run that used to succeed may now fail. Nothing here is found by a search for an old name, so check it even if nothing else on this page applies to you.

These are limits of Anthropic's API and SDK, and of LangChain. 0.1 let them through; the next release refuses them (provider limits). There is no setting that turns either check off.

docs.title: 1. An output model that Claude cannot fill
docs.text:
Who: an agent on claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5 or claude-fable-5-2 (and a model that you added to a Claude subclass with native_output=True). Not claude-haiku-5-5, Gemini, Gemma or OpenAI, and not a streaming agent.

In the output model, or a model inside it In 0.1 Now A dict of any kind, also in a list or optional; a model with extra="allow" The run said SUCCESS and the field was empty Refused A recursive model, such as a tree whose nodes hold nodes Refused by the API, in the run Refused More than 24 optional fields (a field with a default is optional; open_questions is one) Refused by the API, in the run Refused

If you stored results from such an agent with a dictionary in its output, look at them: the data may never have been there.

When it raises. Not when the class is declared: when the agent is built, as MyAgent(). The runner builds it, so runner.run(MyAgent, ...) raises a Pydantic ValidationError, as for any wrong agent. It does not return a FAILED result, and no attempt is logged. It names the model and the problems:

claude-sonnet-5-5 cannot fill Out: free-form objects (answers): a `dict`, or a model that takes extra fields, would always
come back empty. Use a list of a small model, for example one with `key` and `value`. ...

Check, before you run anything: build every agent once. It calls no model and needs no key. A test does it:

@pytest.mark.parametrize("agent", [Triager, Reporter])  # every agent of your project
def test_the_agent_builds(agent):
    agent()

An agent that is built from data (create_model, jobs_lookup) is checked when it is built, so build one for each kind of definition that you have. If you choose the model at run time, check each model that you can choose.

Do:

  • A dictionary becomes a list of a small model. Change the code that reads it too:
# before
class Out(AgentOutput):
    answers: dict[str, str] = {}


# after
class Entry(BaseModel):
    key: str
    value: str


class Out(AgentOutput):
    answers: list[Entry] = []  # to read it as before: {e.key: e.value for e in output.answers}
  • A recursive model becomes a flat list with ids: each node holds its id and its parent_id.
  • Too many optional fields: make some required (no default), group the fields in fewer models, or split the work over two agents. A required field must be filled even when the model does not know it, so it can be invented.
  • Or choose a model that is not held to these limits. Test it: each provider differs.

A changed output model is a changed agent: its hash differs, so a job that is resumed across the change runs that step again. A result that was kept in the old shape is not valid in the new one.

docs.title: 2. An answer given before the tools' results were seen
docs.text:
Who: an agent with tools (or sub-agents, skills, MCP servers or background jobs) whose output is asked for as a tool call. Of the built-in Claude models that is claude-haiku-5-5, the default of Claude().

The model can give its answer in the same reply in which it calls a tool. In 0.1 the run succeeded, with an answer written before the tool's result was seen: empty, or made up. Now the attempt fails with EarlyAnswerError and is retried, up to max_attempts (3). If every attempt does it, the result is FAILED.

Do:

  • A retry runs the tools again, and by the time the attempt fails they have already run. A tool that sends, writes or pays must be safe to run twice, as for any failed attempt.
  • If you run with max_attempts=1, handle the FAILED result.
  • It depends on what the model does in a run, so no build or search finds it. After the upgrade, look in the run log for attempts whose error_type is EarlyAnswerError.

docs.title: Settings, logs and spans
docs.text:
Warning

An old variable name is ignored without a word, and the default takes its place. If you lowered a limit, it is loose again: MAX_AGENT_DEPTH=1 now gives the default of 3, MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES=2 gives 10, and MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENT_RUNS gives 10. Look in every place that sets them: .env files, compose and deployment files, CI, and the settings of your host.

Before After Notes the environment variable MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENT_RUNS FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS It limits the attempts (the model calls) that run at once. The argument max_concurrent is unchanged. the environment variables MAX_AGENT_DEPTH, MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES FTW_MAX_AGENT_DEPTH, FTW_MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES Every variable of featherweight starts with FTW_. The old names do nothing. the arguments AgentRunner(observer_timeout=), JobWorker(lease=, heartbeat=, receive_timeout=, cancel_poll=), SqliteQueue(lease=, max_deliveries=) FTW_OBSERVER_TIMEOUT, FTW_JOB_LEASE, FTW_HEARTBEAT, FTW_WORKER_RECEIVE_TIMEOUT, FTW_WORKER_CANCEL_POLL, FTW_QUEUE_LEASE, FTW_QUEUE_MAX_DELIVERIES These tune a deployment and are environment-only; passing the argument is a TypeError. The list. the span attribute ftw.invocation.id ftw.run.id the span attribute ftw.run.id ftw.attempt.id ftw.run.id now means something else (a run, not an attempt): change dashboards and alerts that read it before you upgrade the attribute they read. the span attribute ftw.reused_from_agent_run_id ftw.reused_from_attempt_id the log lines invocation_started, invocation_finished run_started, run_finished One per run. the log lines run_created, run_running, run_finished (the run log's rows) attempt_created, attempt_running, attempt_finished One per attempt. Mind the order if you rewrite them by script: run_finished is both a before and an after. the keys agent_run_id= and invocation_id= in the log lines attempt_id= and run_id= the key reused_from= in the log lines of a resume reused_from_attempt_id= The three lines of a resume (run_reused, run_reuse_rejected, result_missing) also carry run_id= now.

Also gone from featherweight.runner: ENV_MAX_CONCURRENT, ENV_MAX_DEPTH, ENV_MAX_LAUNCHES, DEFAULT_MAX_CONCURRENT, DEFAULT_MAX_DEPTH, DEFAULT_MAX_LAUNCHES, DEFAULT_MAX_BACKGROUND, max_concurrent_from_env(), max_depth_from_env() and max_launches_from_env(). To read the limits in force, read runner.max_concurrent, runner.max_depth, runner.max_launches and runner.max_background_jobs. Also gone: featherweight.tools.NO_JOB, a message of the removed run store. An import of any of these fails with ImportError.

The span names do not change (invoke_workflow, invoke_agent, chat, execute_tool).

docs.title: Your database upgrades by itself
docs.text:
SqliteDatabase and PostgresDatabase apply the migrations they have not applied when they connect, in a transaction each, and keep every row:

Migration What it does 2, identity_hash Adds agent_runs.identity_hash. Runs from before it have none. 3, queue_identity Adds the column of the identity to the sqlite queue table. 4, attempts Renames the table and the columns of the run log (the spec). 5, queue_identity_kind Adds the column of the identity's kind to the sqlite queue table. A message that is queued with an identity when it is applied has no kind, and its job fails (InvalidJobIdentity). 6, attempt_constraints Renames the Postgres constraints of attempts (agent_runs_pkey and the others) to attempts_.... Nothing on sqlite.

Take a copy of a database that matters before you connect to it with the new version, as you would for any upgrade. There is no way back: a database that was migrated cannot be opened by 0.1.

docs.title: What is new
docs.text:
None of this needs a change; it is here so that you know it exists.

  • Who is asking: a typed identity for a run, for tools, in your process and on workers (identity_type, identity=).
  • Jobs that are not declared in code: jobs_lookup on a worker.
  • Reading a skill from somewhere else: Skill.aread.
  • Attachments in a chat: images, documents, audio and video, with limits (max_attachments, max_bytes). This one can need a change: they are on by default (above). A file for an agent or a job is passed as a reference, and not carried.
  • Configuration: one list of FTW_ variables. New: FTW_MAX_BACKGROUND_JOBS and FTW_WORKER_CONCURRENCY (an argument wins over them), FTW_JOBS_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT and FTW_SKILL_READ_TIMEOUT (15 s each; environment only).
  • Approvals: agents propose and your code executes (a pattern, with two recipes and a chapter of the book), and what is not supported on purpose.
  • Recipes and a glossary that says which name to use.

docs.title: For coding agents
docs.text:
You are changing a project that uses featherweight 0.1 to the next release. Work in this order, and stop to ask the owner where the page says to.

  1. Find the uses. From the project root, run this and read every hit (rg or git grep -n). Search hidden files too (rg --hidden -g "!.git"), where .env and CI files are:
rg -n "RunStore|store_get|store_set|background_agents|agent_run_id|invocation_id|AgentRunRow|AgentRunFailed|RunStatus|ReusedRun|RunStart|RunEnd|max_background=|MAX_AGENT_DEPTH|MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES|ENV_MAX_|DEFAULT_MAX_|_from_env|NO_JOB|observer_timeout|receive_timeout|cancel_poll|heartbeat=|lease=|max_deliveries|list_runs|get_run|create_run|finish_run|mark_run_running|find_reusable_run|agent_runs|MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENT_RUNS|ftw\.run\.id|ftw\.invocation\.id|reused_from_agent_run_id|\binvocation_(started|finished)\b"
  1. Remove what is gone, by hand: the run store (the first section). It has no replacement; ask the owner where the state should live if the code relied on it across agents.
  2. Rename mechanically, with whole-word matches, in this order (a later row can match what an earlier row wrote):
# Find Replace with Only in 1 parent_agent_run_id parent_attempt_id code and SQL 2 reused_from_agent_run_id reused_from_attempt_id code and SQL 3 agent_run_id attempt_id code, SQL and logs 4 CURRENT_AGENT_RUN_ID CURRENT_ATTEMPT_ID code 5 invocation_id run_id code and SQL 6 AgentRunRow AttemptRow code 7 AgentRunFailed RunFailed code 8 list_runs, get_run, create_run, finish_run, mark_run_running, find_reusable_run list_attempts, get_attempt, create_attempt, finish_attempt, start_attempt, find_reusable_attempt calls on a database object, and a Database you implement 9 agent_runs attempts SQL 10 background_agents background_jobs code, docs and prompts 11 MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENT_RUNS FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS deployment files, .env, docs 11e MAX_AGENT_DEPTH FTW_MAX_AGENT_DEPTH deployment files, .env, docs. Leave a name that already has FTW_ 11f MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES FTW_MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES the same 11b RunStatus Status code (the import and every use) 11c ReusedRun RunReused code that implements an observer 11d max_background= max_background_jobs= AgentRunner(...) calls 12 ftw.run.id ftw.attempt.id span queries, dashboards, alerts: before row 13 13 ftw.invocation.id ftw.run.id span queries, dashboards, alerts 14 ftw.reused_from_agent_run_id ftw.reused_from_attempt_id span queries 15 the log lines run_created, run_running, run_finished attempt_created, attempt_running, attempt_finished log queries and alerts: before row 16 16 invocation_started, invocation_finished run_started, run_finished log queries and alerts
  1. Move what has no one-word replacement, and tell the owner what you moved:
  2. AgentRunner(observer_timeout=), JobWorker(lease=, heartbeat=, receive_timeout=, cancel_poll=) and SqliteQueue(lease=, max_deliveries=) become variables (settings): put the same values where the deployment sets its environment, and drop the arguments. testing.MemoryQueue(lease=) stays as it is.
  3. An import of a removed name of featherweight.runner, or of NO_JOB (what is gone): read the limit from the runner, or drop the use.
  4. Files (attachments): find every StreamingAgent and every use of the Vercel or AG-UI adapter. No search for an old name finds this. Ask the owner whether each chat should take files, and do what they choose before the upgrade is deployed.
  5. Build every agent, and fix what is refused (typed output). No search finds this: write or run a test that calls TheAgent() for every agent class, and every model it can be given. It calls no model. For each agent on Haiku with tools, check that every tool that acts is safe to run twice, and tell the owner which are not.
  6. Ask the owner about: a chat that looks up the row of a stream by the run_id of its events (get_attempt( or get_run( with a stream's id, which is now None: use the stream's attempt_id, or list_attempts(run_id=...)), a Database or a queue the project implements (change them as the two sections above say, then run the kits), dashboards, alerts and log queries that are not in the repository, and what the stricter checks and the attachments table list: one job_id given to runs for several identities, an identity model with an exclude=True field and no default, job names built from user input, a skill whose aread can return None, how to reshape an output model that is refused (it changes the code that reads the output, and results already stored from a dictionary field may be empty), an except ValueError around runner.stream() (answer AttachmentLimitError with a 413), and a client that matches the text of an error message.
  7. Check. Run the search from step 1 again: outside this page it must return only what you have read and meant to keep, such as MemoryQueue(lease=), a name that already starts with FTW_, or a word of the project's own. Run the project's tests. If the project has a database that matters, test the upgrade on a copy. Then run git diff --stat and read it: every change should be one of the rows above.
  8. Do not rename a variable that happens to be called run_id or attempt_id in the project's own code, and do not touch the OpenTelemetry span names.

docs.title: Models and providers
docs.text:
An agent's model says which model runs it and how hard it thinks. Each provider has its own class, because the controls differ: a thinking level, an effort, an on/off switch.

from featherweight import Claude


class Triager(AgentBase):
    model: ModelSettings = Claude(model="claude-haiku-5-5", effort="low")

The reasons and the details are in the spec. This page is how to use it.

  • The providers
  • Install and keys
  • What is checked
  • No temperature
  • Add a model: GPT-5.x
  • Add a provider: Ollama
  • Testing your agents
  • Tokens and the run log
  • Limits

docs.title: The providers
docs.text:
Class Models Control Default Gemini gemini-3.8-flash, gemini-3.6-flash, gemini-3.5-flash-lite thinking: minimal, low, medium, high (3.8-flash has no minimal) gemini-3.5-flash-lite, medium Gemma gemma-4-26b-a4b-it, gemma-4-31b-it thinking: minimal (off) or high gemma-4-26b-a4b-it, minimal Claude claude-haiku-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-opus-5-5, claude-fable-5-2 effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max. thinking: adaptive, or off where allowed claude-haiku-5-5, medium OpenAI gpt-6-luna, gpt-6.1-terra, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6-astra, gpt-6.2-sol, gpt-6.2-astra effort: none, low, medium, high, xhigh, max, as each model allows gpt-6-luna, medium

Every class also has max_output_tokens, the most the model may produce, thinking included. Claude needs it, so it defaults to 16,000 there: raise it at xhigh and max.

Every class also has show_thoughts (default False): it asks the provider to return the model's thoughts, so that a streaming agent can show them. How hard the model thinks is the other setting. What comes back differs by provider: Claude returns a summary of its thinking (newer models return none unless asked, so Claude sends display: "summarized"), OpenAI a reasoning summary (the raw reasoning stays hidden), Gemini and Gemma their thought summaries. It is refused where there is nothing to show: Claude(thinking="off") and OpenAI(effort="none"). A class you write reads self.show_thoughts in build().

An agent with no model uses Gemini(). Because show_thoughts is part of the settings, it is part of the agent's hash: a run recorded before it existed is no longer matched when a job is resumed.

docs.title: Install and keys
docs.text:
Gemini and Gemma come with featherweight. The other two are extras:

pip install 'featherweight[anthropic]'     # ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
pip install 'featherweight[openai]'        # OPENAI_API_KEY

A package that is missing, or a key that is not set, fails the run at once with a message that says what to do, and is not retried.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
When the agent is defined:

  • the model must be one of the class's models, and the message lists them;
  • the effort must be one that that model accepts: gemini-3.8-flash has no minimal, and gpt-6.2-sol does not accept none;
  • Claude(thinking="off") is accepted only for a model that allows it (claude-haiku-5-5), and only at high effort or below;
  • show_thoughts needs a model that thinks (see above);
  • the output model must be one the model can fill (provider limits);
  • a field the class does not have is an error.
Gemini(model="gemini-3.8-flash", thinking="minimal")
# ValidationError: gemini-3.8-flash does not accept thinking='minimal'. It accepts: low, medium, high

docs.title: No temperature
docs.text:
None of the classes takes temperature, top_p or top_k. The current models either ignore them (Gemini 3.6), reject them with a 400 (Claude 5), or ask you to omit them (GPT-6.2), and a setting that is silently dropped hides a mistake. Claude(temperature=0) says so:

Claude has no `temperature`: the current models of this provider refuse or ignore it, ...

To make output more repeatable, give the agent clear rules in its prompt, use enums in the output model, and use check_output. No provider documents a switch for it. A class for a model that does accept temperature can declare the field (Ollama below).

docs.title: Add a model: GPT-5.x
docs.text:
The built-in OpenAI class lists the GPT-6 models. To use GPT-5.5, subclass it and add the model to its catalog:

from typing import ClassVar

from featherweight import ModelInfo, OpenAI


class OpenAI5(OpenAI):
    models: ClassVar[dict[str, ModelInfo]] = {
        **OpenAI.models,
        "gpt-5.5": ModelInfo(efforts=("none", "low", "medium", "high"), default="medium"),
    }


class Reader(AgentBase):
    model: OpenAI5 = OpenAI5(model="gpt-5.5", effort="low")

efforts is what the model accepts. Everything else, including build(), is inherited, so the new model gets the same validation: OpenAI5(model="gpt-5.5", effort="max") is an error, and so is OpenAI(model="gpt-5.5"), because the built-in class is unchanged.

Check what the older model needs. GPT-5 models, for instance, refuse a temperature other than 1 unless the effort is none. If you want a field, add it to the subclass and override build().

docs.title: Add a provider: Ollama
docs.text:
Any provider that LangChain has a chat model for works. Write a subclass with its fields, and build():

from typing import ClassVar

from pydantic import Field

from featherweight import ModelSettings


class Ollama(ModelSettings):
    provider: ClassVar[str] = "ollama"
    temperature: float | None = Field(default=None, ge=0, le=1)  # its own field, so it is accepted
    reasoning: bool | None = None

    def build(self):
        from langchain_ollama import ChatOllama  # imported here, so `featherweight` does not need it

        return ChatOllama(model=self.model, temperature=self.temperature, reasoning=self.reasoning)


class Local(AgentBase):
    model: ModelSettings = Ollama(model="gpt-oss:20b", temperature=0.2)
  • build() is required. It is the only method you must write, and it returns the LangChain chat model. The base class does not provide one: if you leave it out, the class can still be created and put on an agent, but the first run fails with NotImplementedError: <Class> must write build(). A setup error is not retried, so the run fails at once. The runner calls agent.model.build() for every attempt.
  • With no models catalog, any model name is accepted and efforts are not checked. Add a models catalog, and an effort_field naming the field that holds the effort, to get the checks of the built-in classes.
  • label() is the short text the run log keeps. It is the effort field by default, and can be overridden.
  • Raise SetupError (from featherweight.errors) for a problem that a retry cannot fix. require("langchain_ollama", "ollama") imports a package and raises one that names the install command.

Ollama's tool support depends on the model you pull, and its docs list token usage as unsupported, so check what your model reports.

docs.title: Testing your agents
docs.text:
The runner has no argument for choosing a model: an agent's own model settings decide it, and the runner calls agent.model.build(). So a fake is model settings too. Write a settings class whose build() returns a fake chat model, and run the agent with it:

from typing import Any, ClassVar

from pydantic import Field

from featherweight import ModelSettings


class FakeSettings(ModelSettings):
    provider: ClassVar[str] = "fake"
    model: str = "fake-model"
    chat: Any = Field(default=None, exclude=True)  # the fake chat model; not part of the settings' data

    def build(self):
        return self.chat


fake = ...  # a chat model that replays a script


class UnderTest(PeopleExtractor):  # the same agent, run by the fake
    model: ModelSettings = Field(default_factory=lambda: FakeSettings(chat=fake))


result = await AgentRunner(db).run(UnderTest, ExtractInput(text="..."))

Nothing in the runner exists for tests, so the test runs the same code as production. The recipes have a whole test file with a fake chat model.

docs.title: Tokens and the run log
docs.text:
input_tokens and output_tokens on the result mean the same for every provider: all input, and all output with thinking. The runner sums them over the model calls of the successful attempt.

The run log has one row for each attempt. For the model it keeps:

Column model_name, reasoning The model, and the effort or thinking level as text reported_model_name What the API reported provider google, anthropic, openai, or your class's provider settings All the settings as JSON, so a run can be reproduced

Rows written before these columns have NULL in provider and settings.

docs.title: Provider limits
docs.text:
How a provider is asked for typed output differs by model, and each way has limits. They come from Anthropic's API and SDK, and from LangChain, which featherweight builds on. featherweight does not work around them. It refuses what would go wrong, and says why.

Warning

Claude Opus, Sonnet and Fable do not take every output model. An agent with one of these is refused when it is built:

  • No dictionaries. A dict of any kind (also in a list, or optional), and a model with extra="allow". Anthropic's SDK sends it as an object that may hold nothing: the field would always come back empty, and the run would succeed.
  • No recursive models, such as a tree whose nodes hold nodes. The API refuses the request.
  • At most 24 optional fields, counted over the model and the models inside it. open_questions is one of them, so a flat output has room for 23 of your own. A field with a default is optional.

Use a list of a small model in place of a dictionary:

class Entry(BaseModel):
    key: str
    value: str


class Out(AgentOutput):
    entries: list[Entry] = []  # not `dict[str, str]`

Warning

A model can answer before it has seen what its tools returned. For Claude Haiku 5.5, the default Claude model, the typed output is one more tool. The model can call it in the same reply as your tools. LangChain then takes that answer, runs your tools and ends, so the answer is empty or made up.

featherweight fails that attempt (EarlyAnswerError) and retries it, like any failed attempt. Your tools have run by then, and run again on the retry: a tool that sends or writes something must be safe to run twice. With max_attempts=1, the run is FAILED.

Warning

A reply that does not fit the schema is not always sent back to the model. Where the output is a tool call (Haiku), LangChain returns the error to the model within the same attempt. With a provider's structured output (Claude Opus, Sonnet and Fable, and OpenAI), the attempt fails and is retried. Claude is not given numeric or length limits (ge, max_length) as rules, only as text in a description, so a reply can break them.

The schema is checked by a method of the model settings, check_model_output_schema, so a settings class of your own can add its provider's limits. The early answer is checked by the runner, for every model. The decisions, and what was seen on the real APIs, are in the specs of models and the runner.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Gemma and tools. With tools and an output model in one agent, both hosted Gemma models answered in JSON at once and did not call the tool, where Gemini did. Prefer Gemma for agents without tools.
  • Claude's bounds. The API does not enforce numeric bounds in an output model (ge, le), so use check_output.
  • Typed output differs by model: see provider limits before you choose a Claude model.
  • OpenAI. Tested with gpt-6-luna only. Every OpenAI model here uses the Responses API.
  • Older models (Gemini 2.x, Claude 4, GPT-5) are not built in. Add them as above.
  • Not available: token budgets (thinking_budget, budget_tokens), verbosity, reasoning.mode: pro, a different model on a retry, and a cost report. A subclass can add the fields it needs.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
See what your jobs and agents do, in the tool you already use, and run evaluations on the traces you collect. featherweight emits the spans. Where they go, and what you do with them, is yours.

Spec: Observers and OpenTelemetry. Example: examples/observability (make example-observability).

  • How it works
  • OpenTelemetry
  • What is on the spans
  • Content
  • Your own spans
  • Across the queue
  • Evaluation
  • Writing your own observer
  • Versions of the conventions
  • What is not here

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
An observer is a class that the runner calls as things happen: a job starts and ends, an attempt starts and ends, a step is reused, a model call or a tool call starts and ends. featherweight stores nothing that an observer receives, and an observer never changes a run: one that raises or is too slow is logged and ignored.

runner = AgentRunner(db, observers=[OTelObserver()])

A job run by run_job and a job run by a worker report the same, because the worker uses its runner. Without observers nothing changes.

Metadata always, content on request. An observer always receives ids, names, status, tokens, timing, hashes and the type of an error. The inputs, outputs, messages, tool arguments and results, and the text of an error go only to an observer that asks for them.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
OTelObserver is the one we ship, because every observability and evaluation platform reads OpenTelemetry.

pip install 'featherweight[otel]'      # opentelemetry-api only

from featherweight import AgentRunner, OTelObserver

runner = AgentRunner(db, observers=[OTelObserver()])

featherweight uses the OpenTelemetry API only. You configure the SDK and the exporter for your backend, as for any application (examples/observability prints to the console). Without an SDK it does nothing and costs nothing.

docs.title: What is on the spans
docs.text:
The spans follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, so the platforms read them as they are.

What Span Under A job invoke_workflow {job name} the span of whoever submitted it, if there is one An attempt of an agent invoke_agent {agent name} the job, or the tool call that launched the agent A model call chat {model} its attempt A tool call execute_tool {tool name} its attempt A step reused by a resumed job invoke_agent {agent name}, with ftw.reused the job
  • A retry is a span of its own, a sibling of the attempt it follows. They share ftw.run.id, and the attempt that counted has ftw.attempt.final = true. A rejected attempt ends with an error status and error.type: the type of the exception, and never its text.
  • A reused step has no model calls under it. ftw.reused_from_attempt_id and ftw.resumed_from say where it came from, so you can find the original run.
  • The conventions' attributes are used for what they cover (the operation, the agent and its version, the model, the tokens, the finish reasons, the tool name and call id). Ours are in the ftw. namespace: the job's id, name, version and hash, the agent's hash, the attempt number and how many are allowed, an attempt's token totals, and the ids that link a reused step. The full list is in the spec.

docs.title: Content
docs.text:
Off by default. To put the messages, the tool arguments and results, and the typed input and output of jobs and agents on the spans:

OTelObserver(capture_content=True)

or set OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_CONTENT=SPAN_ONLY, the convention's own switch (an explicit capture_content wins). The content is set as the conventions' attributes (gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, gen_ai.tool.call.arguments, ...), as JSON strings. It will contain whatever your users sent, so it goes where you decide: your exporter and your backend, and nowhere that featherweight keeps. The values that send content as events are not supported, and are treated as off.

docs.title: Your own spans
docs.text:
A span around your own code is yours: use the OpenTelemetry API, and featherweight offers nothing for it.

tracer = trace.get_tracer("my_app")


@job
async def summarise(ctx: JobContext, input: In) -> Out:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("load documents"):
        docs = await load(input)
    return await ctx.run(Summariser, docs)

OTelObserver makes the job's span and each attempt's span the current one while the work runs, so your span is under the job, and the attempts started inside your span are under it. That is OpenTelemetry's own rule, not a featherweight feature. Without OTelObserver there is no job span, and your spans are simply roots.

docs.title: Across the queue
docs.text: A job that a client submits and a worker runs is one trace. JobClient(db, queue, observers=[OTelObserver()]) puts the W3C trace context in the message, and the worker's job span joins it. Both sides need an observer; the context travels in the message only, and is stored in no table.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Evaluation platforms (Langfuse, Phoenix and others) read traces. featherweight does not run evaluations or score anything: it emits traces that make that easy.

  • To judge the answer: turn content on. The job and attempt spans have the input and the final output, and the model calls have the messages.
  • To judge the path: the tool calls are spans, in order, with their arguments and results (with content on), under the attempt that made them.
  • To know which attempt counted: ftw.attempt.final, and error.type on the rejected ones.
  • To compare versions: the agent's name, version and hash, the job's name and version, and the model are on the spans. Set the OpenTelemetry resource attribute service.version to your release (a git sha or a tag) for the code around them: platforms group by it.

docs.title: Writing your own observer
docs.text:
Subclass Observer and override only what you need: every method does nothing by default.

from featherweight import ModelCallEnd, Observer


class Tokens(Observer):
    def __init__(self):
        self.total = 0

    async def model_call_finished(self, call: ModelCallEnd) -> None:
        self.total += (call.input_tokens or 0) + (call.output_tokens or 0)

The job and attempt hooks (job, attempt) wrap the work, so an observer can keep a context (a span) open while it runs. Set capture_content = True on the class to receive the content fields. Check yours with the kit:

await testing.check_observer(lambda: Tokens())

Calls are made inline, so an observer that does slow work (a network call per event) should buffer for itself.

docs.title: Versions of the conventions
docs.text:
The GenAI conventions are in the Development status, so attribute names may change. featherweight pins the version it follows, and a test checks every attribute it emits against a list kept with the code. A rename is a breaking change in the changelog.

featherweight GenAI conventions 0.1.0 semantic-conventions-genai@622b2b6, core conventions 1.45.0

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
• Running evaluations, scoring, datasets, or a feedback API.
  • Metrics and logs through OpenTelemetry: spans only.
  • Content as events, and an event per token for a streaming run.
  • gen_ai.tool.definitions, and a span link from a reused step to its original span: we store no trace or span ids.
  • A tracing helper for your own code: use the OpenTelemetry API.

docs.title: Persistence: what is kept, and what is not
docs.text:
featherweight keeps the state of the orchestration, and none of the data that flowed through it. The run log says what ran, in what order, with what outcome, at what cost. It never holds an input, an output, a message or the text of an error. Where data has to be kept for a feature (resuming a job), you provide the place.

The design is in the spec.

  • What the run log holds
  • A result store of your own
  • Choosing a database
  • Migrations
  • Adding another database
  • Tenants

docs.title: What the run log holds
docs.text:
Kept Never kept Jobs: status, timing, whether a retry points to an earlier job The input of an agent Every attempt: agent, model, status, tokens, timing The output of an agent, or the result of a job The launch tree (which agent launched which) The messages of a conversation Hashes of what was declared, given and produced The words of a prompt or a tool result The type of an error, and a hash of its message The text of an error, and the names of tools

A hash says that something changed without saying what it was: agent_hash (the whole declaration, input and output schemas included), system_prompt_hash (so that you can see the prompt changed), tools_hash, input_hash, output_hash and identity_hash (the hash of who the run was for: the identity itself is not kept). A failed attempt keeps error_type (the class, such as ValidationError) and error_hash, because a message can quote data. You still get the error text in the AgentResult you are returned, in the logs, and (for a streaming run) in the RUN_ERROR event. The columns are below.

Content leaves featherweight in two ways only: in what AgentRunner.run returns to you, and through an observer that asks for it (observability): never into the run log. The two exceptions are the sqlite queue and the sqlite result store, for local work: they hold a submitted job's input until a worker acknowledges it, and its result. For a deployment those are yours (a production stack).

docs.title: The tables
docs.text:
Two tables record everything. jobs: id, name, status, whether it is resumable, resumed_from (the job this one resumes, or empty), for a submitted job its job_hash and input_hash, cancel_requested, the error's type and hash, and when it was created, started and completed. A job whose task is cancelled is CANCELLED. attempts: one row per attempt:

Column seq, attempt_id The order the rows were made in, and the attempt run_id, attempt The attempts of one run share a run_id job_id The job parent_attempt_id, depth For an agent launched by another: the attempt that launched it, and its depth (1 for a top-level run) agent_name, agent_version The agent, readable agent_hash The hash of the whole agent: its prompt, version, limits, model settings (and the settings class), tools, sub-agents, skills and MCP servers, and the JSON schemas of its input and output models. Same hash, same agent system_prompt_hash, tools_hash The hash of the assembled system prompt, and of the tools bound to the model. They say what changed when agent_hash does (a tool's name can be client-specific, so tool names are not kept) provider, model_name, reasoning, settings, reported_model_name What was asked for (the provider, the model, the effort, all settings as JSON), and what the API reported status INIT (queued for a slot), RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED (the task that awaited it was cancelled, or a streaming run was stopped) error_type, error_hash For a failed attempt: the class of the exception (ValidationError, RateLimitError) and the hash of its message. Recurring errors group; the text is in the logs and in the AgentResult you get back, not in the run log (a message can quote the data) input_hash, output_hash The SHA-256 of the input and of the output, as canonical JSON. A reused or repeated step is recognised by them, with no content kept identity_hash The SHA-256 of the run's identity (its kind, the name of its class, and its fields as canonical JSON without the excluded ones), NULL when it had none. A resume reuses only a step of the same identity; the identity itself is kept nowhere reused_from_attempt_id For a run that reused an earlier one (resuming a job): the row it took its output from thread_id For a streaming run: the conversation the client named input_tokens, output_tokens, latency_ms Of the attempt created_at, started_at, completed_at Created (queued for a slot), holds a slot and runs, ended. Times are datetimes 
sqlite3 featherweight.db "select agent_name, attempt, status, depth, error_type from attempts where job_id = '<job id>' order by seq"

A failed pipeline can be diagnosed from those rows (which step failed, and with what kind of error), and resumed from them (resuming a job). To see what went in and out of a step, use the logs, or keep the content yourself.

Log lines go to stdout through setup_logging() (featherweight.log), such as attempt_started attempt_id=... attempt=1/3.

Why sqlite, and not OpenTelemetry or Langfuse? To keep it as small and simple as possible: two tables, no collector, no account. A real deployment will want a proper backend, and an observer sends traces to it (observability).

docs.title: A result store of your own
docs.text:
Where results live (a folder, a bucket, a database per tenant) is your decision, so the store is an abstract class you implement: put(key, output), get(key) and delete_job(job_id). The key is a ResultKey (the job and the hashes of the agent and the input), and an output is a JSON dict. One that misses a method cannot be built, and the conformance kit checks the rest:

class FileResultStore(ResultStore): ...  # three methods, see examples/results/store.py


await testing.check_result_store(lambda: FileResultStore(folder))  # raises AssertionError: which rule it breaks

examples/results is a whole store, in about a dozen lines (make example-results, no model or key). testing.MemoryResultStore is the smallest, for tests. There is no Postgres result store: how results are kept in a deployment is for you to decide.

docs.title: Choosing a database
docs.text:
Database is an abstract class, and choosing one is a line of code; the runner does not change:

db = SqliteDatabase("featherweight.db")  # local development
db = PostgresDatabase("postgresql://...", schema="featherweight")  # deployment
runner = AgentRunner(db)
  • sqlite is for local development. Its tables are made by numbered migrations when you connect, and a database from before migrations is refused: delete it.
  • Postgres (pip install 'featherweight[postgres]', psycopg 3) is the deployment choice. It uses native types (timestamptz, jsonb) and keeps its tables in their own schema, so they never collide with your application's. It has no default result store: pass results=. To try it, docker compose up -d postgres starts one (postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/postgres), and make test runs the tests of PostgresDatabase against it.

Rows come back as Pydantic models (JobRow, AttemptRow) with timezone-aware datetimes, whichever database it is.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
The tables are made by numbered migrations, written by hand for each dialect (featherweight/migrations.py): a version, a name, and the SQL for sqlite and for Postgres.

  • They run when you connect. async with SqliteDatabase(...) or async with PostgresDatabase(...) applies every migration that is not applied yet, in order, in whichever process connects. There is no separate command and no CLI, and a connection cannot skip them.
  • They are recorded. Each applied migration is a row in the schema_migrations table (version, name, applied_at), so a later connect skips it. Each one runs in a transaction: a failing migration leaves nothing behind.
  • A new featherweight version with a schema change brings a new migration. It is applied the first time something connects with that version. A migration that has been released is never edited, and there are no down-migrations.
  • Postgres creates its schema. The first connect runs CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS for the schema you named (featherweight by default), so the database user needs permission to create a schema and tables, at least that once.
  • An old database is refused. One from before migrations existed raises SetupError ("delete it and run again"): nothing is carried over.
  • Processes can connect at the same moment. On Postgres, creating the schema and applying the migrations happen under an advisory lock on the schema, so an API and several workers started together on a fresh database wait for each other: one makes the tables, and the rest find them done.

The rules and the reasons are in the spec.

docs.title: Adding another database
docs.text:
Implement Database (write every abstract method) and run the conformance kit against it:

await testing.check_database(lambda: MyDatabase(...))  # an unopened database; the kit opens and closes it

Records go in as frozen Pydantic models (AttemptRecord, AttemptFinish), so statuses, hash formats and non-negative numbers are checked once, for every database. The schema (every column, its type and constraint) is in the spec, and the migrations are in featherweight/migrations.py: a new database adds the SQL of its dialect to each.

docs.title: Tenants
docs.text: There is no tenant column: the run log holds nothing of a client's, so one database can be shared. To attribute runs to a tenant, choose the job id (create_job(name, job_id="acme-...")) or the name. A result store that must separate tenants can route by the job id of its keys, or be one per tenant.

docs.title: A production stack
docs.text:
featherweight is the harness. The infrastructure is yours. This page is one coherent, production-shaped way to put the pieces together, and what to reach for in each place.

This is a suggestion, and one way of many. Every component here can be swapped for whatever you want or already run, and your own stack always wins over this page. featherweight requires none of these choices: it asks only that what you plug in implements its interface (a Database, a JobQueue, a ResultStore, an Observer). Use Redis where it says Postgres, keep results in object storage, run workers on a platform of your choice: it is all your call.

flowchart LR
    user([your users]) --> api["your API<br/>JobClient"]
    api -->|enqueue| queue[("job queue<br/>yours")]
    queue -->|receive| w["workers (as many as you need)<br/>JobWorker + AgentRunner"]
    api -->|status, events| db[("metadata database<br/>PostgresDatabase")]
    w -->|status, events, leases| db
    w -->|results| store[("result store<br/>yours")]
    api -->|results| store
    w -->|model calls| models["model providers"]
    w -.->|spans| otel["OpenTelemetry collector"]
    otel -.-> backend["your observability<br/>or evaluation platform"]

docs.title: What to use where
docs.text: Piece What featherweight ships A good choice (swap it freely) Metadata database (jobs, events, the run log, leases) SqliteDatabase and PostgresDatabase Postgres, in anything that is not a toy. The API and every worker point at the same one. sqlite is for local work: one machine, one file. Job queue SqliteQueue (one machine) and MemoryQueue (tests) Implement JobQueue over what your environment already runs. Good choices: Postgres (a table with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and LISTEN/NOTIFY to wake a worker), Redis streams, or a cloud queue (SQS, Pub/Sub). We do not ship these: they are thin and specific to where you run. The interface asks for a lease, extend and a delivery count, which these already have: see your own queue. Result store SqliteResultStore You own the schema. Keep only what you need for resume, audit and your product. A table in Postgres is the usual start. For large outputs, keep the output in object storage (S3, GCS) and store a reference. See persistence. The API none: featherweight runs no server Your web framework (FastAPI, for example). It submits with JobClient and streams a job's events to the browser over SSE (sse.encode). Workers JobWorker The same image as the API, a different command. Run as many as you need: a worker that dies loses its lease and another takes the job over. Give long jobs a timeout. Observability OTelObserver Send spans to an OpenTelemetry collector, and from there to the backend or evaluation platform you already use. Content stays off unless you turn it on. See observability. Models Gemini, Gemma, Claude, OpenAI, or your own provider class Provider keys from your secrets manager, as environment variables.

docs.title: The wiring
docs.text:
A sketch. MyQueue and MyResultStore are the two classes you write.

import os

from featherweight import AgentRunner, JobClient, JobWorker, OTelObserver, PostgresDatabase

# the same in every process
queue = MyQueue(...)  # your JobQueue
results = MyResultStore(...)  # your ResultStore

# the API process
async with PostgresDatabase(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) as db:
    client = JobClient(db, queue, results, observers=[OTelObserver()])
    job_id = await client.submit(summarise, Report(text=text))  # then follow it: client.events(job_id)

# a worker process
async with PostgresDatabase(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) as db:
    runner = AgentRunner(db, results=results, observers=[OTelObserver()])
    await JobWorker(db, queue, runner, jobs=[summarise], results=results).run()

If your tools act for a user, declare the identity_type on the runner and on the worker (the runner's must accept the worker's; the client's is optional), and pass identity= to submit: the identity travels in the queue message, so keep it small and keep secrets out of it, and secure the queue as you secure the input (who is asking). If users define their own agents, a worker finds them with jobs_lookup (jobs that are not declared in code).

docs.title: Before you rely on it
docs.text:
• Check what you wrote. Each piece you implement has a conformance kit in featherweight.testing: check_queue, check_result_store (and check_database and check_observer). Run them in your own tests.
  • A job must be safe to run twice. A queue delivers at least once, and a worker can be lost mid-job: see several workers.
  • Where your data lives is your decision. featherweight stores metadata and nothing else: status, tokens, timing, hashes. Inputs, outputs and results are in the queue and the result store you chose, under your own retention and access rules.

To see the same shape run on one machine, the finished project of the book submits jobs to two workers over a sqlite queue.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: How a release is made. It is for the maintainers. main is protected, so a release goes through a release pull request, and merging that pull request is the approval.

docs.title: Merging into main
docs.text:
• A pull request is needed, and all its CI checks must pass, with every conversation resolved. This holds for maintainers too.
  • A contribution needs one approval. A ruleset asks for it, and a repository admin may bypass that rule alone when merging a pull request: GitHub does not let anyone approve their own. The checks above are in the branch protection, which nobody bypasses.
  • Squash is the only way to merge. The title of the pull request becomes the message of the commit on main, so the title must be a Conventional Commit: the version and the changelog are made from it. CI tests its form, and cannot tell whether the type is right, so read the title before you merge. Give a pull request that has a fix or a feature a fix: or feat: title, or keep it to one change.

docs.title: Cut a release
docs.text:
Only the release pull request is a manual step. Merging it is how you choose when a release is made.

  1. Run the workflow. In GitHub, Actions, release, Run workflow (or gh workflow run release). It reads the commit messages since the last release and opens, or updates, one release pull request. The pull request changes the version in pyproject.toml, __version__ in src/featherweight/__init__.py, version in .claude-plugin/plugin.json, the project's own version in uv.lock and the manifest, and adds a new section at the top of CHANGELOG.md. The docs and the book show a "docs for" badge that reads the version from pyproject.toml on main, so a release does not edit them. A new place that holds the version goes in extra-files of release-please-config.json. Nothing is tagged or released yet.
  2. Review and merge it when its checks are green. Read the version and the changelog section first.
  3. That is all. The merge makes the tag vX.Y.Z and a GitHub release whose notes are the changelog section, by itself, and then the publish job builds the package and publishes it to PyPI. The built files are attached to the release. Then the docs job publishes the documentation site for the release (below). A push to main that is not a merged release pull request does nothing.

No pull request is opened unless someone runs the workflow, and nothing is tagged or released until a release pull request is merged.

docs.title: Entries listed twice
docs.text:
The release tool reads every commit on main. A merge commit repeats the title of its pull request in its body, so the tool listed the change twice: once for the merge and once for the commit it merged. That is why 0.1.0 lists many changes twice, and why the first notes of 0.2.0 did before they were edited.

  • Squash is the only way to merge (above), so no new merge commit reaches main.
  • A line in a squash commit's body that begins with a type (feat: ...) is read as a change of its own. That is wanted only when you mean it. A bulleted list of the commits, and a Co-Authored-By line, add nothing.
  • A test fails when a release in CHANGELOG.md lists an entry twice, and it runs on the release pull request, so such a pull request cannot be merged. It compares the text, so the same change in other words still needs your eyes. If it fails, edit the section in CHANGELOG.md and the same text in the description of the release pull request, which the release tool reads when it makes the GitHub release. Do not run the workflow again after that: it writes both anew.

docs.title: The bump commit
docs.text: The release pull request, and so its commit, is a semantic commit: chore(release): bump version to X.Y.Z. It is a chore, so it is not a line of the changelog.

docs.title: How the version is chosen
docs.text:
From the commit messages on main (Conventional Commits), which are the titles of the merged pull requests, since the last release:

Commit Bumps fix:, perf: the patch version feat: the minor version feat!:, or a BREAKING CHANGE: line in the body the major version, or the minor version below 1.0

Other types (docs, refactor, test, ci, chore, build) never start a release by themselves. docs and refactor appear in the changelog when a release is made, and test, ci, chore and build do not. The changelog is written from the commit messages, so write them as you want them read. Commits that are not in this form are ignored.

The first release was 0.1.0: the manifest started at 0.0.0, and its changelog lists everything since the repository was opened.

docs.title: The token
docs.text:
A pull request made with the default GITHUB_TOKEN does not start other workflows, so the required checks would never run on the release pull request, and it could not be merged. The workflow therefore uses the secret RELEASE_TOKEN: a fine-grained personal access token for this repository, with Contents and Pull requests read and write. Create it once in Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions.

Without the secret the workflow falls back to GITHUB_TOKEN. That works only if the setting "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" (Settings, Actions, General) is on, and even then the release pull request's checks do not run, so the secret is the way to go.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: File .github/workflows/release.yml The workflow: by hand it opens the release pull request, and on a push to main it makes the tag and the GitHub release if that push is the merged release pull request release-please-config.json The release type, the pre-1.0 rule, the title of the bump commit, the changelog sections .release-please-manifest.json The last released version. The workflow keeps it up to date .github/workflows/docs.yml Publishes the documentation site for a release (called by release.yml), or for any tag, by hand mkdocs.yml, scripts/docs_hooks.py The site: its theme, the navigation, the API reference, the links to GitHub .github/workflows/publish-testpypi.yml A dry run of publishing, by hand, to TestPyPI CHANGELOG.md The changelog. Written by the release pull request; edited by hand only as above, or to add what an upgrade needs to know

docs.title: The documentation site
docs.text:
The site is https://ftw.asankar.de: the book, the guides and the specs of docs/, and an API reference made from the docstrings. It is built with MkDocs Material and mkdocstrings, and each release publishes its own version of it with mike, so there is nothing to do by hand.

  • Per release. After publish, the docs job runs docs.yml on the release tag: it builds the site (strict, so a broken link stops it), and mike deploy adds it to the gh-pages branch. The links to code in the pages point at that tag on GitHub.
  • One version per minor release. v0.2.1 replaces the pages of 0.2, and the alias latest points at them. The root of the site redirects to latest, and the version list is in the header. Below 1.0 a minor release is the breaking one, so this is where the pages should differ.
  • gh-pages is output. One branch, a folder per version, committed by the workflow. Nobody edits it, and it needs no branch protection. The source is main.
  • Nothing is published between releases. The docs on main are the docs of the next release.
  • A fix to the docs of a release already out: Actions, docs, Run workflow, with the tag (v0.2.1). It builds from that tag, so to fix the pages of 0.2, the fix must be in the tag you give.
  • Locally, in the container: make docs serves it at http://localhost:8001 (make docs DOCS_PORT=9000 for another port), and make docs-build builds it into site/ (git-ignored). Both the pull request check and the commit hook run the strict build.

One-time setup, by the owner:

  1. After the first release (it creates gh-pages): Settings, Pages, Source: Deploy from a branch, gh-pages, / (root).
  2. DNS for asankar.de: CNAME ftw → aadhithya.github.io. Then in Settings, Pages, set the custom domain ftw.asankar.de and tick Enforce HTTPS (GitHub issues the certificate). The workflow keeps the CNAME file in the branch, so a release does not remove the setting.
  3. Optional: verify the domain in your account's Pages settings, so nobody else can claim the subdomain.
  4. A longer name, such as featherweight.asankar.de, can only be a redirect to https://ftw.asankar.de: a Pages site has only one custom domain. Make it an HTTP redirect (URL forwarding) at the DNS provider, or a small repository of its own that publishes a page with a redirect.

docs.title: Publishing to PyPI
docs.text:
The publish job of the release workflow runs only after the tag and the release were just made (needs: release, on the release_created output), so merging the release pull request is the decision to publish. It checks out the tag, builds the sdist and the wheel (python -m build), runs twine check --strict, uploads with pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish, and attaches the files to the GitHub release.

It uses trusted publishing: no PyPI token is stored in the repository. PyPI is told once that this repository, this workflow and this environment may publish the project.

One-time setup, by the owner (it cannot be done from the repository):

  1. On pypi.org, Your projects, Publishing, add a pending publisher for the project featherweight: owner aadhithya, repository featherweight, workflow release.yml, environment pypi. (A pending publisher creates the project at the first upload.) Do the same on test.pypi.org with the workflow publish-testpypi.yml and the environment testpypi.
  2. In the repository, Settings, Environments: pypi and testpypi are created the first time a workflow uses them. Add a required reviewer to pypi if you want a second gate before the upload; without one, the publish follows the merge.
  3. The repository must be named featherweight on GitHub: the trusted publisher names it.

A dry run. Actions, publish-testpypi, Run workflow: it builds the package at the branch you pick and uploads it to TestPyPI. Install it to look (pip install -i https://test.pypi.org/simple/ featherweight). It never makes a tag or a release.

Check the build by hand, at any time:

uv build && uvx twine check --strict dist/*

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
A skill is a set of instructions that an agent reads when it needs them. featherweight follows the Agent Skills specification: a skill is a directory with a SKILL.md and, optionally, other files. Defining agents is in agents.md.

  • Using a skill
  • How an agent uses its skills
  • The skill model
  • Loading a skill
  • What is supported
  • Writing a good skill

docs.title: Using a skill
docs.text:
from featherweight import Skill


class Writer(AgentBase):
    ...
    skills: list[Skill] = [Skill.from_directory("examples/skills/meeting-notes")]

A skill can also be written in code:

Skill(
    name="release-notes",
    description="Turns changes into release notes. Use when asked for a changelog.",
    instructions="1. Start with the version.\n2. ...",
)

examples/skills is an agent with three skills to run (make example-skills): the agent is agent.py, and each other folder is a skill.

docs.title: How an agent uses its skills
docs.text:
Skills are loaded in steps, so that an unused skill costs almost nothing. This is the specification's "progressive disclosure".

Step What the agent has How 1. Known The name and description of every skill In the system prompt, always 2. Activated The instructions (the body of SKILL.md) The agent calls get_skill(name) when a skill fits the task 3. Used Other files of the skill The agent calls get_skill(name, resource=path) when the instructions point to a file

The system prompt lists the skills and tells the agent to read the one that applies before it starts:

You have these skills, which are instructions for particular kinds of work:
- meeting-notes: Turns raw meeting text into short tagged notes. Use when asked to ...
When a skill applies to your task, call `get_skill` with its name before you start, and follow what it says. ...

The tool, get_skill(name, resource=""), is built by the runner for each attempt:

Call Returns get_skill("meeting-notes") # Skill: meeting-notes, the instructions, and a list of the skill's other files get_skill("meeting-notes", "references/tags.md") The text of that file An unknown skill 'x' is not one of your skills. Your skills: ... An unknown file, or a path that leaves the skill The skill 'x' has no file '...'. Its files: ...

Nothing raises: the agent reads the text and carries on. The agent decides whether and when to read a skill; nothing activates a skill for it. An agent reads only the skills it lists. Skills are not passed on to an agent it launches: each agent has its own.

In the log: the tools= of the attempt's attempt_started line includes get_skill, and each read logs skill_read agent=... skill=... resource=.... Reads are not stored as rows of their own.

The tokens are the usual ones: the instructions the agent reads are tool results, so they are in its input tokens from then on. That is why a skill's body should stay short (see below).

docs.title: The skill model
docs.text:
Skill is a frozen Pydantic model. Everything the specification limits is checked when a skill is built; a skill that breaks a rule raises a ValidationError (a ValueError).

Field Required Rule name yes 1-64 characters: lowercase letters a-z, digits and single hyphens, not starting or ending with a hyphen. pdf-processing is valid; PDF-Processing, -pdf and pdf--processing are not description yes 1-1024 characters. Say what the skill does and when to use it; this is all the agent knows before it reads the skill instructions no The Markdown body of SKILL.md. No format is imposed license no Text compatibility no 1-500 characters when given: environment requirements metadata no Text keys to text values allowed_tools no A space-separated text, written allowed-tools in SKILL.md. Kept, not enforced resources no The other files: path relative to the skill, and its text. A path must be relative, must not contain .. and must not be SKILL.md

Methods: - skill.read(resource=""): what get_skill returns. - Skill.from_markdown(text, resources=None) and Skill.from_directory(path): see below. Both raise SkillError (a ValueError) for a file that is not a skill, and ValidationError for a field that breaks a rule.

Two skills of one agent cannot have the same name.

docs.title: Loading a skill
docs.text:
Skill.from_directory(path) loads a directory in the specification's layout:

meeting-notes/
  SKILL.md              required: frontmatter, then the instructions
  references/tags.md    any other files, in any folders
  scripts/  assets/     the conventional folders; no folder is special
  • SKILL.md must start with YAML frontmatter between --- lines. name and description are required.
  • The name must match the directory name, as the specification says.
  • Every other file below the directory is loaded as a resource, with its path relative to the directory.
  • Files that start with a dot (such as .DS_Store) are skipped. Files that are not UTF-8 text (images, binaries) are skipped and logged as skill_file_skipped, because the agent can only read text.
  • Frontmatter keys the specification does not define are ignored, because skills written for other tools carry extra ones. metadata values that YAML reads as numbers (version: 1.0) are turned into text.
  • A body longer than 500 lines is logged (skill_long), as the specification recommends keeping it shorter. It is not refused.

Skill.from_markdown(text) parses the text of one SKILL.md, with the resources you give it.

docs.title: Reading a skill from somewhere else
docs.text:
A skill whose text lives in a database or an object store is a Skill subclass that fetches it when the agent asks. The agent's get_skill tool awaits skill.aread(resource). The default returns skill.read(resource), so a skill that holds its text needs nothing; a subclass overrides aread:

class BucketSkill(Skill):
    etag: str  # changes when the text does

    async def aread(self, resource: str = "") -> str:
        return await bucket.get_text(f"{self.name}/{resource or 'SKILL.md'}")  # your client, awaited: it must not block
  • The name and the description are plain fields, because they are in the prompt. Only the instructions and the files are read late.
  • Give the subclass a field that changes when the text does (an etag, a version). The agent's hash is made from the fields of its skills, and a fetched text is not one of them: without it, an edit in the store leaves the hash as it was, and resuming a job reuses results made with the old text.
  • A read that fails does not fail the run. The agent is told The skill 'x' could not be read: <the type of the error>, and the error goes to the log as skill_read_failed, because its message can name a bucket or a key. These are failures too: aread returns something that is not text (a client that answers None for a missing key), and a read that takes longer than FTW_SKILL_READ_TIMEOUT seconds (15 by default, and it must be safe to cancel).
  • The path is checked before aread sees it. The model chooses resource, and a prompt injection can too. The runner gives aread only a path that is inside the skill (./a.md and a//b.md are tidied to a.md and a/b.md), and answers The skill 'x' has no file '...' itself, without asking your skill, for a path that starts with /, has a .., a backslash or a control character, or is over 256 characters. It does not decode %2e%2e: a client that does must treat what it gets as untrusted, and check again.
  • Who is asking: a subclass that keeps skills per tenant can read the identity of the run from CURRENT_IDENTITY (from featherweight.context import CURRENT_IDENTITY) to check what it may fetch. featherweight does not check it for you (who is asking).
  • featherweight ships no store and no client. Where the skills live, who may edit them and which ones an agent gets is your application's. The spec has the rules.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
What the specification defines, and what featherweight does with it:

In the specification In featherweight SKILL.md with name and description Supported, with every length and character rule license, compatibility, metadata Supported: validated, kept, available on the Skill allowed-tools (experimental) Parsed and kept; not enforced. An agent's tools are only those in its tools Markdown body as the instructions Supported; returned by get_skill Other files, references/, assets/ Supported as text files, read on request with get_skill scripts/ Kept as text for the agent to read. Nothing runs a script: featherweight has no code execution Binary assets (images, PDFs) Not supported: skipped when loading Progressive disclosure, steps 1 to 3 Supported as described above The name matches the directory Checked by from_directory Instructions under 500 lines and about 5,000 tokens A line count is logged; the token count is not checked File references one level deep from SKILL.md Not checked Validation with the skills-ref tool Not used; Skill checks the same rules itself

Beyond the specification, in featherweight: - A skill is a typed Pydantic model that can also be written in code, with no directory. - An agent can have both skills and subagents (launching-agents.md); they are independent.

Not built yet: - Finding skills. An agent knows only the skills it lists. A tool that finds skills by keyword is not built. The matcher that finds MCP tools (tool discovery) could serve it. - Loading skills from an archive or a registry, or sharing a skill between processes. - Reading a part of a long file, or a size limit on a file.

docs.title: Writing a good skill
docs.text:
• The description is what makes a skill get used. Say what it does and when: "Use when asked to summarise a meeting, a call or minutes", not "Helps with meetings". Include the words a request would use.
  • Keep SKILL.md short and put detail in other files that the instructions name. The agent reads a file only when it needs it, so a long reference costs nothing until then.
  • Name the files in the instructions ("the tags are in references/tags.md; read it first"). The agent is told which files exist, but not what is in them.
  • Write steps an agent can follow, with the rules it must keep (a word limit, a format) stated plainly. Test the skill by running an agent on a few requests and reading the output, as examples/skills/agent.py does.

docs.title: Streaming agents
docs.text:
An agent that talks to a person while it works, such as a chat. The answer arrives as events while the model writes it, and nothing is validated at the end.

Examples: examples/chat. Design: the spec.

  • A streaming agent
  • Streaming a turn
  • Thoughts
  • AG-UI

  • Keeping the conversation
  • Vercel AI SDK
  • Stopping a response
  • The example

  • How it differs from an agent
  • Background work
