docs.title: A streaming agent
docs.text:
from featherweight import Claude, StreamingAgent


class Support(StreamingAgent):
    name: str = "support"
    description: str = "Answers questions about the product"
    version: str = "1"
    prompt: str = "You help customers. Be short."
    model: ModelSettings = Claude(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", effort="low")
    tools: list[BaseTool] = [lookup_order]

It is declared like any agent: tools, skills, MCP servers and sub-agents work the same. It has no output_model or check_output, and a failed turn is not retried, because a word that is out cannot be taken back. A sub-agent it launches is a tool call that returns when the sub-agent is done, and its text is not streamed. A streaming agent cannot be a sub-agent. allow_user_questions and raise_conflicts do nothing, because a person is already in the chat.

docs.title: Streaming a turn
docs.text:
from ag_ui.core import UserMessage
from featherweight import ChatInput

chat_input = ChatInput(messages=[UserMessage(id="1", content="Where is my order?")], thread_id="t-17")
run = runner.stream(Support, chat_input)
async for event in run:
    print(event.type, getattr(event, "delta", ""))

runner.stream() returns at once. The run starts when you loop over it, and can be looped over once. The events are AG-UI's (from the ag-ui-protocol package), in the order the protocol requires:

Event When RUN_STARTED First. It has the thread_id (made up when the client named none) and the run_id STEP_STARTED, STEP_FINISHED One step per model turn, named model. A step also holds the tool results that follow the turn TEXT_MESSAGE_START, TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT (one per chunk), TEXT_MESSAGE_END The model writes text REASONING_START, REASONING_MESSAGE_START, REASONING_MESSAGE_CONTENT, REASONING_MESSAGE_END, REASONING_END The model's thoughts, only with show_thoughts REASONING_ENCRYPTED_VALUE A provider's opaque or signed value for a thought (Claude's signature, OpenAI's encrypted content) TOOL_CALL_START (name, id), TOOL_CALL_ARGS (the arguments, in pieces), TOOL_CALL_END The model calls a tool TOOL_CALL_RESULT The tool returned (the text of its result, or of its error) RUN_FINISHED Last, on success: outcome is success, and usage has the tokens RUN_ERROR Last, on failure

A text message, a thought or a tool call is closed before another kind opens, and everything open is closed before a step ends and before RUN_FINISHED or RUN_ERROR. A tool call carries the id of its turn's assistant message in parent_message_id. A launched sub-agent shows as a tool call (launch_agent) with its result.

When the loop ends, run.status is SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED, run.error says why it failed, and run.usage has the tokens. run.run_id is the id of the run in the run log.

stream() raises for a mistake in your code: an agent that is not a StreamingAgent or an input that is not a ChatInput (TypeError), or a job_id that does not exist (raised when the loop starts). A StreamingAgent passed to runner.run() is a TypeError too. Failures at run time, such as a provider that is down, are events, not exceptions.

docs.title: Thoughts
docs.text:
model: ModelSettings = Claude(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", effort="medium", show_thoughts=True)

show_thoughts is a setting of every model class. It asks the provider for the model's thoughts, which the reasoning events carry; off by default, and then there are no reasoning events. For most providers it is a summary, not the raw reasoning. Thoughts that must go back with the next request are kept whether shown or not, in run.new_messages.

docs.title: AG-UI
docs.text:
The events are already AG-UI's, so the adapter (featherweight.adapters.agui) is only the edge with HTTP. It has no server or router and needs no web framework:

parse_request(body) The JSON body of an AG-UI request (a dict, text or bytes) as a ChatInput. threadId is kept. The client's tools, state, context and forwardedProps are ignored (the agent has its own tools); sending tools logs a warning encode(run) The events of a run as server-sent events, one string each. Leaving the loop early stops the run CONTENT_TYPE, HEADERS text/event-stream, and headers that stop the stream being cached or buffered BadRequest What parse_request raises (a ValueError) for a body that is not JSON, is not an AG-UI request, or has a message a ChatInput refuses (system, developer, a last message that is not the user's). The message says what is wrong. AttachmentLimitError is a BadRequest too (see Attachments): runner.stream() raises it, and a handler for it can answer 413

With Starlette (FastAPI is the same):

from featherweight import AttachmentLimitError, BadRequest
from featherweight.adapters import agui
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse, StreamingResponse


async def chat(request):
    try:
        chat_input = agui.parse_request(await request.body())
        run = runner.stream(Support, chat_input)  # raises AttachmentLimitError over the agent's attachment limits
    except AttachmentLimitError as exc:
        return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc)}, status_code=413)
    except BadRequest as exc:
        return JSONResponse({"error": str(exc)}, status_code=422)
    return StreamingResponse(agui.encode(run), media_type=agui.CONTENT_TYPE, headers=agui.HEADERS)

Binary (protobuf) events are not supported.

docs.title: The conversation is yours
docs.text:
featherweight keeps no conversation. A ChatInput is the whole conversation so far, and it is all the agent sees:

  • the last message is from the user;
  • system and developer messages are refused: the agent has its own prompt, and a client must not be able to replace it;
  • thread_id is optional. It names the conversation in the run log. It does not load anything.

The history can hold text, assistant messages with tool calls, tool results (with their error), and thoughts with their signature. A user message may also carry attachments.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
A user message can carry images, documents, audio and video next to its text. featherweight only transports them, as LangChain content blocks. The provider decides what it can read.

from ag_ui.core import DocumentInputContent, InputContentDataSource, TextInputContent, UserMessage

pdf = DocumentInputContent(
    source=InputContentDataSource(value=base64_of_the_pdf, mime_type="application/pdf"),
    metadata={"filename": "report.pdf"},  # OpenAI wants a name for an inline file
)
chat_input = ChatInput(messages=[UserMessage(id="1", content=[TextInputContent(text="Summarise this."), pdf])])
  • Only inline data. A part's source must be data: base64 bytes with a mime_type, in the form that base64.b64encode (Python) and btoa (JavaScript) give: standard alphabet, padded, in one line, with no data: prefix. A wrong form is refused when the ChatInput is built, and the error says the likely mistake (a data: URL from a browser's FileReader, line breaks, the URL-safe alphabet, missing padding). An empty attachment is refused too. A url source is refused, because featherweight fetches nothing: your application downloads and checks the file, and sends the bytes. A file you uploaded to a provider (a file_id) is not an AG-UI source: build the LangChain message yourself.
  • Round trip. ChatInput.from_langchain and to_agui turn the blocks into parts again, so a stored conversation keeps its attachments.
  • Limits. Every turn resends the whole conversation, so the limits count the attachments of all messages. They are set on the agent; the defaults are 10 attachments and 15 MiB of decoded data (max_attachments = 0 turns attachments off for that agent):
class Support(StreamingAgent):
    max_attachments = 20
    max_bytes = 30 * 1024 * 1024

Over a limit, runner.stream() raises an AttachmentLimitError before any run exists. It is a BadRequest (so a ValueError): a web application answers it with a 413, and the other bad requests with a 422, as the examples above do. Files do not travel between agents, or through a job's queue: for files that are not in a chat, keep them in your own store and pass a reference.

The server's body limit comes first. Both adapters take an attachment as base64 inside the JSON body, a third larger than the file (the default 15 MiB is about 20 MiB of body), and every turn sends the whole conversation again. A web server or a proxy in front of your application often has a lower limit on the body of a request: a body over it never reaches featherweight, and the person gets the server's refusal and none of these messages. max_bytes is the agent's policy: set the server's limit above max_bytes x 4/3 plus the text. - Errors. A wrong input is raised (a URL, bad base64, an empty attachment, no mime type, over a limit: an AttachmentLimitError). What the provider refuses (a type the model cannot read, a file too big for it) is a failed turn: a RUN_ERROR event and a FAILED row, not retried. - No checks. featherweight does not know what a model can read. What the providers accept is a dated snapshot; read the providers' own pages before you design around a type or a size. - The Vercel AI SDK sends an attachment as a file part with a data: URL, which is read. Any other URL is refused with a BadRequest. - Not logged. The run log, the events and the default observers hold no attachment. An observer that captures content (capture_content=True, or OpenTelemetry with content capture on) gets the bytes with the other messages: leave it off, or filter, if attachments are private. featherweight puts no attachment bytes in an event or a log line, and guarantees nothing about what a provider's endpoint puts in its error text or keeps in its own logs: the text of a failure is passed on as it is. - Some providers drop or refuse a type without warning (Anthropic raises for audio and video; OpenAI's Responses API silently drops audio). The provider page has the table.

Details and decisions: the attachments spec.

docs.title: Keeping the conversation
docs.text:
featherweight stores nothing: the application keeps the messages, wherever it likes, as LangChain's messages. LangChain's chat message histories read and write them, and they hold what the model needs on the next request (tool call ids, results, thoughts with their signature). The wire format with a client is AG-UI's, and featherweight converts between the two:

run = runner.stream(Support, ChatInput.from_langchain([*history.messages, user_message], thread_id=thread_id))
async for event in run:
    yield encoder.encode(event)  # to the browser
history.add_messages([user_message, *run.new_messages])  # to your store
run.new_messages The LangChain messages of the turn: the assistant messages (with their tool calls and thoughts) and the tool results, in order. They fill up while the turn runs and are complete when the loop ends. After a failure it holds what had finished ChatInput.from_langchain(messages, thread_id=None) The conversation from LangChain messages, such as history.messages. The last one is the user's ChatInput.from_agui(request_or_messages, thread_id=None) The conversation from what an AG-UI client sent: a RunAgentInput (its thread_id is kept) or its messages featherweight.messages.to_langchain(messages), to_agui(messages) The converters, in both directions

The converters keep tool call ids, tool results and signed thoughts, so a stored conversation can go back to the model. A round trip gives the same messages, except:

  • A thought is a message of its own in AG-UI (reasoning) and a content block of the assistant message in LangChain. The converter folds it into the assistant message that follows it, and unfolds it again.
  • A failed tool result has an error in AG-UI and one text with status="error" in LangChain, so the two texts are one.
  • An AG-UI activity message is a UI element, not part of the conversation, and is left out.
  • A provider's own block format (Claude's thinking) is read through LangChain's standard reasoning blocks, and kept in that form when it comes back from AG-UI.

Any store that takes LangChain messages works: a BaseChatMessageHistory, or a list in your own table. There is no LangGraph checkpointer.

docs.title: Vercel AI SDK
docs.text:
featherweight.adapters.vercel speaks the UI message stream that useChat and the other AI SDK clients read. It is not a server: it reads a request and gives you strings to send with any web framework.

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException, Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

from featherweight import AttachmentLimitError, BadRequest
from featherweight.adapters import vercel

app = FastAPI()


@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(request: Request):
    try:
        chat_input = vercel.parse_request(await request.json())
        run = runner.stream(Support, chat_input)  # raises AttachmentLimitError over the agent's attachment limits
    except AttachmentLimitError as exc:
        raise HTTPException(413, str(exc))
    except BadRequest as exc:
        raise HTTPException(422, str(exc))
    return StreamingResponse(vercel.encode(run), headers=vercel.HEADERS)
  • The request. useChat posts {"id": ..., "messages": [UIMessage, ...]}. id becomes the thread_id. A UIMessage's text parts are joined; an assistant message with tool parts becomes what the model saw (the assistant message with its tool calls, then the tool results, then the next step's message), and its reasoning parts become reasoning messages. A user message's file parts are read as attachments; in an assistant message, files, sources and data-* parts are ignored. The same rules as any ChatInput: no system message, and the last message is the user's. parse_request raises BadRequest (a ValueError, also raised by the AG-UI adapter) for a body it cannot use, with the reason.
  • The response. Each AG-UI event becomes the part that the protocol page shows:
AG-UI Part RUN_STARTED start (its messageId is the run id) STEP_STARTED, STEP_FINISHED start-step, finish-step TEXT_MESSAGE_* text-start, text-delta, text-end REASONING_START, REASONING_MESSAGE_CONTENT, REASONING_END reasoning-start, reasoning-delta, reasoning-end TOOL_CALL_START, TOOL_CALL_ARGS, TOOL_CALL_END tool-input-start, tool-input-delta, tool-input-available (the arguments, parsed) TOOL_CALL_RESULT tool-output-available (the result, parsed when it is JSON) RUN_FINISHED finish, or abort when the run was stopped RUN_ERROR error

The stream ends with data: [DONE]. HEADERS has x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1. Events with no part (state, activity, and the opaque value of a thought) are dropped: the Vercel client does not need them, and you keep the messages yourself. - A client that goes away. Stop iterating encode(...) (a web framework does when the connection drops) and the run stops. - The version. Written against the protocol as documented on 2026-11-19, and versioned by its header (v1).

docs.title: Stopping a response
docs.text:
The person stops the agent while it answers, then corrects it. Two things stop a run:

run.cancel()  # from anywhere in the same process
runner.cancel(run_id)  # by the id of RUN_STARTED, for a stop button's request; False when no such run is going on here

and a reader that leaves: when the client drops the connection, your web framework closes the stream and the run stops. If you stop reading early, close it yourself with async with contextlib.aclosing(aiter(run)) as events:. A plain break leaves the run going until the generator is collected.

A stop ends the stream cleanly. The model call is cancelled, everything open is closed, and the last event is RUN_FINISHED with the cancelled outcome (Vercel: abort), so the code after your loop runs. The row is CANCELLED, its output holds the length of the text so far, and the concurrency slot is free at once. A stop also works while the run waits for a slot, and before the loop has started. A second cancel(), or one after the run ended, does nothing.

The partial turn is kept, so the next message has its context. run.new_messages holds what the turn said and did, cleaned up so it is valid to send back:

When it was stopped What new_messages has Text was streaming An assistant message with the text so far A tool call's arguments were still streaming Nothing of that call: it is not complete A tool call was complete and the tool had not returned The call, and a tool message that says it did not return (status="error": "cancelled by the user"), because a provider rejects a call with no result A tool had returned The call and its real result A thought was streaming The thought only if it has its signature (a provider rejects one without); the text is kept either way

new_messages is filled when the run ends, whatever ended it, including a reader that left. Save it in a finally, after the stream is closed (use aclosing, as below, or the run may not be over yet). A turn that fails is closed the same way: its text so far, no call without a result.

from contextlib import aclosing

run = runner.stream(Support, ChatInput.from_langchain([*history.messages, user_message]))
try:
    async with aclosing(agui.encode(run)) as pieces:
        async for piece in pieces:
            yield piece
finally:
    history.add_messages([user_message, *run.new_messages])

What a stop cannot undo - A synchronous tool runs in a thread and cannot be interrupted, and an MCP call may finish on the server, so its effect can still happen after the person pressed stop. An async tool is cancelled where it waits. - A launched sub-agent is cancelled with its parent, and its row is CANCELLED too. - The tokens of a cancelled call are those counted when it stopped; the provider may bill for more. - cancel() works only in the process that runs the stream.

docs.title: What is logged
docs.text:
One attempts row per turn, in the same run log as any run. It holds no content: no messages, no text.

Column input_hash, output_hash SHA-256 of the ChatInput, and of the text (set when the turn succeeds) thread_id The conversation, when the client named one status INIT while it waits for a concurrency slot, RUNNING while it streams, then SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED error_type, error_hash For a failed turn: the class of the exception and the hash of its message. The client gets the text in the RUN_ERROR event tokens, latency, agent, model, the hashes of the agent As for any run

The words stay with your application: save run_id next to each turn you store, to join your messages to the log. The slot is held for the whole stream. A streaming run is never reused when a job is resumed.

docs.title: How it differs from an agent
docs.text: AgentBase StreamingAgent Run with runner.run() runner.stream() Input its own input_model ChatInput Output output_model, validated, check_output text, in events, not validated Retries up to max_attempts none Rows one per attempt one per turn System prompt the prompt, plus the instructions for questions and conflicts the prompt

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
examples/chat has one agent (support.py: a support chat with one tool, on claude-haiku-5-5) and two ways to talk to it:

  • cli.py, a terminal chat in about 30 lines. It prints the answer as it is written, keeps the conversation in a list with run.new_messages, and Ctrl-C stops the answer so you can correct the agent. make example-chat.
  • api.py, the same agent behind FastAPI in about 50 lines: POST /agui, POST /vercel and POST /stop/{run_id}. The client sends the conversation, so there is no store. make example-chat-api.

docs.title: Background work
docs.text: A streaming agent can start another agent and carry on: a background job. The turn does not wait for it. The stream carries two events (background_started and background_finished), and when the child is done your application starts the next turn with the history and the child's result (runner.background_message(job_id)). A launched sub-agent (subagents) blocks the turn until it returns.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Retries. A failed turn is an error event and a FAILED row.
  • Streaming sub-agents: a launched agent is a tool call with a result.
  • Client-side tools, shared state and interrupts of AG-UI: ignored.
  • Stored conversations, sessions, a LangGraph checkpointer. Keep the messages yourself.
  • Structured or validated output from a streaming agent.
  • Stopping across processes: cancel() works in the process that runs the stream.
  • A web server or router. The adapters give you strings, you send them.
  • Background jobs are their own feature, and jobs across processes are submitted jobs.

docs.title: Submitted jobs
docs.text:
A client submits a named, typed job. A separate worker takes it from a queue and runs it. The result goes to your result store. featherweight keeps the status and the events of the job, never its input or its result.

Spec: Submitted jobs. Example: examples/jobs (make example-jobs).

  • The model
  • Defining a job
  • Submitting and following
  • Who the job is for: the identity
  • Cancelling
  • Events and SSE
  • Running a worker
  • Several workers
  • Your own queue
  • What is not here

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
JobClient --submit--> database (job row, "queued" event) + JobQueue --> JobWorker --> your ResultStore
    ^                                                                       |
    +---------------------- status, events, result -------------------------+

The client and the worker never talk to each other. The queue and the database are their only connection, so they can be two processes, or two machines. A job is the same thing as in Jobs: a row with a status. Submitting only adds queued to it; the worker is what runs it.

docs.title: Defining a job
docs.text:
The example of this page, declared with the decorator (jobs says more):

from featherweight import job, JobContext
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Text(BaseModel):
    text: str


class Shouted(BaseModel):
    shouted: str


@job
async def shout(ctx: JobContext, input: Text) -> Shouted:
    return Shouted(shouted=input.text.upper())

How to declare a job (@job, a Job class, the version, the timeout, ctx.run) is in jobs. An agent is a job too: pass an agent class to submit and the worker runs it.

docs.title: Submitting and following
docs.text:
client = JobClient(db, queue)  # results="default" uses the default result store
job_id = await client.submit(shout, Text(text="hello"))

await client.status(job_id)  # the JobRow
async for event in client.events(job_id):  # queued, running, succeeded
    ...
print(await client.result(shout, job_id))  # Shouted(shouted='HELLO'), read from your result store

The same job runs in your process with run_job(runner, shout, Text(text="hello")): it writes the same row, events and result, and returns the outcome. result is None until the job succeeded. wait(job_id, timeout) polls the database until the job is final: fine in a script or a test, but a web handler should return the job id and let the caller follow events.

docs.title: Who the job is for: the identity
docs.text:
A tool on a worker can act for the user who started the job, as a tool in your process can (who is asking). submit takes identity=, the message carries it as JSON together with its kind (the name of its class), and the worker rebuilds it as the model that the kind names, from its own identity_type:

runner = AgentRunner(db, identity_type=Teacher)
worker = JobWorker(db, queue, runner, jobs=[shout], identity_type=Teacher)
client = JobClient(db, queue, identity_type=Teacher)  # optional: it only checks the identity before a job is made

job_id = await client.submit(shout, Text(text="hello"), identity=Teacher(user_id="u1", tenant="uni"))
  • The worker's type is the authority. A message without an identity, when the worker's type does not allow None, fails its job (InvalidJobIdentity), and so does an identity that does not fit the type, one whose kind the type does not have (a Student's message for a worker that declares only Teacher), or one when the worker declares no type. The job is not run, and it is not retried. The error names the fields, never the values.
  • A worker can serve several kinds of people: declare a union (identity_type=Teacher | Student) and the worker rebuilds each message as the model it was sent as, even when the models have the same fields. The kind is the name of the class, so a rename of an identity class while a job is queued fails that job, as a renamed job does. Two models of one union cannot have the same name.
  • The runner must accept the worker's type. JobWorker raises TypeError when it is built if the runner's identity_type does not accept every type the worker rebuilds (and None, if the worker allows no identity): otherwise every job that runs an agent would fail. A worker may be stricter than its runner.
  • Fields marked exclude=True are not sent, so a value that exists only in your process stays there. The worker's copy has their default, so such a field needs one (a model without one is refused when it is declared), and a tool that wants the value on a worker asks for it by user id.
  • A job that an agent starts in the background on a worker (a runner with background=JobClient) is submitted with the identity of its parent.
  • It is data in the queue message, until the message is acknowledged: the queue is trusted, so keep the identity small and keep secrets out of it, and secure the queue the way you secure the input. A tool on a worker gets a credential from the identity with its own code; featherweight has no provider for it. The identity spec has the rules and what is yours.

docs.title: Cancelling
docs.text:
await client.cancel(job_id)  # False if the job is already final, or does not exist

A queued job becomes CANCELLED at once, and the worker skips its message. A running job is asked to stop: the worker sees the request within about a second (at once when the worker is in the same process), and the job ends CANCELLED. The client and the worker race for a queued job, and exactly one of them wins: a job is never both cancelled and run.

docs.title: Events and SSE
docs.text: client.events(job_id, after=n) is the stream of the job's events that jobs describes (job_events): the stored ones after n, then each new one, ending at the final one. A worker writes the same events as run_job does. To send them to a browser, sse.encode(client.events(job_id, after=after)) with sse.HEADERS, as in that section; examples/jobs/api.py is this behind FastAPI.

docs.title: Running a worker
docs.text:
worker = JobWorker(db, queue, AgentRunner(db), jobs=[shout], concurrency=10)
await worker.run()  # until stop() or cancellation
await worker.stop(grace=30)
  • It runs only the jobs you list (and the ones your jobs_lookup finds, below); a message for another name fails that job.
  • It never retries a failed job. If the job was resumable, you resume it with a new job (Persistence).
  • The result is written to your result store, keyed by the job id, the job hash and the input hash. If it cannot be written, the job fails.
  • While it runs jobs, the worker holds a lease on each (FTW_JOB_LEASE, 60 seconds) and renews it, and the queue's lease of the message, every third of it (FTW_HEARTBEAT). A worker that finds a job taken from it stops that job at once and writes nothing more to it. A job must be safe to run twice.
  • On stop, the worker takes no new messages, waits up to grace seconds, then cancels what is left, puts those messages back on the queue and sets those jobs back to INIT, so they run again.

docs.title: Jobs that are not declared in code
docs.text:
A worker is given its jobs when it starts. If your users define their own agents (kept in your database, built into classes when they are needed), a worker cannot have been given them. jobs_lookup is a fallback for those: jobs is tried first, and the lookup is called only for a name jobs does not have.

async def jobs_lookup(name: str, job_hash: str | None, identity: Teacher):  # the worker declares `Teacher`: never None
    definition = await my_agents.get(identity.tenant, name)  # your storage; the identity can scope the search
    return build_agent(definition) if definition else None  # an agent class or a Job class; None: unknown


worker = JobWorker(
    db, queue, AgentRunner(db, identity_type=Teacher), jobs=[], jobs_lookup=jobs_lookup, identity_type=Teacher
)
  • It gets the name from the message, the job_hash recorded when the job was submitted, and the identity the worker rebuilt (an application that does not need it ignores it).
  • The worker checks what it returns before anything runs: the name must be the one asked for, and job_hash() must be the recorded hash. If the user edited their agent while the job waited, the job fails (JobLookupError) instead of running the new definition. A lookup that keeps old versions of a definition can use job_hash to load the exact one. None is UnknownJob; a lookup that raises, or returns something that is not a job, fails the job with JobLookupError. The worker never retries a job, so a lookup that can fail for a transient reason retries inside itself.
  • The worker caches nothing. The hash is made from the content, so you may cache what you built by (name, job_hash).
  • The lookup has a timeout: FTW_JOBS_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT seconds (15 by default). It runs inline in the worker's receive loop, so one that hangs would stop the worker taking messages; past the limit it is cancelled (so it must be safe to cancel) and the job is FAILED with JobLookupError. There is no way to switch it off: set a large value.
  • Names are yours. A job's name is a string you choose, unique in what your lookup searches (with the identity, unique within a tenant is enough) and stable: a rename breaks the jobs queued under the old name. It must match [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*, and the worker fails a job whose name does not (UnknownJob) without asking your lookup.
  • On the client side nothing changes: submit takes the class that you built from the same definition.

The spec has the rules. It is not a registry: where definitions live, who may define one and which tools a user may pick are your application's.

docs.title: Several workers
docs.text:
Run as many workers as you like on one queue: a message goes to one of them, and one wins the job. (SqliteQueue is for one machine; for several, share one database (PostgresDatabase ships in the package) and use a queue of your own: your own queue.)

  • A worker that dies. While a worker runs a job it renews two leases about every 20 seconds (a third of lease, 60 seconds by default): the job's, in the database, and its message's, in the queue. If the worker dies, the leases run out. The message comes back to another worker, which sees that the job's lease expired and takes it over: the same job, with executions one higher and a lost event in its events (queued, running, lost, running, succeeded). A message that arrives while the job's lease is still alive is a duplicate: it is acknowledged and the job is left alone.
  • What the new worker reuses. If the job is resumable, the steps that finished before the worker died are reused, as in a resume; otherwise the job runs again from the start. A resume is you running a job that ended again, as a new job; a takeover is the system running a job that did not end again, as the same job.
  • A worker that only stalled. If a worker was paused (not dead) and wakes up after a takeover, its writes are refused, because every write of a running job checks that the worker still owns it. It stops the job at once and writes nothing more. Only featherweight's writes are checked: a job must be safe to run twice, because what its own code already did (a mail sent, an API called) is not undone.
  • A job that hangs. The heartbeat only shows that a worker is alive. Each job has a timeout (@job(timeout=...), 600 seconds by default, None for no limit): when it passes, the job is cancelled and fails with error type JobTimeout. It is not retried; you resume it.
  • How often a message may come back is your queue's policy. SqliteQueue marks a message dead after FTW_QUEUE_MAX_DELIVERIES (3) deliveries and fails its job (DeadLettered). If your own queue dead-letters a message, call client.fail(job_id) from its dead-letter handler to end the job.

examples/jobs/takeover.py does it: it kills a worker with SIGKILL in the middle of a job, and another one takes the job over (make example-takeover).

docs.title: Your own queue
docs.text:
SqliteQueue is the only queue that featherweight ships, for local work. For production, subclass JobQueue (enqueue, receive, ack, nack, extend) over the queue you run, and check it with the kit. The kit gives your factory the lease in seconds (a short one, to see a message come back):

await testing.check_queue(lambda lease: MyQueue(visibility_timeout=lease))

The lease. A received message is yours for a limited time. If you do not ack it, nack it or extend it before the lease ends, it is delivered again to another receiver, and its Delivery.delivery_count is higher. extend renews the lease; a delivery that has been replaced (a stale one) must change nothing. You do not have to build it: a broker has it. On SQS the lease is the visibility timeout (extend is ChangeMessageVisibility, and the delivery count is ApproximateReceiveCount); on a Redis stream it is the pending list (XAUTOCLAIM takes a message over, extend is a XCLAIM of your own entry to reset its idle time, and the delivery counter is in XPENDING). How many times a message may be delivered is your broker's policy, with its own dead-letter queue. The kit asks that a message can be delivered at least three times. SqliteQueue(db) is the one we ship (FTW_QUEUE_LEASE, FTW_QUEUE_MAX_DELIVERIES): after that many deliveries it marks the message dead.

A message also carries a trace_context (a small mapping of strings, empty unless the client has an observer that gives one) and an identity (a JSON mapping, or None) and its identity_kind (a string, or None: who the job is for): carry them unchanged, and the kit checks that you do. A queue that drops the identity or its kind fails the kit.

A dead-letter queue is yours to configure on your queue: a message that is nacked without requeue is yours to keep or drop.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text:
• A worker registry, a scheduler, priorities, and a sweeper for a job whose message never comes back.
  • An event channel such as pub/sub: events are read from the database for now.

docs.title: What featherweight is
docs.text: Book › Part 0: Start here › What featherweight is

docs.title: What featherweight is
docs.text:
An opinionated agent harness for Python. Pydantic is the spec. Everything else follows.

You declare an agent as a typed class: its input, its output, its prompt, and what it may use. featherweight runs it, checks what comes out, retries what fails, and records what happened. You write the part that is yours: the pipeline around it.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Typed agents. What goes in and what comes out is a schema. A bad answer is caught and retried before your code sees it.
  • Abilities. Tools, MCP servers, skills and sub-agents, declared on the agent.
  • Jobs. A pipeline is a job: a declared class that runs in your process or on a worker, with a status, events and a result.
  • Chat. A streaming agent, for a browser or a terminal.
  • Background jobs. An agent starts another agent and goes on.
  • Traces. OpenTelemetry spans for jobs, attempts, model calls and tool calls.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not a workflow engine. A pipeline is plain Python: if and for, no graph to draw.
  • Not a store for your data. The framework stores metadata and nothing else. You bring the storage.
  • Not a server or a UI. It runs no server. You send its events wherever you like.

Want durable execution or built-in evals? Look at Pydantic AI. Want a graph that pauses and resumes? Look at LangGraph.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
A small incident report assistant: a report goes in, a structured summary comes out. It grows through the book, from one agent to a chat and a pipeline on workers. See how to read this book.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
How the parts fit. Each box is a chapter, or a few.

flowchart TD
    agent["Agent: a typed class"] -->|run by| runner["AgentRunner"]
    runner -->|calls| model["A model: Gemini, Claude, OpenAI"]
    runner -->|uses| abilities["Tools, MCP servers, skills, sub-agents"]
    runner -->|records metadata in| db[("Database: the run log")]
    job["Job: a typed class that runs agents"] -->|run here by| runjob["run_job"]
    job -->|submitted by| client["JobClient"]
    client -->|message| queue[("JobQueue")]
    queue --> worker["JobWorker"]
    runjob --> runner
    worker --> runner
    runner -->|result| store[("ResultStore: yours")]
    runner -.->|events| observers["Observers: OpenTelemetry"]
  • An agent is a typed class. The runner runs it, against a model, with its abilities, and records metadata about every attempt in the database, the run log.
  • A job is a typed class that runs agents. run_job runs it in your process. A client submits it to a queue, and a worker runs it elsewhere. The same job, the same record, in both places.
  • Results go to a result store that you own. The framework keeps no data.
  • Observers receive what happens, and send it where you want: OpenTelemetry is the one we ship.
  • What ships, and what is yours. Model providers: Gemini, Gemma, Claude, OpenAI. Databases: sqlite and Postgres. Result stores and queues: sqlite. Observers: OpenTelemetry. MCP servers: stdio and HTTP. Chat protocols: AG-UI and the Vercel AI SDK. For databases, result stores, queues, observers and providers, yours is a class you write: Part 6.

docs.title: The philosophy
docs.text: Book › Part 0: Start here › The philosophy

docs.title: The philosophy
docs.text:
featherweight has opinions. Take them, or fork off. Each one shaped features you will meet, and each is argued in a spec.

Principle What it means Where you will see it Pydantic is the spec An agent's input and output are models, checked on the way in and on the way out. A bad declaration fails when the class is written. A typed agent, agents spec Failures are values A failed run returns a status and the error. It does not raise. Running it, Failures and check_output, runner spec Plain Python pipelines Order, loops and branching are if and for. No graph, no workflow syntax. What a job is, jobs spec Least privilege Everything an agent can do is an allow-list that the developer wrote: its tools, the MCP servers and the tools it may use from them, its skills, the sub-agents it may launch, the background jobs it may start. Nothing is granted by default. Tools, MCP, Skills, Sub-agents, Background jobs, the tools spec Metadata only, and your storage The framework stores metadata and nothing else. Inputs, outputs and results go where you decide. Results and the result store, persistence spec One concept, two places A job runs in your process or on a worker, by the same code, with the same record. What a job is, Submit and a worker, submitted jobs spec We run no server We emit events, and SSE is the one streaming protocol. Your API sends them. Status and events, In the browser, streaming spec What you plug in is an abstract class, with a kit A database, a result store, a queue or an observer is a class you implement, and a conformance kit checks it. Bring your own storage, persistence spec Agents propose, code executes An agent does not hold a permission. It returns a typed proposal, a person approves it, and your own code acts, once. Approvals, approvals spec, the recipe Seams, not solutions featherweight takes what you give it, as typed definitions, and runs it durably. How you store them, who your users are, who may do what, and what things are called is your application's. Where your code meets ours is a typed seam, checked at the boundary and closed when misused. A use case is a recipe, not a feature. Who is asking (the identity: you define it, the tool checks it), jobs_lookup (a job that is not in the worker's code), a skill from a database or S3, files: pass a reference, Tenants (we have no tenant column: you choose the job id or the name), Bring your own storage, the recipes

These are not a style guide for your code. They are why featherweight works the way it does, so that its behaviour is never a surprise.

docs.title: How to read this book
docs.text: Book › Part 0: Start here › How to read this book

docs.title: How to read this book
docs.text:
In order, or through the map: go straight to what you want to build.

  • Short chapters. Each is a goal, the code, how to run it, and what to notice. A "why" box links to the spec when a choice needs its reasons.
  • One small project. You build an incident report assistant: a report goes in, a structured summary comes out. It gains one thing per chapter, so each chapter starts from the code of the one before.
  • Code you can run. Every chapter's code is a file in code/, in a folder per chapter (code/<part>-<chapter>/). Each folder runs on its own, so you can start at any chapter. The last one is the finished project.
  • In a container. The code runs in a container by default, so nothing touches your machine. code/README.md says what the container does, how to start it, and how to run it without Docker.
  • A model key. The default model is Gemini: set GOOGLE_API_KEY in .env. Other providers take their own key (choosing a model).

When you need an exact rule, the guides and the specs are the reference (Part 7).

Also possible

  • Upgrading from an earlier version? See the migration guide.
  • Short patterns to copy: the recipes.

docs.title: Install and set up
docs.text:
Get featherweight running in a container, with a model key.

You need Docker, and a key for Gemini (the default model). Everything runs in a container, so nothing is installed on your machine.

cd docs/book/code
cp .env.example .env     # put your Gemini key in GOOGLE_API_KEY
make build               # once
make chapter N=1-1

"""Chapter 1-1: is featherweight installed, and is there a key? No model is called."""

import os

from featherweight import __version__

print("featherweight", __version__)
for key in ("GOOGLE_API_KEY", "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", "OPENAI_API_KEY"):
    print(key, "is set" if os.environ.get(key) else "is not set")

featherweight 0.1.0
GOOGLE_API_KEY is set
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set
OPENAI_API_KEY is not set

What to notice

  • No model was called: this only checks the install and the key. Only GOOGLE_API_KEY has to be set.
  • The chapter code is mounted into the container, so you can edit a file and run it again.
  • No Docker? code/README.md shows the same files in a virtual environment.

Why a container. The agents, their tools and the MCP server of Part 2 all run inside it, and only the keys you list get in. What it does, line by line: what the container does.

docs.title: A typed agent
docs.text: Book › Part 1: Your first agent › A typed agent

docs.title: A typed agent
docs.text:
Write an agent as a typed class: its input, its output and its prompt.

"""Chapter 1-2: the agent, as a typed class. Nothing is run against a model."""

from typing import ClassVar, Literal

from featherweight import AgentBase, AgentInput, AgentOutput


class Report(AgentInput):  # what goes in: a typed model, checked before the model is called
    text: str


class Summary(AgentOutput):  # also carries `open_questions: list[str]`
    title: str = ""  # every field has a default: a model that does not know is not forced to invent
    # only these values, or None when the report does not say
    severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] | None = None
    service: str | None = None
    impact: str = ""
    next_steps: list[str] = []


class IncidentSummariser(AgentBase):
    name: str = "incident_summariser"  # how the run log and the traces name the agent
    description: str = "Turns an incident report into a short, structured summary"
    version: str = "1"  # change it when the prompt or the behaviour changes: runs are told apart by it
    prompt: str = (
        "Summarise the incident report. Use only what the report says. "
        "If the severity or the service is not stated, leave it out and ask in open_questions."
    )
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = Report  # the contract is set on the class: the same for every run
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = Summary


if __name__ == "__main__":
    agent = IncidentSummariser()  # a malformed agent is refused here, before any model is involved
    print(agent.name, agent.version)
    print(list(Summary.model_fields))

incident_summariser 1
['open_questions', 'title', 'severity', 'service', 'impact', 'next_steps']

What to notice

  • The input and the output are Pydantic models. The runner checks both, so a summary with severity="urgent" is never handed to your code.
  • The output fields have defaults. If the report does not say, the model can leave a field empty and ask in open_questions, which AgentOutput carries, and does not have to invent an answer to pass the check.
  • The class is checked when it is built. IncidentSummariser() refuses a malformed agent (a model that does not exist, a recursion_limit out of range, duplicate tool names) before any model is involved.
  • A class can also be built from data (a file, a database row): the runner sees a class either way. See agents built from JSON.
  • name, description and version identify the agent in the run log: change the version when the prompt or the behaviour changes.

Why typed. Pydantic is the spec: what goes in and what comes out is a schema, enforced, and not a convention. See the philosophy and the agent spec.

More on defining agents: agents guide.

Next: run it.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
Run the agent on a report, and read the result.

"""Chapter 1-3: run the agent on a report, and read the result."""

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path
from typing import ClassVar, Literal

from featherweight import AgentBase, AgentInput, AgentOutput, AgentRunner, SqliteDatabase, Status, default_db_path


class Report(AgentInput):  # what goes in: a typed model, checked before the model is called
    text: str


class Summary(AgentOutput):  # also carries `open_questions: list[str]`
    title: str = ""  # every field has a default: a model that does not know is not forced to invent
    # only these values, or None when the report does not say
    severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] | None = None
    service: str | None = None
    impact: str = ""
    next_steps: list[str] = []


class IncidentSummariser(AgentBase):
    name: str = "incident_summariser"  # how the run log and the traces name the agent
    description: str = "Turns an incident report into a short, structured summary"
    version: str = "1"  # change it when the prompt or the behaviour changes: runs are told apart by it
    prompt: str = (
        "Summarise the incident report. Use only what the report says. "
        "If the severity or the service is not stated, leave it out and ask in open_questions."
    )
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = Report  # the contract is set on the class: the same for every run
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = Summary


async def main() -> None:
    report = Report(text=Path("reports/01-checkout-outage.txt").read_text())
    async with SqliteDatabase(default_db_path()) as db:  # the run log: a sqlite file, /data/book.db in the container
        # the class, not an instance: the runner builds the agent
        result = await AgentRunner(db).run(IncidentSummariser, report)
    if result.status == Status.SUCCESS:
        print(result.output)
    else:
        print("failed:", result.error)  # a failed run is a value, not an exception
    print(result.status.value, f"attempts={result.attempts}", f"tokens={result.input_tokens}+{result.output_tokens}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

open_questions=[] title='Checkout was down' severity='high' service='checkout' impact='About 1,200 orders affected ...' next_steps=[...]
SUCCESS attempts=1 tokens=312+96

What to notice

  • run takes the class, not an instance. The runner builds the agent, and returns an AgentResult: status, output, error, attempts and the tokens.
  • A failed run is a value, not an exception. You check result.status. (A wrong input type does raise: that is a bug in your code.)
  • SqliteDatabase(default_db_path()) is the run log. In the container it is /data/book.db, in a volume that survives between runs. The next chapter reads it.

Why a value. A pipeline decides what a failure means. See the philosophy and the result.

Also possible

  • Test an agent without a real model: a fake model.

Next: what the run log recorded.

class IncidentSummariser(AgentBase):

    description: str = "Turns an incident report into a short, structured summary"
    version: str = "1"  # change it when the prompt or the behaviour changes: runs are told apart by it
    prompt: str = (
        "Summarise the incident report. Use only what the report says. "
        "If the severity or the service is not stated, leave it out and ask in open_questions."
    )
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = Report  # the contract is set on the class: the same for every run
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = Summary


async def main() -> None:
    report = Report(text=Path("reports/01-checkout-outage.txt").read_text())
    async with SqliteDatabase(default_db_path()) as db:
        job_id = await db.create_job("incident-report")  # a job id groups the runs of one piece of work
        # the class, not an instance: the runner builds the agent
        result = await AgentRunner(db).run(IncidentSummariser, report, job_id=job_id)
        print(result.status.value, result.output)
        for row in await db.list_attempts(
            job_id=job_id
        ):  # one row for each attempt: metadata, never the report or the summary
            print(
                f"attempt {row.attempt}: {row.status.value}, {row.model_name}, tokens={row.input_tokens}+{row.output_tokens}, "
                f"{row.latency_ms or 0:.0f} ms, input_hash={row.input_hash[:8]}"
            )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

SUCCESS open_questions=[] title='Checkout was down' ...
attempt 1: SUCCESS, gemini-3.5-flash-lite, tokens=312+96, 2210 ms, input_hash=2d368048

What to notice

  • One row for each attempt: its status, the model, the tokens, the time and the hashes. A retry is its own row (the next chapter).
  • Metadata and nothing else. The row has the hash of the report, never the report, and not the summary either. The framework stores metadata and you bring the storage: where the report and the summary live is your decision.
  • create_job gives a job id, which groups the runs of one piece of work. Jobs get their own part, Part 3.
  • The run log is a Database: SqliteDatabase here, PostgresDatabase for a deployment, or your own (Part 6).
  • The file is /data/book.db. make clean in docs/book/code resets it.

Why only metadata. What went through the agent is yours, and so is how it is kept. See the rule and the run log.

Also possible

  • Log what the runner does: setup_logging() and FTW_LOG_LEVEL, in Configuration.

docs.text:
Reject an answer the schema cannot catch, and see what a failed attempt looks like.

"""Chapter 1-5: a rule the schema cannot say, and what a rejected attempt looks like."""

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path
from typing import ClassVar, Literal

from featherweight import AgentBase, AgentInput, AgentOutput, AgentRunner, SqliteDatabase, default_db_path


class Report(AgentInput):  # what goes in: a typed model, checked before the model is called
    text: str


class Summary(AgentOutput):  # also carries `open_questions: list[str]`
    title: str = ""  # every field has a default: a model that does not know is not forced to invent
    # only these values, or None when the report does not say
    severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] | None = None
    service: str | None = None
    impact: str = ""
    next_steps: list[str] = []


class IncidentSummariser(AgentBase):
    name: str = "incident_summariser"  # how the run log and the traces name the agent
    description: str = "Turns an incident report into a short, structured summary"
    version: str = "1"  # change it when the prompt or the behaviour changes: runs are told apart by it
    prompt: str = (
        "Summarise the incident report. Use only what the report says. "
        "If the severity or the service is not stated, leave it out and ask in open_questions."
    )
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = Report  # the contract is set on the class: the same for every run
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = Summary

    def check_output(self, agent_input, output):  # a rule the schema cannot say: raise to reject the attempt
        if output.service and output.service.lower() not in agent_input.text.lower():
            raise ValueError(f"The report does not name the service {output.service!r}")


async def main() -> None:
    report = Report(text=Path("reports/02-sign-in-trouble.txt").read_text())  # this report names no service
    async with SqliteDatabase(default_db_path()) as db:
        job_id = await db.create_job("incident-report")  # a job id groups the runs of one piece of work
        # the class, not an instance: the runner builds the agent
        result = await AgentRunner(db).run(IncidentSummariser, report, job_id=job_id)
        print(result.status.value, f"attempts={result.attempts}", result.output if result.output else result.error)
        for row in await db.list_attempts(job_id=job_id):
            print(f"attempt {row.attempt}: {row.status.value} {row.error_type or ''}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

SUCCESS attempts=2 open_questions=['What was the cause?', ...] title='Sign-in trouble' severity=None service=None ...
attempt 1: FAILED ValueError
attempt 2: SUCCESS

What to notice

  • check_output(agent_input, output) holds rules between the input and the output, which a schema cannot express. Raise ValueError to reject the attempt.
  • A rejected attempt is retried, up to max_attempts (3). The retry samples again with the same input: the error is in the log (error_type) and is not sent back to the model.
  • If every attempt fails, you get a FAILED result, with the last error, and not an exception. Your code decides what that means.
  • A reply that breaks the schema (a wrong type, a value outside a Literal) goes back to the model within the same attempt where the output is a tool call. With a provider's own structured output it fails the attempt, which is retried (provider limits). The book's Gemini agent was not checked for which it is.

Why it works this way. Each attempt is a row, so a failure can be diagnosed from the log. See attempts and retries and checking the output.

Also possible

  • Tell the next attempt what went wrong: a retry that knows the last error.

Next: choose the model.

Choose the model: it is a setting of the agent. This is the assistant that the next parts build on.

"""Chapter 1-6: the model is a setting of the agent. This is the assistant that the next parts build on."""

import asyncio
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import ClassVar, Literal

from featherweight import (
    AgentBase,
    AgentInput,
    AgentOutput,
    AgentRunner,
    Gemini,
    ModelSettings,
    SqliteDatabase,
    default_db_path,
)


class Report(AgentInput):  # what goes in: a typed model, checked before the model is called
    text: str


class Summary(AgentOutput):  # also carries `open_questions: list[str]`
    title: str = ""  # every field has a default: a model that does not know is not forced to invent
    # only these values, or None when the report does not say
    severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] | None = None
    service: str | None = None
    impact: str = ""
    next_steps: list[str] = []


class IncidentSummariser(AgentBase):
    name: str = "incident_summariser"  # how the run log and the traces name the agent
    description: str = "Turns an incident report into a short, structured summary"
    version: str = "1"  # change it when the prompt or the behaviour changes: runs are told apart by it
    prompt: str = (
        "Summarise the incident report. Use only what the report says. "
        "If the severity or the service is not stated, leave it out and ask in open_questions."
    )
    model: ModelSettings = Gemini(model="gemini-3.5-flash-lite", thinking="low")  # the one line to change
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = Report  # the contract is set on the class: the same for every run
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = Summary

    def check_output(self, agent_input, output):  # a rule the schema cannot say: raise to reject the attempt
        if output.service and output.service.lower() not in agent_input.text.lower():
            raise ValueError(f"The report does not name the service {output.service!r}")


async def main(path: str = "reports/01-checkout-outage.txt") -> None:
    report = Report(text=Path(path).read_text())
    async with SqliteDatabase(default_db_path()) as db:
        job_id = await db.create_job("incident-report")  # a job id groups the runs of one piece of work
        # the class, not an instance: the runner builds the agent
        result = await AgentRunner(db).run(IncidentSummariser, report, job_id=job_id)
    print(result.status.value, result.model_name, result.output or result.error)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main(*sys.argv[1:2]))

model: ModelSettings = Claude(model="claude-haiku-5-5", effort="low")

The models of a provider are in its class: docker compose run --rm --no-deps book python -c "from featherweight import Gemini; print(list(Gemini.models))".

What to notice

  • The settings are checked when the agent is built. A model that does not exist, or an effort that model does not accept (Gemini(model="gemini-3.8-flash", thinking="minimal")), fails at once with a message that says why.
  • The settings are part of the run log, so two runs can be told apart by the model that made them.
  • This file is the project's base. Later chapters keep Report, Summary and IncidentSummariser, and add one thing at a time.
  • The providers are Gemini, Gemma, Claude and OpenAI: each is a class with the controls of its provider (the providers).
  • Not every output works on every model. Read the box below before you change the model.
  • Your own provider is a subclass. Any provider that LangChain has a chat model for works: subclass ModelSettings and write build(). Add a provider shows it for Ollama.

Warning

The providers differ in what they do with typed output. Claude Opus, Sonnet and Fable take no dictionaries, no recursive models and at most 24 optional fields: such an agent is refused when it is built. Claude Haiku can answer in the same reply in which it calls a tool, before it has seen the result: that attempt fails and is retried, and the tools run again. These come from Anthropic and LangChain. See provider limits.

Why a setting. The model is part of what the agent is, so it is declared and checked like the rest. See the model spec.

Also possible

  • Another model or provider: a different provider.

Next: Part 2 gives the assistant abilities.

docs.text:
Give the agent a tool it can call.

This part adds abilities to the assistant from Part 1. Parts 2, 3 and 4 do not depend on each other: you can read this one without the others.

Every ability in this part is an allow-list: the agent has what its declaration names and nothing else, and each one is a step you take on purpose (see the philosophy).

"""Chapter 2-1: a tool. The summariser works out how long the incident lasted."""

import asyncio
import sys
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import ClassVar, Literal

from langchain_core.tools import BaseTool, tool

from featherweight import (
    AgentBase,
    AgentInput,
    AgentOutput,
    AgentRunner,
    Gemini,
    ModelSettings,
    SqliteDatabase,
    default_db_path,
)


@tool
def minutes_between(start: str, end: str) -> str:
    """The minutes between two timestamps, each written as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM'."""
    return str(int((datetime.fromisoformat(end) - datetime.fromisoformat(start)).total_seconds() // 60))


class Report(AgentInput):  # what goes in: a typed model, checked before the model is called
    text: str


class Summary(AgentOutput):  # also carries `open_questions: list[str]`
    title: str = ""  # every field has a default: a model that does not know is not forced to invent
    # only these values, or None when the report does not say
    severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] | None = None
    service: str | None = None
    impact: str = ""
    duration_minutes: int | None = None  # new: the model cannot subtract timestamps reliably, the tool can
    next_steps: list[str] = []


class IncidentSummariser(AgentBase):
    name: str = "incident_summariser"  # how the run log and the traces name the agent
    description: str = "Turns an incident report into a short, structured summary"
    version: str = "2"  # change it when the prompt or the behaviour changes: runs are told apart by it
    prompt: str = (
        "Summarise the incident report. Use only what the report says. "
        "If the severity or the service is not stated, leave it out and ask in open_questions. "
        "If the report gives a start and an end time, use minutes_between for duration_minutes."
    )
    # the model is a setting of the agent
    model: ModelSettings = Gemini(model="gemini-3.5-flash-lite", thinking="low")
    tools: list[BaseTool] = [minutes_between]  # an allow-list: only these tools are bound to the model
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = Report  # the contract is set on the class: the same for every run
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = Summary

    def check_output(self, agent_input, output):  # a rule the schema cannot say: raise to reject the attempt
        if output.service and output.service.lower() not in agent_input.text.lower():
            raise ValueError(f"The report does not name the service {output.service!r}")


async def main(path: str = "reports/04-batch-delay.txt") -> None:
    report = Report(text=Path(path).read_text())
    async with SqliteDatabase(default_db_path()) as db:
        job_id = await db.create_job("incident-report")  # a job id groups the runs of one piece of work
        # the class, not an instance: the runner builds the agent
        result = await AgentRunner(db).run(IncidentSummariser, report, job_id=job_id)
    print(result.status.value, result.model_name, result.output or result.error)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main(*sys.argv[1:2]))

Run it with make book-chapter N=2-1. It reads reports/04-batch-delay.txt, which says when the batch started and when it ended. Something like:

SUCCESS gemini-3.5-flash-lite open_questions=[] title='Nightly batch was late' severity='low' service='batch' impact='Reports were a day old' duration_minutes=1170 next_steps=['Alert when the disk is 80% full']

What to notice

  • A tool is a plain function with LangChain's @tool: featherweight is built on LangChain, so its tools are LangChain tools. The model reads its name, its docstring and its argument names, so write them for the model.
  • tools is an allow-list, and a guardrail. Only the tools the agent declares are bound to the model, so nothing else is reachable. The runner checks the list before the model sees it, together with any tools the runner adds.
  • The tool does the subtraction, not the model. The report says 14:05 on 2 March and 09:35 on 3 March: 1170 minutes. duration_minutes is a new field of Summary, so the answer is typed like the rest.
  • Ready-made tools (calculate, current_datetime, days_between, add_to_date) are in featherweight.tools: see the tools guide.

Why a list on the class. The tools are part of what the agent is, and the run log keeps a hash of them, so a change shows. See tools on an agent.

Next: tools that live in another process.

"""Chapter 2-2: an MCP server. The summariser asks who owns the service."""

import asyncio
import sys
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import ClassVar, Literal

from langchain_core.tools import BaseTool, tool

from featherweight import (
    AgentBase,
    AgentInput,
    AgentOutput,
    AgentRunner,
    Gemini,
    HttpMCPServer,
    ModelSettings,
    SqliteDatabase,
    StdioMCPServer,
    default_db_path,
)


@tool
def minutes_between(start: str, end: str) -> str:
    """The minutes between two timestamps, each written as 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM'."""
    return str(int((datetime.fromisoformat(end) - datetime.fromisoformat(start)).total_seconds() // 60))


class Report(AgentInput):  # what goes in: a typed model, checked before the model is called
    text: str


class Summary(AgentOutput):  # also carries `open_questions: list[str]`
    title: str = ""  # every field has a default: a model that does not know is not forced to invent
    # only these values, or None when the report does not say
    severity: Literal["low", "medium", "high"] | None = None
    service: str | None = None
    impact: str = ""
    duration_minutes: int | None = None
    owner: str | None = None  # new: the answer of the MCP server
    next_steps: list[str] = []


class IncidentSummariser(AgentBase):
    name: str = "incident_summariser"  # how the run log and the traces name the agent
    description: str = "Turns an incident report into a short, structured summary"
    version: str = "3"  # change it when the prompt or the behaviour changes: runs are told apart by it
    prompt: str = (
        "Summarise the incident report. Use only what the report says. "
        "If the severity or the service is not stated, leave it out and ask in open_questions. "
        "If the report gives a start and an end time, use minutes_between for duration_minutes. "
        "If the report names a service, find who owns it with your tools and put the team in owner."
    )
    # the model is a setting of the agent
    model: ModelSettings = Gemini(model="gemini-3.5-flash-lite", thinking="low")
    tools: list[BaseTool] = [minutes_between]  # an allow-list: only these tools are bound to the model
    mcp_servers: list[StdioMCPServer | HttpMCPServer] = [  # the runner starts this server when the agent needs it
        StdioMCPServer(
            name="services",
            command=sys.executable,
            args=("services_server.py",),
            description="Who owns a service, and who is on call",
        )
    ]
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = Report  # the contract is set on the class: the same for every run
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = Summary

    def check_output(self, agent_input, output):  # a rule the schema cannot say: raise to reject the attempt
        if output.service and output.service.lower() not in agent_input.text.lower():
            raise ValueError(f"The report does not name the service {output.service!r}")


async def main(path: str = "reports/03-search-latency.txt") -> None:
    report = Report(text=Path(path).read_text())
    async with SqliteDatabase(default_db_path()) as db:
        job_id = await db.create_job("incident-report")  # a job id groups the runs of one piece of work
        # the class, not an instance: the runner builds the agent
        result = await AgentRunner(db).run(IncidentSummariser, report, job_id=job_id)
    print(result.status.value, result.model_name, result.output or result.error)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main(*sys.argv[1:2]))

The server is services_server.py in docs/book/code/: about 20 lines with FastMCP and one tool, owner_of. Any MCP server plugs in the same way. Run the chapter with make book-chapter N=2-2. It reads reports/03-search-latency.txt, which asks to tell the team that owns search. Something like:

SUCCESS gemini-3.5-flash-lite open_questions=[] title='Search was slow' severity='medium' service='search' impact='...' owner='discovery team, on call: Ben' ...

What to notice

  • StdioMCPServer declares a server the runner starts as a subprocess when a run needs it, and stops afterwards. In the container the subprocess runs inside the container too.
  • Tool search is how the agent reaches an MCP tool, unless you turn it off. discover is on by default: the server's tools are not bound to the model. It gets search_tools(keywords), which finds the best matches, and call_tool(name, args_json), which runs one, and the prompt names the server and what it is for (description). call_tool needs no earlier search. discover=False binds the server's tools directly, which suits a small server. See finding tools by search.
  • There are two kinds of MCP server. StdioMCPServer is a process the runner starts (command, args, and the names of the environment variables to pass it). HttpMCPServer is a remote server over streamable HTTP (url, and bearer_from, the name of the variable that holds a token). Both take tools= to allow only some of the server's tools.
  • The tool's name carries its server: the model calls services_owner_of. Your agent's own tools stay as they are.
  • What the server returns is yours. The run log keeps metadata only, never a tool's result.

Why search by default. Tool schemas stay out of the context until the agent needs them. See tool discovery.

For a real server, examples/mcp points an agent at GitHub's MCP server (it needs a token): the declaration is the same with HttpMCPServer. See also the MCP guide.

Next: instructions the agent reads when it needs them.

from langchain_core.tools import BaseTool, tool

    AgentBase,
    AgentInput,
    AgentOutput,

    default_db_path,

    text: str

    # only these values, or None when the report does not say

    service: str | None = None
    impact: str = ""
    duration_minutes: int | None = None
    owner: str | None = None  # new: the answer of the MCP server

    name: str = "incident_summariser"  # how the run log and the traces name the agent
    description: str = "Turns an incident report into a short, structured summary"

    prompt: str = (
        "Summarise the incident report. Use only what the report says. "
        "If the severity is not stated, decide it with your skill. If the service is not stated, leave it out and ask in open_questions. "
        "If the report gives a start and an end time, use minutes_between for duration_minutes. "
        "If the report names a service, find who owns it with your tools and put the team in owner."
    )
    # the model is a setting of the agent
    model: ModelSettings = Gemini(model="gemini-3.5-flash-lite", thinking="low")
    skills: list[Skill] = [Skill.from_directory("2-3/severity-rubric")]  # read on demand, not in every prompt
    tools: list[BaseTool] = [minutes_between]  # an allow-list: only these tools are bound to the model
    mcp_servers: list[StdioMCPServer | HttpMCPServer] = [  # the runner starts this server when the agent needs it
        StdioMCPServer(
            name="services",
            command=sys.executable,
            args=("services_server.py",),
            description="Who owns a service, and who is on call",
        )
    ]
    input_model: ClassVar[type[AgentInput]] = Report  # the contract is set on the class: the same for every run
    output_model: ClassVar[type[AgentOutput]] = Summary

    def check_output(self, agent_input, output):  # a rule the schema cannot say: raise to reject the attempt
        if output.service and output.service.lower() not in agent_input.text.lower():

async def main(path: str = "reports/02-sign-in-trouble.txt") -> None:
    report = Report(text=Path(path).read_text())
    async with SqliteDatabase(default_db_path()) as db:
        job_id = await db.create_job("incident-report")  # a job id groups the runs of one piece of work
        # the class, not an instance: the runner builds the agent
        result = await AgentRunner(db).run(IncidentSummariser, report, job_id=job_id)

    asyncio.run(main(*sys.argv[1:2]))

The skill is a folder next to the code:

---
name: severity-rubric
description: Decides the severity of an incident (low, medium or high). Use when an incident report does not state its severity.
---

# Severity rubric

Pick the highest level that fits.

- **high**: customers cannot do what they came for (pay, sign in, reach the product), or data was lost.
- **medium**: the product works but is slow or partly broken, or only some customers are affected.
- **low**: no customer noticed, or only internal work was delayed.

If the report gives too little to choose, leave the severity out and ask in `open_questions`.
Worked examples are in `references/examples.md`.

Run the chapter with make book-chapter N=2-3. It reads reports/02-sign-in-trouble.txt, which states no severity. Something like:

SUCCESS gemini-3.5-flash-lite open_questions=['What was the cause?'] title='Sign-in trouble' severity='medium' service=None ...

What to notice

  • A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md. Its name and description are always in the prompt, and the agent reads the rest, with get_skill, only when a skill applies. Other files (references/examples.md) are read when the instructions point to them. An unused skill costs a line of prompt.
  • Skill.from_directory takes the folder, relative to where the code runs (/code in the container).
  • The format is the Agent Skills specification, shared with other tools. See the skills guide for what is supported.
  • Nothing runs from a skill. A skill is text for the agent to read; it executes no code.

Why a skill and not a longer prompt. A rubric in the prompt costs tokens in every run, even the ones that do not need it. See how an agent uses a skill.

Also possible

  • A skill kept in a database or S3, read when the agent asks: the recipe.
  • One agent, the skills of whoever is asking: a skill for each department.
