Spec Covers Units of work The words job, execution, run, attempt and step, the ids and names that follow from them, and the rename from the old words Agents The agent definition, what is checked when it is built, input and output, the system prompt Agent runner Running, results, attempts and retries, concurrency, launching agents, limits Models and providers ModelSettings: Gemini, Gemma, Claude and OpenAI, the catalog, temperature, extending it, tokens Tools and the registry Tools on an agent, the tool registry, the ready-made tools, the run context MCP tools MCP servers: declaring, connections, failures, what the model gets Tool discovery Finding MCP tools by keyword: discover, search_tools, call_tool, matching Skills The skill model, loading, how an agent reads a skill, the Agent Skills specification Approvals Agents propose, code executes: the proposal, the executor, who talks to the user, asking in a job, and what is not supported Identity Who a run is for: a typed identity the application passes, how tools read it, how it crosses the queue, and the identity hash for resuming; what stays the application's Streaming agents StreamingAgent, runner.stream(), AG-UI events, thoughts, stopping a response, messages, the AG-UI and Vercel adapters Attachments Images, documents, audio and video in a chat message: what a client can send, what the model gets, limits, failures Run log and persistence What featherweight keeps and never keeps, hashes, Database and ResultStore, migrations, the schema, resumable jobs, Postgres Jobs Jobs, the run log, statuses, logging Submitted jobs A job as a declared class, JobQueue, JobClient, JobWorker, cancelling, job events and SSE Background jobs A job exposed to an agent as a tool, here or on a worker, getting its result back, events, how long a child lives Configuration The environment variables (FTW_...), which settings can also be passed in code, and the rule for both Observers and OpenTelemetry The Observer class and what it receives, OTelObserver and the GenAI conventions, spans for jobs, attempts, model calls and tool calls, evaluation

docs.title: Where things belong
docs.text:
A change goes in the spec of the thing it changes, and not in the spec of the epic that happens to touch it. Each spec owns:

Spec Owns Units of work Job, execution, run, attempt and step: what each is, its id, where it appears (the API, the database, the spans, the logs, the settings) Agents The agent definition, what is checked when it is built, input and output, the system prompt Agent runner Running an agent: results, attempts and retries, concurrency, launching agents, how a step is resumed, when observers are called Models and providers ModelSettings, the catalog, what is checked per provider, tokens Tools and the registry, MCP tools, tool discovery, skills What their names say Approvals A proposal as a typed value, the executor's checks, who talks to the user, asking at a boundary, and what is left out on purpose Identity The identity of a run: declaring and passing it, RunContext.identity, who inherits it, its field in the queue message, identity_hash, the developer's responsibilities Streaming agents StreamingAgent, runner.stream(), the events, the adapters Attachments The parts a user message may carry, how they reach the model, the limits on them Run log and persistence The metadata-only rule, hashes, the Database class, the schema of every table, migrations, the result store, Postgres, tenants Jobs A job: run_job, running a job class, its version, statuses, what the run log records, logging Submitted jobs The Job class and @job, the queue and its message, the client, the worker, cancelling, job events and SSE Background jobs background_jobs, start_background, where a child runs, the result message, the events, how long a child lives Configuration Every environment variable, its default, and whether an argument may override it Observers and OpenTelemetry The Observer class and its records, OTelObserver, the GenAI mapping, your own spans, evaluation

A spec says what it owns, and links to the spec that owns the rest.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
Status: implemented. How to use it is in agents.md. The code is models.py.

  • Goal
  • The definition
  • Checked when an agent is built
  • Input and output
  • The system prompt
  • Decisions
  • Not supported
  • Tests

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: An agent is a static, typed definition. Pydantic is the specification: the input, the output, the tools, the skills, the sub-agents and the MCP servers are declared on the class and enforced by Pydantic, not by convention. A running agent is complete before it runs: nothing about it is decided while it runs, so it can be read, tested and versioned like any class, and its hash identifies it. The class can be written in code, or built from data (a file, a database row) when it is needed: the runner sees a class either way, and a definition built from data is checked as strictly as one written by hand. A malformed definition fails when it is built, before any model is called.

docs.title: The definition
docs.text:
A subclass of AgentBase. The runner instantiates it (agent_cls()), so a subclass supplies defaults for every field.

Field Type, default Rule name, description, version, prompt str, required name and version are recorded on every attempt. description is what a parent's model reads before it launches this agent model ModelSettings, Gemini() Which model runs the agent and how hard it thinks. A setting the model does not accept fails when the agent is built (models) tools list[BaseTool], empty Only these are bound to the model, besides the tools the runner adds (tools and the registry) recursion_limit int, 25, at least 1 Passed to langgraph. Stops a runaway tool loop inside one run; a run that hits it fails allow_user_questions, raise_conflicts bool, False Each only adds a sentence to the prompt. Neither is enforced subagents list[type], empty Agent classes this agent may launch (runner) background_jobs list[type], empty Agent or job classes this agent may start in the background (background jobs) skills list[Skill], empty Skills this agent can read (skills) mcp_servers list[StdioMCPServer \| HttpMCPServer], empty MCP servers whose tools this agent may use (MCP tools) input_model, output_model ClassVar, AgentInput and AgentOutput The agent's contract

A subclass re-annotates a field it overrides (name: str = "x"), because Pydantic rejects an unannotated override.

docs.title: Checked when an agent is built
docs.text:
Each of these raises a ValidationError (a programming error, not a failed run):

  • the output model: one that the agent's model cannot fill is refused by its model settings, which are in charge of everything that depends on the provider or the model (model settings). Claude is the example: some of its models take no dictionary.

  • subagents: every entry is an AgentBase subclass; none is the agent's own class; the names of the sub-agents are distinct.

  • background_jobs: every entry is a non-streaming agent class or a Job class; none is the agent's own class; the names are distinct; an agent may be in subagents too, to be run inline or in the background (the model chooses); an agent that is in a background_jobs list does not declare its own (background jobs).
  • skills: the names are distinct.
  • mcp_servers: the names are distinct. Each server model checks itself too (name format, timeouts, caps).
  • tools: the names are distinct, and none is launch_agent, get_agent_schema, get_skill, search_tools or call_tool, which the runner uses for its own tools.
  • model, recursion_limit: the allowed values above. model checks itself (models).

Agent A listing B while B lists A is allowed. The runner's depth limit stops it.

docs.title: Input and output
docs.text:
• AgentInput forbids extra fields (extra="forbid"). The runner raises TypeError for an input that is not an instance of the agent's input_model: a wrong type is a bug, so it raises. The input is sent to the model as indented JSON, in a single user message.
  • AgentOutput always carries open_questions: list[str], where a model reports a question or a conflict instead of guessing. It is never a failure. The task fields of an output should have defaults, so that a model that needs to ask is not forced to invent an answer to pass validation.
  • The output is enforced twice. The output model is the structured-output schema the model is given (response_format), and the reply is validated against it again. A reply that does not validate is a failed attempt.
  • check_output(agent_input, output) is the place for rules between the input and the output ("everything the model returned is in the input"). It raises ValueError to reject, which is a failed attempt and is retried. The default accepts everything. Rules about the output alone belong in validators on the output model.

docs.title: The system prompt
docs.text:
Assembled by build_system_prompt(can_launch=True), in this order, and joined by blank lines:

  1. prompt
  2. one sentence for allow_user_questions, whichever way it is set, and one for raise_conflicts
  3. if the agent has subagents or background_jobs and can_launch: the agents it may start, each once, by name and description, in groups: the ones to launch inline, the ones to start in the background, and the ones that can be either (an agent in both lists), and how to use each tool. Their schemas are not in the prompt
  4. if the agent has skills: each skill's name and description, and how to read one
  5. if the agent has an MCP server with discover on (the default): the servers it can search, by name and description, and how to use search_tools and call_tool

The runner sets can_launch to false for an agent at the depth limit. Its SHA-256 is recorded on every attempt (system_prompt_hash), so two runs can be compared by prompt. The discovery section is built from the declaration, so the hash is known before any server starts. Bound MCP tools add nothing to the prompt.

docs.title: The agent hash
docs.text:
Every attempt also records agent_hash, the SHA-256 of the whole declaration, so that "this run used exactly this agent" can be checked. If system_prompt_hash is the same and agent_hash differs, the model, a tool or a limit changed, not the prompt. Resuming a job uses it: a run is reused only when the hash is the same (runner). The hash covers:

  • name, version, description, prompt, recursion_limit, allow_user_questions, raise_conflicts
  • the model settings, all fields
  • each tool's name, description and argument schema, as the model sees them
  • each sub-agent's own declaration, recursively. A sub-agent already being described further up is named only, so a cycle ends
  • each agent in background_jobs the same way (a job class by its name, version and job_hash), only when there are some, so that an agent without any keeps the hash it had
  • each skill in full, and each MCP server as declared (environment variable names, never values)
  • the assembled system prompt
  • the JSON schema of the input_model and of the output_model, so that a changed field, type, description or default is another agent (check_output is code and is not hashed: version is its signal, and a reused output is checked against it again)

The declaration is built as a plain structure, written as JSON with sorted keys and fixed separators, and hashed, so equal declarations give the same hash in any process. The code inside tools and in check_output is not covered: version is the signal for that. Rows from before the column existed have NULL.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Static, and classes, not instances. A definition has no per-run state. A run passes the class and the input, and the runner builds the agent. A different prompt is a different class, with a new version. Static means complete before the run, not written in the source: an application may build the class from data, when a request arrives, with its own rules about what a user may choose. What the runner needs is a validated class, and its hash says which agent ran. How the class is made is the application's.
  • Who runs an agent is not part of it. An identity is an argument of the run, so the same agent runs for every user, and it is not in agent_hash (identity).
  • The instruction flags are not enforced. allow_user_questions and raise_conflicts only tell the model what it may do. An output that asks a question when asking is forbidden is not rejected.
  • A failing rule is the pipeline's, not the agent's. check_output only rejects. It cannot fix the output or decide what a failure means: the pipeline does.
  • Flat output schemas for Gemini. A nested or nullable structured-output schema can come back silently truncated (a tree with only its root). Prefer flat lists with ids, avoid X | None on nested objects, and add a check_output that compares the output with the input. The example pipeline builds its trees from flat lists for this reason.
  • The model is typed, one class per provider. A typo, or an effort a model does not accept, fails at build time. Other models and providers are a subclass (models).

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Per-run overrides of the prompt, model or tools.
  • Models other than the three Gemini models, and provider-specific settings (a thinking budget).
  • Enforcing allow_user_questions and raise_conflicts.
  • Output validation that feeds the error back to the model. A retry resamples with the same input (runner).
  • Streaming from an ordinary agent. A streaming agent is a subclass (StreamingAgent) with its own input, no output model and no retries.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: test_models.py covers the defaults, that declarations are frozen, the prompt flags and the prompt hash, that a class built from data (create_model) is refused for the same malformed definitions as one written with class, with the same message, and test_model_settings.py the models and efforts each provider class accepts; test_runner.py covers input type errors, output validation and check_output; the build-time checks are in test_subagents.py (sub-agents), test_skills.py (skills), test_mcp.py (servers and the reserved tool names) and test_registry.py (duplicate tools).

docs.title: Approvals: agents propose, code executes
docs.text:
Status: implemented as a pattern, in issue #271. There is no new class or argument: it is how the parts that exist are put together. How to use it is in the agents guide, a recipe and a chapter of the book.

  • Goal
  • The rule
  • The proposal
  • The executor
  • Who talks to the user
  • Asking in a job: ask at a boundary
  • Two ways to propose
  • Decisions
  • Not supported
  • Tests

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Some things must not happen without a person's yes: a booking, a payment, an email, a deletion. featherweight's answer is two stages. An agent does its research and comes back with a proposal; the application shows it to a person; and after the yes, something that is not the agent executes it: plain code (an API call, a pipeline), another job, or another agent. The agent never holds the permission, so a mistake, or a prompt injection, can only produce a proposal.

This is the principle of the framework applied to approvals (seams, not solutions): the proposal is a typed value that Pydantic checks, and who may approve, what is shown and how it is executed are the application's. The reference is the fw-concierge application, where a booking is created only by POST /api/bookings: "plain application code: no agent decides", with an idempotency key and a row lock.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
1. An agent does not ask for approval and does not hold a permission. It proposes.
  2. Do not give an agent a tool that does what needs approval. Its allow-list holds read tools and, if it proposes in the middle of a conversation, a propose_* tool that only writes a proposal. A sub-agent or a background job has its own tools and never its parent's, so "read-only" is a matter of what is in its list.
  3. The application, not the model, decides what is shown, who may approve and how the action runs.

docs.title: The proposal
docs.text:
• A typed value: a Pydantic model. It is the output_model of the agent, or what a propose_* tool writes. It is validated when the agent answers, so a malformed proposal never reaches a person.
  • Kept by the application, with its hash, an expiry and a status (pending, approved, rejected, expired). The run log keeps only hashes, and never the content (persistence); the result store is the application's.
  • Shown from the typed value. The approval screen is drawn by your code from the fields of the proposal. A text that a model wrote about it is decoration: the concierge writes its confirmation text from the verified provider and slot, and the person confirms the slot.
  • Referenced by id. The client sends back the id, the choice (an option of the proposal) and the hash it was shown, never the arguments of the action.

docs.title: The executor
docs.text:
A function of your code, with no model in it. For one approval it:

  1. finds the proposal by id and refuses one that is not pending or has expired;
  2. checks the hash that the person was shown against the stored proposal (the proposal did not change), and that the choice is one of its options;
  3. checks that the approver may approve this: the approver's identity, from your authentication, never anything the model said (identity, who is asking);
  4. revalidates what can have changed (the slot is still free, the price is still the price);
  5. executes once: an idempotency key makes a second approval of the same proposal return the first result and change nothing, and a lock or a transaction makes two approvals of one thing safe;
  6. records who approved what and when (your records; the run log holds hashes only).

It never executes arguments that came from the model's prose or from the client's conversation: a chat sends its whole history back, so anything in it can have been changed.

docs.title: Who talks to the user
docs.text: Only the streaming agent talks to the user. A sub-agent or a background job never asks: it returns a result, open_questions or a proposal to its parent, and the streaming agent relays it in its own turn (a background job's result arrives as a message, background jobs). A pipeline reaches the user through the application: a notification, a page, then a new job. This is the shape of the major products: their background work only reads, and comes back to the user for permission to write.

docs.title: Asking in a job: ask at a boundary
docs.text:
An agent that needs something from the user does not stop in the middle of its loop. It ends its run with the typed work it has done and its open_questions (a successful run; AgentOutput carries the field). The job returns a typed outcome (what is done, the questions, the draft) and succeeds. The application keeps its own "awaiting" row and tells the user; when they answer, it submits a new job with resume_from the old one (resuming): the finished stage is answered from the result store, with no model call and no tool call, and the next stage runs with the compact findings and the answers.

  • Nothing is held while waiting: no run, slot, lease or timeout. A day is as good as a minute.
  • What a rerun wastes is the output tokens that it regenerates and the tools that it calls again, not the input that it reads again: resume_from avoids both. A provider's cache lasts minutes to about an hour (check the provider), so a person's answer finds a cold cache whatever the framework does.
  • A stage that carries a summary costs less than a replay of the whole transcript.

docs.title: Two ways to propose
docs.text:
• The output is the proposal. For a job or a pipeline: the agent's output_model is the proposal (options, a recommendation, open_questions). The run ends, and the application takes it from there.
  • A propose_* tool. For a chat: the agent calls a tool that writes a proposal to your store and answers "proposed as #id, waiting for the user". The tool cannot act, so it is safe in the allow-list. The agent may propose several things, and the interface shows a card for each. After the approval your code executes, and the outcome is added to the conversation as a message for the next turn.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Agents propose, code executes. The only design that needs no suspended run, so a proposal can wait as long as it must and no worker is held. It also makes the model unable to act: the permission is not in its hands.
  • The proposal is data, and is bound by its hash. An approval means "this exact thing", not "something like it".
  • No approval flag on a tool, and no policy engine. What needs approval is the application's rule, and it is written where the proposal is made and where it is executed.
  • No new status for a job. A status says how an execution ended; "needs input" is the meaning of a result, so it is in the typed outcome of a job that succeeded.
  • Read-only background work. The tools of a child are its own, so a background job reads and proposes.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
Each is left out on purpose, and what to do instead is in the right column. The last column says when to think again.

Not supported Do this instead Think again when A flag or policy on a tool ("needs approval", read-only) A tool that does not act, and an executor that does Many applications write the same policy by hand, and a seam that is not a solution is clear A status or an exception "needs input" for a job A typed outcome of a successful job, and resume_from Never for the status; an exception that pauses is suspension Pausing a live run in the middle of its loop (LangGraph interrupt with a checkpointer, OpenAI RunState, Pydantic AI deferred tools) Stages, and a new job with resume_from; for a chat, the turn ends and the next turn starts A chat needs to continue the same turn: see below Replaying a run's messages (an AgentResult.messages, an AgentRunner.from_messages, an input that builds its first messages) Typed state in the output; tools backed by your own cache, so that a rerun repeats model calls and not tool calls A real long loop that needs its verbatim tool outputs, and stages do not express it. Then: opt-in for one agent, stored by the application, on the input and not on the runner, with a check of the agent's hash

The honest limit: one long agent loop that asks at its fortieth step and needs its verbatim tool outputs after the answer. A replay would cascade (a pipeline of seven agents has seven histories), is valid only for the same agent (its prompt, tools, tool-call ids and reasoning signatures), puts content in memory, and a runner method would grow the runner. Stages cover almost every case.

For a chat, AG-UI 1.0 has a model for a pause that is a turn ending: a run can finish with an interrupt outcome (an id, a reason, a message, a tool_call_id, a response_schema, an expiry), and the next request carries resume entries. featherweight does not use it yet: it emits the success and cancelled outcomes, ignores resume, and a ChatInput must end with a user message. A later feature for streaming agents, spec first, with the rule that an interrupt names a proposal stored on the server and resume carries only the decision.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• The recipe approving what an agent proposes, with a fake model: the agent has no tool that books; a second approval books once; a changed proposal, an expired one and an unauthorised approver are refused; the propose_* variant writes a proposal and acts on nothing.
  • The recipe asking the user in the middle of a job: a job ends with questions and succeeds; the second job reuses the first stage, so its model is called once across both.
  • The book's chapter 5-6, whose code needs no model: the proposal and the executor run, and are checked for a double approval and a changed proposal.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
Status: implemented, in epic #170: the converters and what ChatInput refuses (#171), the limits (#172), the provider tests (#173), the adapters (#174), and the guide (#175). It changes streaming agents (ChatInput, to_langchain, to_agui, the Vercel adapter), and nothing else.

  • Goal
  • What a client can send
  • What the model is given
  • Limits
  • Failures
  • Decisions
  • Not supported
  • Findings
  • Tests

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
A person in a chat attaches an image, a PDF, a recording or a video to a message, and the model reads it. A user message of a ChatInput carries them next to its text (streaming).

featherweight is the transport. It takes what the client sent and hands it to the LangChain model underneath, in LangChain's provider-independent content blocks. It does not check what the model can read, it does not download, upload, convert, resize or store anything. Whether an attachment suits the model is the application's responsibility, and the provider says so when it does not. The application decides how files reach it: uploads, a store, fetching, scanning.

docs.title: What a client can send
docs.text:
AG-UI 1.0 messages from a user can hold text, image, audio, video and document parts. Each media part has a source:

Source Meaning Here data the bytes, base64-encoded, with a required mime_type accepted url a URL, "fetched by whoever needs them" refused

A url source is refused because nothing in featherweight should fetch a URL that a client chose, and because what happens to one depends on the provider: langchain-google-genai downloads an http(s) URL in the server process, langchain-anthropic and langchain-openai pass it to the provider. An application that wants URLs fetches them itself, checks them as it sees fit, and sends the bytes as a data source. We offer no hook for that: how to fetch safely is the application's decision.

The legacy binary part of AG-UI 0.x is retired in 1.0 and is not supported.

What data is. Standard base64 (the alphabet of RFC 4648, section 4), padded, in one line, with no data: prefix: what Python's base64.b64encode and JavaScript's btoa give, and nothing else. It is checked when the ChatInput is built, so a wrong one is raised before a run exists. These are refused, and the error names the likely cause (it never quotes the data):

What was sent Why it is refused The way out a data:image/png;base64,... URL (what a browser's FileReader.readAsDataURL gives) it is a URL, not base64 send only the part after the comma line breaks or spaces (Python's base64.encodebytes wraps every 76 characters) not one line send it in one line - or _ the URL-safe alphabet send the standard alphabet (+ and /) a length that is not a multiple of 4 no padding pad it with = any other character, or = before the end not the base64 alphabet, or padding in the middle the error says which of the two an empty value an empty attachment is refused: there is nothing to send, and the provider would say no after a run exists send a file with bytes in it, or no attachment

The check decodes the value in chunks of 64 KB and drops each one, so the memory it needs does not grow with the size of the attachment. The limits of the agent (below) are checked later, from the length of the text, without decoding.

docs.title: What the model is given
docs.text:
to_langchain turns each part into a LangChain standard content block, and the provider's package turns that into its own request:

AG-UI part LangChain block image {"type": "image", "base64": ..., "mime_type": ...} document {"type": "file", "base64": ..., "mime_type": ..., "filename": ...} audio {"type": "audio", "base64": ..., "mime_type": ...} video {"type": "video", "base64": ..., "mime_type": ...}
  • filename comes from the part's metadata["filename"] when there is one. OpenAI wants a name for an inline file, and LangChain otherwise puts in a placeholder and warns. We never invent one.
  • Parts of a message keep their order, and the text parts around them.
  • to_agui is the inverse, so a stored conversation with an attachment survives from_langchain and back.
  • An assistant, tool or system message carries no attachments; they stay text.
  • Provider-side files (an uploaded file's file_id) cannot be said in AG-UI. An application that uses them builds its own LangChain message with a {"type": "file", "file_id": ...} block. Nothing here blocks that, and nothing here helps with it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Every turn sends the whole conversation, so an attachment in an earlier message is sent again and counts again. The limits apply to all the attachments of the conversation, not to the last message.

Limit Default Counts max_attachments 10 the media parts of all messages max_bytes 15 MiB (15,728,640 bytes) the decoded size of all of them

The application sets them on the agent, with a class attribute, and the runner checks them when a turn starts. A limit is a whole number of 0 or more. max_attachments = 0 turns attachments off for that agent: any attachment is refused, and a message with only text passes. A conversation over either limit raises AttachmentLimitError before any run exists.

Where the defaults come from. The size is a cautious value that Anthropic, Google and OpenAI all accept; the count is our own choice. The providers' figures are in what the providers accept (read it with its warning: it is a dated snapshot, and the providers' pages are the source):

Provider Count per request Size of a request Anthropic 100 images (600 for some models) 128 MB Google no count stated for documents; 3,600 images (unconfirmed) 100 MB inline, 50 MB for PDFs; one page still says 20 MB OpenAI 1,500 images; none stated for files 512 MB of images; 50 MB for all files together

The default count is 10, a design choice, not a provider's limit: every provider accepts more (the lowest is Anthropic's 100 images), but a chat that takes 100 files in one go is a different job: a pipeline that keeps the files in a store and passes references (below). 10 is also what the Gemini app allows. An application that needs more raises max_attachments. For size the pages disagree: the lowest figure on any of them is Google's 20 MB, the next is OpenAI's 50 MB for files. Base64 makes data a third larger, so 15 MiB of decoded bytes is exactly 20 MiB on the wire: that lowest figure and no more (and over it, if "20 MB" is read as 20 million bytes). It is under every other figure. The default is the cautious one: Google has since raised its inline limit to 100 MB, and an application that has checked its provider raises it. Anthropic also applies a stricter pixel limit past 20 images or documents: that is the provider's to report. These are ceilings against a request that cannot work, not a promise that every request under them does: a provider also limits pages, pixels and the type of each file, and says so in its error.

docs.title: Failures
docs.text:
Consistent with the rest of featherweight: a thing that is wrong with the input is raised; a thing that goes wrong in the run is a result.

  • Raised, before any run exists: a url source; a part type that is not supported; data that is not base64; an empty attachment; a missing mime type; more attachments or bytes than the agent allows. Nothing is started, and nothing is written to the run log.
  • The limits raise AttachmentLimitError, a subclass of BadRequest (so a ValueError, and a handler for BadRequest answers it too), from runner.stream(). The input cannot refuse it earlier: the adapters build a ChatInput before they know the agent and its limits. A web application answers it as a request that cannot be taken: 413 for AttachmentLimitError (a handler for the subclass wins over the one for BadRequest), and 422 for every other BadRequest. The message says by how much, and that the application can raise the limit. BadRequest is defined in featherweight.errors, where streaming.py can import it; featherweight.adapters.errors still exports it.
  • A result: everything the provider says no to (a type the model cannot read, a file that is too large for it, too many pages). The turn ends FAILED with the provider's error, an error event is sent, and nothing is retried, as for any streaming agent.

docs.title: Files for agents and jobs
docs.text:
Attachments are a feature of the chat. By design, an agent does not pass binary data to another agent, and a job does not carry it: not to a launched agent, not to a background job, not to an agent wrapped in a job (as_job), and an agent that a pipeline runs has no field that takes a file either. Their input is JSON that a model or a queue carries. A model cannot write bytes; a queue message, the job store, the input hash and the traces would all carry them; and the run log keeps no content. The other frameworks work the same way (checked 2026-11-25): Claude Code's sub-agents get only the prompt string, Pydantic AI's delegation passes text and shared dependencies, OpenAI's Agent.as_tool takes text or structured parameters, and Google ADK and LangChain Deep Agents share named files that are loaded on demand. So there is no attachments field on AgentInput and no argument of the runner for it, and none is planned.

What to do instead: pass references. Keep the file in a store that you manage (a database, a disk, S3) and put its reference, an id or a name, in the input of the job or the agent. A tool fetches it:

  • The input says what to work on, the identity says who may read it (identity), and the tool does both the fetch and the check. The model sees the reference, and may pass another one: the tool checks that the identity may read the one it was given.
  • The tool returns the text of the file, which every provider takes, or an image or a file block, which reaches the model as it is and is read where the provider accepts it (what was verified).
  • A pipeline that downloads a file stores it, and passes the reference on to the agent. That is one more step, for a case that is rare.
  • A resume reuses a step for the same input and the same identity, so for the same reference, even if the file behind it changed (resuming). Put a version or a hash in the reference when that matters.

A recipe shows it, with a test.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Attachments are for a chat; agents and jobs pass references. A file does not travel between agents, or through a queue. See above.
  • Transport only. No capability checks, no conversion, no fetching, no uploads. The application knows its model and its users.
  • data only. Safe by construction, and the one source that every provider's package accepts.
  • One form of base64, and an error that says which mistake. Strict and predictable: what b64encode and btoa give. A lenient reader (taking a data: prefix, line breaks, the URL-safe alphabet) would guess, and the size of an attachment is counted from its length. The error says what the likely mistake is, so the developer does not have to find out.
  • An empty attachment is refused, as a wrong input is raised and not left to fail in the run.
  • Validate without a decoded copy. The input is built before the agent's limits are known, so it cannot refuse a conversation that is too large first; what it can do is not to hold a second copy of every attachment while it checks.
  • All four media types. They map in the same way, so supporting two and refusing two would add code and not remove any.
  • Limits are on the agent, with cautious defaults that all three big providers accept, so that most applications need no setting.
  • The run log keeps no content. It holds no message text today, and holds no attachment now: not the bytes, not the name.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Fetching URLs, uploading to a provider's store, and file_id sources: the application's.
  • Converting a PDF into page images, resizing, transcribing or OCR, for a model that cannot read the original.
  • Checking that a model can read a type, or the provider's own limits (pages, pixels, duration).
  • Attachments on an assistant or tool message, and in the input of an agent or a job: a launched agent, a background job, an agent wrapped in a job, or one that a pipeline runs. They pass references (above).
  • Stored attachments. The application keeps them, as it keeps the conversation.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Checked while writing this (2026-11-22):

  • ag-ui-protocol 1.0.0: ContentPart is text, image, audio, video or document; a source is data (value, mime_type required) or url; there is no source for a provider's file id. BinaryInputContent is kept only for importing.
  • langchain-core 1.8.3 has standard blocks image, audio, video, file and text-plain, each with base64, url, file_id and mime_type. The three provider packages here translate them.
  • Anthropic (langchain-anthropic 1.7.11): base64 and URL for images and documents, and file_id.
  • Google (langchain-google-genai 4.4.2): base64 for all types; gs://, YouTube and Google-hosted URLs go through; any other http(s) URL is downloaded by our process and inlined.
  • OpenAI (langchain-openai 1.8.2): base64 images; PDFs inline as file_data, on Chat Completions (PDF only) and Responses (more types); audio inline; file_url for files on Responses only; file_id.
  • Ollama takes images only, as base64 in an images array, on vision models; no PDFs. featherweight has no Ollama provider, and langchain-ollama was not checked: an application that adds one (see models) finds out which blocks it accepts.
  • What the LangChain packages do with our blocks (checked offline, nothing sent, tests): Anthropic sends images and PDFs as base64 blocks and raises for audio and video while it builds the request; OpenAI Chat Completions sends images, PDFs (a LC_AUTOGENERATED name and a warning without a filename) and audio, and raises for video; OpenAI Responses sends images and files, raises for video, and drops audio without any error, so the model sees only the text; Google sends every block inline. Only OpenAI gets the filename. A text file passes through Anthropic and Chat Completions, although Chat Completions takes only PDFs. This is the packages' behaviour on the dates above and it changes: the tests describe the versions of uv.lock, the floors in pyproject.toml let an application install others, and a test of the Google package that fails after an upgrade says that the package changed (its private function is imported inside the helper, so only those tests fail).
  • Observers: an observer that captures content (capture_content=True, and OpenTelemetry with content capture on) is given the attachment bytes with the rest of the messages. That is the documented opt-in. By default no event, run log row, observer record or span holds any of it.
  • What a provider returns or logs is the provider's: featherweight puts no attachment bytes in an event or a log line, and guarantees nothing about what a provider's endpoint puts in its error text or keeps in its own logs. The text of a failure is passed on as it is, to the client (RUN_ERROR) and to the application's log; the run log keeps only the error's type and a hash of its text.
  • A file returned by a tool (2026-11-25, real calls, the smallest model of each provider, one small file each: a 200 px JPEG and a one-page PDF). A tool that returns [text block, image or file block] reaches the model as a list of content blocks, unchanged, and the model read both files with Anthropic (claude-haiku-5-5), Google (gemini-3.5-flash-lite) and OpenAI (gpt-6-luna, on the Responses API, the only one that featherweight's OpenAI settings build). Google's Gemma (gemma-4-26b-a4b-it) did not call the tool: it answers at once when an agent has a reply schema, so nothing is known for it. This is one run each, a snapshot and not a promise: text is the result that every provider takes, and media is for a provider that you have tried.
  • The body of a request carries each attachment as base64 inside the JSON, a third larger than the file, and every turn sends the whole conversation again. A server or a proxy in front of the application often has a lower limit on a body, and a body over it never reaches featherweight: the guide says so, and that max_bytes is the agent's policy and not the server's.
  • The Vercel adapter read only the text of a user message and dropped its file parts, so an attachment was lost. It now converts a file part with a data:...;base64, URL into an image, audio, video or document part by its mediaType, and refuses any other URL with a BadRequest. The AG-UI adapter needed no change.
  • What each provider accepts, with the limits, is in its own page: a dated snapshot, a suggestion and not a duty of a release. It says that it is not maintained and that the providers' pages are the source, and a developer checks them for the provider and the model that they use. It changes: Google raised its inline limit from 20 MB to 100 MB in January 2026, and its pages still disagree.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Never a real model, and no network.

  • The conversion: each part type to its block and back; the order of parts; filename; a message with only attachments.
  • Refusals: a url source, bad base64 (each of the mistakes of the table above, with its message), an empty attachment, a missing mime type, an unsupported part, a limit that is exceeded by count, by bytes, and by the attachments of earlier messages; the agent's own limits over the defaults.
  • The check agrees with Python's: over many generated strings, and at the edges of the chunks, it accepts what base64.b64decode(..., validate=True) accepts and refuses what it refuses (an empty value apart).
  • Memory: checking a large attachment does not allocate a decoded copy of it (the peak is measured).
  • The limit error: it is an AttachmentLimitError, a BadRequest and a ValueError; a limit of 0 refuses an attachment and passes text; a limit that is not a whole number of 0 or more is refused when the class is declared; over HTTP, a handler answers the limit error with 413 and its message, and a malformed body with 422.
  • The provider's side, offline: build the request that each of the three packages would send for each block, and check its shape without sending it.
  • A fake model that fails on a block: the run is FAILED, the error event is sent, and there is no retry.

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text:
Status: implemented. The declaration, the tool and the child job (#116), the result and the run that waits (#117), and the events, the cancel and the trace (#118) and the guide, the skill reference and the example (#119, #120) are done. It is tracked in epic #115, and each part has its own issue (listed at the end). When a part is built, this page says so, and the guide docs/background-jobs.md shows how to use it.

It builds on submitted jobs (a job is a declared class that runs in your process or on a worker, with events and a result in your store), the runner (launching agents, and its limits) and streaming agents (the events of a chat run). What it changes in them is in them, and not here (what changes).

  • Goal
  • The principle
  • The tool
  • Where it runs
  • Getting the result back
  • Events
  • How long a child lives
  • Limits
  • What changes
