docs.title: Goal
docs.text: An agent hands work to another agent and goes on. A launched sub-agent (runner) blocks its parent until it returns. A background job does not: the agent starts it, gets a job id at once, and carries on, and the result comes back when it is ready. A streaming agent can start a long piece of research and keep talking; a pipeline agent can start several and collect them.

docs.title: The principle
docs.text:
A background job is a job that is exposed to an agent as a tool. It is not a new kind of thing: it has a job row, events, a result in the user's store, and it can run in your process or on a worker, as any job does.

  • featherweight wakes nothing. It emits events, and the application decides what to do with them. The model never polls. The one thing that waits for a child is a run that is not a chat (how long a child lives).
  • featherweight is stateless about conversations. It keeps no pending result for a parent whose turn is over. A restart loses what the application has not stored, and the guide says so.
  • A session that wakes itself is not part of the framework. It is an example, built on jobs and these events.
  • The result is read from the user's result store, because we keep none. Background jobs need a result store.

docs.title: The tool
docs.text:
An agent declares which agents it may start in the background, as it declares subagents:

class Researcher(AgentBase):
    background_jobs = [WebSearcher, Summariser]  # agent classes, or Job classes
  • Every entry is an agent class (not a streaming one) or a Job class, as submit takes; none is the agent's own class; the names are distinct. An agent may be in both subagents and background_jobs: then the model chooses, per call, between launch_agent (it waits and gets the output) and start_background (it goes on). A Job class can only be in background_jobs. An agent that is itself in a background_jobs list may not declare background_jobs: a background job cannot start background jobs (a bound on fan-out).
  • The model gets one more tool, start_background(agent_name, input_json). The prompt lists each agent once, by name and description, in three groups: inline (only in subagents), background (only in background_jobs) and either (in both), so that an agent in both lists is not described twice (agents). get_agent_schema(agent_name) covers all of them. input_json is a string, for the same reason as in launch_agent.
  • It returns at once, and as text, and never raises into the parent's run:
Case What comes back Started {"status": "STARTED", "agent": "...", "job_id": "..."} A name that is not in background_jobs 'x' is not an agent you can start in the background. You can start: ... The input does not fit The input for 'x' is not valid: ... Check get_agent_schema and try again. The limit of live children is reached A sentence saying so
  • The child is a job with its own id. Its row records parent_attempt_id, the attempt that started it (metadata only), so that the tree of a trace is one query. Its agent runs are those of an ordinary job: its own retries, tools and sub-agents. It does not share the parent's job.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
Where a child runs is the application's configuration, and nothing else changes with it: the same job, here or on a worker.

  • Here (the default). The child runs in the parent's process, as an asyncio task, by the same code as run_job (running a job class). Nothing but the runner is needed.
  • On a worker. AgentRunner(db, background=client), where client is a JobClient: the child is submitted to the queue with client.submit, and a worker runs it. The workers must list the child's job in their jobs; a worker that does not know it fails the job, as it does for any job.

Either way the child's events and its result are those of any job, and an application that wants to follow it uses client.events(job_id). The runner needs a result store (results=) to read the result from; an agent with background_jobs run on a runner with results=None is a SetupError before any model call.

docs.title: Getting the result back
docs.text:
The spawn tool has returned and has its result ("started"). When the child finishes, its result cannot be a second result of that call: the providers reject an orphan tool result, and a call with no result. So the result arrives as new information, as a user message:

<background_result job_id="…" agent="Summariser" status="SUCCESS">
{ the output, as JSON }
</background_result>

A failed child has status="FAILED" and its error_type, and a cancelled one status="CANCELLED"; there is no output.

  • While the parent's loop runs, the runner adds the message of every child that has finished before the parent's next model call, after the results of the tool calls of the round (never between a call and its result), once for each child. It is a hook before the model call (LangChain's agent middleware, before_model, which runs once the round's tool results are in the state). A message the loop gave is in new_messages of a streamed turn, so the application keeps what the model saw.
  • After a chat turn has ended, it is the application's: it starts the next turn with the history and the message. await runner.background_message(job_id) builds the same user message from the job's status and the result store, so that no application writes the format by hand (and it is how the example's session does it). It returns a LangChain HumanMessage, built from what the job's row and the result store hold, and what it can: a job that has not ended says its status and has no output; a job that succeeded and whose result is gone says output="missing"; an unknown job is a LookupError. The error text of a failed child is never in it, only its type.
  • A run that is not a chat waits (how long a child lives): the same hook, after the model's reply. When the reply would end the loop (it asks for no tool, or every tool it asked for has its result) while a child that was not given yet is still running, the run waits for the next one to end (handing its concurrency slot back meanwhile, because a child that runs here needs one), adds the messages of those that have ended, and sends the loop back to the model (jump_to="model"). It is bounded by recursion_limit: a child that ends after the limit is reached fails the run as the limit does. A streamed turn never waits.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
• On the parent's stream (a streaming agent, while the stream is open), two AG-UI CUSTOM events, as the streaming spec reserves (streaming): background_started (job_id, agent), sent when the tool starts the child, and background_finished (job_id, agent, status, error_type), sent when the child's job is final (for a child here and on a worker alike: the runner waits on the job's events). They are metadata only: the result is not in the event, the application reads it. They travel as any other event, over the adapters (streaming says what each does), and so over SSE. When the stream ends, the runner stops watching: a child that finishes after that is not announced.
  • After that stream has ended, the application follows the child through its job events (client.events(job_id), over SSE with sse.encode), as for any job. There is no new protocol and no new channel.
  • Observers: the child's job span is under the tool call's span (observability). For a child on a worker the client's submitted hook gives the carrier, as for any submitted job; for a child that runs here the runner calls the same hook itself and hands the carrier to the job's scope. In both the hook is told which tool call started the job (parent_tool_call_id), so that the carrier is that call's span; the id is for the observers and is stored nowhere.

docs.title: How long a child lives
docs.text:
• A chat turn (a streaming agent) does not wait. The turn ends when the model ends it, and its children carry on, in this process or on a worker. The application follows them with the events above. If the user stops the response (run.cancel(), runner.cancel(run_id), or a client that disconnects), the children of that run that are still live are cancelled with it. A turn that fails is not a stop: its children carry on.
  • A run that is not a chat waits. When the model would end its run while it has live children, the run waits for the next one to finish, adds its result as above, and the model goes on, within recursion_limit; so a pipeline agent can start several children and collect them. Cancelling the run (its task) cancels its live children.
  • Cancelling a child is cancel as for any job: the task is cancelled (here, and its job ends CANCELLED), or cancel_requested is set (on a worker). A child that fails or is cancelled is a result like any other: the parent is told, and it is up to the model.
  • A parent that outlives its children's process (a restart) loses the results that were not stored by the application. A child on a worker carries on and its result is in the store.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Live children (max_background_jobs, default 3): the most children of one attempt of one agent that may be running at one time. A start over the limit is refused with a sentence, and does not count. Finished children do not count.
  • No recursion: a background job cannot start background jobs (the tool), and it is a job of its own, so max_depth and max_launches count within it, as in any job.
  • The concurrency limit of the runner holds as for any run.

docs.title: What changes
docs.text: Each in the spec that owns it: agents (the background_jobs field and its checks); the runner (the tool, the limits, the hook before the model call, AgentRunner(background=), runner.background_message, cancel propagation); persistence (jobs.parent_attempt_id); streaming (the two CUSTOM events); observability (the child's span); submitted jobs (nothing: a child is a job).

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• The field is background_jobs (#204; it was background_agents). It holds agent classes and Job classes, and an agent class in it runs as a job of its own (its own id, status, events and result), so the name says what the list holds. The tool and the events keep their names (start_background, background_started, background_finished). The agent hash still names this entry background_agents in the declaration, so renaming the field changed no hash and a resume of an older job still reuses its steps. There is no alias for the old name (0.x), and it is not ignored: a class that still declares a field background_agents is refused when it is declared (TypeError, naming background_jobs), so that an agent written for 0.1 does not lose its background jobs without a word.
  • A background job is a job exposed as a tool, and one concept runs here or on a worker, by configuration.
  • An agent may be inline, background or both, by which lists it is in; the model chooses for an agent in both, and the prompt describes each agent once.
  • The result comes back as a user message, never as a second tool result, and only where every call of the round has its result.
  • featherweight wakes nothing: events, and a helper that builds the message. A self-waking session is an example.
  • A chat turn does not wait, and a run that is not a chat does.
  • A background job cannot start background jobs, and a child is not detached from its parent's cancel.
  • Metadata in the events, and the result from the user's store.

docs.title: Later
docs.text:
• Arbitrary statuses from a background job ("searching 3 of 5 sources"): a stream of updates, as progress, from a child to its parent and the application. It needs a place for them (a job event with content? a channel?), and the content question comes with it, so it is not decided here.
  • A child that outlives its parent by design (detach) is a client.submit, and needs no new feature today.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Arbitrary statuses and progress with content, for now (later).
  • A durable inbox or a session in the framework: pending results are the application's.
  • Background jobs that start background jobs.
  • A tool for the model to wait, check or poll a child.
  • Streaming agents as background jobs (they stream to a person, as for jobs).
  • A registry of running children, or a way to list them: the jobs table has them (parent_attempt_id).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
No live model call. Fake models, MemoryQueue, the dict result store.

  • The declaration: the checks of background_jobs, a background job that declares its own refused, an agent in both lists accepted, the prompt (each agent once, in its group) and the tool.
  • The tool: every row of the table; a child here and on a worker (MemoryQueue and a worker); the same job, row, events and result in both; results=None refused before the model call; the limit of live children.
  • The result: a child that finishes mid-loop is added after the round's tool results and once; a failed and a cancelled child; a model that starts several; the message of runner.background_message; no orphan tool result in any case.
  • The lifecycle: a chat turn that ends with live children leaves them running; stopping the response cancels them; a run that is not a chat waits, goes on with the result, and cancels its children when it is cancelled.
  • The events and observers: the two events on a stream and over the adapters; the child's span under the tool call's.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
Tracked in epic #115. One issue and one pull request each, in this order:

  1. #116 The child job and the tool: background_jobs, start_background, jobs.parent_attempt_id, here and on a worker, the limit.
  2. #117 The result: the hook before the model call, runner.background_message, and a run that waits for its children.
  3. #118 Events and cancel: the two CUSTOM events, stopping a response cancels its children, observers.
  4. #119 The guide and the skill.
  5. #120 An example: a session that wakes itself (a streaming agent that starts a background job and goes on).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Status: implemented, in issue #231. How to use it is in the guide. The code is config.py.

The numbers that tune a whole deployment, and where they are set. What each one does is in the spec that owns the thing it tunes (the runner, submitted jobs, skills, observers).

  • Goal
  • The rule
  • The settings
  • What is not configuration
  • Decisions
  • Not supported
  • Tests

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A setting that applies to a whole deployment is set where a deployment is configured: the environment. One that you also change by hand, while you try something out, can be passed in code. And there is one list: every variable featherweight reads has the prefix FTW_, is in the table below, and is read by one function, so there is no variable that you find only by reading the code.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
• Every environment variable of featherweight starts with FTW_. (The keys of the model providers, the names that an MCP server's env_from and headers_from point to, and OpenTelemetry's own OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_CONTENT are not featherweight's, and keep their names.)
  • Two kinds of setting.
  • Both ways: the argument of the constructor wins; if there is none, the variable; if there is none, the default. These are the numbers you change by hand when you try something out: how many attempts run at once, how far agents launch agents, how many jobs a worker runs at once.
  • Environment only: the variable, else the default. There is no constructor argument. These are the numbers that tune a platform and that nobody sets for one worker: leases, timeouts, polling.
  • Read when the object is built, not at import, and kept as an attribute. A test sets the variable, then builds the runner or the worker. A change of the variable later does not reach an object that exists.
  • A variable that is set but empty counts as not set, for a number and for FTW_LOG_LEVEL. A compose file or a .env hands over an empty value when you chose none (${FTW_LOG_LEVEL:-}).
  • A value that is not a positive number raises ValueError that names the variable (or the argument), when the object is built. A count must be an integer. There is no way to switch a timeout off: a very large value does it.
  • The effective values are logged at INFO when a runner or a worker is built (runner_configured, worker_configured), so that a setting that came from the environment is not invisible.

docs.title: The settings
docs.text:
Variable Default Argument What it sets FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS 10 AgentRunner(max_concurrent=) Model attempts running at once, per runner (runner) FTW_MAX_AGENT_DEPTH 3 AgentRunner(max_depth=) Most agents in one chain of launches. 1 turns launching off FTW_MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES 10 AgentRunner(max_launches=) Most launches per attempt of one agent FTW_MAX_BACKGROUND_JOBS 3 AgentRunner(max_background_jobs=) Most children one attempt may have running in the background FTW_WORKER_CONCURRENCY 10 JobWorker(concurrency=) Jobs one worker runs at once FTW_OBSERVER_TIMEOUT 1 s none How long an observer hook may take before the runner goes on (observers) FTW_WORKER_RECEIVE_TIMEOUT 1 s none How long a worker waits for a message before it looks again whether it is stopping FTW_WORKER_CANCEL_POLL 1 s none How often a worker asks whether a job it runs was cancelled in another process FTW_JOB_LEASE 60 s none How long a worker holds a job without renewing it, before another may take it over (submitted jobs) FTW_HEARTBEAT a third of the job's lease none How often a worker renews the leases of its jobs and of their messages FTW_QUEUE_LEASE 60 s none How long a message that was received stays invisible to other receivers, in the queues featherweight ships (SqliteQueue) FTW_QUEUE_MAX_DELIVERIES 3 none How many times SqliteQueue delivers a message before it marks it dead FTW_JOBS_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT 15 s none How long jobs_lookup may take (submitted jobs) FTW_SKILL_READ_TIMEOUT 15 s none How long a skill's aread may take (skills) FTW_DB_PATH featherweight.db the path given to SqliteDatabase The sqlite file FTW_LOG_LEVEL INFO the level given to setup_logging() The log level

FTW_DB_PATH and FTW_LOG_LEVEL are not numbers and are read where they were, by SqliteDatabase and setup_logging(): an argument wins there too.

docs.title: What is not configuration
docs.text:
• How long this call waits is an argument of the call: JobClient.wait(timeout), JobQueue.receive(timeout), JobWorker.stop(grace).
  • A timeout that belongs to a typed definition differs per job or per server, so it is in the definition: a job's timeout, an MCP server's timeout_s.
  • The attachment limits (max_attachments, max_bytes) are class attributes of the streaming agent: they differ per agent, so they are in the definition (attachments). There is no variable for them and no runner argument.
  • A runner's own behaviour in code: max_attempts and retry_delay_s stay arguments of AgentRunner.
  • MemoryQueue(lease=) (in featherweight.testing, for tests) is an argument: the queue kit builds queues with make_queue(lease), and a queue that someone else writes reads its own setting.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• One list and one reader. Before this, some numbers were variables, some were arguments and the limits were both; that made each one a thing to look up. The list is the table above, and featherweight.config reads it.
  • Both ways only where a person changes it by hand. A notebook or a local run should not need an environment to try max_depth=1; nobody sets a lease for one worker, so a lease has no argument and the constructors do not grow a parameter for every knob.
  • The FTW_ prefix on every variable, so that a bare name cannot collide with another tool's in a deployment.
  • Two leases, two variables. The job's lease and the queue's lease have different jobs (submitted jobs) and are set apart.
  • Read once, when built. A value that changed under a running worker would be a cause of failures that cannot be reproduced.
  • No off switch for a timeout, because a timeout that can be turned off is the one that is off when it is needed.
  • Pre-release: no alias. The old names (MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS, MAX_AGENT_DEPTH, MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES) and the removed arguments are gone.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• A configuration file, and a settings object that is passed around.
  • Changing a setting of a running runner or worker.
  • A way to switch a timeout off.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• For each setting: the default; the variable; for a "both ways" setting, that the argument wins; a value that is not a number, is zero or is negative raises ValueError that names the variable; an object built before the variable was set does not see it.
  • The table here, the list in featherweight.config and the Configuration table of the guide say the same (a test compares them).
  • The runner and the worker log their effective values when they are built.
  • The old names do nothing.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Status: implemented, in epic #190: the runner and the tools (#195: identity_type, identity=, RunContext.identity, CURRENT_IDENTITY, JobContext.identity and the inheritance), the identity hash (#197: the identity_hash column, fingerprint.identity_hash and the reuse check) the queue and the worker (#196: the identity field of the message, JobClient(identity_type=) and submit(identity=), JobWorker(identity_type=), InvalidJobIdentity, the migration of the sqlite queue table, and the kit's check), Skill.aread (#198) and jobs_lookup (#199), which skills and submitted jobs own. The guides are who is asking and the identity across the queue.

It builds on the runner, tools and the registry, submitted jobs and persistence, and adds a few lines to each. What it owns is the identity itself.

  • Goal
  • The identity
  • Declaring and passing it
  • How tools read it
  • Who inherits it
  • Across the queue
  • Resuming a job
  • What featherweight never does with it
  • The developer's responsibilities
  • Decisions
  • Not supported
  • Tests
  • The work

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
A tool often has to act for someone: read this user's files, send this user's mail, count against this tenant's quota. The model must not choose who, and the answer cannot come from the model's input. An identity is what the application tells a run about who it is for. It is a typed value that reaches the tools and nothing else, and it is the same value, apart from the fields marked exclude=True, whether the run happens in your process or on a worker ("one concept, two places": a tool that works in a process must not silently get nothing on a worker).

featherweight carries the identity. It does not authenticate anyone, decide what they may do, get a credential for them or keep them: those are the application's (the developer's responsibilities). This is the principle of the framework applied once more: a typed seam, checked at the boundary and closed when misused, and no solution built behind it (the philosophy).

docs.title: The identity
docs.text:
An identity is a Pydantic model that the application defines:

class Teacher(BaseModel):
    user_id: str
    tenant: str
    roles: list[str] = []
    language: str = "en"
  • It holds what the tools need to know about who the run is for: ids, a tenant, roles, a language. Whatever it holds is the application's: featherweight does not read its fields.
  • Small. It travels in the queue message of a submitted job, so it holds ids, not names or addresses.
  • No secrets. A token in it would sit in the queue until the message is acknowledged, and a queued job can outlive a token. A tool gets a credential from the identity with the application's own code (the responsibilities). A field marked exclude=True is the one exception: it is not serialised, so it is dropped when a job is submitted, and it is not part of the hash. It is there for a value that exists only in your process (a token that the tool would otherwise ask the vault for). It needs a default (jwt: str | None = Field(None, exclude=True)): the worker rebuilds the identity without it, and a model whose excluded field has none would fail every job on the worker, late, after submit had made and queued it. So identity_type is refused when the runner, the worker or the client is built if a model has an excluded field with no default. The pattern for a tool: in a process it may find the value; on a worker it is the default, and the tool falls back to the vault by user id.
  • One job, one identity. A job is for one identity: every run that carries its job_id has the same identity, or none. To run something for another identity, use another job (a resume is a new job, so a support person can resume a user's job under their own identity). run_job and submit give the whole job one identity by construction; only a developer who passes the same job_id to run, run_many or stream with different identities can break it, and the runner refuses it.

  • Read-only, by recommendation. An identity is a value the application hands over: do not change it after a run has it. The hash is computed from the object at each run, so a tool that changes it changes what later runs record. featherweight does not enforce this (a frozen model is the application's choice).

  • It is a model, not a field of an agent. An agent is a static definition and is not changed by who runs it: the same agent class runs for every user, and the identity is not in agent_hash.

docs.title: Declaring and passing it
docs.text:
The application declares the type once, where the framework needs it to check and to rebuild the identity:

runner = AgentRunner(db, identity_type=Teacher)
worker = JobWorker(db, queue, runner, jobs=[...], identity_type=Teacher)
client = JobClient(db, queue, results, identity_type=Teacher)  # optional

result = await runner.run(Summarise, summarise_input, identity=teacher)

identity= is an argument of run, run_many, stream, run_job and JobClient.submit. The declared type says what it must be:

Declared as A run without identity= A run with identity= nothing fine: no identity TypeError: the framework could not rebuild it on a worker Teacher TypeError checked: it must be a Teacher Teacher or None (a union) fine: no identity checked: it must be a Teacher Teacher or Student (a union of models) TypeError checked: it must be one of them Teacher, Student or None fine: no identity checked: it must be one of them
  • identity_type is a Pydantic model class, or a union of model classes, with or without None. Anything else, and a union that has two classes with the same __name__ (two Teacher classes in two modules), raises TypeError when the runner, the worker or the client is built, not at the first run. A union is for one agent or job that serves different kinds of people, a teacher or a student: the application says which kinds, and the identity says which one this run is for (the kind).
  • A missing identity is a programming error and raises, like an input of the wrong type, and before anything runs. The case it prevents: one code path of an application forgets identity=, and a tool runs as nobody. A union of the type and None (identity_type=Teacher | None) is how an application says that some runs (a nightly job) have none.
  • run_many gives every input the same identity, and checks it once, at the call, whatever the number of inputs (also none). run_job and submit give it to the job: every agent the job runs with ctx.run has it.
  • A run refuses an identity that is not its job's. When a run has a job_id and the job already has a run with another identity (or with none, and this one has one, or the reverse), the runner raises ValueError ("a job is for one identity") before anything is written, naming no identity value. run and run_many check at the call; stream is not async, so it checks when the loop starts, where it also raises for a job_id that does not exist. A run with no job_id is not checked. It is a guard against a mistake, not a security boundary: two first runs of one job with different identities at the same instant can both pass.
  • The worker's type must be one its runner accepts. The worker rebuilds the identity from the message with its type and gives it to the run, so every model of the worker's type must be a model of the runner's (or a subclass of one), and if the worker allows no identity, so must the runner. JobWorker raises TypeError when it is built, naming both types, if not: otherwise every job that runs an agent would fail at its first ctx.run. The two types need not be equal: a worker for Teacher over a runner of Teacher | None is fine (the runner also serves runs in the process that have none), and a job can be a pipeline of several agents, because they all run with the job's one identity on the one runner. The client's declaration is optional: with it, submit checks the identity before it creates a job (TypeError); without it, submit accepts any Pydantic model and serialises it, and the worker is where the declared type is the authority.

docs.title: How tools read it
docs.text:
RunContext becomes generic and gets a field:

@dataclass
class RunContext(Generic[IdentityT]):
    job_id: str | None
    run_id: str  # the run that the tool is called in
    attempt_id: str  # the attempt that is running now
    identity: IdentityT | None = None

run_id and attempt_id are the units of the units spec: a run is one call of an agent, and an attempt is one try of it.

A tool declares runtime: ToolRuntime[RunContext[Teacher]] and reads runtime.context.identity. LangChain fills the parameter in and hides it from the model, so the model never passes it and cannot see it (tools and the registry). A tool that does not declare runtime cannot see it.

  • The shared (MCP) tools cannot take a RunContext, because one tool object serves many attempts. The runner sets a context variable around each attempt, as it does for the attempt's id, and code that cannot take runtime reads it: CURRENT_IDENTITY.
  • A tool on a runner that declares a union annotates RunContext[Teacher | Student] and checks the kind (isinstance) before it acts. Nothing links the annotation to the runner's identity_type: a mismatch fails at run time, not in the editor.
  • Pipeline code reads the identity of its job with ctx.identity on the JobContext, for a job that has to behave differently for a tenant.
  • The identity is the same object that was passed, in a process. On a worker it is a new object, rebuilt from the message, and equal to it apart from the fields marked exclude=True, which have their default.

docs.title: Who inherits it
docs.text:
• A launched agent (launch_agent) runs with the identity of its parent, and so does an agent started in the background in the same process.
  • A background job on a worker (a runner with background=JobClient) is submitted with the identity of its parent.
  • Both read it from the attempt that started them (its RunContext): how a background job runs, here or on a worker, does not change where its identity comes from.
  • The model cannot set, change or drop it. launch_agent and start_background take no identity argument.

Why identity is inherited and capabilities are not. A launched agent does not get its parent's tools, skills or sub-agents: each agent has the allow-lists its own definition gives it, and that is least privilege. An identity is not a capability. It is who the whole run acts for, and a child that ran as nobody, or as someone else, would make its tools act for the wrong person or for no one. So a child can never have more, or less, than its parent's identity: it is the same one. What the child can do with it stays limited by its own allow-lists.

docs.title: Across the queue
docs.text:
A submitted job is the one place where a run leaves the process, so it is the one place where the identity is serialised, and the only place where it could be read or changed by anything but the application.

  • JobMessage gets two fields: identity: dict[str, Any] | None, the identity as JSON, from model_dump(mode="json"), without the fields marked exclude=True, and identity_kind: str | None, which model it is: the name of its class (type(identity).__name__). Both are None when the run has no identity, and the kind is sent always, also when the declared type is a single model. Two fields, and not one that holds both, so that a queue carries the same flat message as before.
  • The worker rebuilds it with its declared type, and gives it to the run, so a tool sees on a worker what it sees in a process. It chooses the model by the kind, and validates the data against that one model: pydantic's own choice among the members of a union is the first one that fits, which is the wrong model when a teacher and a student have the same fields. A kind that no member of the worker's type has fails the job, so a message of a Student never passes as a Teacher, also when the worker declares a single Teacher.
  • It fails closed. A message whose identity does not validate against the worker's type, one whose kind the worker's type does not have, one that has an identity and no kind, and a message without an identity when the worker's type does not allow None, make the job FAILED with InvalidJobIdentity (the way an input that does not validate does): the job is not run, and the worker does not retry it.
  • Every queue carries it, and testing.check_queue checks that a queue returns the identity and its kind unchanged, so that a queue that drops a field fails the kit. SqliteQueue stores them in the job_queue table (two migrations: the identity, then its kind) until the message is acknowledged, on the same terms as the input.
  • The queue is trusted. featherweight does not sign or encrypt a message: a deployment secures its queue (access control, TLS, encryption at rest) as it does for the input. An application that wants a signature or encryption of its own writes or wraps a queue: JobQueue is the seam, and a wrapper that signs the message on enqueue and checks it on receive is a recipe, run through check_queue like any queue.

docs.title: Resuming a job
docs.text:
Resuming reuses a step of an old job when the agent hash and the input hash match. That assumes a step depends only on its agent and its input. A tool that reads the identity makes it depend on who ran it, and if the identity has changed, so may the permissions, so the old result cannot be relied on. So the identity takes part, as a hash:

  • Each run records identity_hash: the SHA-256 of the identity as canonical JSON (keys sorted, no spaces: the form input_hash uses) of {"kind": <the class name>, "data": <its fields>}, without the fields marked exclude=True, so that it is the same in a process and on a worker. NULL when the run had no identity. The framework stores no identity. The kind is in it because two models can have the same fields: a Teacher and a Student with the same data are two identities, and a step of one is not a step of the other.
  • The hash is of the identity, never of the message. It is computed from the identity object (its class and its fields): in a process from the object that was passed, on a worker from the object the worker rebuilt by the kind and the data. Because the worker chooses the model by the kind, both give the same class name and the same fields, and so the same hash. The two fields of the message are how the object travels; the {"kind", "data"} text is what is hashed, and it is never sent.
  • A step is reused only when the old run's identity_hash equals the new run's. NULL equals only NULL: a step that ran with no identity is not reused by a run with one, and the other way round.
  • This is a rule about which steps are the same step. Whether a person may resume a job at all, or see its result, is the application's check (the responsibilities).
  • A support person who resumes a user's job under their own identity reruns every step. An application that wants the job to keep acting as the user passes the user's identity, once it has decided that it may. Identity should therefore stay small and stable: a roles list that changes between two runs stops the reuse.

docs.title: What featherweight never does with it
docs.text:
• It is never shown to the model: not in the prompt, not in a tool's arguments, not in a tool's result that the runner writes, and not in the events of a stream.
  • It is never in agent_hash, system_prompt_hash or tools_hash: only its hash is recorded, on the run.
  • It is never stored. No table holds it. The queue message holds it until it is acknowledged, as it holds the input.
  • It is never logged, and never in a span or an observer record (observers hear metadata): OTelObserver does not put it on a span. An application that wants a tenant on its traces adds it itself, in its own observer.

docs.title: The developer's responsibilities
docs.text:
These stay the application's, on purpose, and the guides, the book and the recipes say so:

  • A tool checks authorization itself. Carrying an identity does not make a tool safe: a tool that ignores it acts for everyone. A tool should check what the identity may do before it acts, and refuse in text, as the ready-made tools do.
  • An identity is a snapshot taken when the job was submitted. A queued job can run minutes or hours later: roles may have changed, a user may have left, and a token will have expired. For a sensitive action, a tool re-checks with the application by user id, and does not trust a list of roles in the identity.
  • A tool gets credentials from the identity with its own code, at each call (a long job outlives a token). The usual ways: a stored refresh token in a vault keyed by the user id, a service credential plus the user id (the service decides), a token exchange or impersonation, or a grant made at submit time and looked up by the job id.
  • Check who owns a job before resume_from. The identity hash makes a resume reuse only steps of the same identity, and does not decide who may resume a job or read its result: that is a check the application makes with its own records of who started which job.
  • If you pass a job_id to run, run_many or stream yourself, pass the same identity every time: a job is for one identity.
  • An identity says who, not what. A file or a record that a run works on is a reference in the input, and the tool checks that the identity may read it (files for agents and jobs). A resource in the identity would make "a job for this identity" differ per file.
  • Keep it small, and keep secrets out of it. Do not change an identity after a run has it.
  • Do not let users declare stdio MCP servers. A StdioMCPServer runs a command on your server. An application that builds agents from what users write allows only HttpMCPServer, or servers from a list it controls.
  • The name of an identity class is a name in the queue. The kind is the class name, so a rename of an identity class between submit and the worker running the job fails that job (InvalidJobIdentity), as a renamed job fails a queued job, and changes the identity_hash of the runs after it, so a resume reruns their steps once. Rename when the queue is empty, or keep the old name.
  • Names are the application's. A job's name is a plain string it chooses, unique in what its jobs_lookup searches, and stable: a rename breaks the jobs queued under the old name. The pattern is ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*$: a letter first, then letters, digits, _, . and -.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• An identity is an argument of the run, not a field of the agent, so the same agent runs for every user, and the hash of an agent says what it is, not who ran it.
  • Typed, declared, and required when declared: the type says what a run must pass, and a union with None is how an application allows none. A missing identity raises, instead of letting a tool run as nobody.
  • It crosses the queue as a field of the message, rebuilt with the declared type, and a message that does not fit fails the job. It is the one place where a run leaves the process.
  • The kind of an identity is the name of its class, sent in its own field, always. A union of models is wanted (one agent serves a teacher or a student), and a plain JSON of the fields does not say which model it was: pydantic would rebuild a student as the first model that fits. The class name is the simplest kind that works; the cost, a rename of the class while a job is queued, is documented, not engineered around (the application names its jobs the same way). It is sent always, so there is one rule, and a worker that declared a single type does not accept the data of another model with the same fields. The hash includes it for the same reason.
  • The worker keeps its own type, and it must be compatible with its runner's. The worker's type is what it accepts from the queue, the runner's what a run accepts; a worker may be stricter than its runner, never looser.
  • Inherited by what a run launches, and the model cannot touch it. It is who the run is for, not a capability.
  • A job is for one identity, and the runner refuses a run that is not. The design does not support several identities in one job (the key of a result is the job, the agent and the input), so the rule is stated and checked at run time, rather than the key changed. It is checked on each run that names a job: one indexed lookup of the run log.
  • An excluded field has a default, because the worker rebuilds the identity without it, and a failure that shows only on a worker is found when the type is declared instead.
  • Identity, not credentials. The framework has no credential provider and no protocol for one: where tokens live and how they are exchanged is the application's.
  • A hash on the run, so that resume reuses only the same step. The framework keeps a hash, as it keeps input_hash, and never the identity.
  • No codec, no signing and no encryption in the framework. The queue is the seam; a deployment secures it, and a wrapper queue is a recipe.
  • Plain strings for names, no key. How an application names and keys what it defines is its own; the framework runs a job by the name it is given.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Authenticating a user, deciding what they may do, and getting a credential for them.
  • An identity per tool call, or a tool that changes it: a run has one.
  • Several identities in one job: a job is for one identity. The result store's key does not carry the identity, and a resume finds a step by the job and the identity: a job that held two would hand one identity's output to the other.
  • Per-identity MCP servers (a connection and headers for each identity). Deferred: the connection of a server is shared by every run of a runner today, and a server that acts for a user needs its own connection and a token issued for that server. It is its own piece of work.
  • Signing or encrypting a message, and an identity that is a secret.
  • Storing identities, a tenant column, and attributing runs to a user in the run log: the application keeps its own record of who started which job (see tenants).
  • A key on agents and jobs, and an agent builder: how an application stores and names what its users define is its own.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
No live model call. Fake models, MemoryQueue.

The identity cases of Skill.aread are in skills, and those of jobs_lookup in submitted jobs: each spec owns its own.

  • Declaring and passing: a missing, a wrong and an extra identity, for each of the three declarations; Teacher | None; each entry point (run, run_many, stream, run_job, submit).
  • Tools: a tool of the parent, a tool of a launched agent and a sync tool (which runs in a thread) see the identity; the shared tools read CURRENT_IDENTITY; two runs with two identities on one runner at once do not mix; ctx.identity in a job.
  • Never: the hash of an agent does not change with it; it is not in the prompt, the log, the run log or a span.
  • Inheritance: a launched agent and an in-process background job have it; a background job submitted to a worker carries it.
  • A job is for one identity: a second run of a job for another identity raises before the model is called and writes nothing, for run, run_many (also with no inputs) and stream; the same identity twice is fine; none then an identity and the reverse are refused; a run with no job_id is not checked; a resume under another identity is a new job and works; the Database kit on sqlite and Postgres.
  • Excluded fields: one with no default is refused when the runner, the worker and the client are built (for a model, and for a member of a union); a tool sees the value in a process and the default on a worker.
  • The kind: a union of two models with the same fields is rebuilt as the model that was sent, in both orders of the union; a single declared type refuses the data of another model; a kind that the type does not have, and an identity with no kind, fail the job; two members with one class name are refused when built; the worker's type is checked against its runner's (accepted and refused cases).
  • The queue: check_queue against SqliteQueue and MemoryQueue (a queue that drops a field fails it); a job submitted with an identity whose tool reads it on a worker; a message without an identity for a worker that requires one, and a message that does not validate, fail the job and are not run.
  • Resume: the same identity reuses, another one reruns, NULL matches only NULL; a job that failed on a worker and is resumed on a worker, and a takeover, reuse a step of the same identity only; the hash is the same in a process and on a worker, two models with the same data have two hashes, and a field marked exclude=True is not in it; the Database kit on sqlite and Postgres.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
Status: implemented. How to use it is in jobs.md, persistence.md. The code is db.py (the abstract class, the records and rows), sqlite.py, migrations.py, jobs.py and log.py. The run log holds metadata only: see the persistence spec for why, and for PostgresDatabase.

Jobs can also be submitted to a queue and run by a separate worker: see the submitted jobs spec.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Every attempt of every agent is on record, tied to the job it belongs to and to the agent that launched it, so that a failed pipeline can be diagnosed from its rows, and replayed against them, without new model calls. A pipeline that is declared and recorded is a job.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
A job is a pipeline. It is declared as a Job class (submitted jobs), and it runs either in your process or on a worker. run_job(runner, job, input, *, job_id=None, resume_from=None, resumable=False) runs it in your process:

  1. creates the job (or uses job_id, which must exist), with the job's name, version, hash and the hash of the input, and starts it (start_job, the same compare-and-set step as a worker's), so it is RUNNING;
  2. runs job.run(ctx, input), where the JobContext holds the runner and the job's id;

  3. writes the output through the runner's result store, if it has one, and marks the job SUCCESS, or FAILED with the error; it returns a JobOutcome (job_id, status, result (the output model) on success, error on failure).

  4. job is a Job class, or a plain (non-streaming) agent class, as for submit; the input must be an instance of its input model (TypeError otherwise). A plain function is not a job: @job makes one from it.

  5. A job that raises is a failed outcome, not an exception. The error is ExceptionType: message, up to 2,000 characters.
  6. A cancelled task marks the job CANCELLED and re-raises the cancellation.
  7. A job that was cancelled before it could start is not run: the outcome has the status the job has, no result, and an error that says so.
  8. run_job(..., resume_from=old_job_id) and db.create_job(name, resume_from=old_job_id) create a new job that records resumed_from (an unknown job raises LookupError; run_job refuses job_id and resume_from together). See resuming a job.
  9. To run in the background and hand the caller the id first: db.create_job, then asyncio.create_task(run_job(runner, job, input, job_id=job_id)).
  10. set_job_status keeps error only for FAILED, and sets completed_at only for SUCCESS and FAILED. A job that does not exist raises LookupError.

docs.title: Running a job class
docs.text:
A job is one thing: a declared class, and it runs in your process or on a worker.

@job
async def summarise(ctx: JobContext, input: In) -> Out: ...


outcome = await run_job(runner, summarise, In(...))  # you run it, in your process
job_id = await client.submit(summarise, In(...))  # a worker runs it
  • Parity. The only difference between running a job in your process and on a worker is who runs it, and where. One function, execute_job, is used by run_job and by the worker: it runs the started job, writes the result, sets the final status and so writes the events. So both write the same job row, hashes and events (events() cannot tell them apart); write the result to the result store if there is one (run_job uses the runner's, the worker its own), and keep nothing if it is None (run_job still returns the output); resume the same way; and fail the same way. A job whose output cannot be kept fails, because the output is its product.
  • What stays different: a submitted job's input is JSON, because it crosses a queue; in your process it is the model as you built it. A submitted job is cancelled through the database (client.cancel), and one in your process by cancelling its task. The worker also settles the queue's message, and puts a job back on the queue when it shuts down.
  • No file, no service: SqliteDatabase(":memory:") (persistence) runs it all in memory.
  • Observers. That one function enters the observers' job scope around the pipeline and finishes it with the status and the error type, so both report the same (the runner); a worker also gives it the message's trace context.
  • Streaming agents cannot be jobs, as before.
  • trace_context is an optional argument of run_job: the carrier of the trace of whoever started the job (a runner that starts a background job here), which the job's scope joins. It is empty otherwise.
  • A job run in your process has an owner and no lease: run_job starts it as process-<id> (executions 1) and every write to it is conditional on that owner, as a worker's are (several workers); nothing renews a lease or takes the job over, so it has none to lose.
  • The timeout (Job.timeout, default 600 seconds) applies to both: it is in the shared function (several workers).
  • Tests: the same job run both ways gives the same row, hashes, events and result; :memory:; results=None; resume; a failing and a cancelled job.

A job has a version, as an agent has: Job.version, set by hand when the pipeline's behaviour changes (@job takes version=, default "1"). It is stored on the job (jobs.job_version) and the job's trace carries it. A pipeline's code is not hashed: arbitrary Python cannot be fingerprinted in a way that means anything (closures, imports, everything they call). job_hash covers the declaration: the name, the version and the two models. The code release is the user's, as the OpenTelemetry resource attribute service.version.

docs.title: Resuming a job
docs.text:
A resume is the user running a job that ended again, as a new job. (A job that did not end, because its worker died, is taken over by another worker as the same job: several workers. Both reuse finished steps with the mechanism below.)

A pipeline that failed at step 2 is run again with resume_from=<failed job>, if the failed job was created resumable=True (decided before it ran; otherwise nothing was kept and create_job raises). This is replay with memoised agent calls, not pausing: the pipeline's own code, loops and decisions run again, and the runner answers a run from the old job's kept results when it can (runner has the rules). A job created with resume_from is resumable too. The new job's trace has every step: a reused step is a SUCCESS row with zero tokens and reused_from_attempt_id pointing at the original, so the totals of the new job count only the calls it made. The old job is not changed.

The limits:

  • The code between agents must be deterministic (no clock, no random, no unordered iteration). It is the user's code and the user's responsibility; nothing checks it. If it takes another path, the inputs change, nothing matches, and the agents run again.
  • State kept in memory is not used for resumption; the result store is. A reused step does not run, so what it kept in memory is not rebuilt.
  • Side effects of tools in the failed job are not undone or repeated. An agent that failed halfway runs whole.
  • Rows from before agent_hash existed are never reused. Neither are FAILED, INIT and RUNNING rows.
  • A reference stands for the file behind it. A step is reused for the same input and identity, so for the same reference even if the file it points to has changed. When that matters, put a version or a hash in the reference (files for agents and jobs).
  • Depth 1 only. Sub-agent runs are not looked up. A parent that succeeded is reused whole; one that failed runs again with its children. Child reuse is not included.

docs.title: The run log
docs.text:
The orchestration, and no data. Database is an abstract class (see the persistence spec), and SqliteDatabase (a file, FTW_DB_PATH, default featherweight.db) implements it for local development. Records go in (AttemptRecord, AttemptFinish) and rows come out (JobRow, AttemptRow) as frozen Pydantic models, so the same constraints hold for every implementation; timestamps are timezone-aware datetimes. The tables are made by numbered migrations (persistence); a database from before migrations is refused (SetupError). There is no input, output, message or error text in any table, except the queue's message until it is acknowledged. The columns of every table, their types and constraints are in the schema. What they record:

  • jobs: one row per job. A job made without a job class has no job_hash and no input_hash.
  • job_events: one row for every change of a job's status, written in the same transaction as the change.
  • attempts: one row per attempt, so a retry is visible and a failed attempt keeps its error. run_id is shared by the attempts of one run() call. agent_hash covers the whole agent declaration, input and output schemas included (agents). system_prompt_hash and tools_hash say what changed between two runs. input_hash and output_hash are of the canonical JSON (a streaming run: of the ChatInput and of its text). A failed attempt records the class of the exception and the hash of its message: the text can quote data, so it is in the logs and the result, never the log.

completed_at - started_at is the run, and started_at - created_at the wait for a slot. A reused run, or one cancelled while queued, has no started_at. The whole launch tree of a job is one query on parent_attempt_id and depth, and the indexes on the job, the run, the parent and (job_id, agent_hash, input_hash) (the lookup for reuse) keep the queries cheap.

docs.title: Statuses
docs.text:
Status Jobs Attempts INIT Created Created, waiting for a concurrency slot RUNNING The pipeline runs Holds a slot and runs SUCCESS The pipeline returned The output validated FAILED The pipeline raised, or was cancelled The attempt failed CANCELLED The task running the pipeline was cancelled (run_job), or the job was cancelled before it ran The attempt was cancelled: the task that awaited it was cancelled, a launched agent whose parent was, or a streaming run that was stopped

finish_attempt accepts only a terminal status (SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED).

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
setup_logging() sends featherweight.* logs to stdout as plain text (time level logger key=value ...). The level is the argument, else FTW_LOG_LEVEL, else INFO. Calling it twice adds one handler. The libraries only use logging.getLogger(__name__); entry points call setup_logging.

The events: db_connected, db_migrated, job_created, job_status, job_started, job_finished, job_failed, job_cancelled, attempt_created, attempt_running, attempt_finished, run_reused, run_reuse_rejected, and the runner's lines (runner). Failures log at warning or error.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• sqlite for the run log, and OpenTelemetry as an observer. The log is small: two tables, no collector, no account. A real deployment sends traces to its own backend through an observer (observers and OpenTelemetry), and the log stays the source of truth.
  • One row per attempt, so a retry is visible, and a failed attempt keeps its error.
  • The prompt is recorded as a hash, not as text: enough to tell two runs apart, and it keeps secrets and size out of the table.
  • Inputs and outputs are not in the log. It keeps metadata only (persistence); content leaves only through an observer that asks for it.
  • A failed job is a value (JobOutcome), the same rule as for a failed run.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Exporting traces from the log. That is an observer (observers and OpenTelemetry), not a table.
  • Rows for tool calls. Skill reads and MCP calls are log lines only.
  • Redaction of inputs and outputs, and retention or cleanup.
  • Several processes writing one database.
  • Resuming from a crash inside the pipeline's code, mid-step. The code runs again; runs are answered from the log.
  • Reusing the runs of sub-agents.

docs.title: Goal and scope
docs.text:
An agent declares the MCP servers it uses, as typed, frozen Pydantic models. Their tools are added to the agent like any other tool: allow-listed per agent, bound to the model, traced, and with failures returned as values.

This spec is how MCP tools are connected and bound. Finding them by search (discover, search_tools, call_tool) was added after, and is in tool-discovery.md: by default a server's tools are discoverable, and the sections below about binding apply to a server with discover=False.

docs.title: Findings from the adapter
docs.text:
Checked with a fake stdio server, and once with a real Gemini call through create_agent.

It fits. - Tools come back as langchain StructuredTools, so they go into the registry like any other tool. - A session passed to load_mcp_tools(session) is reused. Five concurrent calls ran in 0.51s for a 0.5s tool, all in one subprocess. - tool_name_prefix=True prefixes tool names with the server name (server_tool). - env values reach a stdio server, and HOME and PATH are still inherited. - An MCP error result (isError) comes back as error text the model can read (handle_tool_errors=True). - Tool annotations (readOnlyHint and so on) arrive in tool.metadata. tool_interceptors wrap every call and get the server name. - Gemini accepted the tools, including a nested and nullable schema, and called them correctly. - mcp brings jsonschema, which call_tool (tool discovery) uses. About 50 packages in all, so it is an optional extra.

It does not fit, and what we do. 1. By default each tool call starts a new session, which for stdio is a new subprocess. We hold the sessions ourselves and pass them in. 2. A session must be opened and closed by the same task. Opening in one task and closing from another raised Attempted to exit cancel scope in a different task. An owner task per server, which opens the session and waits for a stop signal, works. 3. A server that dies raises (McpError: Connection closed, or FileNotFoundError for a missing command), and the run dies with it. The adapter handles only isError results. We wrap every MCP tool.

Gemini's schema conversion is lenient and lossy. It never raised, but: nested optional fields became required; a oneOf collapsed to its first type; a dict with typed values became a bare object; format, minimum and maximum were dropped. The server still validates the call and its error text reaches the model, so most of it is recoverable. Document it next to the existing structured-output caveat.

docs.title: Declaration
docs.text:
class MCPServer(BaseModel, frozen=True):
    name: str  # lowercase letters, digits and single underscores; the tool prefix
    description: str = ""  # what the server is for; the model reads it, to know what to search for
    discover: bool = True  # False: bind the tools directly (see tool-discovery.md)
    tools: tuple[str, ...] | None = None  # None: every tool of the server. A tuple: only those
    timeout_s: float = 60  # per call
    max_result_chars: int = 20_000  # cap on the text of one result; at least 1


class StdioMCPServer(MCPServer):
    command: str
    args: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    env_from: tuple[str, ...] = ()  # names of environment variables, never values
    cwd: str | None = None


class HttpMCPServer(MCPServer):  # streamable HTTP
    url: str
    bearer_from: str | None = None  # name of a variable; sent as `Authorization: Bearer <value>`
    headers_from: dict[str, str] = {}  # header name -> name of an environment variable


class AgentBase:
    mcp_servers: list[StdioMCPServer | HttpMCPServer] = []

Checked when the agent is built (a programming error that raises): - server names are unique within the agent; - a name is valid, and short enough that name_tool fits in 64 characters for typical tools; - an allow-list has no empty or duplicate entries; - timeout_s is above 0 and max_result_chars is at least 1.

Secrets are names. The agent definition holds environment variable names. They are resolved when the connection opens. A missing variable is a setup failure that names the variable. Values never appear in a log, a run row or a prompt hash.

The models import without the extra. Only the runner imports mcp and the adapter, lazily, and a missing install raises a message that says pip install featherweight[mcp].

docs.title: The tool registry
docs.text:
An internal class, built by the runner for each attempt. It holds every tool the attempt may use, with its source (local, mcp:<server> or runner) and its mode (direct or discoverable; see tool-discovery.md).

  • Naming. MCP tools are named by the adapter: load_mcp_tools(session, server_name=<the agent's name for the server>, tool_name_prefix=True) gives server_tool. The registry does not rename tools. It loads once per connection and agent-side server name, and caches the result.
  • Collisions. A name used twice, across local tools, MCP tools and the injected launch_agent, get_agent_schema and get_skill, is a setup failure. (A single underscore can clash: server a_b with tool c, and server a with tool b_c.) A local tool against an injected tool is caught when the agent is built.
  • Filtering. tools on a server keeps only the listed tools. A listed name the server does not have is a setup failure, because it is usually a typo.
  • Binding. The direct entries are what the model is bound to. The attempt_started log line lists them (tools=); the run log keeps tools_hash.

docs.title: Separation of concerns
docs.text:
Two parts, with different lifetimes:

Scope Owns Does not know MCPConnections (mcp_connections.py) One per runner, shared by agents, runs and retries The server processes and sessions An agent's names for servers, filters, timeouts, caps, modes ToolRegistry (registry.py, with mcp_tools.py) One per attempt of one agent Nothing live: the tools it was given Whether a server is shared, or when it stops

Rule: what can differ between two agents that share a server is on the registry side; what cannot is on the connection side. The connection key holds only connection settings, so name, tools, timeout_s, max_result_chars (and later discover) never reach it.

lease = Lease(connections)  # one per run, from its first attempt to its last
await lease.list_tools(server)  # the server's own tool list, unprefixed and unfiltered
await lease.session(server)  # the session the tools call through
await registry.add_mcp(server, lease)  # the agent's view: allow-list, prefix, timeout, cap, failures as text
await lease.release()  # the run is done

docs.title: Connections and lifecycle
docs.text:
• Nothing connects when the runner is created. A server opens when a run first needs it.
  • Each server is held by an owner task: it opens the session, publishes it, and waits for a stop signal. Calls from any task share the session.
  • Concurrent first uses open one connection (a lock per server).
  • Connections are shared between agents whose connection settings are equal: the command, args, cwd and environment names for stdio; the URL and header names for HTTP.
  • A run holds a lease on its servers from its first attempt to its last, so a retry does not start a server again. A server is stopped when its last lease is released.
  • The context manager is optional. async with AgentRunner(db) (or aclose() at the end) keeps servers up between runs and stops them at the end of the block. Without it, each run starts what it needs and stops it when it is done, unless another run still holds it. Nothing raises either way, and a runner needs no setup to run an agent with MCP servers, also when the agent is launched by another agent.
  • An attempt gets its servers before it takes a concurrency slot, so a slow start (npx) does not hold one.
  • aclose() stops every server, whatever holds it, and can be called twice. A later run starts them again.
  • A dead connection is replaced. When a call finds the connection broken, or its owner task ends, it is forgotten, and the next attempt that needs the server opens a new one. The runner's retries therefore cover a crashed server.

docs.title: Failures are values
docs.text:
Case Result Missing environment variable, command not found, an allow-listed tool the server lacks, a name collision The attempt fails at once, without retry. The message names the server (never a secret's value) The connection fails to open for another reason An ordinary failed attempt, which is retried The tool returns an MCP error (isError) Error text the model can read (the adapter's handle_tool_errors) The server dies, or the connection drops, during a call The model gets MCP server 'x' is unavailable: .... The connection entry is cleared A call exceeds timeout_s The model gets The call to 'x_tool' timed out after 60s Bad arguments The server validates them and its error text reaches the model

Every MCP tool is wrapped when the registry is built, so that no exception from the adapter or the connection reaches the agent loop. Without the wrapper a dead server ends the whole run (checked).

docs.title: What reaches the model
docs.text:
• Text, images and embedded files pass through as the adapter converts them. Checked with gemini-3.5-flash-lite: it named the colour of a returned PNG, and read a code out of a returned PDF.
  • A resource link is turned into text (Resource link: <uri> (<mime type>)), not passed through. The adapter makes it a file block with a URL, and the Gemini client then fetches that URL itself, when the next model call is prepared. That has two problems: a server can make our process fetch any address, and a failed fetch raises outside the tool, so the tool wrapper cannot catch it (checked: a 404 killed the run).
  • Audio makes the adapter raise. The wrapper turns that into text: The tool returned audio, which is not supported.
  • structuredContent is not shown to the model separately: the adapter puts it in the message's artifact, and a server that declares an output schema must also return the same data as text. If a result has no content but has structured content, the registry renders the structured content as JSON text.
  • Size. The text of a result is capped at the server's max_result_chars (default 20,000 characters, about 5,000 tokens). Longer text is cut at the limit and ends with [truncated: 48,213 characters, showing the first 20,000]. The cap is per result, counted over all its text blocks together. It applies to text only: images and embedded files are not capped in this version. A result counts in the next model call's input tokens, and an oversized one can exceed the context limit and fail the attempt.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
• Each call logs mcp_call attempt_id=... server=... tool=... status=ok|error|timeout ms=.... Arguments and results are not logged.
  • Opening and closing log mcp_open server=... transport=... and mcp_close server=....
  • No new tables or columns.

docs.title: Not in this version
docs.text:
• Discovery of tools other than MCP's (tool-discovery.md).
  • SSE and websocket transports.
  • OAuth flows for HTTP servers; MCP resources, prompts and sampling.
  • A refresh of a server's tool list. It is read when a connection is opened.
  • Using tool annotations (destructiveHint and so on) as policy.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
A real stdio fake server (FastMCP, about 0.3s to start) with a scripted fake chat model, so no API calls.

  • Tools appear named server_tool and are bound; a local tool and an MCP tool work in one attempt.
  • Concurrent calls share one session and one process.
  • A retry does not start the server again.
  • Two agents with equal connection settings share a process; with different settings, they do not.
  • A server that dies mid-call gives text to the model, and the next attempt gets a new connection.
  • A call over timeout_s gives text.
  • Each setup failure fails at once, with one attempt.
  • A name collision is refused. A typo in an allow-list is refused.
  • A secret's value is in no log line, run row or exception message.
  • A server stops when the run ends without async with, and when the block ends with it; two runs share a server inside the block, and parallel runs share one outside it. aclose() leaves no child process; closing twice is fine.
  • An MCP agent runs on a runner that is not open (no async with), and its server is stopped when the run ends.
  • A resource link reaches the model as text, with no fetch. Audio becomes a text note.
  • An image and a PDF returned by the server reach the real model and are read (e2e, gemini-3.5-flash-lite).
  • Unit tests for the empty-content-with-structured-content rule, and for the cap: a result at the limit is untouched, one over it is cut with the note, and several text blocks are counted together.
  • One e2e test against the real model and the fake server, and, if Node is available, one against a small real server.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• The runner's context manager is optional: a server starts when a run needs it and stops when the last run using it ends, unless the runner is inside async with. (First decided the other way, that an MCP agent on a runner that was not open raises. That made the rule depend on the whole tree of launched agents, and it was dropped.)
  • Connections are shared and per runner; the registry is per attempt and owns nothing. The agent's declaration is applied on the registry side.
  • tools not given means every tool of the server; given, only those. An allow-list is therefore optional per server.
  • Images and embedded files pass through; resource links become text (see the check above).
  • Text results are capped, per server, at max_result_chars (default 20,000).

docs.title: Models and providers
docs.text:
Status: implemented. How to use it is in models.md. The code is model_settings.py.

It was designed in issue #2. It changes agents (the model_name and reasoning fields), the runner (the model factory is removed) and jobs (two columns).

  • Goal
  • The model
  • What is in the catalog
  • Rules that hold for every provider
  • Per provider
  • Extending it
  • Tokens and the run log
  • Testing
