docs.title: Goal
docs.text: An agent says which model runs it, and how hard it thinks, with a typed object that checks itself. Each provider has its own class with its own fields, because the providers do not share their controls: a thinking level, an effort, an on/off switch. A setting that a model does not accept fails when the agent is defined, not on the first call. Anyone can add a provider, or a model, by writing a class.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
ModelSettings is a frozen Pydantic model that rejects unknown fields (extra="forbid"). An agent has one:

class Triager(AgentBase):
    model: ModelSettings = Claude(model="claude-haiku-5-5", effort="low")
Member provider A class attribute: "google", "anthropic", "openai". Stored in the run log models A class attribute: the catalog of the class, model id to ModelInfo model The model id. Must be in models max_output_tokens Optional. The most tokens the model may produce, thinking included show_thoughts False by default. Asks the provider to return the model's thoughts (see streaming agents). Gemini and Gemma send include_thoughts, Claude thinking.display = "summarized", OpenAI reasoning.summary = "auto". Refused for Claude(thinking="off") and OpenAI(effort="none") build() Returns the LangChain chat model. Imports the provider's package when called. Required: the only method a new class must write. The base class raises NotImplementedError("<Class> must write build()"), when the model is built for a run, not when the class is defined label() A short text for the log, such as medium, off or high. By default the effort or thinking field check_model_output_schema(output_model) Refuses an output model that this model cannot fill (provider limits). The default accepts everything

ModelInfo is frozen: efforts (the allowed values, in order), default (what the provider uses when none is sent, for the docs), and for Claude can_disable_thinking and native_output (provider limits).

docs.title: The model settings validate what an agent asks of its model
docs.text:
The model settings are in charge of validating everything that depends on the provider or the model: which model and options an agent names, and which output it asks the model to fill. What a provider takes differs by provider and by model, so the class that knows the model holds the rule, and the runner and AgentBase know no provider: AgentBase calls the hook. A settings class that a user writes states its own provider's rules in the same place. This does not change who validates data: the data of a run is validated against the agent's input_model and output_model, and by check_output. Nor is a reply the settings' to judge: the runner refuses an early answer, whatever the model.

What is validated By When The model and its options The setting's own validators When the setting is built The agent's output model check_model_output_schema When the agent is built

Why: Anthropic is the example, and the reason this was added (2026-11-26). Claude Opus, Sonnet and Fable take only some output schemas, and one of the others, a dictionary, is not refused by anyone: Anthropic's SDK empties it, and the run succeeds without the data. The rule is not true of every provider, nor of every Claude model (Haiku takes those schemas), so it belongs neither in the agent nor in the runner (provider limits).

Validation, when the setting is built:

  • model must be in the catalog, and the effort (or thinking level) must be one of that model's efforts. The message lists what is allowed.
  • A field the class does not declare is an error. In particular temperature, top_p and top_k are not fields of any built-in class, and passing one raises a message that says why (below).

AgentBase.model replaces model_name and reasoning. The default is Gemini().

docs.title: What is in the catalog
docs.text:
Class Models Controls Gemini gemini-3.8-flash, gemini-3.6-flash, gemini-3.5-flash-lite thinking: minimal, low, medium, high, as each model allows Gemma gemma-4-31b-it, gemma-4-26b-a4b-it thinking: minimal (off) or high Claude claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5, claude-fable-5-2 effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max. thinking: adaptive or off OpenAI gpt-6.2-astra, gpt-6.2-sol, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6.1-terra, gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-luna effort: none, low, medium, high, xhigh, max, as each model allows

Only Gemini 3 and later, Gemma 4, Claude 5 and later, and GPT-6 are built in. Older models are for a user class (Extending it). The exact efforts of each model are in the code and the table below.

docs.title: Rules that hold for every provider
Temperature
docs.text:
No built-in class has temperature, top_p or top_k.

  • Gemini 3.6: "deprecated and ignored", and a 400 in later generations. The advice is a system instruction with explicit rules.
  • Claude 5: a non-default value is a 400, and so is top_p=1 (its default is 0.99) and sending temperature and top_p together. From API version 2026-10-21 any value is a 400.
  • GPT-6.2: the migration guide says to omit temperature and top_p.
  • langchain-openai drops a non-1 temperature silently on GPT-5 models, and langchain-google-genai sets it to None on Gemini 3. A silent drop hides a mistake, so these classes refuse it.

A class whose models accept temperature declares it itself (the Ollama example). To make an agent more repeatable, use the prompt, an output schema with enums, and check_output. No provider documents a switch for repeatable output.

docs.title: Thinking is counted in tokens
docs.text: max_output_tokens includes thinking on all three providers. For Claude it is required by the API, so Claude has a default of 16,000 and the docs advise 64,000 or more at xhigh and max.

docs.title: Setup errors
docs.text: A provider package that is not installed, a missing key, and an invalid setting at build time are a ModelSetupError: not retried, as before. A package that is not installed says which extra to install (pip install 'featherweight[anthropic]').

docs.title: Per provider
docs.text:
Gemini Gemma Claude OpenAI Package langchain-google-genai (always installed) same langchain-anthropic, extra anthropic langchain-openai, extra openai Key GOOGLE_API_KEY same ANTHROPIC_API_KEY OPENAI_API_KEY Sent as thinking_level thinking_level reasoning_effort, and thinking={"type": "adaptive"} or {"type": "disabled"} Responses API, reasoning={"effort": ...} Can thinking be off? No (minimal is nearly off) minimal Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable: no. Haiku 5.5: yes, at high or below none, on gpt-6.1-terra and gpt-6-luna only Tools and the reply schema Native Caveat below Opus, Sonnet, Fable: native. Haiku: the reply is a tool call (limits). Forced tool_choice is rejected on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable, which LangChain does not use Responses API; Chat Completions only at effort none on Luna

Efforts per model:

Model Efforts Default gemini-3.8-flash low, medium, high medium gemini-3.6-flash minimal, low, medium, high medium gemini-3.5-flash-lite minimal, low, medium, high minimal gemma-4-31b-it, gemma-4-26b-a4b-it minimal, high claude-opus-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5 low, medium, high, xhigh, max medium claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-fable-5-2 low, medium, high, xhigh, max high gpt-6.2-astra, gpt-6.2-sol, gpt-6.1-sol, gpt-6-astra low, medium, high, xhigh, max medium (not stated for the 6.2 models; medium is the docs' advice) gpt-6.1-terra, gpt-6-luna none, low, medium, high, xhigh, max medium

The class default is not always the provider's default. Gemini, Claude and OpenAI all default effort or thinking to medium (Gemma to minimal), so that a bare Claude(model=...) behaves alike across providers. The table says what the provider would use.

Gemma. It takes thinking_level through ChatGoogleGenerativeAI, and reports thinking tokens. With a tool and a reply schema in one agent, both hosted models answered in JSON at once and did not call the tool, where Gemini did. Gemma is supported, and this is documented as a limit: prefer Gemma for agents without tools, until it is tested further. Hosted Gemma has image input, no audio, and a 256K context.

OpenAI. OpenAI.build() always uses the Responses API, because tool calling needs it on the models above. It is tested with gpt-6-luna at none and low: a tool call and our reply schema, with a defaulted field and a bounded integer, both worked.

Claude. Claude(thinking="off") sends {"type": "disabled"}, and is refused for a model that cannot (info) or at xhigh or max. How the output is asked for differs by model, and so do the limits (provider limits): Opus, Sonnet and Fable get Anthropic's structured output, and Haiku gets a tool call. The API does not enforce a numeric bound, so check_output is the guard.

docs.title: Provider limits
docs.text:
An output schema that a provider cannot fill is refused by the model settings, because that differs by provider and by model. featherweight passes the output model to LangChain as it is: LangChain chooses how to ask for it, and the provider's own SDK converts the schema. We add no converter and no middleware. We only refuse.

ModelSettings.check_model_output_schema(output_model) is called when an agent is built (not for a streaming agent: it has no typed output), and by default accepts everything.

Schemas that Claude's structured output does not take. Claude.check_model_output_schema applies to the models whose ModelInfo.native_output is true (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.2), which is where LangChain asks for Anthropic's structured output. It raises ValueError, so the agent is not built, and the message names every problem:

Output model has Without the check A free-form object: a dict of any kind, also in a list or optional, or a model with extra="allow" Anthropic's SDK (transform_schema) sends an object with no properties that allows no others. The field comes back empty, and the run succeeds A recursive model The API refuses the request (400) More than 24 optional fields, those of nested models and open_questions included The API refuses the request (400)

The optional fields are counted from the model's JSON schema, with a definition that is used twice counted once, so the count is never higher than the provider's, and an output that the API takes is not refused for it. A model that a user adds to the catalog says native_output=True itself. Claude(model="claude-haiku-5-5") is not held to these limits: LangChain asks it for the output as a tool call, which sends the schema as it is. Types without a JSON schema type (Any, a bare list, object) are not checked: the SDK raises for them before anything is sent.

An early answer is the other limit seen with Claude Haiku, which gets its output as a tool call: it can give the answer before it has seen its tools' results. The runner refuses that, whatever the model (an early answer).

When the answer does not validate. With the output as a tool call, LangChain sends a validation error back to the model within the attempt. With a provider's structured output (Claude's native models, and OpenAI), a reply that does not validate fails the attempt.

Decided (2026-11-26). Refuse, and document. Rejected:

  • Middleware that sends an early answer back to the model. It works in a prototype, with one call more, but it makes featherweight own the agent loop's edge cases, one middleware after another.
  • A schema converter of our own. The conversion is the provider's, and a second one would drift from it.
  • Asking Haiku for native output (by changing what LangChain knows about it). In an offline prototype it removes the early answer, and brings all three schema limits to the default Claude model. It was not run against the real API.
  • Only documenting the dictionary. The data is lost while the run succeeds, so a warning that is missed costs data.

Seen on the real API on 2026-11-26: Haiku 5.5, with thinking on, gave an empty answer in one reply with a tool call (inferred: one model call, the tool ran, every field empty; the reply itself was not kept, and the case was reproduced with a fake). Sonnet 5.5 returned {} for a dict[str, str] it was asked to fill, and refused a recursive schema and one with 31 optional fields. Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 were not run: LangChain asks them the same way.

docs.title: A model of a provider that is built in
docs.text:
Subclass the class and add to its catalog. For example, GPT-5.x:

from typing import ClassVar

from featherweight import ModelInfo, OpenAI


class OpenAI5(OpenAI):
    models: ClassVar[dict[str, ModelInfo]] = {
        **OpenAI.models,
        "gpt-5.5": ModelInfo(efforts=("none", "low", "medium", "high"), default="medium"),
    }


class Reader(AgentBase):
    model: OpenAI5 = OpenAI5(model="gpt-5.5", effort="low")

build() is inherited. Rules of the older models (such as GPT-5's refusal of a temperature) are the user's to add, by overriding build() or adding a field.

docs.title: A provider: Ollama
docs.text:
Write build(), name the fields:

class Ollama(ModelSettings):
    provider: ClassVar[str] = "ollama"
    models: ClassVar[dict[str, ModelInfo]] = {}  # empty: any model name the server has
    temperature: float | None = Field(default=None, ge=0, le=1)
    reasoning: bool | None = None

    def build(self):
        from langchain_ollama import ChatOllama

        return ChatOllama(model=self.model, temperature=self.temperature, reasoning=self.reasoning)

An empty catalog means any model id is allowed, and efforts are not checked. Nothing else is needed: the runner calls agent.model.build(), and the log stores provider and the settings.

label() can be overridden when the class has no effort or thinking field.

docs.title: Tokens and the run log
docs.text:
Tokens. The runner sums usage_metadata["input_tokens"] and ["output_tokens"] of the model's replies. This was checked in the source of each LangChain package, and with live calls:

input_tokens output_tokens Gemini, Gemma Prompt tokens (cached included) plus tool-use prompt tokens Reply tokens plus thinking tokens, added by the package Claude Input plus cache reads plus cache writes, added back by the package As the API reports, thinking included OpenAI Prompt tokens, cached included Completion tokens, reasoning included

All three give input_tokens as the whole input and output_tokens as the whole output with thinking, so _usage needs no change. The reported model name is response_metadata["model_name"] for Gemini, Gemma, Claude and OpenAI. A class that does not set it (Ollama puts model) leaves AgentResult.model_name empty. Cache reads and writes are available in input_token_details and are not stored.

The run log records the requested model, the effort (the label()), the provider (google, anthropic, openai, or the class's own) and the settings as JSON, so that a run can be reproduced. The columns are in the schema.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: A fake is model settings. A test defines a ModelSettings subclass whose build() returns a scripted chat model, and runs the agent with its model replaced by that settings object. The runner calls agent.model.build() as in production, and nothing in the runner exists for tests. The suite does this with FakeSettings in tests/fakes.py, which looks up the scripted model a test registered under a key, so that an agent can be declared once and a test can choose its model. The guide and the agent skill show the pattern for users, with the fake chat model held by the settings.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• What depends on the model is validated by its settings (above), not by the runner or by AgentBase, which would need to know each provider and each model (2026-11-26).
  • One class per provider, with its own fields. The controls differ in kind, so a shared reasoning: Literal[...] would be wrong for one of them. The label in the log is what is shared.
  • A catalog per class, checked when the setting is built. A typo, or an effort a model refuses, fails at definition time. The cost is a change in featherweight when a model ships, and a user class is the way round it.
  • No hook on the runner. A second way to choose the model, used only by tests, would let a run use a model its declaration does not name, and would leave the declaration unable to say what ran. Tests use fake settings instead.
  • No registry. The class is the extension point and the runner calls build(). Nothing is registered.
  • No temperature. The vendors have removed or discourage it, and silently ignoring it is worse than refusing it.
  • Only current families. Older models need other parameters (budget_tokens, thinking_budget), and a user class can add them.
  • Settings are stored as JSON in the log. A run can be reproduced, and a new field needs no new column.
  • Gemma is in, with a limit. The limit is in the docs and not hidden.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Older models (Gemini 2.x, Claude 4 and earlier, GPT-5) in core. Add them as in Extending it.
  • Token budgets (thinking_budget, budget_tokens), the OpenAI verbosity setting and reasoning.mode: pro, and Claude's task_budget. A user class can add each.
  • Choosing a model by a string alone (model="claude-sonnet-5-5").
  • Different settings per attempt (a stronger model on a retry).
  • Checking an output schema against a provider's whole schema subset. Only what is in provider limits is checked.
  • Cost, or storing cached-token counts.
  • Provider-side features: built-in tools, web search, prompt caching.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
What the vendors say, and what was run (2026-11-18).

Claude, live (haiku-5-5, sonnet-5-5, opus-5-5, low effort) Tool call, then reply as JSON: native structured output. Defaulted field and a bounded integer worked. Usage and model name reported OpenAI, live (gpt-6-luna: Chat Completions none, Responses none and low) The same, three times. Identical token counts in all three, and 0 reasoning tokens even at low, so it is not shown that the effort reached the API. Strict mode is not shown to be on Gemma, live (both hosted models) Reply schema, usage and model name work. Tool calling works when the tool is bound alone. With a reply schema in the same agent, the tool was skipped Ollama (docs only) reasoning is True, False or None; temperature 0 to 1; the default structured-output method is json_schema; the docs list token usage as unsupported and show counts in one example

Sources: the vendors' documentation for Gemini thinking, Claude effort, Claude thinking, Claude structured outputs, OpenAI reasoning and OpenAI structured outputs, and the installed source of the three LangChain packages. Parts of the vendor pages were read through a summary, not verbatim.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Offline, and with no key. For each class: the catalog (a model not in it, an effort the model refuses, a field it does not have, temperature with its message), label(), and build() with a fake key, which checks what the LangChain object holds (reasoning_effort, thinking, max_tokens, use_responses_api, reasoning, thinking_level). A missing package is a ModelSetupError that names the extra. A user class (GPT-5 and Ollama as in the examples above), the log columns and the migration, and an agent with a Claude and one with a Gemini setting. Provider limits: each refused schema, the boundary of the optional fields, the models and providers that are not held to them, the early answer and its retry (the runner), and two facts of the dependencies that the checks rest on (which Claude models LangChain asks for native output, and that Anthropic's SDK still empties a dictionary). One real-model test per provider, claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-6-luna and a small Gemma, run only on request.

docs.title: Observers and OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
Status: implemented. #92 (the Observer class, its records, testing.check_observer, and the runner's calls), the job scope and the trace context across the queue (#93) and OTelObserver (#94, pinned to semantic-conventions-genai@622b2b6, which refers to core semantic conventions 1.45.0) and the guide, the example and the skill reference (#95) are done. It is tracked in epic #90, and each part has its own issue. When a part is built, this page says so, and the guide docs/observability.md shows how to use it.

It builds on the persistence spec (the rule that featherweight keeps metadata only, and that content never goes into the run log, even by option). It is about what an observer is, what it receives, and the OpenTelemetry observer. What the other specs do about it is in them, and not here: the runner (when it calls observers, and how it sees model calls and tool calls), submitted jobs (the trace context in the message), and jobs and tracing (a job runs the same way in your process and on a worker, and has a version), which the spans of a job depend on.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Let a developer see what their pipelines do, and run evaluations on what they collected, without featherweight keeping or seeing their data.

  • Observers: an abstract class that the runner calls as things happen. featherweight stores nothing from it. What an observer does with the events is the user's.
  • OpenTelemetry: one observer that we ship, because every observability and evaluation platform reads it. It follows the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, so the traces are readable by those platforms as they are.

docs.title: The principle
docs.text:
featherweight emits spans for its own concepts. The user uses the OpenTelemetry API for their own.

  • Ours: a job, an agent attempt, a model call, a tool call, and a reused step. Nothing else.
  • Yours: any span around your own code. There is no featherweight API for it, no helper, no wrapper.
  • Metadata always, content on request. The records an observer receives always carry ids, names, status, tokens, timing, hashes and error types. Inputs, outputs, messages, tool arguments and results and error text are there only for an observer that asks for them. Nothing leaves the process by default.
  • The run log is the source of truth. Resume and status never read from an observer, and nothing an observer receives is stored by us. In particular no trace id or span id is stored in any table: they are application and telemetry state.
  • Observers never change a run. One that raises or is slow is logged and ignored, so a broken exporter cannot fail a job.
  • We do not run evaluations or score anything. We emit traces that make that trivial on a platform of the user's choice.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
class Observer(ABC):
    capture_content: ClassVar[bool] = (
        False  # an observer that wants content says so; nothing is built for one that does not
    )

    def job(self, start: JobStart) -> AbstractAsyncContextManager[Scope]: ...
    def attempt(self, start: AttemptStart) -> AbstractAsyncContextManager[Scope]: ...
    async def reused(self, run: RunReused) -> None: ...
    async def model_call_started(self, call: ModelCallStart) -> None: ...
    async def model_call_finished(self, call: ModelCallEnd) -> None: ...
    async def tool_call_started(self, call: ToolCallStart) -> None: ...
    async def tool_call_finished(self, call: ToolCallEnd) -> None: ...
    async def submitted(
        self, job: JobSubmitted
    ) -> Mapping[str, str] | None: ...  # the carrier that travels in the message

(The exact shape is settled in the issue for the class; this is what it has to cover.)

  • Every method has a default that does nothing. An observer overrides what it cares about. The class is abstract in the same sense as Database: it is the interface, with a conformance kit (testing.check_observer) that calls every method with sample records and checks that none of them fails or changes anything.
  • job and attempt wrap the work. The runner enters them around the pipeline and around one attempt, and calls scope.finish(end) with the outcome before leaving. This is what lets an observer make its span the current one while the work runs (see your own spans). model_call and tool_call are start and finish events: they come from a callback in another task, so they cannot wrap anything.
  • Inline, and harmless. Every call is awaited, with a timeout and with its errors logged and ignored (the runner). A slow observer buffers for itself. OpenTelemetry's own exporters already batch in the background, so ours is cheap.
  • Where they are set. On the runner (AgentRunner(db, observers=[...]): see the runner for when it calls them), and on the client (JobClient(db, queue, observers=[...]), for submitted only).

docs.title: What an observer sees
docs.text:
Records are frozen Pydantic models, as everywhere. Always present (metadata): ids (job_id, attempt_id, run_id, parent_attempt_id), names and versions, hashes, attempt and max_attempts, the provider and model, tokens, timing, status, and the error type (never the text). Only for an observer with capture_content = True: the job input and output, the agent input and output, messages, system instructions, tool definitions, tool arguments and results, and error text.

  • A job (JobStart/JobEnd): job_id, name, version, job_hash, input_hash, resumable, resumed_from, and the trace carrier that came with the message (see OpenTelemetry); at the end: status, error type.
  • An attempt: one per row of attempts. Agent name, version, description and hash, run_id, attempt, parent_attempt_id (the agent that launched it), parent_tool_call_id (the tool call that launched it), depth, provider, model, whether it is a streaming run; at the end: status, tokens, final (the attempt succeeded, or it was the last one allowed), error type.
  • A reused step (RunReused): a step of a resumed job that was answered from the result store, with reused_from_attempt_id and the resumed_from job. It is not an attempt, and has no model calls.
  • A model call: provider, model, the model the API reported, the finish reasons, input and output tokens, duration; with content: the messages.
  • A tool call: tool name and call id (the id the model gave it; the OpenTelemetry tool type is always function); with content: arguments and result. A tool that launches an agent (the runner's launch tools) has the launched agent's attempt as its child.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry
docs.text:
OTelObserver ships in the package. It needs opentelemetry-api only (the extra featherweight[otel]). With no SDK configured the API does nothing, so it costs nothing to use. The user configures the SDK and the exporter as for any application.

The spans follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions:

Ours Span Kind A job invoke_workflow {job name} internal An attempt of an agent invoke_agent {agent name} internal A model call chat {model} client A tool call execute_tool {tool name} internal A reused step invoke_agent {agent name}, with ftw.reused internal
  • Nesting: a job holds the attempts of its pipeline; an attempt holds its model calls and tool calls; a tool that launches an agent holds that agent's attempt. The parent of an attempt comes from the tool call that launched it (parent_tool_call_id) or else from parent_attempt_id, and not only from the current span, because a launched agent runs in another task. Retries are siblings that share ftw.run.id. The job of a background job is under the tool call that started it: the submitted hook is told the tool call (JobSubmitted.parent_attempt_id and parent_tool_call_id, which are for observers and stored nowhere), and OTelObserver gives the carrier of that call's span.
  • Attributes from the conventions: gen_ai.operation.name (invoke_workflow, invoke_agent, chat, execute_tool), gen_ai.agent.name (an agent's name, and a job's name: the conventions call it the name of "the GenAI agent or workflow"), gen_ai.agent.version, gen_ai.agent.description, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.tool.name, gen_ai.tool.call.id, gen_ai.tool.type (always function), and error.type (the error type, never the text). On a model call also gen_ai.provider.name (required there, and only there: gcp.gen_ai for Google, and anthropic and openai as they are), gen_ai.response.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens and gen_ai.response.finish_reasons. An attempt does not repeat the token counts as gen_ai.usage.*, so that a platform that sums them over a trace counts each token once; its totals are ftw.tokens.*.
  • Content, opt-in: gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, gen_ai.system_instructions, gen_ai.tool.call.arguments, gen_ai.tool.call.result, in the JSON structure the conventions give (a job's or an agent's typed input and output are the text of one user or assistant message, as JSON). Python span attributes cannot hold an object, so they are JSON strings. gen_ai.tool.definitions is not emitted: the records do not carry the tool definitions. Content is set only when it is on. OTelObserver(capture_content=...) decides, and its default follows the conventions' own switch, OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_CONTENT: NO_CONTENT (the default) or SPAN_ONLY are supported; the values that send content as events are not, and are logged and treated as NO_CONTENT.
  • Ours, in the ftw. namespace: ftw.job.id, ftw.job.name, ftw.job.version, ftw.job.hash, ftw.job.execution (1 for the first execution of the job, one more for each takeover: several workers), ftw.agent.hash, ftw.attempt.id (the attempt_id), ftw.run.id, ftw.attempt and ftw.attempts (the number, and how many are allowed), ftw.attempt.final, ftw.tokens.input and ftw.tokens.output (the attempt's totals), ftw.reused, ftw.reused_from_attempt_id, ftw.resumed_from.
  • A rejected attempt ends its span with an error status and error.type (the exception type, for example the type that check_output raised). The attempt that counted has ftw.attempt.final = true.
  • A reused step is a span with no model-call children and ftw.reused = true, with the ids that say where it came from. The ids are how you find the original run; no span link, because we do not store span ids.
  • The trace crosses the queue. JobClient asks its observers for a carrier on submit (the W3C traceparent and tracestate of the current span), and the message carries it as trace_context. The worker passes it to its observers, so that the job's span joins the client's trace. It travels in the message only, and is stored nowhere by us.

Pinned to the conventions. The GenAI conventions are in the Development status and live in their own repository, with no release and no schema URL yet, so they will change.

  • One constant in the code names the version we follow (GENAI_CONVENTIONS in otel.py: the repository and the commit that was read, now 622b2b6073b15e5ed886c3c12a65a892b9cd5c70 of 2026-11-20, with CORE_CONVENTIONS, the core version it refers to), and docs/observability.md will have a table from each featherweight version to the convention version it follows.
  • A test checks every attribute name we emit against ATTRIBUTES, a list kept with the code, and the list is updated by hand when we move to a newer convention. A change to an attribute name is a breaking change in the changelog.
  • The extra pins opentelemetry-api to a range. We use the attribute names as strings, so we do not depend on the package that carries the constants.

docs.title: Your own spans
docs.text:
A span around your own code is yours. You use the OpenTelemetry API directly:

with tracer.start_as_current_span("load documents"):
    docs = await load()
    result = await ctx.run(Summariser, docs)
  • featherweight offers nothing for it. The one connection is OpenTelemetry's own rule, that a span that is current while your code runs is the parent of the spans started inside it. OTelObserver makes the job span and the attempt span current while the work runs (this is what the wrapping hooks are for), so your span is under the job, and our attempts are under your span.
  • Without OTelObserver there is no job span, and your spans are simply roots. That is not an error.
  • A tool that you write and that starts a span nests under the attempt's tool span only when the callback runs in the tool's own context; the guide says that your own spans inside a tool may be attached to the attempt and not to the tool call.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Evaluation platforms read traces. For a trace to be useful to them it needs the path and the content, which is why model calls and tool calls have their own spans, and why content is an opt-in switch and not a different feature.

  • To evaluate the answer: turn content on. The span of an attempt has the input and the final output; the model call has the messages.
  • To evaluate the path: the tool calls, in order, with their arguments and results, under the attempt that made them.
  • To tell which attempt counted: ftw.attempt.final, and error.type on the ones that were rejected.
  • To compare versions: the agent name, version and hash, the job name and version (a job's version), and the model are on the spans. The code release is the OpenTelemetry resource attribute service.version, which the user sets (a git sha or a tag), and which evaluation platforms already group by.
  • We do not run evaluations, score, or have a feedback API.

docs.title: What changes
docs.text:
• New: Observer and its records, testing.check_observer, OTelObserver, and the extra featherweight[otel].
  • Elsewhere, each in the spec that owns it: the runner calls observers (runner); JobMessage.trace_context and JobClient(observers=) (submitted jobs); run_job runs a job class, and the job version (jobs); SqliteDatabase(":memory:") and jobs.job_version (persistence).
  • Not changed: the run log's tables for attempts, the result store, resuming, the job events, SSE.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• One concept, observers; OpenTelemetry is one of them, and the one we ship.
  • Inline calls, with a timeout and no failures. Simple, ordered, and it is what lets a span be current while the work runs.
  • Metadata always, content on request, by a flag on the observer, so nothing is built for content that nobody wants.
  • The GenAI conventions, with our own attributes under ftw., so that the platforms read our traces on day one.
  • Spans for model calls and tool calls, because evaluation needs the path. The cost is the callback handler.
  • No trace or span ids in the run log. They are the application's. The reuse reference is the ids we already store.
  • No API for your own spans. The principle is a clean line between what we offer and what you do.
  • Observers are on the runner, so a job run by run_job and a job run by a worker report the same way, and nothing is reported twice.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Running evaluations, scoring, datasets, or a feedback API.
  • A featherweight API for spans around your own code, or span links to a reused run's original span.
  • Content as events (the conventions' EVENT_ONLY and SPAN_AND_EVENT), and per-token events for a streaming run.
  • Metrics and logs through OpenTelemetry. Spans only. The logger lines stay as they are.
  • Storing any trace data, and an observer that changes a run.
  • A different tracing library than OpenTelemetry as a product feature. Write an observer.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
No live model call. Fake models (with tool calls), MemoryQueue, an in-memory span exporter from the OpenTelemetry SDK (a dev dependency only).

  • Observers: every hook is called in order and with the right records; an observer that raises, or is too slow, changes nothing; content is built only when an observer asks; check_observer against a no-op observer and a recording one.
  • The callback handler: model calls and tool calls of a fake model, with timings, and with a launched agent under its tool call.
  • OpenTelemetry: the span tree of a job with retries, a launched agent and a reused step; every attribute name against the list; content off and on; the status and error.type of a rejected attempt; ftw.attempt.final; the trace context from a client to a worker; your own span inside a job; no SDK means no spans and no errors.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
Tracked in epic #90. One issue and one pull request each, in this order. The first, #91, is specified in jobs, and the others depend on it:

  1. #91 run_job runs a job class (built; specified in the jobs spec, as above).
  2. #92 The Observer class, its records, check_observer, the runner's calls, the callback handler for model and tool calls, and the content switch.
  3. #93 Jobs, and the trace across the queue: the job scope for run_job and the worker, JobMessage.trace_context, JobClient observers, the queue kit.
  4. #94 OTelObserver: the GenAI mapping, the ftw. attributes, the pinned version and its test, featherweight[otel].
  5. #95 The guide, an example, the skill, and dropping "OpenTelemetry? Too big" from the README.

docs.title: Run log and persistence
docs.text:
Status: implemented (epic #58 is done: #59 the agent hash, #60 resumable jobs and the result store, #61 the Database abstract class and the metadata-only schema, #62 PostgresDatabase, #63 the guide and the example). It is tracked in epic #58, and each part has its own issue (listed at the end). When a part is built, this page says so, and the guide docs/persistence.md shows how to use it.

It changes jobs (the database, the schema, the migrations, resumable jobs), the runner (resuming reads through a result store), agents (what agent_hash covers, resuming a job) and streaming agents (the run log of a streaming run).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
featherweight is a harness, not a data store. It keeps the state of the orchestration: what ran, in what order, which agent launched which, with what outcome, at what cost, and which hashes identify the declaration and the input. It does not keep the data that flowed through it: inputs, outputs, messages, results. Where data has to be kept for a feature (resuming a job), the user provides the place.

This keeps the framework small and neutral. A deployment decides where its data lives, who can read it and how long it stays, and the metadata can be shared and read freely because it holds nothing of a client's.

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
featherweight keeps featherweight never keeps Jobs: status, timing, whether a retry points to an earlier job The input of an agent Every attempt: agent, model, status, tokens, timing The output of an agent, or the result of a job The launch tree (parent, depth) The messages of a conversation Hashes of what was declared, given and produced The words of a prompt or of a tool result The type of an error, and a hash of its message The text of an error What a run matched (which row it reused), and the thread of a chat The names of tools

There is one exception, and it is the user's to place: a result store holds the outputs that resuming a job reads back, only for a job that opted in, in a store that the user implements. We ship one for sqlite, which is a local development database.

docs.title: Hashes
docs.text:
A hash says that something changed without saying what it was, so it can stand where content or client information could show.

Column What it identifies Why it is separate agent_hash The whole declaration: prompt, version, limits, model settings, tools, sub-agents, skills, MCP servers, the assembled system prompt, and the input and output schemas Same hash, same agent system_prompt_hash The assembled system prompt When a step reruns after a resume, this says the prompt changed tools_hash The tools bound to the model (names, descriptions, argument schemas) Replaces tool_names: a tool's name can be client-specific. It says the tools changed input_hash The input, as canonical JSON Matches the same input again output_hash The output, as canonical JSON (every agent, and a streaming run's text) Compares two runs without keeping either identity_hash The SHA-256 of the identity of the run (its kind, the name of its class, and its fields as canonical JSON, without its excluded fields); NULL when there is none A resume reuses only a step of the same identity, and no identity is stored (identity)

agent_hash and the schemas. (Done in #59.) Before it, agent_hash left out input_model and output_model, which are class attributes and not instance fields, so a changed output model does not change the hash. That is an oversight: the declaration includes them. Their JSON schemas are added, and every hash changed (this was before the first release). check_output is code and cannot be hashed: version is its signal, and a reused output is checked against it again.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A failed run keeps error_type (the class name, such as ValidationError or RateLimitError) and error_hash (SHA-256 of the message), not the text. Messages come from places we do not write: Pydantic quotes the offending value, check_output is the user's code (the README's own example puts names in it), tools and providers say what they like. No formatting of ours can promise that a message holds no data.

  • Recurring errors still group (same type, same hash), and a failure can be told from another without the words.
  • The full text is in the logs (a deployment keeps them if it wants to) and in the RUN_ERROR event of a streaming run, which the client sees.
  • A job that fails keeps the same two columns.

docs.title: The database
docs.text:
Database is an abstract class: what the runner and run_job need, and nothing about sqlite. An implementation that does not write every abstract method cannot be built.

Method connect(), close(), async with Open and close; connect() runs the migrations create_job(...), insert_job(...), get_job(job_id), set_job_status(...) Create, read and change a job. A change of status writes its event in the same transaction start_job(job_id), cancel_queued_job(job_id), fail_queued_job(job_id, error_type, error_hash), request_job_cancel(job_id), list_cancel_requested(job_ids) The compare-and-set steps that take or cancel a job, so that exactly one of a worker and a client wins (cancelling) list_job_events(job_id, after, limit), poll_job_events(job_ids, after) The events of one job, or of many in one query renew_job_leases(worker_id, jobs, lease), owns_job(job_id, owner) A worker's heartbeat (one in-place update for all of its jobs, returning the ones it still owns), and a cheap read of whether it still owns one (several workers). set_job_status(..., owner=) and the lease renewal are conditional on the owner, in the statement, and raise JobLost when it is not take_over_job(job_id, worker_id, lease) Taking a job whose lease expired: one transaction, a lost event and then a running event, executions + 1, a new lease; False if the lease is live. Where the database has a clock, it decides (several workers) create_attempt(AttemptRecord), start_attempt(...), finish_attempt(AttemptFinish), get_attempt(...), list_attempts(...) Attempts job_has_other_identity(job_id, identity_hash) Whether the job has a run whose identity hash differs from this one (None differs from any hash, and the reverse): the check that a job is for one identity (identity) find_reusable_attempt(job_id, agent_hash, input_hash, identity_hash, before_execution=None) The attempt of a job that succeeded, at depth 1 (a step), with this agent, input and identity (NULL, no identity, matches only NULL): metadata only. With before_execution, only attempts of an earlier execution of the job (a takeover looks in its own job)

Typed in, typed out. create_attempt and finish_attempt take frozen Pydantic records (AttemptRecord, AttemptFinish), and the methods return Pydantic rows (JobRow, AttemptRow). Statuses, hash formats and non-negative numbers are checked once, in the model, whichever database sits behind it; a wrong type from an implementation fails when the row is built. Timestamps are datetime objects: each implementation converts what its database stores.

Two implementations, and a third is possible. SqliteDatabase(path) is for local development, and PostgresDatabase(dsn) is for deployment. Choosing is one line, and the runner does not change:

db = SqliteDatabase("featherweight.db")  # local
db = PostgresDatabase("postgresql://...")  # deployed
runner = AgentRunner(db)

In memory. SqliteDatabase(":memory:") keeps everything (the jobs, the events, the run log and the default result store) in memory: no file and no service, and it is gone when the database closes. It is the same code and the same migrations. It is for trying a job and for tests .

Another database is an implementation of the class. To make that safe, the schema is documented (every column, its type, nullability and constraint), the rows and records are models, and a conformance kit (featherweight.testing) runs the contract against any implementation. Our two pass it.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
The schema is made by hand-rolled, numbered, dialect-aware migrations: a list of Migration(version, name, sqlite, postgres), applied in order by connect(), each in a transaction, and recorded in schema_migrations (version, name, applied_at). The sqlite-only patching of added columns is gone. A later change is a new migration with the SQL of each dialect, and a migration is never edited once released. Migration 2, identity_hash, adds attempts.identity_hash (NULL for every run from before it). Migration 3, queue_identity, adds job_queue.identity; migration 5, queue_identity_kind, adds job_queue.identity_kind. Migration 6, attempt_constraints, renames the Postgres constraints of attempts from agent_runs_... to attempts_... (ALTER TABLE ... RENAME does not), and does nothing on sqlite. The migrations are not squashed into one baseline: each says what changed, and when.

The baseline migration creates the schema of the first release, and is never edited. It carried nothing over from the database that came before migrations existed, which was never released: that one is not read. A database that has attempts but no schema_migrations raises SetupError ("this database is from before migrations: delete it and run again").

Concurrent first connects. Processes that connect to a fresh database at the same moment (an API and workers started together) must not race on the schema and the tables. On Postgres, connect() takes a session advisory lock, keyed on the schema (pg_advisory_lock on a hash of featherweight:<schema>), around creating the schema and applying the migrations, and releases it after: one connection makes the tables, and the others wait and then find them applied. Different schemas do not block each other. sqlite takes the write lock for each migration (BEGIN IMMEDIATE), reads what is applied inside it, and skips a migration that another process applied while it waited: its file locking alone is not enough, because each process reads the applied versions first, and with several migrations a late process would run an old one on a schema that another had already changed (found with eight processes on one fresh file, five trials: no such table: agent_runs). A database that is up to date takes no lock. A connection waits for another's lock up to 30 seconds.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
Types are given as Postgres / sqlite. A CHECK is in both.

attempts, one row per attempt:

Column Type seq bigint identity / integer autoincrement Monotonic, for ordering (sqlite's rowid has no equal everywhere) attempt_id text primary key (sqlite: unique, seq is the key) The attempt run_id text not null Attempts of one call share it attempt integer not null, >= 1 job_id text null, foreign key jobs parent_attempt_id text null The launch tree depth integer not null, >= 1 1 at the top agent_name, agent_version text not null The agent, readable agent_hash, system_prompt_hash, tools_hash text not null, 64 hex See hashes provider, model_name text not null What was asked for reported_model_name text null What the API reported reasoning text not null The effort or thinking level, as a short label settings jsonb / text not null All the model settings input_hash text not null, 64 hex identity_hash text null, 64 hex The hash of the run's identity (its kind and its fields), NULL when it had none (identity); added by a migration output_hash text null, 64 hex Set when the attempt produced one reused_from_attempt_id text null For an attempt answered from an earlier one job_execution integer null The execution of the job that made the attempt (several workers): given by the task that runs the job, or else the job's executions when the attempt is created. NULL without a job thread_id text null For a streaming run: the conversation the client named status text not null, one of INIT, RUNNING, SUCCESS, FAILED, CANCELLED error_type, error_hash text null Set for FAILED input_tokens, output_tokens integer null, >= 0 latency_ms double precision / real null created_at, started_at, completed_at timestamptz / text (ISO 8601, UTC) Created (waiting for a slot), holds a slot, ended

Indexes: job_id, run_id, parent_attempt_id, and (job_id, agent_hash, input_hash) for the lookup of a step to reuse.

Gone from today's table: input, output (data), tool_names (names can be client-specific; tools_hash replaces it), and error (replaced by error_type and error_hash). New: seq, tools_hash, started_at, error_type, error_hash, and output_hash for every agent. The placeholders a streaming run used for input and output are gone. The column count is about the same: the change is in what the table holds. Audited and kept: agent_version (a hash is not readable), system_prompt_hash (says what changed), reasoning and settings, reported_model_name, latency_ms.

jobs, one row per job:

Column Type job_id text primary key name text not null status text not null, as for attempts See statuses resumable boolean / integer not null, default false Decided when the job is created: it keeps the results of its steps resumed_from text null, foreign key jobs The job this one resumes job_hash, input_hash text null A submitted job: the hash of its declaration and of its input. NULL for a job made without a job class cancel_requested boolean / integer not null, default false A running job that was asked to stop parent_attempt_id text null The attempt that started this job as a background job. NULL for any other job worker_id, lease_expires_at text null, timestamptz / text null The worker that runs the job (the last one, once it ended), and when its lease ends (NULL while queued, when final, and for a job run in your process). Renewed in place; Postgres uses its own clock executions integer not null, default 0, >= 0 How many times a worker started the job; 1 for the first, one more each time it is started again error_type, error_hash text null Set for FAILED created_at, started_at, completed_at timestamptz / text started_at is cleared when the job goes back to the queue

job_events, one row for every change of a job's status, written in the same transaction as the change: seq (monotonic, across all jobs), job_id (foreign key jobs), type (queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled, cancel_requested, lost), status (the status after the change), error_type, error_hash, at. Index: (job_id, seq). Metadata only; submitted jobs says how they are read and streamed.

job_queue (sqlite only: the queue we ship, see the queue): seq, job_id, job_name, input (JSON: this is the one table that holds a job's input, until the message is acknowledged), trace_context (JSON: the submitter's trace context, if an observer gave one; the one place it is kept, and gone with the message), identity (JSON) and identity_kind (the class name): who the run is for, kept with the input until the message is acknowledged and nowhere else, state (ready, claimed or dead), enqueued_at, claimed_at, lease_expires_at (when the claim's lease ends) and delivery_count (how many times it has been delivered).

results (the sqlite result store only): job_id, agent_hash, input_hash (together the primary key), output (text, JSON), created_at. schema_migrations: version (primary key), name, applied_at.

docs.title: The result store
docs.text:
The outputs that resuming a job reads back go through an abstract class that the user implements:

class ResultStore(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    async def put(self, key: ResultKey, output: dict[str, Any]) -> None: ...
    @abstractmethod
    async def get(self, key: ResultKey) -> dict[str, Any] | None: ...
    @abstractmethod
    async def delete_job(self, job_id: str) -> None: ...


class ResultKey(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)

    job_id: str
    agent_hash: str = Field(pattern=r"^[0-9a-f]{64}$")
    input_hash: str = Field(pattern=r"^[0-9a-f]{64}$")

ResultKey is a frozen Pydantic model, like every typed class here (records, rows, settings): no dataclasses. A malformed hash is refused when the key is built, for every store; the conformance kit uses real hashes.

The contract. An output is JSON (a dict). get returns what put stored for the key, equal as JSON, or None. put on a key that exists replaces it. Calls can be concurrent. delete_job removes every result of a job and does not fail when there are none. A conformance kit (featherweight.testing.check_result_store) runs these rules against any store, so that an implementation is checked, not trusted; it is how a tenant-scoped store, a bucket or Redis is verified.

What we ship. SqliteResultStore (a results table in the file of the run log) is the default with a SqliteDatabase, and MemoryResultStore (a dict, in featherweight.testing) is for tests and is the smallest example of the class. There is no Postgres store: how results are kept in a deployment (a database per tenant, a table per tenant, something else) is for the user to decide. With a PostgresDatabase the default is no store: pass results=, or resume is unavailable.

Opt-in, per job. Results are stored only for a job created resumable=True, decided before the pipeline runs (run_job(runner, job, input, resumable=True), db.create_job(name, resumable=True)). A job that does not need to be resumed holds nothing. A job created with resume_from is resumable too, so that a third attempt is possible.

What is stored. The output of a top-level run (depth 1) that succeeds inside a resumable job. Not a run with no job, a launched agent (reusing launched agents is parked), a streaming run, or a failure.

docs.title: Resuming a job
docs.text:
Which steps of a failed job are reused, and the checks on them, are the runner's (resuming); what a resumed job means for a pipeline is the job's (resuming a job). What is persistence's is where the pieces are kept:

  1. The old job must have been resumable. If it was not, create_job raises, before any model call, saying that nothing was kept (a full rerun is a run without resume_from).
  2. The log answers the metadata question: find_reusable_attempt(old_job, agent_hash, input_hash, identity_hash) is a SUCCESS run of the old job at depth 1, with the same identity.
  3. The store answers the data question: get(ResultKey(old_job, agent_hash, input_hash)). A runner with no store, for a job that resumes another, is a SetupError.
  4. A reused step's result is copied forward under the new job's key (a takeover has no new job, so nothing is copied: several workers). Each job then holds its own results, deleting an old job never affects a newer one, and a chain of attempts works. The duplication is only the output; the trace is complete and the cost is counted once.

docs.title: Postgres
docs.text:
PostgresDatabase(dsn, schema="featherweight") implements Database with psycopg (version 3, async), behind the extra featherweight[postgres] (a SetupError with the install line when it is missing; importing featherweight never imports it). It runs the same migrations with the postgres SQL of each, with native types (timestamptz, jsonb, boolean, an identity column), because Postgres is the deployment choice. The tables live in their own schema (a lowercase identifier, created when it does not exist), so they never collide with an application's tables. The session is UTC and each statement commits (a migration runs in one transaction). One connection per PostgresDatabase, like sqlite; a pool is a later step.

There is no results table and no Postgres result store: with a PostgresDatabase the runner has no default store, so pass results= (or resume is unavailable).

Testing: the Database conformance kit, the migration tests and the type checks run against Postgres. A postgres service in compose.yaml (a healthy dependency of the featherweight service, and on 127.0.0.1:5432) makes the Docker unit tests run them with FTW_TEST_POSTGRES_URL set; without it those tests are skipped, so a plain pytest still runs. Each test gets a schema of its own and drops it.

docs.title: Tenants
docs.text: There is no tenant column and no tenant label: the metadata holds nothing of a client's, so one database can be shared. A user who needs to attribute runs to a tenant chooses the job id (create_job(name, job_id="acme-...")) or the job name. An identity is carried to the tools and never stored: only its hash is recorded. A result store that must route by tenant can do so from the job id of its keys, or be one per tenant.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• Metadata only, for every agent. The rule is the framework's, not a streaming special case.
  • Hashes where names or content could show: tools_hash instead of tool_names, error_type and error_hash instead of the text.
  • Pydantic for every typed class (records, rows, keys, settings), not dataclasses: one way to define a typed object, with validation for free. (The three dataclasses that exist today are internal runtime objects, left as they are.)
  • Abstract classes (Database, ResultStore), not protocols: an implementation that misses a method cannot be built. A conformance kit checks behaviour, which neither a protocol nor an abstract class can.
  • A result store only for sqlite, opt-in per job, keyed by (job, agent hash, input hash), with the result copied forward.
  • A retry is a new job that points to the old one; resuming from a job that was not resumable is an error.
  • One baseline migration, no carry-over from before it: the database that came before migrations was never released.
  • Native types on Postgres, text on sqlite; the conversion is each implementation's job, and the rows are datetimes.
  • psycopg 3, own schema, hand-rolled migrations.
  • Logs and the streaming RUN_ERROR keep the full error text: a deployment keeps logs only if it wants to, and the client deals with what it is sent.
  • Job ids and thread ids are the user's: we do not hash them.
  • No tenant label.
  • Content leaves only through an observer, one that asks for it (observers and OpenTelemetry); it is never stored by us.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Reading an old database. Delete it.
  • Content in the run log, for any agent, even by option.
  • A Postgres result store. The user writes one.
  • Results for a run with no job, a launched agent, a streaming run or a job that is not resumable.
  • A TTL, size limit or encryption in the store contract: the implementation's business.
  • A pool for Postgres: later.
  • Jobs across processes (queue, workers, leases): the jobs epic, which builds on this one.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
No live model call. Fake models, and the dict store.

  • Conformance kits: the Database contract against sqlite and, when a URL is set, Postgres; the ResultStore contract against the sqlite store and the dict store.
  • Migrations: applied once, in order, recorded; a second connect() does nothing; an old database is refused; several processes connecting to a fresh Postgres schema at the same moment all connect, and the migration is applied once.
  • Metadata only: after runs of every kind (success, failure, retry, reused, launched, streaming, stopped), no table holds an input, an output, a message or an error text, and no column named input, output, tool_names or error exists.
  • Typed models: a wrong status, a malformed hash or a negative token count is refused when the record or row is built.
  • Resume: success, a rejected check_output, a missing result, a failing put, a chain of three attempts with the first job's results deleted, no store, a non-resumable old job, nothing stored for the cases listed above.
  • The agent hash: a change to either schema changes it.
  • The rest of the suite moves to the new records and rows.

docs.text: Issue #58 The epic #59 The agent hash includes the input and output schemas #60 Resumable jobs and the ResultStore; resume through it #61 The Database abstract class, typed records and rows, SqliteDatabase, migrations, the metadata-only schema #62 PostgresDatabase #63 The guide, an example and the skill reference

docs.title: Agent runner
docs.text:
Status: implemented. How to use it is in agents.md and launching-agents.md. The code is runner.py.

  • Goal
  • Running
  • The result
  • Attempts and retries
  • Concurrency
  • Launching agents
  • Tools and connections
  • Configuration
  • Logging
