docs.title: Goal
docs.text: AgentRunner runs agent definitions: it validates, calls the model, checks what came back, retries, limits concurrency, lets an agent launch other agents, and records every attempt (jobs). It is not a workflow engine. Order, loops, branching and when to stop are the caller's code. A runner is not tied to one agent: the agent is chosen on each call, and one runner can run any number of different agents.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
result = await runner.run(AgentClass, agent_input, job_id=job_id)
results = await runner.run_many(AgentClass, inputs, job_id=job_id)
  • run takes the class and an input that is an instance of its input_model.
  • run_many runs one agent over many inputs at the same time and returns the results in input order. It has no limit of its own: the concurrency limit bounds it.
  • job_id is optional. Runs of one pipeline share a job. Without one, the runs have no job.
  • identity= is who the run is for. Whether it is optional or required depends on the type the runner declares (AgentRunner(db, identity_type=...)): a declared type makes it required, a union with None allows none, and with nothing declared passing one is an error. run, run_many and stream take it. See identity.
  • Runtime failures are values. run returns a FAILED result. It does not raise.
  • Programming errors raise: an input of the wrong type (TypeError), a job_id that does not exist, an identity that is missing, of the wrong type, or given when no type is declared (TypeError), and an identity that is not the one of the job: a job is for one identity (ValueError, identity). run_many checks the identity once, at the call, also for no inputs; stream checks the job's identity when the loop starts.
  • A streaming agent is not run with run: it raises TypeError and names stream. stream(StreamingAgent, ChatInput, job_id=...) returns a StreamingRun at once, whose events come as the model writes (streaming agents). It takes a concurrency slot like any run, holds it for the whole stream, and is never retried. cancel(run_id) stops a streaming run of this runner by its id and says whether there was one (stopping a response).

docs.title: The result
docs.text: AgentResult[OutT]: status (SUCCESS or FAILED only), output (the validated output model, on success), error (the last error, on failure), attempt_id (the last attempt), input_tokens, output_tokens (thinking included), attempts, latency_ms (across attempts), model_name (as the API reported it, which can differ from the one requested) and reused (see resuming). Tokens are summed over the model calls of the successful attempt. The tool results the model read are in its input tokens. A failed result has no tokens.

docs.title: Resuming
docs.text:
A takeover of a job (several workers) uses the same rules, with one difference: the source is the same job, and only runs of earlier executions (job_execution below the current one) are looked up, so a run never reuses its own execution's rows. The result is read under this job's own key, so nothing is copied forward, and only a resumable job is looked up. A job that resumes another and was taken over looks in itself first, then in the old job. The execution that asks is the one that the task running the job has (not the job row's: a worker that lost the job and has not noticed is still the execution it was).

A job created with resume_from (see jobs) makes the runner look up a run before it runs it. This is replay with memoised agent calls: the caller's code runs again, and only runs are answered from the log.

  • Where. At the start of a run, once per run call, before the attempt loop, and only when depth is 1 and there is a job_id. A sub-agent (depth above 1) is never looked up.
  • The match. In the old job: status = SUCCESS, the same agent_hash, the same input_hash, the same identity_hash (NULL, no identity, matches only NULL: identity), depth = 1. Any matching row will do. A row with no agent_hash or input_hash never matches. The log is the metadata question.
  • The result. The output comes from the runner's ResultStore (get(ResultKey(old job, agent hash, input hash))). No store (results=None) is a SetupError; no result for a step that the log says succeeded logs result_missing and the runs.
  • The check. The kept output is validated against the current output model, then check_output(agent_input, output) runs again. If either fails, run_reuse_rejected reason=... is logged and the agent runs normally.
  • What is kept. The output of a depth-1 run that succeeds inside a resumable job, put in the store after the row is finished. A store that fails does not fail the run (result_not_kept is logged). A reused run copies its result to the new job.
  • The reused run. It writes one SUCCESS row in the new job, with a new attempt_id, zero tokens, the stored output and reused_from_attempt_id. It logs run_reused run_id=... attempt_id=... reused_from_attempt_id=..., calls no model, builds no MCP connection and takes no slot. The result has reused=True, zero tokens and attempts=1.
  • run_many resumes per input, since each input is one run call.
  • Not covered. The determinism of the caller's code between agents (the caller's responsibility, not checked), state that a run kept in memory (a reused run does not run, so it is not rebuilt), side effects of tools, reuse of sub-agent runs, rows from before agent_hash.

docs.title: Attempts and retries
docs.text:
Each attempt is one row in the run log, and goes through these steps:

  1. The tools of the attempt are collected, and MCP servers are started if needed (below). The row is created as INIT.
  2. The attempt waits for a concurrency slot. Then the row becomes RUNNING.
  3. The chat model is built (a failure here is a setup error), the agent is run through langgraph, the structured reply is validated, and check_output runs.
  4. The row is finished as SUCCESS with the output, or FAILED with the error.

Retries. A failed attempt is retried, up to max_attempts (3). The wait between attempts is retry_delay_s (1s), and it does not hold a concurrency slot.

  • A retry resamples with the same input. The error is recorded in the log but is not sent back to the model. If a retry should know what went wrong, the pipeline does that: it builds a new input.
  • Failed attempts: an API error, a reply that does not validate, no structured reply, a rejection by check_output, an early answer, the recursion limit, and any other exception.
  • Not retried (the run fails at once): a SetupError (no API key, an unknown model, an MCP server that cannot start, two tools with one name), and any 4xx response except 408, 409 and 429, found on the exception or its causes.
  • A FAILED result carries the last attempt's error, with its type, at most 2,000 characters.

docs.title: An early answer
docs.text:
Where the output is asked for as a tool call (LangChain's ToolStrategy: Claude Haiku 5.5 today), the model is given the output as one more tool, and it can call it in the same reply as other tools. LangChain then takes the answer, runs the other tools and ends: the model never sees what they returned, and the answer is empty or made up.

The runner refuses a run whose last reply holds the output's call and other calls, with EarlyAnswerError (a ValueError), before check_output. The attempt fails and is retried like any other. By then the other tools have run, and a retry runs them again, which is the rule for every failed attempt: a tool must be safe to run twice. A streaming agent has no typed output, and is not checked.

It is the runner's, and not the model settings' (decided 2026-11-26). It is about how a run ended, it is the same pattern whatever model made it, and no provider needs another rule. A hook on the settings would be a way to switch the check off that nothing needs; if a provider ever needs a rule of its own for a reply, the hook can come with it. Rejected: middleware that sends the answer back to the model (models). Seen once on the real API (Claude Haiku 5.5, thinking on): one model call, the tool ran, and every field was empty. The reply was not kept; the case was reproduced with a fake model.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: A semaphore of max_concurrent slots (FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS, default 10) bounds the attempts that run at once on one runner, across every agent. A queued attempt shows as INIT until it holds a slot. The slot is released between attempts.

docs.title: Launching agents
docs.text:
An agent can hand part of its work to another agent: it launches it, waits, and reads the result.

The identity. A launched agent runs with the identity of its parent, and the model cannot set or change it (identity).

Declaration. subagents is an allow-list of agent classes: the agent can launch exactly those. There is no registry to maintain. The agent definition checks the list (agents).

What the model gets, for an agent with sub-agents and depth left (can_launch = bool(sub-agents) and depth < max_depth):

  • the prompt lists the agents it may launch, by name and description;
  • two tools built for each attempt: get_agent_schema(agent_name), which returns the agent's name, description and input and output JSON schemas, and launch_agent(agent_name, input_json), which validates input_json against the child's input model, runs the child to the end and returns the result.

input_json is a string, because Gemini can reject a function parameter that is an object with no declared properties (checked with the real model).

Both tools always return text and never raise into the parent's run, so that the model can read what happened:

Case What comes back The child succeeds {"status": "SUCCESS", "agent": "...", "output": {...}} The child fails after its own retries {"status": "FAILED", "agent": "...", "error": "..."} A name that is not on the allow-list 'x' is not an agent you can launch. You can launch: ... The input does not fit the child's input model The input for 'x' is not valid: ... Check get_agent_schema and try again. The depth or the launch limit is reached A sentence saying which limit

The child is an ordinary run. It has its own retries, tools, skills, MCP servers and sub-agents, and its own rows in the log. It shares the parent's job. Its row records parent_attempt_id (the attempt that launched it) and depth (1 for a top-level run). The parent sees only the child's output, as a tool result, which counts in the parent's input tokens. A model may launch several agents in one turn, and they run at the same time. A retried parent attempt launches its children again, and the earlier children stay in the log under the failed attempt.

Limits.

  • Depth (max_depth, default 3): the most agents in one chain, the first included. A depth of 1 turns launching off. At the limit an agent gets no launch tools and no mention of them in its prompt, and the tool refuses a call made anyway.
  • Breadth (max_launches, default 10): the most launches one attempt of one agent may make. Launches that fail validation do not count. It is per attempt, not per job, so with the defaults a tree can reach 1 + 10 + 100 = 111 agents before retries. This is different from recursion_limit, which bounds the steps of one agent's own tool loop.

A launched child blocks its parent. One that does not is a background job, which is a job and has its own spec. The runner gives it start_background (and settings max_background_jobs and background=); the rules are there.

The slot hand-over. A parent that waits for its child holds a slot the child needs, and with enough waiting parents nothing could finish. So a parent gives up its slot while its launches run and takes one again when the last of them is done, also when it launched several at once. The limit on model calls at one time still holds, because a waiting parent is not calling the model.

docs.title: Tools and connections
docs.text:
Each attempt builds a tool registry from the agent's tools, the tools of its MCP servers, and the tools the runner adds: launch_agent and get_agent_schema (with sub-agents and depth left) and get_skill (with skills) and search_tools and call_tool (with an MCP server that is found by search). A failure to build it is a setup error.

MCP connections are the runner's, shared by every agent it runs (MCP tools). A run holds a lease on its servers from its first attempt to its last, so a retry does not start a server again, and lets go when it is done. A server stops when its last lease is released. async with AgentRunner(...), or await runner.aclose(), is optional: it keeps servers up between runs and stops them at the end. A runner with no MCP agents needs neither.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Argument Environment variable Default max_attempts 3 At least 1 retry_delay_s 1.0 max_concurrent FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS 10 At least 1 max_depth FTW_MAX_AGENT_DEPTH 3 At least 1 max_launches FTW_MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES 10 At least 1 max_background_jobs FTW_MAX_BACKGROUND_JOBS 3 At least 1

An argument wins over the variable. A value below 1, or an environment variable that is not an integer, raises, and names the variable. The settings of the runner that have no argument, such as the timeout of an observer, and the rule for all of them, are in configuration. The key of the provider (GOOGLE_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY) is needed for the real model. A missing key is a setup error: the run fails at once, without retries.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: run_started and run_finished (with attempts, tokens and latency), attempt_started, attempt_failed (with non_retryable), retry_waiting, waiting_for_slot and slot_acquired, fan_out_started and fan_out_finished, agent_launch (parent, child, depth and launch count), skill_read, and the mcp_* lines. All are plain key=value text through logging.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
Built (#92 and #93). What an observer is, and what it receives, is in observers and OpenTelemetry. What the runner does:

  • Where they are set. AgentRunner(db, observers=[...]); the timeout is FTW_OBSERVER_TIMEOUT (1 second). A worker runs its jobs with its runner, so a job run by run_job and a job run by a worker call the same observers, and nothing is reported twice.
  • When it calls them. Around each attempt (from the moment it holds a slot and runs, until its row is finished; a streamed run: from its row to its end), when a step is reused (resuming: an event, not an attempt), and for each model call and tool call of an attempt. A streaming run is one attempt, with its model calls and tool calls, and none per token. Around the job: the one function that runs a job (execute_job, for run_job and for a worker) enters the observers' job scope before the pipeline and finishes it with the status and the error type, so an observer can make its span current while the pipeline runs (jobs); a worker hands it the message's trace context.
  • Model calls and tool calls. An attempt is one lc_agent.ainvoke(...), so they happen inside LangChain's agent loop. A callback handler added to the config of each attempt (and of a streamed run) turns LangChain's callbacks into the observers' events, with real timings. It does nothing when there are no observers.
  • Inline, and harmless. Every call is awaited, with a timeout (a second by default); an observer that raises or is slow is logged and ignored, so it never changes or fails a run. That includes a hook that raises when it is called, before anything is awaited.
  • Content is built only when asked. The runner builds the content fields of a record only if an observer says it wants content, and passes each observer the record without them unless that observer asked.
  • A launched agent knows its tool call. The callback sets the id of the tool call that is running (CURRENT_TOOL_CALL_ID, a context variable that LangChain copies into the tool's task), and launch_agent passes it as the child attempt's parent_tool_call_id. Without observers it is None.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• The runner does not choose the model. The agent's model settings are the only way to pick one, and the runner calls agent.model.build(). A test replaces the settings with fake ones, so tests take the production path (models).
  • Failures are values. A pipeline decides what a failed run means: skip a document, stop the job, ask again.
  • A retry resamples, and does not feed the error back. Feeding it back is a different feature, and the pipeline can do it by building a new input.
  • Allow-lists of classes, so that there is nothing to register and a rename is a normal refactor.
  • The child's result is text for the parent, not an exception, so that the parent's model can recover.
  • Depth and breadth, not cost. They are simple to explain and to set. A budget is not built.
  • Slots are held by attempts that call the model, which keeps the limit on model calls honest.
  • The runner owns no workflow. It is not a graph engine. Resuming is replay: the caller's code runs again, and the runner answers the runs that already succeeded.
  • AgentResult.reused. A plain flag, so that a pipeline or a test can tell a reused result from a run without reading the log.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Finding agents. An agent knows only its own allow-list. There is no tool to search for agents.
  • Launching in the background. launch_agent waits for the child. An agent that does not wait is a background job.
  • Resuming inside a run. An attempt that failed halfway runs whole. Reusing the result of a sub-agent when its parent is run again is not built: a parent that failed reruns with its children.
  • A limit on launches per job, or on cost or tokens.
  • Streaming from run(). A streaming agent has its own method, stream().
  • Cancelling one run from outside. Cancelling the task that awaits run() cancels the run, and its row is CANCELLED. A streaming run has run.cancel() and runner.cancel(run_id).
  • A runner shared between processes. The slots and the connections are per runner.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: test_runner.py (results, retries, non-retryable errors, token sums), test_limits.py (the three limits: defaults, environment variables, arguments, and the slot limit with run_many), test_concurrency.py (many runs at once do not interfere), test_resume.py (resuming a job), test_subagents.py (the allow-list, the two tools, depth and breadth, the slot hand-over with deadlock tests, tracing), and test_mcp.py (leases). A real-model test of launching is in tests/e2e/test_subagents_e2e.py.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Status: implemented. How to use it is in skills.md. The code is skills.py. It follows the Agent Skills specification.

  • Goal
  • The model
  • Loading
  • How an agent uses a skill
  • Reading a skill from somewhere else
  • What is supported
  • Decisions
  • Not supported
  • Tests

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: A skill is a set of instructions an agent reads when it needs them. It is a typed, frozen Pydantic model that checks everything the specification limits, so a skill that breaks a rule fails when it is built. It costs almost nothing in context until it is used.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Skill is frozen, and ignores frontmatter keys it does not know (skills written for other tools carry extra ones).

Field Rule name Required. 1 to 64 characters: lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, not starting or ending with a hyphen description Required. 1 to 1024 characters, not blank. Says what the skill does and when to use it instructions The Markdown body of SKILL.md. No format is imposed license Text compatibility 1 to 500 characters when given metadata Text keys to text values. Numbers in YAML (version: 1.0) become text allowed_tools Space-separated text, allowed-tools in SKILL.md. Kept, not enforced resources Other files: a path relative to the skill, and its text. The path must be relative, must not contain .., and must not be SKILL.md

A validation failure raises ValidationError; a file that is not a skill raises SkillError. Both are ValueErrors. Two skills of one agent cannot have the same name (agents).

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
• Skill(...): a skill written in code, with no directory.
  • Skill.from_markdown(text, resources=None): parses one SKILL.md: YAML frontmatter between --- lines, then the body. No frontmatter, invalid YAML, or a frontmatter that is not a mapping is a SkillError.
  • Skill.from_directory(path): SKILL.md and every other file below the directory, as a resource keyed by its relative path.
  • The name must match the directory name.
  • Files that start with a dot are skipped. Files that are not UTF-8 text are skipped and logged (skill_file_skipped).
  • A body over 500 lines is logged (skill_long), not refused.

docs.title: How an agent uses a skill
docs.text:
Progressive disclosure, in three steps:

Step The agent has How 1. Known The name and description of every skill In the system prompt, always 2. Activated The instructions get_skill(name), when the agent decides a skill applies 3. Used Other files of the skill get_skill(name, resource=path), when the instructions point to a file

The runner builds get_skill(name, resource="") for each attempt of an agent that has skills. It reads only that agent's skills (with await skill.aread(resource), see below), and returns text, never raising:

Call Returns a known skill # Skill: <name>, the instructions, and a list of the other files a known skill and a file The text of the file an unknown skill 'x' is not one of your skills. Your skills: ... an unknown file The skill 'x' has no file '...'. Its files: ... a path that is not inside the skill (below) The skill 'x' has no file '...'. The skill is not asked, and nothing is raised or logged as an error

The agent decides whether and when to read a skill: nothing activates one for it. Skills are not passed on to the agents an agent launches. Each read logs skill_read agent=... skill=... resource=.... The instructions are tool results, so they count in input tokens from then on, which is why a body should stay short.

docs.title: Reading a skill from somewhere else
docs.text:
A skill whose text lives in a database or an object store (S3) is a Skill subclass that fetches the text when the agent asks for it. The extension point is the read:

Method read(resource="") Synchronous. The instructions (with the other files listed), or the text of one file, from the fields of the skill aread(resource="") Asynchronous, with the same arguments and the same result. The default calls read, so a skill that holds its text needs nothing. The runner's get_skill always awaits aread

A subclass that fetches overrides aread, and never blocks the event loop (every agent of the process shares it).

  • A skill is still data and still a valid Skill: its name, description and the rest are checked as always, and a description is what is in the prompt, so it is not fetched. Only the instructions and the files are read late.
  • The hash. The agent's hash is made from the fields of its skills. A fetched text is not a field, so a subclass adds one that changes when the text does (an etag or a version). Without it, an edit in the store leaves the hash as it was, and resuming a job reuses results made with the old text.
  • A read that fails is text, not an exception. If aread raises, the runner logs skill_read_failed (with the error) and the agent gets The skill 'x' could not be read: <the type of the error>, so the run goes on, as with the other tools that return their errors. The message of the error goes to the log only: it can name a bucket or a key.
  • aread returns text. What it returns is the tool's result, so a value that is not a str (a store client that answers None for a key that does not exist, or bytes) is a read that failed: the same text as an exception (could not be read: TypeError), and skill_read_failed in the log. An empty string is text.
  • aread has a timeout: FTW_SKILL_READ_TIMEOUT seconds (15 by default; configuration), read when the runner is built, with no argument and no way to switch it off. A read that takes longer is cancelled and is a read that failed (could not be read: TimeoutError), so a hung store does not hold the attempt, and its concurrency slot, for ever. An aread must be safe to cancel.
  • aread can ask who the run is for. The identity of the run is CURRENT_IDENTITY (featherweight.context), the same context variable that code which cannot take runtime reads (identity): a subclass that keeps skills per tenant can check what the identity may fetch. It is not an argument of aread, so the signature is the same for every skill. featherweight does not check it: a read is a tool call, and a tool checks authorization itself.
  • Nothing is fetched until the agent asks, and the runner caches nothing: caching for the length of a run is the subclass's.
  • The framework ships no store. There is no S3 or database client in featherweight. The recipes show a skill from a database and a skill from S3.

docs.title: The path the model chooses
docs.text:
resource is written by the model, and a model reads documents and user input, so a prompt injection can choose it. The runner therefore gives aread only a normalised path that is inside the skill, or the empty string, and answers anything else itself, as text, without asking the skill:

  • Refused, flatly: a path that starts with /, one with a backslash, one with a .. segment (it is not resolved: a/../b is refused too), one with a control character (NUL and newline included), one longer than 256 characters, and one that is only . and /. The answer is The skill 'x' has no file '...'. (the path, cut at 80 characters), the same as for a file that is not there, so the model learns nothing about what is outside. It is not an error: the run goes on.
  • Normalised: a . segment is dropped and // is one /, so ./references/a.md and references//a.md are references/a.md.
  • Not decoded: the runner does not URL-decode. A subclass that does (an HTTP store) treats what it gets as untrusted, and checks it again. What a file holds is not checked here.

The default read is unchanged: it looks the path up in the skill's own files. The rule is for every skill, because a subclass's aread replaces that lookup and with it the check.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text: In the specification Here SKILL.md with name and description Supported, with every length and character rule license, compatibility, metadata Validated and kept allowed-tools Parsed and kept, not enforced. An agent's tools are only those in its tools The body as the instructions Supported Other files, references/, assets/ Supported as text scripts/ Kept as text for the agent to read. Nothing runs a script The name matches the directory Checked by from_directory Instructions under 500 lines A line count is logged. The 5,000-token advice is not checked

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• A typed model, also in code. A skill need not be a directory, and a directory is loaded into the same model.
  • Check what the specification limits, ignore what it does not define. Skills written for other tools load.
  • The agent decides. The runner gives it the tool and the prompt, and does not activate a skill on its own.
  • Skills are per agent and are not inherited by launched agents, so each agent reads what its own definition lists.
  • Text only. The agent can only read text, so binary files are skipped, and scripts are never run.
  • The read is async-capable, and the store is not ours. aread is the one hook, and read stays for code that holds the text. A URL is not a resource: the model cannot open one, so the framework would have to fetch it, with a client, limits and the risks that come with it. The path stays the name the model sees, and where the text comes from is the subclass's business.
  • The runner checks the model's path, and the skill still treats it as untrusted. The check is in one place (clean_resource), so that a subclass that joins paths, reads a directory or calls a service that normalises .. cannot be reached by a path that leaves the skill.
  • A read is bounded and returns text. A fetching skill is application code in the middle of an attempt: a timeout and a type check stop a store that hangs or answers with something else from reaching the model or stalling the run.
  • A long skill is logged, not refused, as the specification recommends rather than requires.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Finding skills. An agent knows only the skills it lists. A tool that finds skills by keyword is not built. The BM25 matcher of tool discovery is generic and could serve it.
  • Binary assets (images, PDFs), and scripts that run.
  • Loading from an archive or a registry that we ship, and sharing a skill between processes. aread is the hook, and the recipes show how.
  • A skill list that changes at run time. An agent's skills is fixed when its class is defined; a platform that builds an agent for each request from its own database rows builds the class then.
  • Reading a part of a long file, or a size limit on a file.
  • Enforcing allowed-tools, checking references one level deep, and the skills-ref validator.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: test_skills.py covers the model's rules, from_markdown, from_directory (names, hidden and binary files, resources), read, the prompt, and the get_skill tool. aread is covered with a subclass that reads from a fake in-memory store: the default equals read, the tool awaits it, the hash changes with the subclass's etag, and a read that raises comes back as text and is logged; a value that is not text, and a read that takes longer than the timeout, come back as text too; a path that is absolute, has a .., a backslash, a control character or is too long never reaches aread and a normal one reaches it normalised; an aread sees the identity of the run. A real-model test is in tests/e2e/test_skills_e2e.py.

docs.title: Streaming agents
docs.text:
Status: implemented (epic #29 is done). #33 (stopping a response) and #36 (the example and the guide) are done too. #30 (the class, ChatInput, runner.stream(), the run log), #31 (the events: text, tool calls, thoughts, steps; show_thoughts), #32 (messages in and out: the converters, from_langchain, from_agui, new_messages), #34 (the AG-UI adapter) and #35 (the Vercel adapter) are done; the other issues are not. It is tracked in epic #29, and each part has its own issue (listed at the end). When a part is built, this page says so and the guide docs/streaming.md shows how to use it.

It changes agents (a new kind of agent), the runner (stream(), and run() refuses a streaming agent), models (show_thoughts) and jobs (a thread_id column and a CANCELLED status).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Some agents talk to a person: a chat, or a task that a person watches. They must show the answer while it is written, show what the agent is doing (the tools it calls, and its thoughts), let the person stop it and correct it, and not wait for a finished, validated output. featherweight adds this without a second runtime: a streaming agent is an agent, run by the same runner, with the same tools, skills, MCP servers, limits and run log.

We build abstractions, not a solution. The events are an open protocol's, the HTTP and the storage are the application's.

docs.title: The agent and its input
docs.text:
class Support(StreamingAgent):
    name: str = "support"
    description: str = "Answers questions about the product"
    version: str = "1"
    prompt: str = "You help customers. Be short."
    model: ModelSettings = Claude(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", effort="low", show_thoughts=True)
    tools: list[BaseTool] = [lookup_order]

StreamingAgent extends AgentBase. What changes:

AgentBase StreamingAgent input_model the agent's own ChatInput (fixed) output_model, check_output yes none: nothing is validated, the output is text Retries max_attempts none: once a token is out, it cannot be taken back Run with runner.run() runner.stream()

Passing a StreamingAgent to run() raises TypeError, and so does passing any other agent to stream(), naming the other method. Tools, subagents, skills, mcp_servers and discovery are declared and checked as they are for any agent.

ChatInput is the conversation so far, sent by the client:

ChatInput(messages=[...], thread_id="t-17")  # messages: AG-UI Message types

It is checked when built:

  • The last message is from the user.
  • system and developer messages are rejected. The agent has its own prompt, and a client must not be able to replace it. (The AG-UI request has these roles; a client that sends one gets an error, not silence.)
  • thread_id is optional. It identifies the conversation for the run log; it does not load anything.

docs.title: Streaming a run
docs.text:
run = runner.stream(Support, chat_input, job_id=None)  # nothing happens yet
async for event in run:  # AG-UI events, as the model writes
    send(event)
run.new_messages  # LangChain messages of this turn (after the loop)

StreamingRun:

Member async for event in run The events, once. A second loop is an error run_id The id in RUN_STARTED, and what runner.cancel() takes new_messages The LangChain messages this turn produced. Complete when the stream ends, even on cancel usage Input and output tokens, when known status, error RUNNING, then SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED, and the error text cancel() Stops the run

Under it, the runner builds the agent as it does for run() (tools, MCP lease, skills, discovery, the system prompt) and streams the LangChain agent with astream. The run waits for a concurrency slot (the row stays INIT), holds the slot until the stream ends, and gives it back on success, failure and cancel.

A launched sub-agent is a tool call that blocks until it returns: it shows as a tool call with a result, and its own tokens are not streamed. (The depth and launch rules are the same as in launching agents.)

docs.title: The events
docs.text:
The events are AG-UI's, from the official ag-ui-protocol package (1.0, Pydantic models). featherweight defines none. The runner produces them in the order the protocol requires, and the adapters send them.

What happened Events The run starts RUN_STARTED (thread id, run id) A model turn starts, ends STEP_STARTED, STEP_FINISHED (the step name is model) The model writes text TEXT_MESSAGE_START, TEXT_MESSAGE_CONTENT (one per chunk), TEXT_MESSAGE_END The model thinks (show_thoughts) REASONING_START, REASONING_MESSAGE_START, REASONING_MESSAGE_CONTENT, REASONING_MESSAGE_END, REASONING_END A provider's opaque reasoning value REASONING_ENCRYPTED_VALUE The model calls a tool TOOL_CALL_START, TOOL_CALL_ARGS (the arguments stream), TOOL_CALL_END The tool returns TOOL_CALL_RESULT (with the error text, when the tool failed) The run ends well RUN_FINISHED (success outcome), with the token usage The run is stopped RUN_FINISHED with the cancelled outcome The run fails RUN_ERROR (the open message is closed first)

Rules the runner keeps: a text message is closed before a tool call opens; ids (message, tool call, reasoning) are made by featherweight when the provider gives none; every opened thing is closed, also on error and on cancel; one RUN_STARTED and one ending event per run. A test checks every produced sequence against these rules.

How LangChain's stream maps to this (to be confirmed while building, see Findings): astream with the messages mode gives the chunks of the model's output (text, reasoning and tool call chunks, as content blocks), and the updates mode gives what a tool node returned.

Events with no source here (state, activity, custom, sub-agent events) are not produced. The custom event is used for two events of background jobs, background_started and background_finished.

docs.title: The model's thoughts
docs.text:
ModelSettings gets one field, show_thoughts: bool = False. Each provider class maps it to its own option: Gemini and Gemma ask the model to include its thought summaries, OpenAI asks for a reasoning summary, and Claude asks for its thinking to be returned. (The settings today only set how hard a model thinks.)

  • Off (the default): no reasoning events.
  • On: the reasoning is streamed as reasoning events and kept in the messages.
  • What a thought is differs by provider: Claude returns thinking blocks, OpenAI a summary (its raw reasoning is hidden), Gemini a thought summary. The guide says so.
  • Kept either way. A provider's reasoning, and its opaque or signed value (REASONING_ENCRYPTED_VALUE, a signature), is always kept in new_messages, even when it is not shown, because the provider needs it back on the next request when the model thinks between tool calls.

It is a field of ModelSettings, so it is available to every agent, and it is recorded with the other settings in the run log.

docs.title: Messages and keeping the conversation
docs.text:
featherweight keeps no conversation. The client sends the whole history with each request. That is how both protocols work, and it means any process can serve any turn. The application keeps messages if it wants to, with the tools LangChain already has.

  • Wire format: AG-UI messages. Storage format: LangChain messages, because LangChain's chat message histories read and write them, and because they hold what the model needs (tool call ids, usage, reasoning blocks).
  • Converters, in both directions, between AG-UI and LangChain messages: user, assistant (text and tool calls), tool results (with their error), and reasoning (with its encrypted value).
  • ChatInput.from_langchain(messages, thread_id=None): history loaded from a store.
  • ChatInput.from_agui(messages_or_request): what a client sent.
  • A LangChain to AG-UI converter: to rebuild what a client shows from stored history.
  • StreamingRun.new_messages: the LangChain messages of the turn.
history = SQLChatMessageHistory(session_id=thread_id, connection=...)  # or any BaseChatMessageHistory
run = runner.stream(Support, ChatInput.from_langchain([*history.messages, user_message], thread_id))
async for event in run:
    yield encoder.encode(event)
history.add_messages([user_message, *run.new_messages])

The converters keep tool call ids, tool results, and reasoning (with signatures) exactly; a round trip is tested. Anything the other format cannot hold is listed in the guide.

No LangGraph checkpointer. create_agent supports one, and LangChain recommends it for agents, but it stores the whole graph state per thread, and it is not how featherweight passes state around. It is not forwarded. A later issue can add it if someone asks.

docs.title: Stopping a response
docs.text:
The person stops the agent while it answers, then corrects it: "no, not that one".

Two ways to stop

  1. The client drops the stream (Vercel's stop() aborts the fetch, and an AG-UI client closes the connection). The consumer closes the iterator, and the run is cancelled.
  2. An explicit cancel: run.cancel(), or runner.cancel(run_id) from another request in the same process (the runner keeps its live streaming runs by id). Across processes it belongs to the jobs epic.

An explicit cancel ends the stream cleanly: the model call is cancelled, RUN_FINISHED with the cancelled outcome is sent, and the loop ends, so the application's code after it runs. A disconnect cancels the same way, with no one listening, so it saves in a finally (the guide shows it).

The partial turn is kept. The next request has to contain what the agent already said and did, and a tool that already ran had its effect. So after a cancel, new_messages holds the partial turn, cleaned up so that it is valid to send back:

State when stopped What new_messages has Text was streaming The assistant message with the text so far Thoughts were streaming The reasoning so far, only when it has its signature (or opaque value): a provider rejects a thinking block without one. The text is kept either way A tool call's arguments were still streaming That tool call is dropped (it is not complete: its arguments are not valid JSON yet) A tool call was complete, the tool had not returned The tool call, and a tool message with an error: "This tool did not return: cancelled by the user.", because a provider rejects a tool call that has no result A tool had returned The call and its real result

new_messages is filled when the run ends, whatever ended it, so it is there after a disconnect too. A turn that fails is closed the same way (its text so far, no call without a result, with "the run failed" as the reason).

What a stop does not do

  • A synchronous tool running in a thread cannot be interrupted, and an MCP call may finish on the server. A side effect can still complete after the person pressed stop. The guide says it.
  • A cancelled call's token usage may be unknown. The row records what is known.
  • A launched sub-agent is cancelled with its parent, and its row is CANCELLED (this also changes run(): a run whose task is cancelled is marked CANCELLED, not left RUNNING).
  • The concurrency slot is released (tested at each point above, and while waiting for the slot).

docs.title: The run log
docs.text:
One attempts row per turn, as for any run, with these differences. The run log holds no content for any agent (see the persistence spec): a streaming run has no placeholders for its input and output, only their hashes.

status INIT while it waits for a slot, RUNNING while it streams, then SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED input_hash, output_hash SHA-256 of the ChatInput, and of the text when the turn succeeded thread_id The conversation the client named. NULL when it named none error_type, error_hash For a failed turn: the class of the exception and the hash of its message. The text goes to the client in RUN_ERROR agent_hash Recorded as for any run Reuse None. Resuming a job does not reuse a streaming run

The run's job_id works as for run().

docs.title: The adapters
docs.text:
An adapter has two parts: read the request into a ChatInput, and encode the events for the wire. Neither is a server: no router, no web framework dependency. A one-line Starlette example goes in the guide.

AG-UI (featherweight.adapters.agui, built): the events are already AG-UI's, so this is the thin edge. - parse_request(body): a RunAgentInput (a dict, text or bytes) becomes a ChatInput; a body it cannot read raises BadRequest, a ValueError that a framework turns into a 422. The message of a BadRequest names the part and what is wrong (messages[0].content[1] is image content whose data is not base64: ..., or messages[0].content[0].source.mimeType: Field required), in the same words in both adapters, without pydantic's own path through the unions of the protocol. A conversation over the agent's attachment limits is not known to parse_request: runner.stream() raises AttachmentLimitError (a BadRequest, answered with a 413) (attachments). The client's tools, state and context are ignored (the agent has its own tools), and sending tools logs a warning. - encode(run): SSE strings from the official EventEncoder, plus CONTENT_TYPE and HEADERS for the response. The binary encoding is not supported.

Vercel AI SDK (featherweight.adapters.vercel): a translation from AG-UI events to the documented UI message stream, written by us because no small official package exists (the one from vercel-labs is a whole agent framework, at 0.x).

AG-UI Vercel part RUN_STARTED start STEP_STARTED, STEP_FINISHED start-step, finish-step TEXT_MESSAGE_* text-start, text-delta, text-end REASONING_* reasoning-start, reasoning-delta, reasoning-end TOOL_CALL_START, TOOL_CALL_ARGS, TOOL_CALL_END tool-input-start, tool-input-delta, tool-input-available TOOL_CALL_RESULT tool-output-available RUN_FINISHED (success) finish, then [DONE] RUN_FINISHED (cancelled) abort, then [DONE] RUN_ERROR error, then [DONE] CUSTOM (background_started, background_finished) a data part data-<name>, with the event's value as data, transient (the client gets it with onData, and it is not kept in the message)

The header is x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1. The request is Vercel's list of UIMessage (messages made of parts: text, reasoning, tool parts with a state, and file parts, which are attachments), converted to a ChatInput with the same rules as AG-UI. State and activity events have no Vercel part and are dropped. The guide names the protocol version we wrote against and the date we checked.

A third format is a third adapter: the events are the contract.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• The events are AG-UI's. We write only what does not exist: the mapping from LangChain's stream, the converters, and the Vercel translation. It ties us to a spec we do not control; it is open, at 1.0, and the format that Pydantic AI and others already speak.
  • No retries. A failure is an error event and a FAILED row.
  • Stateless on our side. No sessions, no conversation store, no checkpointer. The run log holds no message content either, only counts, hashes, tokens, status and timing: featherweight is not a persistence layer. The app keeps the words (with LangChain's stores) and saves the run_id from RUN_STARTED next to each turn, so it can join its messages to the log. Where the log should keep content for all agents is a wider question, parked in the ideas notes (the run log and persistence boundary).
  • Client history is untrusted: no system or developer roles; the application still validates what it stores and sends.
  • Cancel keeps the partial turn, with a synthetic result for a tool call that did not return.
  • show_thoughts is a ModelSettings field, default off. (Taken in this spec; to confirm in review: a streaming agent could default it on instead.)
  • thread_id is a column, so a conversation is traceable without a conversation store. (Taken in this spec; to confirm.)
  • A custom StreamingAgent output is text only. Structured output from a streaming agent is a different feature, and is not here.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Background jobs (a sub-agent that runs while the chat goes on): their own spec. The application can do it today with a job and by starting the next turn itself; the guide shows how.
  • Cancelling across processes, and queued or multi-process jobs: the jobs epic.
  • Streaming sub-agents: a launched sub-agent is a tool call.
  • Client-side tools (AG-UI's tools), shared state, activity, interrupts and resume: ignored.
  • Stored conversations, sessions, a LangGraph checkpointer.
  • The AG-UI binary encoding, a router or server.
  • Structured or validated output from a streaming agent.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Checked while writing this (2026-11-19):

  • ag-ui-protocol 1.0.0 on PyPI: depends on Pydantic only, Python >= 3.9. Its models include the text, tool call, reasoning (REASONING_* and REASONING_ENCRYPTED_VALUE), step, run, state and activity events, a cancelled run outcome, TokenUsage, the request RunAgentInput (thread id, run id, messages, tools, state), and messages of the roles developer, system, assistant, user, tool, activity and reasoning. It has an SSE EventEncoder.
  • The Vercel UI message stream is documented, with parts for start, text, reasoning, tool input and output, steps, finish, error and abort, an [DONE] end and the header x-vercel-ai-ui-message-stream: v1.
  • This repository has langchain 1.4.9 and langgraph 1.2.19. A LangGraph graph's astream accepts the messages and updates modes, among others. AIMessage.content_blocks gives provider-independent content blocks. A Claude thinking block comes out as a non_standard block in a test with a hand-made chunk.
  • Pydantic AI ships adapters for AG-UI and the Vercel protocol over one internal event stream. We copy the idea, with AG-UI's events as that stream.

Still to check while building (it needs the real packages, and some of it a live call, which is asked for first): what the three providers return for thoughts through content_blocks and whether show_thoughts maps to the right option for each; whether astream's messages mode gives complete tool call arguments in time for TOOL_CALL_END; and the exact UIMessage shape for tool parts in a request.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
No live model call in the unit tests: a fake streaming chat model in tests/fakes.py, and recorded chunk sequences.

  • Mapping: text, thoughts then text, a tool call with streamed arguments, two tool calls, an error halfway, show_thoughts off; every sequence valid against the protocol's ordering.
  • Input: system and developer rejected, the last message must be the user's, run() and stream() refuse the wrong agent.
  • Messages: round trips both ways with tool calls, results, errors, reasoning with an encrypted value.
  • Cancel: during text, a tool call's arguments, a running tool, the wait for a slot, through runner.cancel, and by dropping the iterator; after each, the row is CANCELLED, the slot is free and new_messages is valid to send back.
  • Run log: the statuses, thread_id, no reuse, tokens.
  • Adapters: a request body from each protocol's docs; the Vercel output equals the protocol page's examples.
  • One live smoke check per provider only on request, with the cheapest model.

docs.title: Submitted jobs
docs.text:
Status: implemented, including several workers (epic #103): the queue's lease (#104), the job lease, the heartbeat and the owner check (#105), takeover (#106), the job timeout (#107), and the guide, the example and the skill reference (#108). #72 (the Job class, JobContext, the job columns and CANCELLED), #73 (the queue), #74 (job events and SSE), #75 (the client), #76 (the worker, with the compare-and-set steps for taking and cancelling a job), #77 (the @job decorator) and #78 (the guide, the example and the skill reference) are done. The jobs_lookup fallback is implemented too (#199, in epic #190).
