docs.title: agui
docs.text: The AG-UI adapter. The events of a streaming run already are AG-UI's, so this is only the edge with HTTP: read a request into a ChatInput, and encode the events of a run as server-sent events. No server and no web framework.

docs.title: parse_request
docs.text:
parse_request(
    body: dict[str, Any] | bytes | str,
) -> ChatInput

The JSON body of an AG-UI request (a RunAgentInput) as a ChatInput.

threadId is kept. The client's tools, state, context and forwardedProps are ignored: the agent has its own tools, and a warning is logged when tools are sent. Raises BadRequest (a ValueError) for a body that is not JSON, is not a RunAgentInput, or is a conversation a ChatInput refuses (a system or developer message, a last message that is not the user's).

docs.title: encode async
docs.text:
encode(run: StreamingRun) -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]

The events of run as server-sent events, one string each (data: {...} and a blank line), for the body of a streaming response. Leaving the loop early stops the run.

docs.title: errors
docs.text: The error of an adapter that is given a request it cannot read, and how it words what is wrong. BadRequest is defined in featherweight.errors (the streaming module raises a subclass of it and cannot import this package); it is exported here too, where it always was.

docs.title: BadRequest
docs.text:
Bases: ValueError

A client's request is not valid. A web framework can answer it with a 4xx (422): the message says what is wrong.

docs.title: problems
docs.text:
problems(exc: ValidationError) -> str

What is wrong in a request, from a pydantic error, in the words of both adapters: one line per problem, where: what. The message of a rule of ours (a ValueError of a validator) already says where, and stands alone, without pydantic's "Value error, ". When a field takes a string or a list, the complaint that a list is not a string is left out when something else is wrong.

docs.title: vercel
docs.text:
The Vercel AI SDK adapter: the UI message stream, for useChat and the other clients of the AI SDK.

It reads a request into a ChatInput, and translates the AG-UI events of a StreamingRun into the parts of the UI message stream. It is not a server: it gives you the strings, you send them with any web framework.

chat_input = parse_request(await request.json())
run = runner.stream(Support, chat_input)
return StreamingResponse(encode(run), headers=HEADERS)

Written against the protocol as documented at ai-sdk.dev (checked 2026-11-19): see docs/streaming.md.

docs.title: Translator
docs.text:
Translator()

Turns the events of one run into the parts of the stream, one event at a time. A part is a dict; encode sends them as server-sent events. A custom event is a data part (data-<name>, transient: the client gets it with onData, and it is not kept in the message); the events that have no part (state, activity, the opaque value of a thought) are dropped.

docs.title: parse_request
docs.text:
parse_request(
    body: dict[str, Any] | str | bytes | list[Any],
) -> ChatInput

The request of useChat ({"id": ..., "messages": [UIMessage, ...]}, or just the list of messages) as a ChatInput. id, the chat's id, becomes the thread_id. Raises BadRequest for a body that cannot be read or a history that ChatInput refuses (a system message, a last message that is not the user's).

docs.title: to_agui_messages
docs.text:
to_agui_messages(
    ui_messages: list[dict[str, Any]],
) -> list[Message]

UIMessages as AG-UI messages. An assistant UIMessage with tool parts becomes the messages the model saw: an assistant message with its tool calls, then the tool results, then the next step's assistant message, and so on.

docs.title: translate
docs.text:
translate(events: Iterable[BaseEvent]) -> list[str]

The events of a whole run as server-sent events, ending with [DONE]. For tests and replays; use encode to stream.

docs.title: encode async
docs.text:
encode(run: StreamingRun) -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]

The server-sent events of a run, as it streams, ending with [DONE]. Send them with the headers in HEADERS. Stopping the iteration (a client that went away) stops the run.

docs.title: client
docs.text:
JobClient: submit a job, follow it, cancel it, and read its result, from any process.

The client and the worker are independent: the queue and the database are all that connects them. The client writes the job row and puts a message on the queue; it never runs a job. The result is read from the user's result store, because featherweight keeps no results of its own. See docs/specs/submitted-jobs.md.

docs.title: JobClient
docs.text:
JobClient(
    db: Database,
    queue: JobQueue,
    results: ResultStore
    | None
    | Literal["default"] = "default",
    observers: Sequence[Observer] = (),
    identity_type: Any = None,
)

Submits jobs to a queue and follows them. results is the user's ResultStore, where the worker wrote the outputs; the default is the sqlite store of a SqliteDatabase, and with another database there is none, so pass one (or None, and result has nothing to read).

docs.title: submit async
docs.text:
submit(
    job: type[Job] | type[AgentBase],
    input: BaseModel,
    *,
    resumable: bool = False,
    resume_from: str | None = None,
    job_id: str | None = None,
    parent_attempt_id: str | None = None,
    parent_tool_call_id: str | None = None,
    identity: Any = None,
) -> str

Create the job and put it on the queue; returns its id. job is a Job class, or a plain (non-streaming) agent class. The input must be an instance of the job's input model (TypeError otherwise).

resume_from is a failed job to resume: a new job that points to it, whose finished steps are reused when it runs (the old job must have been resumable, or ValueError says nothing was kept). If the queue refuses the message, the job is marked FAILED and the error is raised.

parent_attempt_id is set by a runner that starts the job as a background job: the attempt that started it. It is stored. parent_tool_call_id is the tool call that started it: it goes to the observers (so that a trace nests the job under the call) and is stored nowhere.

identity is who the job is for. It goes in the message as JSON, and the worker rebuilds it with its own identity_type; it is stored nowhere. With an identity_type the client checks it first (TypeError); without one it accepts any Pydantic model.

docs.title: status async
docs.text:
status(job_id: str) -> JobRow

The job's row. LookupError for a job that does not exist.

docs.title: cancel async
docs.text:
cancel(job_id: str) -> bool

Cancel a job. A queued job becomes CANCELLED (its message stays on the queue: the worker sees the status when it arrives, and skips it). A running job gets cancel_requested, and its worker stops it. Returns False for a job that is already final, or does not exist.

docs.title: fail async
docs.text:
fail(job_id: str, error_type: str = DEAD_LETTERED) -> bool

End a job that will never run: its message was dead-lettered by a queue that gave up on it. Call it from your dead-letter handler. The job becomes FAILED (a failed event) with this error type, in one atomic step, only if it is not running: it is still INIT, or RUNNING with an expired lease (its worker was lost). Returns False for a job that is running, is already final, or does not exist. The user resumes it, as any failed job.

docs.title: result async
docs.text:
result(
    job: type[Job] | type[AgentBase], job_id: str
) -> BaseModel | None

The output of a job that succeeded, read from your result store and parsed into the job's output model; None while there is none (the job is not SUCCESS, the store has nothing, or results is None). LookupError for a job that does not exist. It never reads our tables, which hold no results.

docs.title: events
docs.text:
events(
    job_id: str, after: int = 0
) -> AsyncGenerator[JobEvent, None]

The events of the job after after: the stored ones, then each as it happens, ending at a final one. Send it as SSE with sse.encode.

docs.title: wait async
docs.text:
wait(job_id: str, timeout: float | None = None) -> JobRow

The job once it is final. TimeoutError after timeout seconds. A convenience for scripts and tests: a web handler should return the job id and let the caller follow events.

docs.title: context
docs.text:
Per-attempt context the runner hands to tools through langchain's ToolRuntime.

Tools declare a runtime: ToolRuntime[RunContext] parameter; langchain fills it in and hides it from the model, so tools stay plain static objects that can sit in an agent's allow-list.

docs.title: RunContext dataclass
docs.text:
RunContext(
    job_id: str | None,
    run_id: str,
    attempt_id: str,
    identity: IdentityT | None = None,
)

Bases: Generic[IdentityT]

What a tool can ask for with runtime: ToolRuntime[RunContext[Teacher]]: LangChain fills it in and hides it from the model.

docs.title: db
docs.text:
The run log: what featherweight keeps of the orchestration, and the abstract class that a database implements.

The log is metadata only: jobs, and one row per attempt of an agent, with status, tokens, timing, the launch tree and hashes. It never holds an input, an output, a message or the text of an error (see docs/specs/persistence.md). Database is the abstract class; SqliteDatabase (local development) and PostgresDatabase (deployment) implement it. Records go in and rows come out as Pydantic models, so the same constraints hold whatever the database is.

docs.title: AttemptRecord
docs.text:
Bases: _Model

What is known when an attempt is created. There is no input in it: only its hash.

docs.title: AttemptFinish
docs.text:
Bases: _Model

What is known when an attempt ends. There is no output and no error text in it: only hashes and the error's type.

docs.title: JobOwner
docs.text:
Bases: _Model

Who owns a running job: the worker, and which execution of the job it is. The writes of a running job are conditional on both, in the statement itself, so that a worker that lost the job cannot change it.

docs.title: JobLost
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

A write for a job that is not this worker's any more: another worker took it over, or it ended, or it was put back in the queue. Nothing was written. The worker that gets it stops the job and writes nothing more to it.

docs.title: JobEvent
docs.text:
Bases: _Model

A change in the life of a job. Metadata only: no content.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

The run log. Subclass it to keep the log in a database of your own: write every abstract method, and run featherweight.testing.check_database against it. The schema is documented in docs/specs/persistence.md.

Rows come back in the order they were made. Timestamps are timezone-aware datetimes: convert what your database stores.

docs.title: connect abstractmethod async
docs.text:
connect() -> None

Open the database and bring its schema up to date (the migrations).

docs.title: create_job async
docs.text:
create_job(
    name: str,
    job_id: str | None = None,
    *,
    resume_from: str | None = None,
    resumable: bool = False,
    job_version: str | None = None,
    job_hash: str | None = None,
    input_hash: str | None = None,
    parent_attempt_id: str | None = None,
) -> str

Create a job. resumable=True keeps the outputs of its steps (in the runner's result store), so that a later job can resume it; it is decided here, before the pipeline runs.

With resume_from, the job resumes that one: its runs may reuse the successful steps of it. The old job must have been resumable, or nothing was kept and ValueError says so. A job that resumes another is resumable itself, so that a third attempt is possible.

docs.title: insert_job abstractmethod async
docs.text:
insert_job(
    job_id: str,
    name: str,
    resumed_from: str | None,
    resumable: bool,
    job_version: str | None,
    job_hash: str | None,
    input_hash: str | None,
    parent_attempt_id: str | None = None,
) -> str

Write a new job in status INIT, and return its id. The rules are checked in create_job.

docs.title: set_job_status abstractmethod async
docs.text:
set_job_status(
    job_id: str,
    status: Status,
    *,
    error_type: str | None = None,
    error_hash: str | None = None,
    owner: JobOwner | None = None,
) -> None

Set the status of a job. The error is kept only for FAILED. RUNNING sets started_at; going back to INIT (a job that returns to the queue) clears it and its owner; a final status ends its lease. LookupError for a job that does not exist.

With owner, the write is conditional, in the same statement, on the job being RUNNING and having that worker_id and executions: if it does not, nothing is written (no status, no event) and JobLost is raised.

docs.title: request_job_cancel abstractmethod async
docs.text:
request_job_cancel(job_id: str) -> bool

Ask for a job that is not final to be cancelled: set cancel_requested and write a cancel_requested event, in one transaction. Returns False, and changes nothing, for a job that does not exist or is already final. Asking twice writes one event. The job's worker does the cancelling.

docs.title: start_job abstractmethod async
docs.text:
start_job(
    job_id: str,
    worker_id: str | None = None,
    lease: float | None = None,
) -> bool

Mark a queued job RUNNING (started_at, a running event) only if it is still INIT and has no cancel_requested, in one atomic step, and say whether it did. It is what a worker calls to take a job: it and cancel_queued_job cannot both succeed, so a job is never cancelled and run at once.

The same step records the owner: worker_id, executions one higher, and, if lease (seconds) is given, a lease_expires_at that far ahead (the database's own clock, where it has one). A job without a lease (one that runs in the process that started it) has no lease to lose.

docs.title: take_over_job abstractmethod async
docs.text:
take_over_job(
    job_id: str, worker_id: str, lease: float
) -> bool

Take a job whose worker was lost: only if it is RUNNING and its lease has expired, in one atomic step, and say whether it did. The step writes a lost event (the job went back to INIT) and then starts the job for worker_id (a running event, executions one higher, a new lease), in one transaction. False means the lease is live (a duplicate delivery, or a slow worker that is still the owner), or the job is final, or another worker won. Where the database has a clock, it is the database's that decides when the lease expired.

docs.title: fail_queued_job abstractmethod async
docs.text:
fail_queued_job(
    job_id: str, error_type: str, error_hash: str
) -> bool

Mark a job FAILED (a failed event with the error) only if it is not running: it is still INIT, or it is RUNNING with an expired lease (its worker was lost), in one atomic step, and say whether it did. It is for a job whose message will never be delivered again (dead-lettered): JobClient.fail calls it. False means the job is running, or is final, or does not exist.

docs.title: renew_job_leases abstractmethod async
docs.text:
renew_job_leases(
    worker_id: str, jobs: Mapping[str, int], lease: float
) -> set[str]

A worker's heartbeat: in one in-place update, move lease_expires_at of each job in jobs (job id to the executions the worker holds) lease seconds ahead, for those that are still RUNNING with this worker_id and that executions. Returns the ids that were renewed: the others are lost. No rows are added, and nothing else changes.

docs.title: owns_job abstractmethod async
docs.text:
owns_job(job_id: str, owner: JobOwner) -> bool

Whether the job is RUNNING and still has this owner. A cheap read, for a check before a step that cannot be made conditional (writing a result to the user's store); it is not atomic with what follows.

docs.title: cancel_queued_job abstractmethod async
docs.text:
cancel_queued_job(job_id: str) -> bool

Mark a job CANCELLED (a cancelled event) only if it is still INIT, in one atomic step, and say whether it did. False means it was taken by a worker (or is final, or does not exist): the caller then asks for a running job to be cancelled with request_job_cancel.

docs.title: list_cancel_requested abstractmethod async
docs.text:
list_cancel_requested(job_ids: Sequence[str]) -> set[str]

Which of these jobs have cancel_requested set and are not final yet, in one query. It is what a worker asks, about the jobs it is running, to learn that a client wants one of them cancelled.

docs.title: list_job_events abstractmethod async
docs.text:
list_job_events(
    job_id: str, after: int = 0, limit: int | None = None
) -> list[JobEvent]

The events of a job after the sequence number after, in order.

docs.title: poll_job_events abstractmethod async
docs.text:
poll_job_events(
    job_ids: Sequence[str], after: int = 0
) -> list[JobEvent]

The events of any of these jobs after after, in order, in one query. It is what the one reader of a process asks for, whatever the number of streams that are open.

docs.title: create_attempt abstractmethod async
docs.text:
create_attempt(run: AttemptRecord) -> str

Write an attempt in status INIT (waiting for a slot), and return its id. A job_id that does not exist is an error.

docs.title: start_attempt abstractmethod async
docs.text:
start_attempt(attempt_id: str) -> None

The attempt holds a slot: status RUNNING, and started_at is now.

docs.title: finish_attempt abstractmethod async
docs.text:
finish_attempt(attempt_id: str, end: AttemptFinish) -> None

End the attempt. LookupError for a run that does not exist.

docs.title: find_reusable_attempt abstractmethod async
docs.text:
find_reusable_attempt(
    job_id: str,
    agent_hash: str,
    input_hash: str,
    identity_hash: str | None,
    before_execution: int | None = None,
) -> AttemptRow | None

The first top-level run (depth 1) of job_id that succeeded with this agent, this input and this identity, or None. The identity matches by its hash, and None (no identity) matches only a run that had none. With before_execution, only a run of an earlier execution of the job (job_execution below it): that is how a takeover looks in its own job without finding the runs of the execution that asks.

docs.title: job_has_other_identity abstractmethod async
docs.text:
job_has_other_identity(
    job_id: str, identity_hash: str | None
) -> bool

Whether job_id already has a run whose identity differs from identity_hash, of any status and depth. None (no identity) differs from any hash and the reverse, so a job that ran with none is not for an identity, and the other way round. It is how a job stays for one identity (docs/specs/identity.md).

docs.title: list_attempts abstractmethod async
docs.text:
list_attempts(
    *, job_id: str | None = None, run_id: str | None = None
) -> list[AttemptRow]

Runs in the order they were made, optionally of one job and/or one run.

docs.title: errors
docs.text: Errors of the library that an application meets by name: a run that cannot work as it is set up, and a request that cannot be taken.

docs.title: SetupError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

The run is set up in a way that cannot work: no API key, an MCP server that cannot start, two tools with one name. The runner does not retry it.

docs.title: BadRequest
docs.text:
Bases: ValueError

A client's request is not valid. A web framework can answer it with a 4xx (422): the message says what is wrong.

docs.title: AttachmentLimitError
docs.text:
Bases: BadRequest

A conversation has more attachments, or more bytes of them, than the streaming agent allows (max_attachments, max_bytes). It is a BadRequest, so a handler for that answers it; a handler for this class can answer 413 (Payload Too Large) and leave 422 for the other bad requests. It is raised by runner.stream() before any run exists.

docs.title: events
docs.text:
Following a job: its events, as an async stream, and waiting for it to end.

The database writes an event in the transaction of every status change (see Database). Here they are read: - in the process that wrote them, the database publishes each event at commit, so a listener hears it at once, with no polling; - from another process, the events table must be read, so each Database object has one reader task that polls it, with a growing delay, for every open stream together (one query, however many streams), and fans the events out. A stream reads the stored events first and listens second, and drops what it has already given, so it misses nothing and gives nothing twice. See docs/specs/submitted-jobs.md.

docs.title: EventHub
docs.text:
EventHub(db: Database)

The listeners of one Database object, and the one reader task that serves the ones in other processes.

docs.title: publish
docs.text:
publish(event: JobEvent) -> int

Give an event to the streams that follow its job and have not had it. Returns how many had it new.

docs.title: hub_for
docs.text:
hub_for(db: Database) -> EventHub

The hub of a database object, made on first use.

docs.title: job_events async
docs.text:
job_events(
    db: Database, job_id: str, after: int = 0
) -> AsyncGenerator[JobEvent, None]

The events of a job, after the sequence number after: the stored ones first, then each as it happens, ending after a final one (succeeded, failed or cancelled). A stream that starts late replays what it missed, and one that reconnects passes the seq of the last event it had. LookupError for a job that does not exist.

docs.title: wait_for_job async
docs.text:
wait_for_job(
    db: Database, job_id: str, timeout: float | None = None
) -> JobRow

The job, once it is final (SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED). It reads the status, and if the job is not final it follows the events, so there is no gap between looking and listening. TimeoutError after timeout seconds, LookupError for a job that does not exist. A convenience for scripts and tests: a web handler should return the job id.

docs.title: identity
docs.text:
The identity of a run: who it is for, as a typed value the application defines.

An identity is a Pydantic model (class Teacher(BaseModel): user_id: str ...). The application declares the type once, where the framework has to check it and to rebuild it (AgentRunner(db, identity_type=Teacher)), and passes a value with identity=. Tools read it as runtime.context.identity. featherweight carries it: it does not authenticate anyone, decide what they may do, get a credential for them or keep them. See docs/specs/identity.md.

docs.title: IdentitySpec
docs.text:
IdentitySpec(identity_type: Any = None)

What a runner (a worker, a client) declared as identity_type, and the checks that come with it.

None declares nothing: runs have no identity, and passing one is an error. A Pydantic model class makes an identity required. A union of one or more model classes and None (Teacher | None) allows a run without one. A union of several models (Teacher | Student) is for an agent or a job that serves different kinds of people: the kind of an identity, the name of its class, says which one it is.

docs.title: describe
docs.text:
describe() -> str

The declaration as words, for an error message.

docs.title: check
docs.text:
check(identity: Any) -> None

Raise TypeError for a programming error: an identity when no type is declared, none when one is required, or one that is not an instance of the declared type.

docs.title: accepts
docs.text:
accepts(other: IdentitySpec) -> bool

Whether a run on this declaration can take every identity that other can produce: each of its models is one of ours (or a subclass of one), and if it allows no identity, so do we. A worker's type is other, and its runner's is self.

docs.title: dump
docs.text:
dump(
    identity: Any,
) -> tuple[dict[str, Any] | None, str | None]

The identity as what travels in a queue message: its fields as JSON-ready data, without the ones marked exclude=True, and its kind (the name of its class). (None, None) for none.

docs.title: load
docs.text:
load(data: Any, kind: str | None = None) -> Any

docs.title: jobs
docs.text:
Jobs: a Job is a declared class, run in your process by run_job or on a worker by name, by the same code (execute_job).

A Job has a name, a version, an input model and an output model (Pydantic), and async run(ctx, input). A plain agent can be a job too (as_job). A job is what a client submits to a queue and a worker runs (see docs/specs/submitted-jobs.md).

docs.title: JobTimeout
docs.text:

A job ran for longer than its timeout. It is the error type that the job fails with.

docs.title: JobContext
docs.text:

What a job gets when it runs: the runner and its own id. run and run_many run agents in this job, so that they share its trace and its resume.

docs.title: Job
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

A job, declared as a class, like an agent. Subclass it, set name, version, input_model and output_model, and write run. A worker is given the classes it can run, and runs one by its name.

The checks are made when the class is defined: a missing or odd name or version, or a model that is not Pydantic, or a timeout that is not a positive number or None, is an error then, not when a job arrives. A class that has not written run cannot be built.

timeout is how many seconds one execution of the job may run (default 600; None for no limit). A job that exceeds it is cancelled and fails with error type JobTimeout, in a worker and in run_job alike. It is not part of job_hash.

docs.text:
job(fn: Callable[..., Awaitable[Any]]) -> type[Job]

job(
    *,
    name: str | None = None,

    /,
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    version: str = "1",
    timeout: float | None = DEFAULT_JOB_TIMEOUT,

Make a Job class from an async function: async def summarise(ctx: JobContext, input: In) -> Out. The name is the function's (or name=), the version "1" (or version=), and the input and output models are the annotations of input and the return value. timeout= is the seconds one execution may run (default 600, None for no limit). The function becomes the class, usable wherever a Job is; the function itself is Summarise.function.

@job
async def summarise(ctx: JobContext, input: SummariseInput) -> SummariseOutput: ...

@job(name="summarise", version="2", timeout=120)
async def summarise(ctx, input: SummariseInput) -> SummariseOutput: ...

docs.text:
as_job(job: type[Job] | type[AgentBase]) -> type[Job]

A Job class as it is, or a plain agent class as a job: its name, its input model, its output model, and agent_hash as the job hash. A streaming agent cannot be a job (it streams to a person).

docs.title: execute_job async
docs.text:
execute_job(
    runner: AgentRunner,
    job: type[Job],
    job_id: str,
    job_input: BaseModel,
    results: ResultStore | None,
    *,
    on_cancel: Callable[[], Awaitable[None]] | None = None,
    trace_context: Mapping[str, str] = {},
    owner: JobOwner | None = None,
    lost: Callable[[], bool] | None = None,
    identity: Any = None,
) -> JobOutcome[BaseModel]

Run a job that has been started (its row is RUNNING), keep its result and set its final status. This is the one function that runs a job, for run_job (in your process) and for the worker, so that the two cannot differ: the same row, hashes, events, result, and the same calls to the runner's observers.

A job that raises is a FAILED outcome, not an exception (the error type and hash go to the run log, the text to the log and the outcome). A cancelled task sets CANCELLED (or runs on_cancel, which the worker uses to put a job back on the queue) and re-raises the cancellation.

The observers' job scope wraps the whole run, so that an observer can make its span the current one while the pipeline runs. trace_context is the carrier that came with the message (a worker), and is empty for run_job.

owner (who started the job) makes every write to the job conditional on it still being the owner, in the statement itself. A write that finds the job taken from it raises JobLost and writes nothing: this function lets it through (the observers' scope ends with error type JobLost, for tracing only) and the caller drops the job. A task that is cancelled because the job was lost (lost() says so) writes nothing to the job either.

docs.title: run_job async
docs.text:
run_job(
    runner: AgentRunner,
    job: type[Job] | type[AgentBase],
    input: BaseModel,
    *,
    job_id: str | None = None,
    resume_from: str | None = None,
    resumable: bool = False,
    trace_context: Mapping[str, str] = {},
    identity: Any = None,
) -> JobOutcome[Any]

Run a job in your process: create it (or use job_id), start it, run it with execute_job (the code a worker runs it with), and return the outcome. job is a Job class, or a plain (non-streaming) agent class; input must be an instance of its input model (TypeError otherwise). The output is the job's output model, in outcome.result, and it is also written to the runner's result store if the runner has one. A job that raises is a FAILED outcome, not an exception; a cancelled task is marked CANCELLED and the cancellation is re-raised.

resumable=True keeps the outputs of the job's steps, so that a later job can resume it. It is decided here, before the job runs: a job that did not keep them cannot be resumed. resume_from is the id of an earlier, resumable job: the new job records it, and a step that the earlier job already finished, with the same agent and input, is answered from the kept result instead of calling the model. resume_from and resumable cannot be combined with job_id: create the job with db.create_job(name, resume_from=...) and pass that.

To run in the background and give the caller the id first: create the job yourself with db.create_job, then asyncio.create_task(run_job(runner, job, input, job_id=job_id)). A job that was cancelled (or started) before it could start is not run: the outcome has the status it has and no result.

trace_context is the carrier of the caller's trace (W3C traceparent), for a runner that starts a job as a background job: the job's span then joins that trace. It is empty otherwise.

identity is who the job is for. It is checked against the runner's identity_type (a TypeError when it is missing, of the wrong type, or given when no type is declared), the job reads it as ctx.identity, and every agent it runs has it.

docs.title: messages
docs.text:
Conversion between the messages of a client (AG-UI) and the messages of the model (LangChain).

The wire format is AG-UI's, the storage format is LangChain's: its chat message histories and stores read and write LangChain messages, and they hold what the model needs on the next request (tool call ids, reasoning with its signature). to_langchain and to_agui keep those exactly.

docs.title: to_langchain
docs.text:
to_langchain(
    messages: Sequence[Message],
) -> list[BaseMessage]

A client's history as LangChain messages.

A reasoning message (a thought, with its signature) is attached to the assistant message that follows it, as a reasoning content block, which is how LangChain carries it. An activity message is a UI element, not part of the conversation, and is left out. A user message may carry images, documents, audio and video as inline data: they become LangChain content blocks, in order. Raises ValueError for an attachment that is not inline data (a URL), is not base64 or has no mime type, for content that is not text in any other message, and for tool call arguments that are not JSON.

docs.title: otel
docs.text:
OTelObserver: featherweight's spans, in the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions.

from featherweight import AgentRunner, OTelObserver

runner = AgentRunner(db, observers=[OTelObserver()])

It needs only opentelemetry-api (pip install 'featherweight[otel]'); with no SDK configured the API does nothing, so it costs nothing. The application configures the SDK and the exporter, as for any other code.

A job is an invoke_workflow span, an attempt of an agent an invoke_agent span, a model call a chat span and a tool call an execute_tool span. Metadata is always on the spans; content (messages, arguments, results) only when capture_content is on. Our own attributes are in the ftw. namespace. The conventions are in the Development status and live in their own repository, so the version we follow is pinned in GENAI_CONVENTIONS, and every attribute we emit is in ATTRIBUTES.

docs.title: OTelObserver
docs.text:
OTelObserver(
    *,
    capture_content: bool | None = None,
    tracer_provider: TracerProvider | None = None,
)

Bases: Observer

Emits OpenTelemetry spans for jobs, attempts, model calls and tool calls, as the GenAI conventions describe them.

capture_content puts messages, tool arguments and results, and a job's or an agent's input and output on the spans. When it is not given, it follows OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_CONTENT (SPAN_ONLY is on; anything else, off). Pass a tracer_provider to use another one than the global one.

docs.text:
PostgresDatabase: the run log in Postgres, for a deployment. SqliteDatabase is the one for local development.

It implements the same Database abstract class with the same records and rows, with native types (timestamptz, jsonb, boolean, an identity column). The tables live in their own schema (default featherweight), so they never collide with an application's tables. There is no result store for Postgres: where a deployment keeps the outputs that resuming needs is for the user to decide, so pass results= to the runner. Needs the extra featherweight[postgres] (psycopg, version 3).

docs.title: queue
docs.text:
The queue that connects a client to a worker, as an abstract class.

featherweight passes what the user gives to a job: the input travels in the message (as JSON, or as a reference inside it). SqliteQueue is our only product implementation, for local development; how jobs travel in a deployment (Redis, SQS, a database) is the user's decision, and featherweight.testing.check_queue checks an implementation against the contract. See docs/specs/submitted-jobs.md.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Bases: BaseModel

A message that was received, and the token that identifies the delivery to its queue (opaque: the queue's own).

docs.title: JobQueue
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Subclass it and write the five methods; one that misses a method cannot be built.

The contract (featherweight.testing.check_queue runs it against any queue): - delivery is at-least-once; - a received message is invisible to other receivers for a lease: until it is acknowledged or nacked, or its lease ends. If the lease ends first (the receiver died, or stalled), the message becomes available again, and its next delivery has a higher delivery_count; - extend renews the lease of a received message. A stale delivery (one whose message was delivered again since) has no effect: not on the message, and not on the lease of the new delivery; - nack(requeue=True) makes it available again; nack(requeue=False) drops it (a broker may dead-letter it); - messages come out in the order they went in, where the implementation can; - receive returns None after the timeout; - calls can be concurrent.

These are what real brokers already have: SQS's visibility timeout (ChangeMessageVisibility is extend) and ApproximateReceiveCount (the delivery count), or a Redis stream's pending list (XAUTOCLAIM, and its delivery counter). How many redeliveries are allowed is the queue's business: a broker has its own policy and dead-letter queue.

docs.title: SqliteQueue
docs.text:
SqliteQueue(db: SqliteDatabase)

Bases: JobQueue

A job_queue table in the run log's sqlite file, for local development. A message is claimed atomically for FTW_QUEUE_LEASE seconds (60 by default); if its receiver does not ack, nack or extend it in time, it is delivered again, with a higher delivery_count. One that has been delivered FTW_QUEUE_MAX_DELIVERIES times (3 by default) and whose lease ends again is marked dead: it stays in the table, and is not delivered. ack deletes the row; nack puts it back in its place or deletes it. A delivery's token names its claim, so that a stale delivery cannot touch the message after it was delivered again. The input stays in the table until the message is acknowledged, on the same terms as the sqlite result store: sqlite is for local development.

docs.title: AgentRunner
docs.text:
AgentRunner(
    db: Database,
    *,
    max_attempts: int = 3,
    retry_delay_s: float = 1.0,
    max_concurrent: int | None = None,
    max_depth: int | None = None,
    max_launches: int | None = None,
    max_background_jobs: int | None = None,
    background: JobClient | None = None,
    results: ResultStore
    | None
    | Literal["default"] = "default",
    observers: Sequence[Observer] = (),
    identity_type: Any = None,
)

max_concurrent caps how many attempts (model calls) run at once across this runner. Default: FTW_MAX_CONCURRENT_ATTEMPTS from the environment, else 10.

max_depth is the most agents in one chain of launches, the first agent included (A launches B launches C is 3). Default: FTW_MAX_AGENT_DEPTH, else 3. At 1 no agent can launch another. max_launches is the most launches one attempt of one agent may make. Default: FTW_MAX_AGENT_LAUNCHES, else 10.

max_background_jobs is the most children one attempt of one agent may have running in the background at one time (FTW_MAX_BACKGROUND_JOBS, else 3). A child runs in this process, as a job of its own, unless background is a JobClient: then it is submitted to the queue and a worker runs it (the worker must list the child's job). Agents with background_jobs need a result store.

results is where the outputs that resuming a job reads back are kept (a ResultStore), for the jobs created resumable=True. With a SqliteDatabase the default is a sqlite store in the same file; with any other database there is no default, so pass your own. None keeps nothing, and then a job that resumes another is a SetupError.

observers hear what the runner does (featherweight.observers): they are called inline, each with a timeout of FTW_OBSERVER_TIMEOUT seconds (1 by default), and what they raise is logged and ignored, so they never change or fail a run.

The settings that come from the environment are read here, once (docs/specs/configuration.md).

identity_type is the type of the identity of a run (a Pydantic model: who the run is for, for the tools; docs/specs/identity.md). A declared type makes identity= required on run, run_many, stream and run_job; a union with None (Teacher | None) allows runs without one; with nothing declared, passing one is a TypeError.

docs.title: aclose async
docs.text:
aclose() -> None

Stop every MCP server this runner started. Safe to call twice.

docs.title: run async
docs.text:
run(
    agent_cls: type[AgentBase],
    agent_input: AgentInput,
    *,
    job_id: str | None = None,
    identity: Any = None,
) -> AgentResult[Any]

Run an agent. Runtime failures come back as a FAILED result; they are not raised.

Programming errors still raise: an input that is not the agent's input_model, a job_id that does not exist, an identity that is missing, of the wrong type, or given when no identity_type is declared, and an identity that is not the one of the job (ValueError: a job is for one identity). A streaming agent is run with stream().

identity is who the run is for. The tools read it from their RunContext, a launched agent inherits it, and it is never shown to the model.

docs.title: stream
docs.text:
stream(
    agent_cls: type[StreamingAgent],
    chat_input: ChatInput,
    *,
    job_id: str | None = None,
    identity: Any = None,
) -> StreamingRun

Run a streaming agent. Returns at once; the run starts when you loop over it, and its events (AG-UI's) come as the model writes. A failure is an RUN_ERROR event and a FAILED row, not an exception; and nothing is retried.

A conversation with more attachments or bytes than the agent allows raises AttachmentLimitError (a BadRequest: the client's request, not a mistake of the application). Programming errors raise, as for run(): an agent that is not a streaming agent, an input that is not a ChatInput, an identity that is missing or of the wrong type, or a job_id that does not exist or a job that is for another identity (raised when the loop starts).

docs.title: cancel
docs.text:
cancel(run_id: str) -> bool

Stop a streaming run of this runner by its id (the run_id of its RUN_STARTED event). It ends as run.cancel() does. Returns False when no such run is going on here.

docs.title: run_many async
docs.text:
run_many(
    agent_cls: type[AgentBase],
    agent_inputs: Sequence[AgentInput],
    *,
    job_id: str | None = None,
    identity: Any = None,
) -> list[AgentResult[Any]]

Run one agent over many inputs concurrently (fan-out), all for the same identity.

Results come back in input order. As with run, runtime failures are FAILED results, not exceptions, so the caller decides what a failure means. There is no limit of its own: the runner's concurrency limit bounds how many attempts run at once.

docs.title: background_message async
docs.text:
background_message(job_id: str) -> HumanMessage

The user message that tells a model how a background job ended, for the application to start the next turn of a chat with (history + message). It is built from the job's status and the result store, and is what the runner adds to the loop of a parent that is still running (<background_result job_id=... agent=... status=...> and the output as JSON). It says what it can: a job that has not ended has its status and no output. LookupError for a job that does not exist.

Auth / config style errors, where another attempt would fail the same way.

docs.title: skills
docs.text:
Skills: instructions an agent can read when it needs them, as typed Pydantic models.

A skill follows the Agent Skills specification (https://agentskills.io/specification): a directory with a SKILL.md (YAML frontmatter, then Markdown instructions) and, optionally, other files such as references/, scripts/ and assets/. Skills are loaded in steps, so that they cost little context until they are needed:

  1. the name and description are in the agent's prompt (that is how the agent knows the skill exists),
  2. the instructions are read with the get_skill tool when the agent decides the skill applies,
  3. other files of the skill are read with get_skill too, only when the instructions point to them.

A Skill is plain data, so it is defined as an instance (or as a subclass with defaults) and listed in an agent's skills; or it is loaded from a skill directory with Skill.from_directory. Scripts are kept as text for the agent to read: nothing here runs them. allowed_tools is kept but not enforced. A skill whose text lives elsewhere is a subclass that overrides aread.

docs.title: SkillError
docs.text:
Bases: ValueError

A skill directory or SKILL.md that does not follow the specification.

docs.title: Skill
docs.text: Bases: BaseModel

docs.title: read
docs.text:
read(resource: str = '') -> str

The instructions, with the other files of the skill listed; or the text of one other file.

docs.title: aread async
docs.text:
aread(resource: str = '') -> str

read, asynchronously: the one the runner's get_skill tool awaits. The default returns read. A skill whose text is somewhere else (a database, an object store) is a subclass that overrides this and fetches without blocking the event loop. It should return text; if it raises, the agent is told the skill could not be read, and the error is logged.

docs.title: from_markdown classmethod
docs.text:
from_markdown(
    text: str, *, resources: dict[str, str] | None = None
) -> Skill

Parse the text of a SKILL.md: YAML frontmatter between --- lines, then the instructions.

docs.title: from_directory classmethod
docs.text:
from_directory(path: str | Path) -> Skill

Load a skill directory: SKILL.md, and every other text file below it as a resource.

The name in SKILL.md must match the name of the directory, as the specification says. Files that are not UTF-8 text are left out (and logged), because the agent can only read text.

docs.title: clean_resource
docs.text:
clean_resource(resource: str) -> str | None

The path that a model asked for, as a path inside the skill, or None when it is not one (docs/specs/skills.md).

The empty string is the skill itself. A . segment is dropped and // is one /. Refused: a path that starts with /, has a backslash, a .. segment (it is not resolved), a control character (NUL and newline included), is longer than MAX_RESOURCE_CHARS, or is only dots and slashes. The model chose it, so this is the one place that decides, for every skill.

docs.title: sqlite
docs.text: SqliteDatabase: the run log in a sqlite file. For local development; deployments use PostgresDatabase.

docs.text:
SqliteDatabase(path: str | Path)

path is the sqlite file, or ":memory:" for a database that lives in memory (no file, gone when it closes).

docs.title: transaction async
docs.text:
transaction() -> AsyncGenerator[Connection]

One write transaction at a time on the connection, committed at the end and rolled back on any error. Everything that writes (the run log, the result store, the queue) goes through it, so that two tasks writing at once cannot commit or roll back each other's half-done work.

docs.title: statements
docs.text:
statements(script: str) -> list[str]

The statements of a migration, one by one, so that they can run in a transaction that was begun by hand.

docs.title: sse
docs.text:
Server-sent events: the one way featherweight streams job events to a client.

encode turns the stream of a job's events (job_events) into SSE text, and HEADERS are the headers of the response. There is no server here: your API sends the response (a StreamingResponse in FastAPI). id is the sequence number of the event, so a browser that reconnects sends Last-Event-ID and the stream resumes after it.

@app.get("/jobs/{job_id}/events")
async def events(job_id: str, request: Request):
    after = int(request.headers.get("last-event-id", 0))
    return StreamingResponse(sse.encode(job_events(db, job_id, after)), headers=sse.HEADERS)

docs.title: format_event
docs.text:
format_event(event: JobEvent) -> str

One event as SSE: id, event (its type) and data (JSON, compact).

docs.title: encode async
docs.text:
encode(
    events: AsyncIterator[JobEvent],
    *,
    keep_alive: float = 15.0,
) -> AsyncGenerator[str, None]

The events as SSE text. A comment line goes out every keep_alive seconds while nothing arrives, to keep the connection open. The stream ends when the events end, and closes the source when the consumer stops.

docs.title: streaming
docs.text:
Streaming agents: an agent that talks to a person while it works.

A StreamingAgent is run with runner.stream(), which returns a StreamingRun: an async iterable of AG-UI events (the events of the ag-ui-protocol package, which featherweight does not redefine). There is no output model, no output check and no retry. See docs/streaming.md.

docs.title: ChatInput
docs.text:
Bases: AgentInput

The conversation so far, sent by the client. featherweight keeps no conversation: this is all the agent sees.

The last message is from the user. system and developer messages are refused, so that a client cannot replace the agent's prompt. thread_id names the conversation in the run log; it does not load anything.

docs.title: from_langchain classmethod
docs.text:
from_langchain(
    messages: Sequence[BaseMessage],
    thread_id: str | None = None,
) -> ChatInput

The conversation from LangChain messages, such as the ones a chat message history holds. The last is the user's.

docs.text:
from_agui(
    request: RunAgentInput | Sequence[Message],
    thread_id: str | None = None,
) -> ChatInput

The conversation from what an AG-UI client sent: a RunAgentInput (its thread id is kept) or its messages.

docs.title: StreamingAgent
docs.text:
Bases: AgentBase

An agent for chat and other user-facing work. It has no output_model and no check_output, and is not retried.

Declare it as any agent (name, description, version, prompt, model, tools, skills, MCP servers, sub-agents). Its input is a ChatInput. A sub-agent it launches is a tool call that returns when the sub-agent is done; its own text is not streamed. allow_user_questions and raise_conflicts do nothing here: a person is already in the chat.

docs.title: check_attachments classmethod
docs.text:
check_attachments(chat_input: ChatInput) -> None

Raises AttachmentLimitError (a BadRequest, so a ValueError) when the conversation has more attachments, or more bytes of them, than this agent allows.

docs.title: StreamingRun
docs.text:
StreamingRun(
    run_id: str,
    start: Callable[
        [StreamingRun, Callable[[BaseEvent], None]],
        Awaitable[None],
    ],
)

One streamed turn. Loop over it to get the events; it can be looped over once.

The run starts when the loop starts, and ends when the loop ends. Leaving the loop early stops the run. status is INIT until the loop starts, then RUNNING, then SUCCESS, FAILED or CANCELLED; error says why it failed. usage is the tokens of the turn, known when the run ends. new_messages is what the turn produced.

docs.title: new_messages property
docs.text:
new_messages: list[BaseMessage]

The LangChain messages this turn produced: the assistant messages (with their tool calls and thoughts) and the tool results, in order. They fill up as the turn goes and are complete when the loop ends. Store them next to the history you sent: history.add_messages(run.new_messages).

docs.title: cancel
docs.text:
cancel() -> None

Stop the run, from anywhere in the same process. The model call is cancelled, the stream ends cleanly (the open things are closed and RUN_FINISHED has the cancelled outcome), the row is CANCELLED, and new_messages has what the turn had said and done. A tool that was running is cancelled where it can be (an async tool); a synchronous tool or an MCP call may finish anyway. Safe to call before the loop starts, after the run ended, or twice.

MemoryResultStore()

docs.title: MemoryQueue
docs.text:
MemoryQueue(lease: float = 60.0)

Bases: JobQueue

A JobQueue in memory: nothing survives the process. For tests, and the smallest example of the class. A received message is leased for lease seconds (pass a very short one in a test): if it is not acked, nacked or extended in time, it is delivered again with a higher delivery_count. There is no limit on redeliveries.

docs.title: check_result_store async
docs.text:
check_result_store(
    make_store: Callable[
        [], ResultStore | Awaitable[ResultStore]
    ],
) -> None

Run the ResultStore contract against a store. make_store returns a fresh, empty store (it may be async). Raises AssertionError that says which rule a store breaks.

async def test_my_store():
    await check_result_store(lambda: MyStore(...))

docs.title: check_database async
docs.text:
check_database(make_db: Callable[[], Database]) -> None

Run the Database contract against an implementation. make_db returns a fresh, empty, unopened database; the kit opens and closes it. Raises AssertionError that says which rule an implementation breaks.

async def test_my_database():
    await check_database(lambda: MyDatabase(...))

docs.title: check_queue async
docs.text:
check_queue(
    make_queue: Callable[
        [float], JobQueue | Awaitable[JobQueue]
    ],
) -> None

Run the JobQueue contract against a queue. make_queue(lease) returns a fresh, empty queue whose lease is lease seconds (it may be async): the kit uses a short one to see a message come back, and needs a queue that delivers a message at least three times. Raises AssertionError that says which rule a queue breaks.

async def test_my_queue():
    await check_queue(lambda lease: MyQueue(visibility_timeout=lease))

docs.title: check_observer async
docs.text:
check_observer(
    make_observer: Callable[
        [], Observer | Awaitable[Observer]
    ],
) -> None

Run the Observer contract against an observer: every hook accepts its record and fails nothing, a scope can be entered, finished and left, submitted returns nothing or a mapping of strings, and no hook changes the record it was given. Raises AssertionError that says which rule an observer breaks.

async def test_my_observer():
    await check_observer(lambda: MyObserver(...))

docs.title: tools
docs.text:
Default tools. Import them and put them in an agent's tools allow-list.

calculate                    exact arithmetic, for totals and subtotals
current_datetime / add_to_date / days_between
                             date operations (UTC, ISO 8601)

All tools return text and do not raise, so the model can read what went wrong and react.

docs.title: calculate
docs.text:
calculate(expression: str) -> str

Evaluate an arithmetic expression exactly, e.g. "320000 + 85000 + 45000" or "(450000 + 200000) * 0.19".

Use plain numbers (no currency signs or thousands separators) and + - * / // % ** with parentheses. Returns the result as a plain number, or an error message.

docs.title: current_datetime
docs.text:
current_datetime() -> str

Get the current date and time in UTC as an ISO 8601 string, e.g. 2026-11-05T10:15:30+00:00.

docs.title: add_to_date
docs.text:
add_to_date(
    date: str = "today",
    days: int = 0,
    weeks: int = 0,
    months: int = 0,
    years: int = 0,
) -> str

Add (or, with negative numbers, subtract) time to a date and return it as YYYY-MM-DD.

date is YYYY-MM-DD, or "today" (the default) for the current UTC date. Months and years are calendar based and clamp to the end of the month, e.g. 2024-01-31 plus 1 month is 2024-02-29. Example: four weeks from now is add_to_date(weeks=4).

docs.title: days_between
docs.text:
days_between(start: str, end: str) -> str

Number of days from start to end (both YYYY-MM-DD, or "today"); negative if end is before start.

docs.title: worker
docs.text:
The worker: the process that runs submitted jobs.

It receives messages from a queue, runs the job each one names, writes the output through the user's result store, and records the outcome in the run log. It holds no state of its own beyond the tasks it is running: everything else is the database, the queue and the user's store. A failed job is never retried here (the user resumes it). See docs/specs/submitted-jobs.md.

docs.title: UnknownJob
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

A message named a job that this worker was not given.

docs.title: InvalidJobInput
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

The input of a message does not fit the input model of its job.

docs.title: JobLookupError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

jobs_lookup raised, returned something that is not a job, returned a job with another name than the one asked for, or returned a job whose hash is not the one recorded when the job was submitted (it changed while the job waited). The job is not run.

docs.title: InvalidJobIdentity
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

The identity of a message is missing and the worker's identity_type requires one, or does not fit that type, or the worker declares no type. The job is not run.

docs.title: JobWorker
docs.text:
JobWorker(
    db: Database,
    queue: JobQueue,
    runner: AgentRunner,
    jobs: Sequence[type[Job] | type[AgentBase]],
    results: ResultStore
    | None
    | Literal["default"] = "default",
    *,
    concurrency: int | None = None,
    worker_id: str | None = None,
    identity_type: Any = None,
    jobs_lookup: JobsLookup | None = None,
)

JobWorker(db, queue, runner, jobs, results): jobs are the Job classes (or plain agent classes) it can run, by name.

results is where the output of a job is written (a ResultStore; the default is a sqlite store in the run log's file for a SqliteDatabase, and none for another database; None keeps nothing). concurrency is how many jobs run at once (FTW_WORKER_CONCURRENCY, else 10).

The job's lease is how long, in seconds, the worker's claim on a job lasts without being renewed (FTW_JOB_LEASE, 60 by default). While it runs jobs, the worker renews the lease of each, and extends the queue's lease of its message, every FTW_HEARTBEAT seconds (a third of the lease by default). A worker that lost a job (another one took it over) stops it and writes nothing more to it. How long it waits for a message and how often it asks about cancellations are FTW_WORKER_RECEIVE_TIMEOUT and FTW_WORKER_CANCEL_POLL (docs/specs/configuration.md): the settings that are not concurrency have no argument. worker_id names the worker in jobs.worker_id (a new id by default).

identity_type is the type of the identity of a run (docs/specs/identity.md): the worker rebuilds the identity of a message with it and gives it to the run. A type that does not allow None makes a message without an identity fail its job (InvalidJobIdentity), and so does an identity that does not fit the type, or one when no type is declared. The job is not run, and not retried.

jobs_lookup is a fallback for jobs that are not declared in code (an agent that a platform's user defined, kept in the platform's own storage): async def jobs_lookup(name, job_hash, identity) returns the job class (or a plain agent class) for the name, or None. jobs are tried first; the lookup is called only for a name jobs does not have, with the job_hash recorded when the job was submitted (None for a job that has none) and the rebuilt identity (None if there is none). The worker checks that what it returns has the name that was asked for and the recorded hash, and caches nothing. None is UnknownJob; a lookup that raises, a result that is not a job, another name and another hash fail the job with JobLookupError. jobs may be empty. See docs/specs/submitted-jobs.md.

worker = JobWorker(db, queue, runner, jobs=[Summarise])
await worker.run()           # until `await worker.stop()` is called, from another task

docs.title: run async
docs.text:
run() -> None

Receive and run jobs until stop() is called. If the task that runs this is cancelled, the running jobs are cancelled and returned to the queue, and the cancellation is raised.

docs.title: stop async
docs.text:
stop(grace: float = 30.0) -> None

Take no new messages, wait up to grace seconds for the running jobs, then cancel the ones still running and return their messages to the queue (nack with requeue=True): those jobs go back to INIT, and run again.

docs.title: cancel
docs.text:
cancel(job_id: str) -> bool

Cancel a job this worker is running, at once (in this process). False if it is not running here. A client in another process sets cancel_requested instead, and the worker finds it within cancel_poll seconds.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
Five kinds of page, from "how do I build it" to "why is it this way". Start at the top and go down only as far as you need.

Level Answers Where Overview What is featherweight, and is it for me? The README The book How do I build something, step by step? book/ Recipes How do I put a few parts together for one job? recipes/ Guides How do I do X? This folder Specs What exactly does it do, what was decided and why, and what is left out? specs/ Examples Show me running code examples/

The book teaches in order; the guides and the specs are for looking things up. A word that means something particular is in the glossary, which also says which of two names to use. The guides and the specs cover the same features. A guide is for using one, and its spec is for relying on it, changing it, or finding out why it behaves as it does.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• I want to build something, step by step. The book: a short chapter at a time, one small project that grows from a typed agent to a chat and a pipeline on workers. Start with the map. The guides and the specs below are the reference.
  • I want a short pattern to adapt. Recipes: a pipeline, resuming a job, a fake model for tests, a worker, a chat that streams, each one small and complete.
  • I'm building a platform where users define skills or agents. Recipes: a skill from a database or S3, agents built from JSON with your own rules, a queue that signs its messages, a tool that acts for the signed-in user. Then who is asking and jobs that are not declared in code.
  • I want a coding agent to build with it. The skill: install it in Claude Code, or copy skills/featherweight into another tool's skills folder. It carries the rules, a working app, the book and the guides.
  • I'm new here. Getting started: install it, write an agent, run it.
  • I want to build an agent. Agents: define one, run it, read the result, handle failures. Then examples/launching or examples/skills to run something.
  • I want my agent to use outside tools. MCP tools: declare a server, and the agent gets its tools. They are found by search by default. Then examples/mcp, which uses GitHub's server.
  • I want to use another model or provider. Models and providers: Gemini, Gemma, Claude and OpenAI, and how to add GPT-5.x or Ollama with a small class.
  • I want agents that delegate. Launching agents: an allow-list of agents, depth and breadth limits.
  • I want to teach an agent a procedure. Skills: instructions in the Agent Skills format, read on demand.
  • I want to see a whole pipeline. Example pipeline: doclearn, five agents and two pipelines built on featherweight. Run it with make pipeline.
  • I want an agent to start another and go on. Background jobs: a job exposed to an agent as a tool, with the result coming back as a message. Then examples/background.
  • I want to run jobs in the background. Submitted jobs: a client submits, a worker runs, and you follow it with events. Then examples/jobs.
  • I want to run it in production. A production stack: what to use where, with Postgres, your own queue and result store.
  • I want to see what my jobs and agents do. Observability: OpenTelemetry spans for jobs, attempts, model calls and tool calls, ready for an evaluation platform. Then examples/observability.
  • I want to work on featherweight itself. Development: the commands, the layout, how to contribute.
  • I want to know why it works this way, or to change it. Specs. Start with the agent runner, which most behaviour passes through.

docs.title: Specs
docs.text:
Each spec has the same shape: goal, the rules, decisions and why, what is not supported, and which tests cover it. The index lists them. How they fit together:

agents ──────────── what an agent is, and what is checked when it is built
  │
runner ──────────── runs agents: attempts, retries, concurrency, launching other agents
  │   │
  │   ├── models ──────── which model and provider, and how hard it thinks
  │   │
  │   └── jobs ────────── a pipeline: its status, events and resuming
  │
  ├── tools ───────────── the tools of an attempt, the registry
  │       │
  │       ├── MCP tools ───────── servers, connections, failures
  │       │       └── tool discovery ── finding MCP tools by search
  │
  └── skills ───────────── instructions an agent reads when it needs them

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
• The README is the landing page: what featherweight is, what it does, and how it differs.
  • A guide is written for someone with a task. It shows code, and says what to expect.
  • A spec is written from the code. It states the rules as they are, the decisions with their reasons, and what was left out on purpose. If a guide and a spec disagree, the spec and the code are right, and the guide should be fixed.
  • An example is a folder you can run (make example-skills, make example-launching, make example-mcp, make example-resume, make example-jobs, make example-observability, make pipeline). Each has a README that says what to look at.
  • Releasing is for the maintainers: Releasing says how a release is made, and the changelog is CHANGELOG.md.
  • The tests are in tests/, and each spec says which files cover it. tests/e2e uses the real model.

docs.title: featherweight [ftw.]
docs.text:
An opinionated agent harness. Pydantic is the spec. Everything else follows.

Build your first agent Read the documentation View on GitHub

An agent is a typed class. Its input, output, tools, skills and sub-agents are declared right there and enforced, not hoped for. The boilerplate every agent project ends up writing (retries, limits, failures, tracing, delegation, workers, resume) is already written. You write the pipeline. That's the part that's yours.

A malformed agent never reaches the model. A running one has a known input and a known output. No guessing.

It has opinions. Take them, or fork off.

And there's a skill, so your coding agent can build with it from the first prompt.

Alpha. The API can still change before 1.0.

docs.title: Built on LangChain, on purpose
docs.text:
featherweight doesn't replace LangChain. It sits on it.

  • Your tools are LangChain tools. Write one with @tool, or take one from the LangChain ecosystem.
  • MCP goes through LangChain's MCP adapters. Stdio or HTTP servers, declared on the agent.
  • Models are LangChain chat models underneath, behind settings classes that are checked when the agent is built.

So what LangChain already gives you, a pile of integrations and adapters, can plug into agents that are typed, bounded and run on workers. We test the providers and tools featherweight ships with. Other LangChain integrations go into the same slots, but we haven't verified them one by one.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text: Typed, declared, enforced An agent is a class. What goes in and what comes out is a schema. A bad declaration fails when it is written, a bad answer is caught and retried before your code ever sees it. Least privilege Everything is an allow-list. A capability an agent has is one the developer gave it, on purpose. Plain Python, failures as values Order, loops and branching are if and for: no graph, no workflow engine. A failed run hands you the error and a status, not an exception. Agents that delegate Sub-agents on a leash, only the ones allowed, only so deep. Or background jobs: one starts another and goes on, and the result comes back when it is ready. Acts for someone A typed identity reaches your tools, in your process and on workers, and never the model. What it may do is your tools' decision: you bring authentication and authorization. Resume instead of rerun A pipeline that dies halfway picks up where it stopped, without paying for the steps that worked. Workers, and a lost worker is fine Submit a job from your API, run it on workers, follow it live, cancel it. Lose a worker mid-job and another takes over. Streams to your UI Chat answers and job status stream over standard protocols (AG-UI, the Vercel AI SDK, SSE), so a browser can listen as is. See what it did OpenTelemetry traces of jobs, attempts, model calls and tool calls, in the format observability and evaluation platforms already read. Content stays off unless you turn it on. Any model, any tool Gemini, Gemma, Claude, OpenAI or your own. MCP servers and skills plug in and stay out of the context until needed. Your data, your storage The framework stores metadata and nothing else. Databases, result stores, queues and observers are interfaces: implement one, run the kit that checks it. SqliteDatabase for local work and PostgresDatabase for deployment both ship, to get you going.

docs.title: What you don't get
docs.text:
A workflow engine No graph to draw, no nodes and edges. Order is if and for, and you already know those. A server or a UI We stream, you serve. Bring your own API and frontend: it speaks AG-UI, the Vercel AI SDK and SSE. Your data No stored conversations, no stored outputs. Metadata only. What happens to the rest is your call, and your problem. An evaluation platform We don't score anything. We emit traces your platform already reads, and it does the judging. A way around the rules An agent that doesn't declare itself properly doesn't run. These are opinions. Take them, or fork off.

Want durable execution or built-in evals? Pydantic AI. Want a graph that pauses and resumes? LangGraph. Want typed, bounded agents on workers, in plain Python? Here.

docs.title: Built for agentic coding
docs.text:
There is a skill. Plug it into your favourite coding agent and it already knows how to build with featherweight: the typed agent, the rules, the patterns, and the whole book. You start building in your editor, not in a docs tab.

In Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add aadhithya/featherweight
/plugin install featherweight@featherweight

OpenAI Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI and the other tools that read Agent Skills: install it with the skills CLI, which puts it where each tool looks (it needs Node.js).

npx skills add aadhithya/featherweight                 # asks which tools to install it for
npx skills add aadhithya/featherweight -a codex        # or name one: codex, cursor, claude-code, ...

Or copy skills/featherweight into the tool's skills folder yourself. There is also an AGENTS.md at the root, for the tools that read that.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The quickest way in is the book: a tiny incident report assistant that grows from a first agent to workers, chapter by chapter, with code that runs in a container.

pip install featherweight
pip install 'featherweight[all]'    # or just: mcp, anthropic, openai, postgres, otel

Python 3.12 or later. Import what you use: from featherweight import AgentBase, AgentRunner. (import featherweight as ftw works too.)

docs.title: fw-concierge ✨
docs.text:
A concierge that books a physio appointment, end to end, built on featherweight.

A chat assistant finds an appointment in Munich. A background worker researches providers while you keep chatting. Nothing is booked until you say yes. One command runs the whole thing.

docs.title: fw-qna 💬
docs.text:
A terminal chat that answers questions about featherweight from its own docs, and writes example code.

Ask "how do I run jobs on a worker?" and get an answer with links to the pages it came from. It reads featherweight's skill, searches the docs of the release you pick, and says when code is untested. A quick way to learn the framework, and a demo of streaming agents, tools and skills.
